M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every closed form is exact.
     b) On a star-shaped open subset of Rⁿ every closed k-form, k ≥ 1, is
        exact.
     c) Every smooth manifold admits a Riemannian metric.
     d) Every manifold admits a Lorentzian metric.
     e) Every vector bundle over a contractible manifold is trivial.
     f) A vector bundle with a nowhere-zero section is trivial.
     g) A closed manifold with χ = 0 has a nowhere-zero vector field.
     h) H¹_dR(M) is finite-dimensional for every manifold M.
     i) ∇_X Y is C^∞-linear in Y.
     j) The difference of two connections is a tensor.
     k) The Christoffel symbols form a tensor.
     l) Gaussian curvature depends only on the metric.
     m) Mean curvature depends only on the metric.
     n) Geodesics minimize length between their endpoints.
     o) In a connected complete Riemannian manifold any two points are
        joined by a minimizing geodesic.
     p) The same holds without completeness.
     q) A closed orientable surface with K > 0 everywhere is diffeomorphic
        to S².
     r) The torus admits a metric with K < 0 everywhere.
     s) Every compact surface embedded in R³ has a point with K > 0.
     t) de Rham cohomology is a homotopy invariant.
     u) The regular value theorem's converse holds: if F⁻¹(c) is a
        submanifold then c is a regular value.
     v) Every orientable rank-2 bundle over S² is trivial.
     Answers:
       a) F: dθ on R² ∖ 0            b) T (Poincaré lemma)
       c) T (partition of unity)     d) F: S² (would need a line field;
                                        χ(S²) ≠ 0)
       e) T                          f) F: Möbius ⊕ ε¹ over S¹ (non-
                                        orientable, so not trivial)
       g) T (Hopf)                   h) F: R² minus Z × {0} (H¹ has
                                        infinite dimension)
       i) F: ∇_X(fY) = (Xf)Y + f∇_X Y (it is C^∞-linear in X)
       j) T                          k) F: 0 in Cartesian, Γ^r_θθ = −r in
                                        polar coordinates of R²
       l) T (Theorema Egregium)      m) F: plane (H = 0) and cylinder
                                        (H = 1/2) are locally isometric
       n) F: a great-circle arc longer than π
       o) T (Hopf-Rinow)             p) F: (−1, 0), (1, 0) in R² ∖ 0
       q) T (Gauss-Bonnet: χ > 0)    r) F: ∫K dA = 2πχ = 0
       s) T (at a point farthest from the origin K ≥ 1/R² > 0)
       t) T                          u) F: f = x², c = 0 (f⁻¹(0) = {0})
       v) F: TS² (Euler number 2)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep ONE worked model for every concept and return to it —
  S² with (θ, φ) for metrics, Christoffel symbols, geodesics, curvature
  and Gauss-Bonnet; H² for negative curvature and "straight lines that
  look curved"; R² ∖ 0 with dθ for closed-versus-exact and for H¹; the
  Möbius band for non-trivial bundles. Always compute a form by first
  writing dx, dy in the new variables, then expanding the wedge (never
  memorize Jacobians), and always check an answer with Stokes or
  Gauss-Bonnet (total curvature 2πχ is a free sanity check). For
  cohomology, first ask "what is it homotopy equivalent to?" and then use
  Mayer-Vietoris only on the small pieces. Harder: prove Sard's theorem
  and the Whitney embedding theorem; prove de Rham's theorem via good
  covers and the Čech-de Rham double complex; prove Poincaré duality for
  compactly supported cohomology; derive the second variation formula
  and use it to prove Bonnet-Myers and Synge's theorem; prove Cartan-
  Hadamard; compute the curvature of a U(1) connection on the Hopf bundle
  and show (i/2π)∫F = −1 (Chern-Weil); and show that Sⁿ has a nowhere-zero
  vector field iff n is odd.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.11 — LIE GROUPS AND LIE ALGEBRAS: STRUCTURE, ROOT SYSTEMS,
CLASSIFICATION OF SEMISIMPLE LIE ALGEBRAS, REPRESENTATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - LIE GROUP: a group G that is a smooth manifold with smooth
    multiplication and inversion. Its LIE ALGEBRA g = T_eG with the
    bracket of left-invariant vector fields. For a closed subgroup G ⊆
    GL(n) (a matrix group, closed by CARTAN'S CLOSED SUBGROUP THEOREM
    automatically a Lie group) g = {X : e^(tX) ∈ G for all t} and
    [X, Y] = XY − YX. Standard list: gl(n) (n²), sl(n): tr X = 0 (n² − 1),
    so(n): Xᵀ = −X (n(n − 1)/2), u(n): X* = −X (n²), su(n) (n² − 1),
    sp(2n, R): XᵀJ + JX = 0 (n(2n + 1)), Heisenberg (3).
  - EXPONENTIAL MAP exp : g → G, t ↦ exp(tX) is the ONE-PARAMETER SUBGROUP
    with velocity X; exp is a local diffeomorphism at 0; det e^X = e^(tr X).
    BAKER-CAMPBELL-HAUSDORFF: log(e^X e^Y) = X + Y + ½[X, Y] + (1/12)([X,
    [X, Y]] + [Y, [Y, X]]) + ..., so the bracket determines the group law
    near e. exp is onto for compact connected G but NOT for SL(2, R):
    tr(exp X) ≥ −2 for X ∈ sl(2, R), so diag(−2, −½) is not exponential.
    A homomorphism Φ : G → H has dΦ : g → h with Φ(exp X) = exp(dΦ X);
    Ad : G → GL(g), Ad(g)Y = gYg⁻¹, and d(Ad) = ad, ad X(Y) = [X, Y].
  - LIE CORRESPONDENCE: Lie subalgebras of g ↔ connected Lie subgroups of G;
    if G is SIMPLY CONNECTED every Lie algebra homomorphism g → h lifts to
    a group homomorphism G → H. Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra
    is the Lie algebra of a unique simply connected group G̃ (Lie III, via
    ADO'S THEOREM: every Lie algebra embeds in some gl(n)); the connected
    groups with Lie algebra g are G̃/Γ, Γ a discrete central subgroup.
    Model: SU(2) ≅ S³ → SO(3) is a double cover (kernel ±I), su(2) ≅ so(3),
    π₁(SO(3)) = Z/2; the universal cover of SL(2, R) is not a matrix group.
  - ABSTRACT LIE ALGEBRAS (over a field, here R or C): bilinear,
    alternating bracket with the JACOBI identity. Ideals, quotients, ad.
    DERIVED series g ⊇ [g, g] ⊇ ...; SOLVABLE if it reaches 0. LOWER
    CENTRAL series Cᵏ⁺¹ = [g, Cᵏ]; NILPOTENT if it reaches 0. Examples:
    strictly upper triangular nₙ (nilpotent), upper triangular bₙ (solvable,
    not nilpotent), aff(1): [x, y] = y (solvable), e(2) (solvable).
  - ENGEL: g is nilpotent iff ad X is nilpotent for every X. LIE'S THEOREM
    (C, char 0): a solvable g ⊆ gl(V) has a common eigenvector, hence is
    upper triangular in some basis; so [g, g] is nilpotent. Fails over R
    (so(2) on R²). The RADICAL rad g = largest solvable ideal; g is
    SEMISIMPLE if rad g = 0 (equivalently no nonzero abelian ideals).
    LEVI: g = rad g ⋊ s with s semisimple (e.g. sl(2) ⋉ C²). REDUCTIVE =
    semisimple ⊕ abelian (gl(n), u(n)).
  - KILLING FORM κ(X, Y) = tr(ad X ad Y): symmetric, ad-invariant
    κ([X, Y], Z) = κ(X, [Y, Z]). For sl(n): κ = 2n tr(XY); so(n): (n − 2)
    tr(XY); sp(2n): (2n + 2) tr(XY); gl(n): 2n tr(XY) − 2 tr X tr Y.
    CARTAN'S CRITERIA: g is solvable iff κ(g, [g, g]) = 0; g is semisimple
    iff κ is NONDEGENERATE. Semisimple ⇒ g = g₁ ⊕ ... ⊕ gₖ (simple
    ideals), g = [g, g], all derivations inner. Compact G semisimple ⇒ κ
    negative definite (su(2): signature (0, 3); sl(2, R): (2, 1)).
  - WEYL'S THEOREM: every finite-dimensional representation of a semisimple
    Lie algebra over C is COMPLETELY REDUCIBLE (proof: the CASIMIR element
    Ω = ∑XᵢXⁱ, dual bases for a nondegenerate invariant form). Fails for
    solvable algebras: b₂ on C² has an invariant line with no invariant
    complement.
  - CARTAN SUBALGEBRA h (maximal toral: abelian, ad-semisimple) of a complex
    semisimple g; ROOT SPACE DECOMPOSITION g = h ⊕ ⊕_{α∈Φ} g_α, g_α = {X :
    [H, X] = α(H)X}. Facts: dim g_α = 1; Φ = −Φ; [g_α, g_β] = g_{α+β} when
    α + β ∈ Φ; each α gives an sl(2)-triple (E_α, H_α, F_α) with
    α(H_α) = 2; κ restricted to h is nondegenerate, and via it Φ spans a
    real Euclidean space E. sl(n): h = traceless diagonal, roots εᵢ − εⱼ.
  - ROOT SYSTEM Φ ⊆ E: finite, spans E, 0 ∉ Φ; Rα ∩ Φ = {±α}; the
    REFLECTION s_α(β) = β − ⟨β, α^∨⟩α maps Φ to Φ, where ⟨β, α^∨⟩ =
    2(β, α)/(α, α) ∈ Z. Then ⟨β, α^∨⟩⟨α, β^∨⟩ = 4cos²θ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}:
    angles 90°, 60°/120°, 45°/135°, 30°/150°, length ratios² 1, 2, 3. The
    WEYL GROUP W = ⟨s_α⟩ is finite and acts simply transitively on the
    Weyl chambers. Rank 2: A₁ × A₁, A₂, B₂, G₂ (4, 6, 8, 12 roots).
  - SIMPLE ROOTS Δ = {α₁, ..., αₗ}: a basis such that every root is an
    integer combination with all coefficients ≥ 0 (POSITIVE Φ⁺) or all ≤ 0.
    CARTAN MATRIX aᵢⱼ = ⟨αᵢ, αⱼ^∨⟩ (aᵢᵢ = 2, aᵢⱼ ∈ {0, −1, −2, −3},
    aᵢⱼ = 0 ⇔ aⱼᵢ = 0, positive definite after symmetrising). DYNKIN
    DIAGRAM: nodes αᵢ, aᵢⱼaⱼᵢ edges, arrow toward the short root. W is
    generated by the simple reflections sᵢ; ρ = ½∑_{α>0} α.
  - CLASSIFICATION (KILLING-CARTAN): complex simple Lie algebras ↔
    connected Dynkin diagrams: Aₗ = sl(l + 1), Bₗ = so(2l + 1), Cₗ = sp(2l),
    Dₗ = so(2l) (l ≥ 4), and E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄, G₂. Dimensions l(l + 2),
    l(2l + 1), l(2l + 1), l(2l − 1), 78, 133, 248, 52, 14; dim g = rank +
    |Φ|. SERRE'S THEOREM rebuilds g from its Cartan matrix. Low-rank
    coincidences: A₁ = B₁ = C₁, B₂ = C₂ (so(5) ≅ sp(4)), A₃ = D₃ (so(6) ≅
    sl(4)), D₂ = A₁ × A₁ (so(4) ≅ sl(2) ⊕ sl(2)).
  - REPRESENTATIONS OF sl(2, C): for each n ≥ 0 exactly one irreducible
    V(n), dim n + 1, h-eigenvalues (WEIGHTS) n, n − 2, ..., −n, basis
    vₖ with h vₖ = (n − 2k)vₖ, f vₖ = (k + 1)vₖ₊₁, e vₖ = (n − k + 1)vₖ₋₁.
    CLEBSCH-GORDAN: V(m) ⊗ V(n) = V(m + n) ⊕ V(m + n − 2) ⊕ ... ⊕ V(|m − n|).
    Casimir Ω = ef + fe + ½h² acts on V(n) by n(n + 2)/2.
  - HIGHEST WEIGHT THEORY: weights λ ∈ h*; the WEIGHT LATTICE P = {λ :
    ⟨λ, α^∨⟩ ∈ Z}, FUNDAMENTAL WEIGHTS ⟨ωᵢ, αⱼ^∨⟩ = δᵢⱼ, dominant P⁺ =
    ∑Nωᵢ, root lattice Q ⊆ P with |P/Q| = det(Cartan matrix) = order of
    the centre of the simply connected group. THEOREM: finite-dimensional
    irreducibles ↔ dominant integral λ (quotients of VERMA modules
    U(g) ⊗_{U(b)} C_λ; PBW: U(g) has basis of ordered monomials).
  - WEYL CHARACTER FORMULA χ_λ = ∑_w ε(w)e^{w(λ+ρ)} / ∑_w ε(w)e^{wρ} and
    WEYL DIMENSION FORMULA dim V(λ) = ∏_{α>0} ⟨λ + ρ, α^∨⟩/⟨ρ, α^∨⟩. For
    sl(3): dim V(a, b) = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2 (3, 8, 6, 10, 27, ...).
    Tensor products: 3 ⊗ 3̄ = 8 ⊕ 1, 3 ⊗ 3 = 6 ⊕ 3̄, 8 ⊗ 8 = 27 ⊕ 10 ⊕ 10̄
    ⊕ 8 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 1.
  - COMPACT LIE GROUPS: bi-invariant HAAR measure; averaging gives an
    invariant inner product, so every representation is unitary and
    completely reducible (the UNITARY TRICK transfers this to sl(n, C)).
    Characters: ∫χ_Vχ̄_W dg = dim Hom_G(V, W); PETER-WEYL: matrix
    coefficients of irreducibles are dense in L²(G). MAXIMAL TORUS T:
    every element is conjugate into T; W = N(T)/T. SU(2): χₙ(θ) =
    sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ, Haar density (2/π)sin²θ dθ on [0, π]. SO(3) has
    irreducibles only of ODD dimension 2l + 1 (spherical harmonics).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Determine the Lie algebras of SL(n, R), SO(n), U(n), SU(n) and
    Sp(2n, R) and their dimensions. (b) Show that for a closed subgroup G ⊆
    GL(n), g = {X : e^(tX) ∈ G ∀t} is closed under the bracket. (c) Show
    that su(2) ≅ so(3) as real Lie algebras.
    Answer: (a) tr X = 0 (n² − 1); Xᵀ = −X (n(n − 1)/2); X* = −X (n²);
    X* = −X, tr X = 0 (n² − 1); XᵀJ + JX = 0 (n(2n + 1)). (b) [X, Y] is
    the derivative of Ad(e^(tX))Y. (c) uₖ = −(i/2)σₖ and Lₖ both satisfy
    [1, 2] = 3 cyclically.
    Teacher explains: (a) Differentiate the defining equation at t = 0.
    det e^(tX) = e^(t tr X) = 1 for all t ⇔ tr X = 0. If A(t)ᵀA(t) = I with
    A(0) = I, A′(0) = X, then Xᵀ + X = 0; conversely (e^(tX))ᵀ = e^(tXᵀ) =
    e^(−tX) = (e^(tX))⁻¹. The same for X* = −X in U(n). For Sp(2n, R),
    J = [[0, I], [−I, 0]], write X = [[A, B], [C, D]]; XᵀJ + JX = 0 gives
    D = −Aᵀ, B = Bᵀ, C = Cᵀ: n² + 2·n(n + 1)/2 = n(2n + 1) parameters.
    (b) g is a vector space: cX ∈ g trivially, and X + Y ∈ g by the Lie
    product formula e^(X+Y) = lim (e^(X/k)e^(Y/k))ᵏ and closedness of G.
    For X, Y ∈ g, e^(tX)e^(sY)e^(−tX) = exp(s e^(tX)Ye^(−tX)) ∈ G for all
    s, so Z(t) = e^(tX)Ye^(−tX) ∈ g; g is a closed subspace, so Z′(0) =
    XY − YX ∈ g. (c) With the Pauli matrices σₖ, σ₁σ₂ = iσ₃, so [u₁, u₂] =
    (−i/2)²·2iσ₃ = −(i/2)σ₃ = u₃, cyclically. In so(3), L₁ = E₃₂ − E₂₃,
    L₂ = E₁₃ − E₃₁, L₃ = E₂₁ − E₁₂ (infinitesimal rotations about the axes)
    satisfy [L₁, L₂] = L₃ cyclically. So uₖ ↦ Lₖ is an isomorphism (both
    are R³ with the cross product). Common mistakes: forgetting that u(n)
    contains iI (so dim u(n) = n², not n² − 1); confusing the real
    dimension of SL(2, C) (6) with its complex dimension (3). Now you try:
    the dimension of Sp(4, R) and of SO(5). (10 and 10: B₂ = C₂)

D2. (a) For X ∈ sl(2, R) show X² = −det(X)·I and obtain a closed formula
    for e^X; compute exp [[0, 4], [1, 0]]. (b) Prove tr(e^X) ≥ −2, with
    equality only for e^X = −I. Deduce that A = diag(−2, −½) and B =
    [[−1, 1], [0, −1]] are not exponentials although SL(2, R) is connected.
    (c) Write A as a product of two exponentials.
    Answer: (a) δ = −det X = λ² > 0: cosh λ I + (sinh λ/λ)X; δ = −θ² < 0:
    cos θ I + (sin θ/θ)X; δ = 0: I + X. exp [[0, 4], [1, 0]] = [[cosh 2,
    2 sinh 2], [½ sinh 2, cosh 2]] ≈ [[3.76220, 7.25372], [1.81343,
    3.76220]]. (b) tr A = −5/2; tr B = −2 but B ≠ −I. (c) A = e^(πJ)
    e^(diag(ln 2, −ln 2)), J = [[0, −1], [1, 0]].
    Teacher explains: Cayley-Hamilton: X² − (tr X)X + (det X)I = 0 and
    tr X = 0 give X² = δI with δ = −det X. Split the power series of e^X
    into even and odd powers: X^(2k) = δᵏI, X^(2k+1) = δᵏX. If δ = λ² > 0
    this gives cosh λ I + (sinh λ/λ)X, trace 2cosh λ ≥ 2. If δ = −θ² < 0
    it gives cos θ I + (sin θ/θ)X, trace 2cos θ ∈ [−2, 2]; the trace is −2
    only when cos θ = −1, and then sin θ = 0 so e^X = −I. If δ = 0 (X
    nilpotent), e^X = I + X, trace 2. Hence tr e^X ≥ −2 always, and −2
    only at −I. For [[0, 4], [1, 0]], δ = 4, λ = 2 and (sinh 2)/2·X gives
    the stated matrix (check det = cosh²2 − sinh²2 = 1). A and B violate
    the trace condition, so exp : sl(2, R) → SL(2, R) is NOT onto. Still
    A = (−I)·diag(2, ½) with −I = e^(πJ) (δ = −π², θ = π) and diag(2, ½) =
    e^(diag(ln 2, −ln 2)): in a connected group every element is a product
    of exponentials. Common mistakes: "connected ⇒ exp onto" (true for
    compact connected groups and for simply connected nilpotent groups,
    false in general); forgetting the case δ = 0. Now you try: exp
    [[0, −1], [4, 0]]. (δ = −4, θ = 2: [[cos 2, −½ sin 2], [2 sin 2,
    cos 2]])

D3. Construct the double cover SU(2) → SO(3) via the adjoint
    representation. Show that exp(θu₃), u₃ = −(i/2)σ₃, maps to the rotation
    by θ about the third axis, and deduce π₁(SO(3)) = Z/2.
    Answer: Ad : SU(2) → SO(su(2), −2tr) ≅ SO(3) is onto with kernel {±I};
    exp(2πu₃) = −I ↦ identity; SU(2) ≅ S³ is simply connected.
    Teacher explains: su(2) ≅ R³ with basis u₁, u₂, u₃ and inner product
    ⟨X, Y⟩ = −2 tr(XY), for which tr(uⱼuₖ) = −½δⱼₖ makes the uₖ
    orthonormal. Ad(g)X = gXg⁻¹ preserves su(2) and the trace form, so
    Ad(g) ∈ O(3); SU(2) = {[[a, −b̄], [b, ā]] : |a|² + |b|² = 1} ≅ S³ is
    connected, so Ad(g) ∈ SO(3). KERNEL: gXg⁻¹ = X for all X ∈ su(2)
    means g commutes with su(2), hence with its complex span sl(2, C);
    as C² is irreducible, Schur gives g scalar, so g = ±I. ONTO: d(Ad) =
    ad is injective (su(2) has zero centre), so the image is a
    3-dimensional compact connected subgroup of SO(3), open and closed,
    hence all of SO(3). For the rotation: Ad(exp θu₃) = exp(θ ad u₃), and [u₃,
    u₁] = u₂, [u₃, u₂] = −u₁, so ad u₃ is the infinitesimal rotation of the (u₁,
    u₂) plane and exp(θ ad u₃) is rotation by θ about u₃. Now exp(θu₃) =
    diag(e^(−iθ/2), e^(iθ/2)); at θ = 2π this is −I, which maps to the identity
    rotation. The loop of rotations θ ↦ R_θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π) lifts to a PATH from I
    to −I, so it is not contractible; SO(3) ≅ S³/{±1} = RP³ and π₁ = Z/2.
    Common mistakes: thinking that isomorphic Lie algebras give isomorphic
    groups; forgetting ±I both map to the identity. Now you try: the image
    of [[0, −1], [1, 0]] = exp(πu₂). (rotation by π about the u₂-axis)

D4. (a) Compute the derived and lower central series of b₂ (upper
    triangular 2 × 2), of the Heisenberg algebra n₃ ([x, y] = z) and of b₃.
    (b) State Engel's and Lie's theorems. (c) Show Lie's theorem fails over
    R and complete reducibility fails for solvable algebras.
    Answer: (a) b₂ ⊃ CE₁₂ ⊃ 0 (solvable), Cᵏ(b₂) = CE₁₂ for all k ≥ 1
    (not nilpotent); n₃ ⊃ Cz ⊃ 0 both ways (nilpotent); b₃ ⊃ n₃ ⊃ CE₁₃ ⊃ 0
    (derived length 3). (c) so(2) on R²; b₂ on C².
    Teacher explains: (a) In b₂ = span(E₁₁, E₂₂, E₁₂): [E₁₁, E₁₂] = E₁₂,
    [E₂₂, E₁₂] = −E₁₂, [E₁₁, E₂₂] = 0. So [b₂, b₂] = CE₁₂, which is
    abelian: derived series reaches 0. But C² = [b₂, CE₁₂] = CE₁₂ again
    (E₁₁ keeps acting by 1), so the lower central series is stuck: b₂ is
    solvable, not nilpotent (ad E₁₁ has eigenvalue 1, not nilpotent,
    consistent with Engel). In n₃, [n₃, n₃] = Cz is central, so [n₃, Cz] =
    0: nilpotent. For b₃: [b₃, b₃] = n₃ (strictly upper), [n₃, n₃] = CE₁₃,
    then 0. (b) ENGEL: g nilpotent ⇔ ad X nilpotent ∀X ∈ g. LIE: if g ⊆
    gl(V) is solvable, V ≠ 0 finite-dimensional over C, there is a common
    eigenvector; by induction V has a g-stable flag, i.e. g is upper
    triangular in a suitable basis. (c) so(2) = R·J, J = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]
    is abelian, but J has no real eigenvector. b₂ acts on C²: the line
    Ce₁ is invariant; any invariant line is an eigenline of E₁₂, i.e. Ce₁
    again, so Ce₁ has no invariant complement. Common mistakes: confusing
    "each element nilpotent as a matrix" with "ad-nilpotent" (I ∈ gl(n)
    is ad-nilpotent but not nilpotent); forgetting Lie's theorem needs an
    algebraically closed field of characteristic 0. Now you try: is e(2)
    ([J, P₁] = P₂, [J, P₂] = −P₁, [P₁, P₂] = 0) nilpotent? (no: solvable,
    Cᵏ = span(P₁, P₂) for all k ≥ 1)

D5. (a) Compute the Killing form of sl(2, C) in the basis (e, h, f) and
    check κ(X, Y) = 4 tr(XY). (b) Compute the Killing form of aff(1)
    ([x, y] = y) and of n₃. (c) Prove: if κ is nondegenerate then g is
    semisimple.
    Answer: (a) Gram matrix [[0, 0, 4], [0, 8, 0], [4, 0, 0]], det −128.
    (b) aff(1): κ(x, x) = 1, others 0 (degenerate); n₃: κ ≡ 0. (c) an
    abelian ideal lies in the radical of κ.
    Teacher explains: (a) [h, e] = 2e, [h, f] = −2f, [e, f] = h. In the
    basis (e, h, f): ad h = diag(2, 0, −2); ad e: e ↦ 0, h ↦ −2e, f ↦ h;
    ad f: e ↦ −h, h ↦ 2f, f ↦ 0. κ(h, h) = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8. ad e ad f sends
    e ↦ ad e(−h) = 2e, h ↦ ad e(2f) = 2h, f ↦ 0: trace 4 = κ(e, f). ad e
    and ad f are nilpotent and shift weights, so κ(e, e) = κ(f, f) =
    κ(e, h) = κ(f, h) = 0. Compare tr(hh) = 2, tr(ef) = 1: κ = 4 tr(XY)
    (the general formula 2n tr(XY) with n = 2). det = −4·8·4 = −128 ≠ 0.
    (b) aff(1): ad x = diag(0, 1) in (x, y), ad y: x ↦ −y, y ↦ 0. So
    κ(x, x) = 1, κ(y, y) = 0, κ(x, y) = tr(x ↦ −y, y ↦ 0) = 0. It kills
    [g, g] = Cy, as Cartan's solvability criterion predicts. In n₃ every
    ad X ad Y maps into the centre and kills it: nilpotent, trace 0.
    (c) If g is not semisimple, the last nonzero term a of the derived
    series of rad g is a nonzero ABELIAN IDEAL. For a ∈ a, y ∈ g, ad a ad y
    maps g into a and a into [a, a] = 0, so (ad a ad y)² = 0 and κ(a, y) =
    0 for all y: a is in the radical of κ, contradiction. (The converse,
    semisimple ⇒ nondegenerate, uses Cartan's solvability criterion on
    the ideal g^⊥.) Common mistakes: using tr(XY) instead of tr(ad X ad Y);
    believing κ ≡ 0 forces nilpotency (only solvability: Cx ⋉ C² with
    ad x = diag(1, i) has κ ≡ 0). Now you try: the Killing form of so(3)
    in the basis L₁, L₂, L₃. (−2δⱼₖ: negative definite, as for any compact
    semisimple group)

D6. Classify the finite-dimensional irreducible representations of
    sl(2, C). Then decompose V(3) ⊗ V(2) and compute the Casimir
    eigenvalue on V(n).
    Answer: one V(n) for each n ≥ 0, dim n + 1, weights n, n − 2, ..., −n;
    V(3) ⊗ V(2) = V(5) ⊕ V(3) ⊕ V(1); Ω = ef + fe + ½h² acts by n(n + 2)/2.
    Teacher explains: Let V be irreducible. From [h, e] = 2e: if hv = μv
    then h(ev) = (μ + 2)ev, so e raises weights by 2 and f lowers by 2.
    Only finitely many eigenvalues of h exist, so there is a HIGHEST WEIGHT
    VECTOR v₀ ≠ 0 with hv₀ = λv₀, ev₀ = 0. Put vₖ = fᵏv₀/k!. Then hvₖ =
    (λ − 2k)vₖ, fvₖ = (k + 1)vₖ₊₁, and by induction evₖ = (λ − k + 1)vₖ₋₁:
       evₖ = (1/k)e f vₖ₋₁ = (1/k)(hvₖ₋₁ + f evₖ₋₁)
           = (1/k)((λ − 2k + 2) + (k − 1)(λ − k + 2))vₖ₋₁ = (λ − k + 1)vₖ₋₁.
    The nonzero vₖ are independent (distinct weights); let vₙ be the last
    nonzero one. Then 0 = evₙ₊₁ = (λ − n)vₙ, so λ = n ∈ N. span(v₀, ...,
    vₙ) is invariant, hence equals V: V ≅ V(n), unique up to isomorphism.
    Tensor product: weights of V(3) ⊗ V(2) are sums of {3, 1, −1, −3} and
    {2, 0, −2}: 5 (×1), 3 (×2), 1 (×3), −1 (×3), −3 (×2), −5 (×1). Peel
    off V(5) (weights 5, ..., −5), then V(3), then V(1): dimensions 6 +
    4 + 2 = 12 ✓. Casimir: Ω commutes with sl(2), so it is scalar on V(n)
    (Schur); on v₀: efv₀ = e v₁ = nv₀, fev₀ = 0, ½h²v₀ = ½n²v₀; total
    n + n²/2 = n(n + 2)/2. Common mistakes: listing weights n, n − 1, ...
    (steps are 2); forgetting |m − n| as the lowest term. Now you try:
    V(2) ⊗ V(2). (V(4) ⊕ V(2) ⊕ V(0))

D7. Find the root space decomposition of sl(3, C): Cartan subalgebra,
    roots, simple roots, Cartan matrix, and the Weyl group. Check
    [g_α, g_β] = g_{α+β} on an example.
    Answer: h = traceless diagonal; roots αᵢⱼ = εᵢ − εⱼ (i ≠ j), 6 roots,
    root vectors Eᵢⱼ; Δ = {ε₁ − ε₂, ε₂ − ε₃}; Cartan matrix [[2, −1], [−1,
    2]] (type A₂); W = S₃, order 6.
    Teacher explains: For H = diag(a₁, a₂, a₃), ∑aᵢ = 0: [H, Eᵢⱼ] = (aᵢ −
    aⱼ)Eᵢⱼ. So g = h ⊕ ⊕_{i≠j} CEᵢⱼ, each root space 1-dimensional, with
    root αᵢⱼ(H) = aᵢ − aⱼ. Positive roots (i < j): α₁ = ε₁ − ε₂, α₂ =
    ε₂ − ε₃, α₁ + α₂ = ε₁ − ε₃; every positive root is a nonnegative
    integer combination of α₁, α₂, so they are simple. The sl(2)-triple
    for α₁ is (E₁₂, H₁ = E₁₁ − E₂₂, E₂₁); the coroot is H₁, and
    ⟨α₂, α₁^∨⟩ = α₂(H₁) = a₂ − a₃ at H₁ = diag(1, −1, 0), i.e. −1.
    Symmetrically ⟨α₁, α₂^∨⟩ = −1. With κ = 6 tr on h, all roots have the
    same length and the angle between α₁, α₂ is 120° (4cos²θ = 1). The
    Weyl group acts on h by permuting the aᵢ: W = S₃, 6 elements, equal
    to N(T)/T for T ⊆ SU(3) diagonal. Example: [E₁₂, E₂₃] = E₁₃ ∈ g_{α₁+α₂},
    while [E₁₂, E₁₃] = 0 since 2α₁ + α₂ is not a root. dim sl(3) = 2 + 6
    = 8 ✓. Common mistakes: taking all diagonal matrices (that is gl(3));
    forgetting negative roots when counting. Now you try: the number of
    roots and positive roots of sl(4). (12 and 6)

D8. State the axioms of a (reduced) root system. Prove that for roots
    β ≠ ±α the product ⟨β, α^∨⟩⟨α, β^∨⟩ lies in {0, 1, 2, 3}, and list the
    possible angles and length ratios. Prove that if (α, β) > 0, β ≠ α,
    then α − β is a root.
    Answer: 4cos²θ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}: θ = 90°; 60°, 120° (ratio 1); 45°,
    135° (ratio 2); 30°, 150° (ratio 3). If (α, β) > 0 one of the Cartan
    integers is 1, and a reflection produces α − β.
    Teacher explains: AXIOMS (E Euclidean): (R1) Φ finite, spans E, 0 ∉ Φ;
    (R2) the only multiples of α in Φ are ±α; (R3) s_α(Φ) = Φ, where
    s_α(v) = v − ⟨v, α^∨⟩α; (R4) ⟨β, α^∨⟩ = 2(β, α)/(α, α) ∈ Z. Now
       ⟨β, α^∨⟩⟨α, β^∨⟩ = 4(α, β)²/(|α|²|β|²) = 4cos²θ ∈ [0, 4],
    and it is an integer by (R4). The value 4 means cos θ = ±1, so β is a
    multiple of α, excluded by (R2). So 4cos²θ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, and both
    integers have the same sign. Also |β|²/|α|² = ⟨β, α^∨⟩/⟨α, β^∨⟩. Table
    (with |β| ≥ |α|):
       ⟨α, β^∨⟩  ⟨β, α^∨⟩   θ       |β|²/|α|²
          0         0      90°     any
          ±1        ±1     60°/120°    1
          ±1        ±2     45°/135°    2
          ±1        ±3     30°/150°    3
    If (α, β) > 0 and β ≠ α, the table shows ⟨α, β^∨⟩ = 1 or ⟨β, α^∨⟩ =
    1. In the first case s_β(α) = α − β ∈ Φ; in the second s_α(β) = β − α
    ∈ Φ, so α − β = −(β − α) ∈ Φ. Dually (α, β) < 0 ⇒ α + β ∈ Φ. Common
    mistakes: forgetting that 90° allows any length ratio (A₁ × A₁ with
    different lengths is still a root system); computing ⟨β, α^∨⟩ with
    |β|² in the denominator. Now you try: the angle and length ratio when
    ⟨β, α^∨⟩ = −3. (150°, |β|² = 3|α|²; then ⟨α, β^∨⟩ = −1)

D9. Describe the root systems B₂, C₂ and G₂: roots, simple roots,
    positive roots, Cartan matrices, highest roots and Weyl groups. Find
    the α-string through β in G₂.
    Answer: B₂ = {±e₁, ±e₂, ±e₁ ± e₂}, α₁ = e₁ − e₂, α₂ = e₂, Φ⁺ = {α₁, α₂,
    α₁ + α₂, α₁ + 2α₂}, Cartan [[2, −2], [−1, 2]], W dihedral of order 8.
    C₂ = {±2eᵢ, ±e₁ ± e₂} ≅ B₂. G₂: Φ⁺ = {α, β, α + β, 2α + β, 3α + β,
    3α + 2β}, Cartan [[2, −1], [−3, 2]], W dihedral of order 12; the
    string is β, β + α, β + 2α, β + 3α.
    Teacher explains: B₂ (so(5)): long roots ±e₁ ± e₂ (length² 2), short
    ±eᵢ. With α₁ = e₁ − e₂, α₂ = e₂: α₁ + α₂ = e₁, α₁ + 2α₂ = e₁ + e₂ =
    highest root, height 3. a₁₂ = 2(α₁, α₂)/(α₂, α₂) = 2(−1)/1 = −2, a₂₁ =
    2(−1)/2 = −1; 4cos²θ = 2: angle 135°. W is generated by reflections in
    lines at 45°; s₁s₂ is rotation by 90°, of order 4, so W is dihedral
    of order 8 = the signed permutations of (e₁, e₂). C₂ (sp(4)) has long
    roots ±2eᵢ and short ±e₁ ± e₂: rotating by 45° and rescaling by
    1/√2 carries it to B₂, the root-level shadow of so(5) ≅ sp(4). G₂:
    take α = (1, 0) and β = (−3/2, √3/2): |β|² = 3, (α, β) = −3/2, cos θ =
    −√3/2, θ = 150°. Then α + β = (−½, √3/2) and 2α + β = (½, √3/2) are short,
    3α + β = (3/2, √3/2) and 3α + 2β = (0, √3) are long; together with negatives
    that is 12 roots, and dim g₂ = 2 + 12 = 14. ⟨α, β^∨⟩ = 2(−3/2)/3 = −1, ⟨β,
    α^∨⟩ = 2(−3/2)/1 = −3. The α-string through β is β − pα, ..., β +
    qα with p − q = ⟨β, α^∨⟩ = −3 and p = 0 (β − α is not a root, both
    simple), so q = 3. The highest root is 3α + 2β (height 5 = h − 1,
    Coxeter number h = 6), and s_αs_β is rotation by 60°: W is dihedral of
    order 12. Common mistakes: mixing up which simple root is long in the
    Cartan matrix (convention aᵢⱼ = ⟨αᵢ, αⱼ^∨⟩); listing 2α + 2β, which is
    not a root. Now you try: ρ = half the sum of the positive roots of
    G₂. (5α + 3β)

D10. State the classification of complex simple Lie algebras and give,
     for each type, the rank, number of roots and dimension. Prove that a
     Dynkin diagram cannot contain a cycle (e.g. the triangle with single
     edges).
     Answer: Aₗ (l ≥ 1), Bₗ (l ≥ 2), Cₗ (l ≥ 3), Dₗ (l ≥ 4), E₆, E₇, E₈,
     F₄, G₂; |Φ| = l(l + 1), 2l², 2l², 2l(l − 1), 72, 126, 240, 48, 12;
     dim = l + |Φ|. Cycles give a nonzero vector of length 0.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: two complex semisimple Lie algebras are
     isomorphic iff their root systems are, and root systems ↔ Cartan
     matrices ↔ Dynkin diagrams; simple ↔ connected. Every connected
     diagram is one of the list, and each occurs (classical matrix
     algebras, Serre relations for the exceptional ones). Table:
        type   algebra      dim        |Φ|        |W|
        Aₗ     sl(l + 1)    l(l + 2)    l(l + 1)   (l + 1)!
        Bₗ     so(2l + 1)   l(2l + 1)   2l²        2ˡl!
        Cₗ     sp(2l)       l(2l + 1)   2l²        2ˡl!
        Dₗ     so(2l)       l(2l − 1)   2l(l − 1)  2ˡ⁻¹l!
        G₂, F₄, E₆, E₇, E₈: 14, 52, 78, 133, 248.
     E.g. dim E₈ = 8 + 240 = 248. WHY NO CYCLES: replace the simple roots
     by unit vectors vᵢ; for joined nodes 2(vᵢ, vⱼ) = −√(aᵢⱼaⱼᵢ) ≤ −1,
     otherwise 0. For v = ∑vᵢ over n nodes,
        0 < |v|² = n + ∑_{i<j} 2(vᵢ, vⱼ) ≤ n − (number of edges),
     since the vᵢ are independent (v ≠ 0). So a connected subdiagram on n
     nodes has fewer than n edges: it is a TREE, and in particular a cycle
     is impossible. For the triangle directly: (vᵢ, vⱼ) = −½, |v|² = 3 −
     3 = 0, contradiction. Similar arguments bound the degree of a node
     (< 4 counted with multiplicity) and exclude all other trees, leaving
     exactly the list above. Common mistakes: listing B₁, C₂, D₃ as new
     types (B₁ = A₁, C₂ = B₂, D₃ = A₃); forgetting the Cartan subalgebra
     when computing dim g from |Φ|. Now you try: dim E₇ from |Φ| = 126.
     (133)

D11. For sl(3, C) define the fundamental weights, find the weights of
     C³, derive dim V(a, b) = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2 from the Weyl
     dimension formula, and decompose 3 ⊗ 3 and 3 ⊗ 3̄.
     Answer: ⟨ωᵢ, αⱼ^∨⟩ = δᵢⱼ; weights of C³: ε₁ = ω₁, ε₂ = ω₂ − ω₁, ε₃ =
     −ω₂; 3 ⊗ 3 = V(2, 0) ⊕ V(0, 1) = 6 ⊕ 3̄; 3 ⊗ 3̄ = V(1, 1) ⊕ V(0, 0) =
     8 ⊕ 1.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM OF THE HIGHEST WEIGHT: every irreducible
     finite-dimensional V has a unique highest weight λ (killed by all
     positive root vectors), λ is dominant integral, λ = aω₁ + bω₂ with
     a, b ∈ N, and each such λ occurs exactly once: V(a, b). On C³ the
     weight of eᵢ is εᵢ; pairing with the coroots H₁ = diag(1, −1, 0), H₂
     = diag(0, 1, −1) gives coordinates (1, 0), (−1, 1), (0, −1). So C³ =
     V(1, 0) with highest weight ω₁, and its dual has weights −εᵢ, highest
     −ε₃ = ω₂: 3̄ = V(0, 1). WEYL DIMENSION: ρ = ω₁ + ω₂ and the positive
     coroots are α₁^∨, α₂^∨, α₁^∨ + α₂^∨, so with λ + ρ = (a + 1)ω₁ + (b +
     1)ω₂,
        dim V(a, b) = (a + 1)/1 · (b + 1)/1 · (a + b + 2)/2.
     E.g. V(1, 1) = 2·2·4/2 = 8 (the adjoint), V(2, 0) = 6, V(3, 0) = 10,
     V(2, 2) = 27. TENSOR PRODUCTS by peeling highest weights: 3 ⊗ 3 has
     highest weight 2ω₁, and V(2, 0) = Sym²C³ (6); the rest Λ²C³ has
     highest weight ε₁ + ε₂ = ω₂: 9 = 6 + 3. 3 ⊗ 3̄ = End C³ = sl(3) ⊕ CI:
     highest weight ω₁ + ω₂, 9 = 8 + 1. Common mistakes: using ε-coordinates
     in the dimension formula without converting; forgetting that V(a, b)*
     ≅ V(b, a). Now you try: dim V(2, 1) and dim V(4, 0). (15 and 15)

D12. Let G = SU(2) and T = {t_θ = diag(e^(iθ), e^(−iθ))}. Using the Weyl
     integration formula ∫_G f dg = (2/π)∫₀^π f(t_θ) sin²θ dθ for class
     functions f, show the characters χₙ(θ) = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ are
     orthonormal, compute ∫_G χ₁⁴ dg, and determine the irreducible
     representations of SO(3).
     Answer: ∫χₘχₙ = δₘₙ; ∫χ₁⁴ = 2 = multiplicity of V(0) in V(1)^⊗4;
     SO(3) has one irreducible of each odd dimension 2l + 1.
     Teacher explains: V(n) = homogeneous polynomials of degree n in two
     variables; t_θ acts on the weight vectors by e^(i(n−2k)θ), so
        χₙ(θ) = e^(inθ) + e^(i(n−2)θ) + ... + e^(−inθ)
              = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ   (geometric series).
     Then χₘχₙ sin²θ = sin((m + 1)θ) sin((n + 1)θ), and
        (2/π)∫₀^π sin((m + 1)θ) sin((n + 1)θ) dθ = δₘₙ.
     Since ∫χ_Vχ̄_W = dim Hom_G(V, W) (Schur plus Haar averaging), this
     reproves that the V(n) are irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic,
     and Peter-Weyl says there are no others. ∫χ₁⁴: χ₁ = 2cos θ, so
        (2/π)∫₀^π 16cos⁴θ sin²θ dθ = (2/π)·16·(π/16) = 2,
     matching V(1)^⊗4 = V(4) ⊕ 3V(2) ⊕ 2V(0). SO(3) = SU(2)/{±I}: an
     irreducible of SO(3) is a V(n) on which −I = t_π acts trivially;
     −I acts by (−1)ⁿ, so n = 2l is even: dimension 2l + 1. These are the
     spherical harmonics of degree l, and a rotation by φ has character
     1 + 2cos φ + ... + 2cos lφ = sin((l + ½)φ)/sin(φ/2) (φ = 2θ). Common
     mistakes: forgetting the density sin²θ (T is not all of G); using
     Haar measure on T alone. Now you try: ∫_{SU(2)} χ₁⁶ dg. (5, the
     Catalan number C₃)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) exp is onto for every connected Lie group.
     b) exp is onto for every compact connected Lie group.
     c) Every Lie group is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of some GL(n).
     d) Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of
        some Lie group.
     e) Groups with isomorphic Lie algebras are isomorphic.
     f) Every finite-dimensional representation of a solvable Lie
        algebra over C is completely reducible.
     g) Every finite-dimensional representation of sl(n, C) is
        completely reducible.
     h) A Lie algebra with Killing form identically 0 is nilpotent.
     i) A Lie algebra with nondegenerate Killing form is semisimple.
     j) Lie's theorem holds over R.
     k) Every subalgebra of a semisimple Lie algebra is semisimple.
     l) Every ideal of a semisimple Lie algebra is semisimple.
     m) The direct sum of two simple Lie algebras is simple.
     n) Root systems with isomorphic Weyl groups are isomorphic.
     o) The sum of two roots is a root or zero.
     p) Every positive root is a sum of simple roots.
     q) Every irreducible finite-dimensional representation of an
        abelian Lie algebra over C is 1-dimensional.
     r) so(4) is simple.
     s) SO(3) has an irreducible representation of dimension 2.
     t) The Killing form of a compact semisimple Lie algebra is negative
        definite.
     Answers:
       a) F: SL(2, R) (diag(−2, −½))       b) T
       c) F: the universal cover of SL(2, R)
       d) T (Ado's theorem + Lie III)      e) F: SU(2) and SO(3)
       f) F: b₂ on C²                      g) T (Weyl)
       h) F: Cx ⋉ C², ad x = diag(1, i) (solvable, by Cartan's criterion)
       i) T (Cartan's criterion)           j) F: so(2) on R²
       k) F: a Cartan subalgebra (abelian), or a Borel b ⊆ sl(n)
       l) T (it is a sum of some of the simple factors)
       m) F: sl(2) ⊕ sl(2) has the ideal sl(2) ⊕ 0
       n) F: Bₙ and Cₙ (n ≥ 3) share W = (Z/2)ⁿ ⋊ Sₙ
       o) F: in A₁ × A₁, α + β is not a root; also α + α = 2α
       p) T (as a sum with repetitions: ∑kᵢαᵢ, kᵢ ∈ N)
       q) T (commuting operators have a common eigenvector)
       r) F: so(4) ≅ so(3) ⊕ so(3)          s) F: only odd dimensions
       t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make everything concrete in sl(2) and sl(3) first — write
  the 3 × 3 matrices Eᵢⱼ, compute [H, Eᵢⱼ] = (aᵢ − aⱼ)Eᵢⱼ by hand, and
  draw the six roots of A₂ as a hexagon before ever saying "root system";
  then draw B₂ (a square with its diagonals) and G₂ (a star of David with
  a hexagon) and read off angles and length ratios from the pictures.
  For every representation question, insist on the routine "list the
  weights with multiplicities, peel off the highest weight, repeat", and
  check the total dimension at the end. Keep the dictionary group ↔
  algebra visible: SU(2) → SO(3) is the example to return to whenever
  someone claims the Lie algebra determines the group. Harder: prove
  Engel's and Lie's theorems and Cartan's criterion; prove Weyl's
  theorem with the Casimir element; show dim g_α = 1 and that the roots
  form a root system; complete the classification of connected Dynkin
  diagrams by excluding every tree outside the list; prove the Weyl
  character formula via the Weyl integration formula for a compact group
  (or via Verma modules and the Casimir), derive Kostant's multiplicity
  formula, and show that |P/Q| equals the order of the centre of the
  simply connected group (Z/n for SU(n), Z/4 or Z/2 × Z/2 for Spin(2n)).


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.12 — PROBABILITY (MEASURE-THEORETIC): CONDITIONAL EXPECTATION,
MARTINGALES, BROWNIAN MOTION, WEAK CONVERGENCE, CHARACTERISTIC FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PROBABILITY SPACE (Ω, ℱ, P): a measure space with P(Ω) = 1. A RANDOM
    VARIABLE is a measurable X : Ω → R; its LAW is μ_X = P ∘ X⁻¹ on 𝔅(R),
    with distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x). E X = ∫X dP, and E g(X) =
    ∫g dμ_X. σ(X) = {X⁻¹(B)} is the information carried by X; Y is
    σ(X)-measurable iff Y = h(X) for a Borel h (Doob-Dynkin lemma).
  - CONDITIONAL EXPECTATION: for X ∈ L¹ and a sub-σ-algebra 𝒢 ⊆ ℱ,
    E[X | 𝒢] is the (a.s. unique) 𝒢-measurable Y ∈ L¹ with E[Y𝟙_G] =
    E[X𝟙_G] for all G ∈ 𝒢. EXISTENCE by Radon-Nikodym (ν(G) = E[X𝟙_G] ≪ P
    on 𝒢), or, for X ∈ L², as the ORTHOGONAL PROJECTION of X onto the
    closed subspace L²(𝒢): E[X | 𝒢] is the best 𝒢-measurable predictor.
  - ELEMENTARY CASES: if 𝒢 is generated by a partition {G₁, G₂, ...} with
    P(Gᵢ) > 0, then E[X | 𝒢] = E[X𝟙_{Gᵢ}]/P(Gᵢ) on Gᵢ. With a joint
    density f(x, y), E[Y | X] = h(X), h(x) = ∫y f(x, y) dy / ∫f(x, y) dy.
    Gaussian vectors: E[Y | X] = EY + (Cov(X, Y)/Var X)(X − EX) (linear!).
  - PROPERTIES (all a.s.): linearity; monotonicity; E[E[X | 𝒢]] = EX;
    TOWER E[E[X | 𝒢] | ℋ] = E[X | ℋ] for ℋ ⊆ 𝒢; TAKING OUT WHAT IS KNOWN
    E[ZX | 𝒢] = Z E[X | 𝒢] for bounded 𝒢-measurable Z; INDEPENDENCE:
    E[X | 𝒢] = EX if X ⫫ 𝒢; conditional JENSEN φ(E[X | 𝒢]) ≤ E[φ(X) | 𝒢]
    for convex φ (so ‖E[X | 𝒢]‖_p ≤ ‖X‖_p); conditional MCT, Fatou, DCT.
    LAW OF TOTAL VARIANCE Var X = E[Var(X | 𝒢)] + Var(E[X | 𝒢]).
  - MARTINGALES: a FILTRATION (ℱₙ) is an increasing sequence of σ-algebras;
    (Mₙ) is ADAPTED if Mₙ is ℱₙ-measurable, and a MARTINGALE if also
    E|Mₙ| < ∞ and E[Mₙ₊₁ | ℱₙ] = Mₙ (SUB: ≥, SUPER: ≤). Examples: sums of
    independent mean-0 steps, Sₙ² − nσ², products of independent mean-1
    factors, exp(θSₙ)/φ(θ)ⁿ, (q/p)^{Sₙ}, Doob martingales E[X | ℱₙ],
    Pólya urn proportions, Zₙ/μⁿ for a branching process. A convex function
    of a martingale is a submartingale (if integrable). DOOB DECOMPOSITION:
    a submartingale is Mₙ + Aₙ with M a martingale, A predictable
    increasing, Aₙ = ∑_{k<n} E[X_{k+1} − X_k | ℱ_k].
  - STOPPING TIMES: τ with {τ ≤ n} ∈ ℱₙ (hitting times yes, "last visit"
    times no). The stopped process M_{τ∧n} is a martingale. OPTIONAL
    STOPPING THEOREM: E M_τ = E M₀ if (i) τ is bounded, or (ii) (M_{τ∧n})
    is uniformly integrable (e.g. |M_{τ∧n}| ≤ K), or (iii) Eτ < ∞ and the
    increments are bounded. It FAILS for simple random walk stopped at the
    hitting time of 1 (E S_τ = 1 ≠ 0). Uses: gambler's ruin, Wald's
    identities E S_τ = μEτ and E(S_τ − τμ)² = σ²Eτ, waiting-time puzzles.
  - DOOB'S INEQUALITIES: for a non-negative submartingale, P(max_{k≤n} X_k
    ≥ λ) ≤ E Xₙ/λ (MAXIMAL); ‖max_{k≤n} X_k‖_p ≤ (p/(p − 1))‖Xₙ‖_p for
    p > 1 (Lᵖ). Kolmogorov's inequality is the case X = Sₙ².
  - CONVERGENCE: the UPCROSSING LEMMA (b − a)E Uₙ[a, b] ≤ E(Xₙ − a)⁺ gives
    DOOB'S THEOREM: sup E|Xₙ| < ∞ ⇒ Xₙ → X∞ a.s., X∞ ∈ L¹. L¹ convergence
    needs UNIFORM INTEGRABILITY (sup_n E[|Xₙ|; |Xₙ| > K] → 0 as K → ∞);
    for martingales, UI ⇔ L¹ convergent ⇔ Mₙ = E[M∞ | ℱₙ]; Lᵖ-bounded
    (p > 1) ⇒ Lᵖ convergence. LÉVY UPWARD: E[X | ℱₙ] → E[X | ℱ∞].
    Counterexample: Mₙ = ∏ξᵢ, ξᵢ = 0 or 2 (prob ½ each): Mₙ → 0 a.s. but
    E Mₙ = 1, so no L¹ convergence. Reverse martingales give the SLLN.
  - BROWNIAN MOTION (B_t)_{t≥0}: B₀ = 0, independent increments, B_t − B_s
    ~ N(0, t − s), continuous paths. Equivalently a centred Gaussian
    process with Cov(B_s, B_t) = min(s, t) and continuous paths. Exists
    (Lévy-Ciesielski series, or Kolmogorov extension + continuity
    criterion E|X_t − X_s|^α ≤ C|t − s|^{1+β}). INVARIANCES: −B, scaling
    c^{−1/2}B_{ct}, time inversion tB_{1/t}, B_{s+t} − B_s (Markov
    property; STRONG MARKOV at stopping times).
  - PATH PROPERTIES: a.s. nowhere differentiable, Hölder of every order
    < ½ but not ½; QUADRATIC VARIATION ∑(ΔB)² → t in L² (and a.s. along
    dyadic partitions), hence INFINITE total variation; LAW OF THE
    ITERATED LOGARITHM lim sup B_t/√(2t log log t) = 1; zero set is a
    perfect null set; BROWNIAN BRIDGE B_t − tB₁, Cov = s(1 − t), s ≤ t.
  - BROWNIAN MARTINGALES AND HITTING TIMES: B_t, B_t² − t,
    exp(θB_t − θ²t/2), B_t³ − 3tB_t are martingales. For τ = exit time of
    (−a, b): P(B_τ = b) = a/(a + b), Eτ = ab. T_a = inf{t : B_t = a} is
    finite a.s. with E T_a = ∞ and E e^{−λT_a} = e^{−a√(2λ)}. REFLECTION
    PRINCIPLE: P(max_{s≤t} B_s ≥ a) = 2P(B_t ≥ a), so max_{s≤t} B_s has
    the law of |B_t|, and T_a has density a(2πt³)^{−1/2}e^{−a²/2t}. With
    drift μ > 0 and unit variance: P(ever reach −a) = e^{−2μa}.
  - WEAK CONVERGENCE (convergence in distribution) μₙ ⇒ μ: ∫f dμₙ → ∫f dμ
    for every bounded continuous f. PORTMANTEAU: ⇔ lim sup μₙ(F) ≤ μ(F)
    for closed F ⇔ lim inf μₙ(G) ≥ μ(G) for open G ⇔ μₙ(A) → μ(A) when
    μ(∂A) = 0 ⇔ (on R) Fₙ(x) → F(x) at continuity points of F. In prob.
    ⇒ in distribution; the converse holds only for a constant limit.
    SLUTSKY, CONTINUOUS MAPPING, SKOROKHOD REPRESENTATION, HELLY
    SELECTION; PROKHOROV: tight ⇔ relatively compact. Weak convergence
    does NOT give E Xₙ → E X without uniform integrability.
  - CHARACTERISTIC FUNCTION φ_X(t) = E e^{itX}: φ(0) = 1, |φ| ≤ 1,
    uniformly continuous, φ(−t) = conj φ(t), positive definite (BOCHNER:
    these characterise ch.f.s); φ_{aX+b}(t) = e^{ibt}φ(at); φ_{X+Y} =
    φ_Xφ_Y for independent X, Y. MOMENTS: E|X|ᵏ < ∞ ⇒ φ ∈ Cᵏ and φ⁽ᵏ⁾(0)
    = iᵏ E Xᵏ. Table: N(μ, σ²) ↦ e^{iμt − σ²t²/2}, Poisson(λ) ↦
    e^{λ(e^{it} − 1)}, Exp(λ) ↦ λ/(λ − it), U[−a, a] ↦ sin(at)/(at),
    Cauchy ↦ e^{−|t|}, Laplace ↦ 1/(1 + t²).
  - INVERSION AND UNIQUENESS: μ(a, b) + ½μ{a, b} = lim_{T→∞} (1/2π)
    ∫_{−T}^{T} (e^{−ita} − e^{−itb})/(it) φ(t) dt; if ∫|φ| < ∞, X has the
    bounded continuous density f(x) = (1/2π)∫e^{−itx}φ(t) dt; for integer
    X, P(X = k) = (1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π} e^{−itk}φ(t) dt. φ determines μ.
  - LÉVY CONTINUITY THEOREM: μₙ ⇒ μ ⇒ φₙ → φ pointwise; conversely if
    φₙ → g pointwise and g is continuous AT 0, then g is a ch.f. and
    μₙ ⇒ μ_g. CLT (Lindeberg-Lévy): i.i.d., mean μ, variance σ² ∈ (0, ∞)
    ⇒ (Sₙ − nμ)/(σ√n) ⇒ N(0, 1). LINDEBERG-FELLER: triangular arrays with
    s_n^{−2}∑E[X_k²; |X_k| > εs_n] → 0. POISSON LIMIT Bin(n, λ/n) ⇒
    Poisson(λ); WLLN via φ(t/n)ⁿ → e^{iμt}; DELTA METHOD; DONSKER: the
    rescaled random walk converges to Brownian motion in C[0, 1].

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Roll a fair die; Ω = {1, ..., 6}, X(ω) = ω. (a) Compute E[X | 𝒢] for
    𝒢 = σ({X even}) and for ℋ = σ({1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}). (b) Verify the
    defining property E[Y𝟙_G] = E[X𝟙_G] for G = {2, 4, 6}. (c) Verify the
    law of total variance for ℋ.
    Answer: (a) E[X | 𝒢] = 4 on evens, 3 on odds; E[X | ℋ] = 1.5, 3.5,
    5.5 on the three blocks. (b) both sides 2. (c) 35/12 = 1/4 + 8/3.
    Teacher explains: When 𝒢 comes from a partition, a 𝒢-measurable Y must
    be CONSTANT on each block, and the defining property with G = the
    block forces the constant to be the average of X over the block:
       E[X | 𝒢] = ∑ᵢ (E[X𝟙_{Gᵢ}]/P(Gᵢ)) 𝟙_{Gᵢ}.
    (a) On {2, 4, 6} the average is (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4; on {1, 3, 5} it is
    3. For ℋ the block averages are 1.5, 3.5, 5.5. (b) Y = E[X | 𝒢]:
    E[Y𝟙_G] = 4 · P(G) = 4 · ½ = 2, and E[X𝟙_G] = (2 + 4 + 6)/6 = 2 ✓.
    (c) Var X = 91/6 − 49/4 = 35/12. Within each block of ℋ, X takes two
    values 1 apart, so Var(X | ℋ) = 1/4 everywhere. E[X | ℋ] takes 1.5,
    3.5, 5.5 with probability 1/3 each: variance (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 8/3. And
    1/4 + 8/3 = 3/12 + 32/12 = 35/12 ✓. Note E[X | ℋ] is a RANDOM
    VARIABLE, not a number, and E[E[X | ℋ]] = 3.5 = EX. Common mistakes:
    giving a single number for E[X | 𝒢]; averaging over the wrong block;
    forgetting to weight by probabilities when blocks are unequal. Now you
    try: two fair dice, S = X₁ + X₂. Find E[X₁ | S]. (S/2, by symmetry:
    E[X₁ | S] = E[X₂ | S] and they add to S)

D2. (a) Prove existence and a.s. uniqueness of E[X | 𝒢] for X ∈ L¹.
    (b) Show that for X ∈ L², E[X | 𝒢] minimises E(X − Z)² over
    𝒢-measurable Z ∈ L². (c) Prove the tower property and "taking out
    what is known".
    Answer: (a) Radon-Nikodym applied to ν(G) = E[X𝟙_G] on (Ω, 𝒢);
    uniqueness from E[(Y − Y′)𝟙_{Y>Y′}] = 0. (b) X − E[X | 𝒢] ⊥ L²(𝒢).
    (c) check the defining identity.
    Teacher explains: (a) First X ≥ 0. ν(G) = E[X𝟙_G] is a finite measure
    on 𝒢 with ν ≪ P|_𝒢 (P(G) = 0 ⇒ ν(G) = 0). Radon-Nikodym gives a
    𝒢-measurable Y = dν/dP ≥ 0 with E[Y𝟙_G] = ν(G) = E[X𝟙_G]. In general
    take X = X⁺ − X⁻. Uniqueness: if Y, Y′ both work, G = {Y > Y′} ∈ 𝒢,
    so E[(Y − Y′)𝟙_G] = 0 with a non-negative integrand; hence P(G) = 0,
    and symmetrically, Y = Y′ a.s. (b) L²(𝒢) is a closed subspace of
    L²(ℱ) (a limit in L² of 𝒢-measurable functions has a 𝒢-measurable
    a.s. limit along a subsequence). Let Y be the orthogonal projection
    of X. Then E[(X − Y)Z] = 0 for all Z ∈ L²(𝒢); taking Z = 𝟙_G gives
    the defining identity, so Y = E[X | 𝒢], and Pythagoras gives E(X −
    Z)² = E(X − Y)² + E(Y − Z)² ≥ E(X − Y)². (c) TOWER (ℋ ⊆ 𝒢): for H ∈
    ℋ ⊆ 𝒢, E[E[X | 𝒢]𝟙_H] = E[X𝟙_H], so E[X | 𝒢] and X have the same
    conditional expectation given ℋ. KNOWN FACTOR: for Z = 𝟙_A, A ∈ 𝒢,
    and G ∈ 𝒢: E[𝟙_A E[X | 𝒢]𝟙_G] = E[E[X | 𝒢]𝟙_{A∩G}] = E[X𝟙_{A∩G}] =
    E[(𝟙_A X)𝟙_G]; extend to simple Z by linearity, bounded Z by DCT.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that uniqueness is only a.s.; using the
    tower property in the wrong direction (E[E[X | ℋ] | 𝒢] = E[X | ℋ]
    trivially, since E[X | ℋ] is already 𝒢-measurable). Now you try: show
    E[X | 𝒢] = EX when X is independent of 𝒢. (E[X𝟙_G] = EX · P(G))

D3. (a) (X, Y) has density f(x, y) = x + y on [0, 1]². Find E[Y | X] and
    check E[E[Y | X]] = EY. (b) (X, Y) is Gaussian with EX = EY = 0,
    Var X = 4, Var Y = 9, Cov(X, Y) = 3. Find E[Y | X] and Var(Y | X).
    (c) Let X, Y be i.i.d. U[0, 1] and M = max(X, Y). Find E[X | M].
    Answer: (a) (3X + 2)/(6X + 3); EY = 7/12. (b) (3/4)X, 27/4.
    (c) 3M/4.
    Teacher explains: (a) The marginal of X is f_X(x) = ∫₀¹(x + y) dy =
    x + ½, and ∫₀¹ y(x + y) dy = x/2 + 1/3. So
       E[Y | X = x] = (x/2 + 1/3)/(x + 1/2) = (3x + 2)/(6x + 3).
    Check: E h(X) = ∫₀¹ ((x/2 + 1/3)/(x + ½))(x + ½) dx = ∫₀¹(x/2 + 1/3) dx
    = 1/4 + 1/3 = 7/12, and EY = ∫₀¹ y(y + ½) dy = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12 ✓.
    (b) Put Y = aX + W with W = Y − aX; choose a so Cov(X, W) = 0: a =
    3/4. For jointly Gaussian vectors, uncorrelated means INDEPENDENT, so
    E[Y | X] = aX + EW = (3/4)X and Var(Y | X) = Var W = 9 − (3/4)²·4 =
    9 − 9/4 = 27/4, a constant. (c) Given M = m, either X is the max
    (probability ½, X = m) or Y is (X uniform on [0, m]). So E[X | M] =
    ½M + ½(M/2) = 3M/4. Check: EM = 2/3 and E(3M/4) = 1/2 = EX ✓.
    Common mistakes: forgetting to divide by the marginal density; in
    (b), using Cov/Var Y instead of Cov/Var X; in (c), treating X as
    uniform on [0, M] without the atom at M. Now you try: X, Y i.i.d.
    Exp(1); find E[X | X + Y]. ((X + Y)/2)

D4. Let ξ₁, ξ₂, ... be i.i.d. with P(ξ = 1) = P(ξ = −1) = ½, Sₙ = ξ₁ +
    ... + ξₙ, ℱₙ = σ(ξ₁, ..., ξₙ). Show that (a) Sₙ, (b) Sₙ² − n,
    (c) e^{θSₙ}/(cosh θ)ⁿ are martingales, and (d) Sₙ² is a
    submartingale; give its Doob decomposition. (e) A Pólya urn starts
    with one red and one blue ball; each draw returns the ball with one
    more of the same colour. Show the red proportion Rₙ is a martingale.
    Answer: in each case compute E[· | ℱₙ] using that ξₙ₊₁ ⫫ ℱₙ;
    Sₙ² = (Sₙ² − n) + n.
    Teacher explains: The recipe: write Mₙ₊₁ in terms of ℱₙ-measurable
    quantities and ξₙ₊₁, take out what is known, use independence.
    (a) E[Sₙ + ξₙ₊₁ | ℱₙ] = Sₙ + Eξ = Sₙ. (b) (Sₙ + ξ)² = Sₙ² + 2Sₙξ + 1,
    so E[Sₙ₊₁² − (n + 1) | ℱₙ] = Sₙ² + 2Sₙ · 0 + 1 − n − 1 = Sₙ² − n.
    (c) E[e^{θ(Sₙ+ξ)} | ℱₙ] = e^{θSₙ}E e^{θξ} = e^{θSₙ}cosh θ; divide by
    (cosh θ)ⁿ⁺¹. (d) By (b), Sₙ² = Mₙ + Aₙ with Mₙ = Sₙ² − n a martingale
    and Aₙ = n predictable increasing: that IS the Doob decomposition.
    Integrability: |Sₙ| ≤ n, so all moments are finite. (e) After n draws
    there are n + 2 balls, of which r = Rₙ(n + 2) are red. The next draw
    is red with probability Rₙ, giving (r + 1)/(n + 3); otherwise r/(n +
    3). So E[Rₙ₊₁ | ℱₙ] = (Rₙ(r + 1) + (1 − Rₙ)r)/(n + 3) = (r + Rₙ)/(n +
    3) = Rₙ(n + 3)/(n + 3) = Rₙ ✓. Common mistakes: forgetting to check
    E|Mₙ| < ∞; conditioning on the wrong σ-algebra (Rₙ is adapted to the
    draws, not to the number of balls alone). Now you try: show Sₙ³ −
    3nSₙ is a martingale. (expand (Sₙ + ξ)³; Eξ² = 1, Eξ³ = 0)

D5. (a) State the optional stopping theorem. (b) A symmetric walk starts
    at 0 and stops at τ, the first hit of b > 0 or −a < 0. Find P(S_τ = b)
    and Eτ. (c) A gambler with 2 units bets 1 unit each time, winning with
    probability p = 0.4, until he has 5 or 0. Find the probability he
    reaches 5 and the expected duration. (d) Show that optional stopping
    fails for τ = inf{n : Sₙ = 1}.
    Answer: (b) a/(a + b), Eτ = ab. (c) 40/211 ≈ 0.18957, 1110/211 ≈
    5.26066. (d) E S_τ = 1 ≠ 0 = S₀.
    Teacher explains: (a) If M is a martingale and τ a stopping time,
    E M_τ = E M₀ provided τ is bounded, or M_{τ∧n} is dominated by an
    integrable variable (e.g. bounded), or Eτ < ∞ with bounded increments.
    Always prove P(τ < ∞) = 1 first. (b) |S_{τ∧n}| ≤ max(a, b), so OST
    applies to Sₙ: 0 = bP + (−a)(1 − P) ⇒ P = a/(a + b). Now Sₙ² − n:
    E S²_{τ∧n} = E(τ ∧ n); let n → ∞ (bounded convergence on the left,
    MCT on the right): Eτ = b²P + a²(1 − P) = (b²a + a²b)/(a + b) = ab.
    (c) Here q = 0.6 and the martingale is r^{Sₙ} with r = q/p = 3/2
    (E r^ξ = p·r + q/r = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1). Start 2, absorb at 0, 5:
       r² = P·r⁵ + (1 − P)·1 ⇒ P = (r² − 1)/(r⁵ − 1) = (5/4)/(211/32)
         = 40/211 ≈ 0.18957.
    For the duration use Sₙ − n(p − q) = Sₙ + 0.2n: E S_τ + 0.2Eτ = 2, and
    E S_τ = 5 · 40/211 = 200/211, so Eτ = (2 − 200/211)/0.2 = 1110/211
    ≈ 5.26066. (d) The symmetric walk is recurrent, so τ < ∞ a.s. and
    S_τ = 1. But Eτ = ∞ and S_{τ∧n} is not bounded below, so none of the
    hypotheses holds — the "doubling strategy" paradox. Common mistakes:
    using the symmetric formula a/(a + b) for a biased walk; forgetting
    to justify n → ∞. Now you try: in (b) with a = 3, b = 7, find Eτ and
    P(S_τ = −3). (21, 7/10)

D6. (a) State and prove Doob's maximal inequality for a non-negative
    submartingale. (b) Deduce Kolmogorov's inequality. (c) For simple
    random walk, bound P(max_{k≤100}|S_k| ≥ 30) and E max_{k≤100} S_k².
    Answer: (a) λP(max_{k≤n} X_k ≥ λ) ≤ E[Xₙ; max ≥ λ] ≤ E Xₙ.
    (c) ≤ 1/9; ≤ 400.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let τ = min{k ≤ n : X_k ≥ λ} (τ = n if none) and
    A = {max_{k≤n} X_k ≥ λ} = {X_τ ≥ λ}. On A, X_τ ≥ λ; so
       λP(A) ≤ E[X_τ; A] = ∑_{k≤n} E[X_k; τ = k] ≤ ∑_{k≤n} E[Xₙ; τ = k]
             = E[Xₙ; A] ≤ E Xₙ,
    where E[X_k; τ = k] ≤ E[Xₙ; τ = k] because {τ = k} ∈ ℱ_k and
    E[Xₙ | ℱ_k] ≥ X_k. (b) If Sₙ is a sum of independent mean-0 L²
    variables, Sₙ² is a non-negative submartingale (Jensen), so P(max
    |S_k| ≥ λ) = P(max S_k² ≥ λ²) ≤ E Sₙ²/λ² = Var Sₙ/λ². (c) E S₁₀₀² =
    100, so P(max|S_k| ≥ 30) ≤ 100/900 = 1/9. Doob's L² inequality: E max
    S_k² ≤ (2/(2 − 1))² E S₁₀₀² = 4 · 100 = 400. Compare Chebyshev for
    the single time 100: the MAXIMUM costs nothing extra in (b). The
    proof pattern (stop at the first time the event happens) is worth
    memorising. Common mistakes: applying the maximal inequality to a
    submartingale that takes negative values (use |M| or M² or M⁺);
    thinking Doob's L¹ version (p = 1) holds — it fails without an
    L log L condition. Now you try: a non-negative martingale with M₀ = 1;
    bound P(sup_n Mₙ ≥ 10). (1/10, letting n → ∞)

D7. (a) State Doob's martingale convergence theorem and sketch the
    upcrossing proof. (b) Let Mₙ = ξ₁⋯ξₙ with ξᵢ i.i.d., P(ξ = 0) =
    P(ξ = 2) = ½. Show Mₙ → 0 a.s. but not in L¹. (c) Same with ξ = ½ or
    3/2. (d) Find the limit law of the Pólya urn proportion of D4(e).
    Answer: (a) L¹-bounded (sub)martingales converge a.s.; (b) Mₙ = 0 as
    soon as one ξᵢ = 0, but E Mₙ = 1; (c) → 0 a.s. since E ln ξ =
    ½ln(3/4) ≈ −0.14384 < 0; (d) Uniform[0, 1].
    Teacher explains: (a) THEOREM: if (Xₙ) is a submartingale with sup E Xₙ⁺
    < ∞, then Xₙ → X∞ a.s. and E|X∞| < ∞. Proof idea: fix rationals a < b
    and let Uₙ be the number of upcrossings of [a, b] by X₀, ..., Xₙ. Bet
    one unit whenever the path has gone below a, until it exceeds b: the
    gains form a martingale transform, and each completed upcrossing
    earns ≥ b − a, giving (b − a)E Uₙ ≤ E(Xₙ − a)⁺ ≤ sup E Xₙ⁺ + |a|. By
    MCT, U∞ < ∞ a.s. If Xₙ did not converge, lim inf < a < b < lim sup
    for some rationals, forcing U∞ = ∞; countably many pairs (a, b), so
    Xₙ converges a.s.; Fatou gives E|X∞| ≤ lim inf E|Xₙ| < ∞.
    (b) E[Mₙ₊₁ | ℱₙ] = Mₙ Eξ = Mₙ; Mₙ ≥ 0 so E|Mₙ| = 1 (L¹-bounded).
    P(Mₙ ≠ 0) = 2⁻ⁿ → 0, so Mₙ → 0 a.s. But E|Mₙ − 0| = 1 ↛ 0: the
    martingale is NOT uniformly integrable (all the mass sits on an event
    of probability 2⁻ⁿ with value 2ⁿ). (c) ln Mₙ = ∑ ln ξᵢ, and by the
    SLLN (ln Mₙ)/n → E ln ξ = ½(ln ½ + ln 3/2) = ½ln(3/4) < 0, so ln Mₙ →
    −∞ and Mₙ → 0 a.s. although E Mₙ = 1. (d) Rₙ ∈ [0, 1] is a bounded
    martingale, hence converges a.s. AND in L¹ to R∞. One checks by
    induction that after n draws the number of added red balls is
    uniform on {0, 1, ..., n}; so Rₙ = (k + 1)/(n + 2) with probability
    1/(n + 1) each, which converges weakly to U[0, 1]. So R∞ ~ U[0, 1] and
    E R∞ = ½ = R₀ (UI!). Common mistakes: "a.s. convergence + martingale
    ⇒ E M∞ = E M₀" (false: (b)); forgetting that non-negative
    martingales are automatically L¹-bounded. Now you try: start the urn
    with 2 red and 1 blue; find P(R∞ > ½). (R∞ ~ Beta(2, 1): 3/4)

D8. Define standard Brownian motion. (a) Show it is the centred Gaussian
    process with Cov(B_s, B_t) = min(s, t). (b) Compute Var(B₁ + B₂ + B₃)
    and E[B₁²B₂²]. (c) Show P(B₁ > 0, B₂ > 0) = 3/8. (d) Prove that
    W_t = tB_{1/t} (W₀ = 0) and c^{−1/2}B_{ct} are Brownian motions.
    Answer: (b) 14 and 4. (c) 1/4 + arcsin(1/√2)/(2π) = 3/8. (d) same
    covariance min(s, t); continuity of W at 0 from B_t/t → 0.
    Teacher explains: DEFINITION: B₀ = 0; for 0 ≤ t₁ < ... < tₖ the
    increments B_{t₂} − B_{t₁}, ..., B_{tₖ} − B_{tₖ₋₁} are independent;
    B_t − B_s ~ N(0, t − s); t ↦ B_t is continuous a.s. (a) Any finite
    vector (B_{t₁}, ..., B_{tₖ}) is a linear image of independent Gaussian
    increments, hence Gaussian. For s ≤ t, Cov(B_s, B_t) = Cov(B_s, B_s
    + (B_t − B_s)) = Var B_s = s. Conversely a Gaussian process with this
    covariance has uncorrelated, hence independent, increments.
    (b) Var(∑B_{tᵢ}) = ∑ᵢ∑ⱼ min(tᵢ, tⱼ) = (1 + 2 + 3) + 2(1 + 1 + 2) = 14.
    Write B₂ = B₁ + Y, Y ⫫ B₁, Y ~ N(0, 1): E[B₁²(B₁ + Y)²] = E B₁⁴ +
    2E[B₁³]E Y + E B₁² E Y² = 3 + 0 + 1 = 4. (c) (B₁, B₂/√2) is a standard
    bivariate normal with correlation ρ = 1/√2. For such a pair, P(X > 0,
    Y > 0) = 1/4 + arcsin(ρ)/(2π) (rotate to independent coordinates:
    the quadrant becomes a wedge of angle π/2 + arcsin ρ). With arcsin
    (1/√2) = π/4: 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8. (d) Both are centred Gaussian. For W:
    Cov(W_s, W_t) = st·min(1/s, 1/t) = st/t = s for s ≤ t. Continuity for
    t > 0 is clear; at 0, W_t = B_u/u with u = 1/t → ∞, and B_u/u → 0
    a.s. by the SLLN for B_n (plus a bound on oscillation between
    integers). For scaling: Cov = c⁻¹ min(cs, ct) = min(s, t). Common
    mistakes: writing Cov(B_s, B_t) = st or = |t − s|; forgetting to check
    path continuity in (d). Now you try: Var(B₁ − 2B₃ + B₄)? (1 + 12 + 4
    + 2(−2 + 1 − 6) = 3)

D9. (a) Show that B_t² − t and exp(θB_t − θ²t/2) are martingales.
    (b) For τ = exit time of (−a, b), prove P(B_τ = b) = a/(a + b) and
    Eτ = ab. (c) For T_a = inf{t : B_t = a}, a > 0, show E e^{−λT_a} =
    e^{−a√(2λ)}; deduce P(T_a < ∞) = 1 and E T_a = ∞. (d) With drift,
    X_t = B_t + μt, μ > 0, find P(X ever reaches −a). Evaluate for μ = 1,
    a = 2.
    Answer: (c) E e^{−T₁/2} = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.36788. (d) e^{−2μa}; e⁻⁴ ≈
    0.01832.
    Teacher explains: (a) For s < t write B_t = B_s + Y, Y ⫫ ℱ_s, Y ~
    N(0, t − s). E[B_t² | ℱ_s] = B_s² + 2B_s·0 + (t − s), so E[B_t² − t |
    ℱ_s] = B_s² − s. E[e^{θB_t} | ℱ_s] = e^{θB_s}E e^{θY} = e^{θB_s}
    e^{θ²(t−s)/2}; rearrange. (b) As in D5, now in continuous time:
    |B_{τ∧t}| ≤ max(a, b) and τ < ∞ a.s., so 0 = bP − a(1 − P), and from
    E B²_{τ∧t} = E(τ ∧ t) with t → ∞, Eτ = b²·a/(a + b) + a²·b/(a + b) =
    ab. (c) Take θ = √(2λ) and M_t = exp(θB_t − λt). Up to T_a, B_t ≤ a,
    so 0 ≤ M_{t∧T_a} ≤ e^{θa}: bounded. On {T_a < ∞}, M_{T_a} = e^{θa −
    λT_a}; on {T_a = ∞}, M_t ≤ e^{θa − λt} → 0. Bounded convergence:
       1 = E M₀ = e^{θa} E[e^{−λT_a}𝟙_{T_a<∞}] ⇒ E e^{−λT_a} = e^{−a√(2λ)}.
    Let λ ↓ 0: P(T_a < ∞) = e⁰ = 1. The derivative d/dλ e^{−a√(2λ)} =
    −(a/√(2λ))e^{−a√(2λ)} → −∞ as λ ↓ 0, so E T_a = ∞. With a = 1, λ =
    1/2: e⁻¹. (d) exp(θX_t) is a martingale iff θμ + θ²/2 = 0: θ = −2μ.
    Stop at hitting −a or b: e^{2μa}P + e^{−2μb}(1 − P) = 1, so P = (1 −
    e^{−2μb})/(e^{2μa} − e^{−2μb}) → e^{−2μa} as b → ∞. With μ = 1, a = 2:
    e⁻⁴ ≈ 0.01832. Common mistakes: applying OST to e^{θB_t} without the
    compensator; using θ = −√(2λ) (then M is unbounded before T_a).
    Now you try: E τ² for the exit time of (−a, a), using the martingale
    B_t⁴ − 6tB_t² + 3t². (5a⁴/3)

D10. (a) State and prove the reflection principle and deduce the law of
     M_t = max_{s≤t} B_s. (b) Compute P(M₁ ≥ 1), the density of T_a and
     the median of T₁. (c) Show ∑_{k=1}^{n} (B_{kt/n} − B_{(k−1)t/n})² → t
     in L², and deduce that Brownian paths have infinite variation.
     Answer: (a) P(M_t ≥ a) = 2P(B_t ≥ a), M_t ~ |B_t|.
     (b) 2(1 − Φ(1)) ≈ 0.31731; a(2πt³)^{−1/2}e^{−a²/(2t)}; ≈ 2.19811.
     (c) the sum has mean t and variance 2t²/n.
     Teacher explains: (a) By the strong Markov property at T_a, (B_{T_a+s}
     − a)_{s≥0} is a Brownian motion independent of ℱ_{T_a}, so it is
     equally likely to be above or below 0 at the remaining time t − T_a:
        P(M_t ≥ a, B_t < a) = P(M_t ≥ a, B_t > a) = P(B_t > a)
     (the last because B_t > a forces M_t ≥ a). Adding, P(M_t ≥ a) =
     2P(B_t ≥ a) = P(|B_t| ≥ a). (b) P(M₁ ≥ 1) = 2(1 − Φ(1)) = 0.31731.
     Since {T_a ≤ t} = {M_t ≥ a}, P(T_a ≤ t) = 2(1 − Φ(a/√t)); differentiate
     in t: f(t) = 2φ(a/√t)·a/(2t^{3/2}) = a(2πt³)^{−1/2}e^{−a²/(2t)}. The
     density decays like t^{−3/2}, so E T_a = ∞ (consistent with D9).
     Median: 2(1 − Φ(1/√t)) = ½ ⇒ 1/√t = Φ⁻¹(3/4) = 0.67449 ⇒ t ≈ 2.19811.
     (c) Let Δₖ be the increments: independent N(0, t/n). So E∑Δₖ² = t
     and Var ∑Δₖ² = n·2(t/n)² = 2t²/n → 0 (Var(Z²) = 2 for Z ~ N(0, 1)).
     Hence Qₙ → t in L². If the path had finite variation V, then Qₙ ≤
     max|Δₖ| · V → 0 by uniform continuity — contradicting Qₙ → t > 0
     (along an a.s. convergent subsequence). Common mistakes: forgetting
     the factor 2 in the reflection principle; "reflecting" at a
     deterministic time instead of a stopping time. Now you try:
     P(M₁ ≥ 1, B₁ ≤ 0)? (reflect: P(B₁ ≥ 2) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.02275)

D11. (a) Define convergence in distribution and prove that, on R, it is
     equivalent to Fₙ(x) → F(x) at continuity points of F. (b) Find the
     limits in distribution of n·min(U₁, ..., Uₙ) (Uᵢ i.i.d. U[0, 1]) and
     of max(E₁, ..., Eₙ) − ln n (Eᵢ i.i.d. Exp(1)). (c) Let Xₙ = n with
     probability 1/n and 0 otherwise: find the weak limit and compare
     E Xₙ. (d) State Slutsky's theorem and apply it to the t-statistic.
     Answer: (b) Exp(1); Gumbel F(x) = exp(−e^{−x}). (c) δ₀, but E Xₙ = 1.
     (d) √n(X̄ − μ)/Sₙ ⇒ N(0, 1).
     Teacher explains: (a) Xₙ ⇒ X means E f(Xₙ) → E f(X) for all bounded
     continuous f. (⇒) Given x with P(X = x) = 0 and ε > 0, take f ≤ 𝟙_{(−∞,
     x]} ≤ g continuous, with f = 1 on (−∞, x − ε], g = 0 on [x + ε, ∞).
     Then F(x − ε) ≤ E f(X) = lim E f(Xₙ) ≤ lim inf Fₙ(x) ≤ lim sup Fₙ(x)
     ≤ lim E g(Xₙ) = E g(X) ≤ F(x + ε); let ε → 0 using continuity at x.
     (⇐) Build Yₙ = Fₙ⁻¹(U), Y = F⁻¹(U) on one space (Skorokhod): Yₙ → Y
     a.s., then use bounded convergence. (b) P(n min > x) = (1 − x/n)ⁿ →
     e^{−x}: Exp(1). P(max − ln n ≤ x) = (1 − e^{−x}/n)ⁿ → exp(−e^{−x}).
     (c) Fₙ(x) = 1 − 1/n → 1 for 0 ≤ x < n, so Xₙ ⇒ δ₀; yet E Xₙ = 1 ↛ 0:
     the sequence is not UI (the mass n · 1/n "escapes to infinity").
     (d) SLUTSKY: Xₙ ⇒ X and Yₙ → c in probability (c constant) ⇒ Xₙ + Yₙ
     ⇒ X + c, XₙYₙ ⇒ cX, Xₙ/Yₙ ⇒ X/c (c ≠ 0). By the CLT √n(X̄ − μ)/σ ⇒
     N(0, 1), and σ/Sₙ → 1 in probability (SLLN), so the product ⇒
     N(0, 1). Common mistakes: requiring convergence at EVERY x (fails for
     δ_{1/n} ⇒ δ₀ at x = 0); applying Slutsky when Yₙ converges only in
     distribution to a NON-constant. Now you try: n(1 − max Uᵢ)?
     (Exp(1))

D12. (a) Compute the characteristic function of N(0, 1) and of Poisson(λ).
     (b) Prove the CLT for i.i.d. variables with finite variance using
     Lévy's continuity theorem. (c) Show Bin(n, λ/n) ⇒ Poisson(λ).
     (d) Estimate P(S ≥ 60) for S = number of heads in 100 fair tosses.
     (e) Show e^{−n}∑_{k=0}^{n} nᵏ/k! → ½.
     Answer: (a) e^{−t²/2}, e^{λ(e^{it}−1)}. (b) φ(t/√n)ⁿ → e^{−t²/2}.
     (c) (1 + λ(e^{it} − 1)/n)ⁿ → e^{λ(e^{it}−1)}. (d) ≈ 0.02872 (exact
     0.02844). (e) CLT for Poisson(n).
     Teacher explains: (a) φ(t) = ∫e^{itx}e^{−x²/2}dx/√(2π). Differentiate
     under the integral (|ix e^{−x²/2}| is integrable) and integrate by
     parts: φ′(t) = −tφ(t), φ(0) = 1, so φ(t) = e^{−t²/2}. Poisson:
     ∑e^{−λ}λᵏe^{itk}/k! = e^{−λ}e^{λe^{it}}. (b) WLOG μ = 0, σ = 1.
     Since EX² < ∞, φ(u) = 1 − u²/2 + o(u²) as u → 0. Then
        φ_{Sₙ/√n}(t) = φ(t/√n)ⁿ = (1 − t²/(2n) + o(1/n))ⁿ → e^{−t²/2},
     (use |aⁿ − bⁿ| ≤ n|a − b| for |a|, |b| ≤ 1). The limit is the ch.f. of
     N(0, 1), continuous at 0, so by Lévy Sₙ/√n ⇒ N(0, 1). (c) The ch.f.
     of Bin(n, p) is (1 − p + pe^{it})ⁿ = (1 + λ(e^{it} − 1)/n)ⁿ →
     exp(λ(e^{it} − 1)). (d) ES = 50, sd = 5. With continuity correction,
     P(S ≥ 59.5) ≈ 1 − Φ(9.5/5) = 1 − Φ(1.9) = 0.02872; the exact binomial
     tail is 0.02844. (e) If Xₙ ~ Poisson(n) = sum of n i.i.d. Poisson(1),
     the sum equals P(Xₙ ≤ n) = P((Xₙ − n)/√n ≤ 0) → Φ(0) = ½. Common
     mistakes: expanding φ to second order without E X² < ∞; forgetting
     that Lévy needs continuity of the limit AT 0 (N(0, n) has φₙ → 𝟙_{t=0},
     no weak limit). Now you try: the ch.f. of Exp(1) and from it E X³.
     (1/(1 − it); φ‴(0) = 6i³ ⇒ E X³ = 6)

    g) (1/n)·Geometric(λ/n) (on {1, 2, ...})
    h) n·min(U₁, ..., Uₙ), Uᵢ i.i.d. U[0, 1]
    i) max(E₁, ..., Eₙ) − ln n, Eᵢ i.i.d. Exp(1)
    j) n(1 − max(U₁, ..., Uₙ))           k) Student's t with n d.f.
    l) (χ²ₙ − n)/√(2n)                   m) density 1 + sin(2πnx) on [0, 1]
    n) max(C₁, ..., Cₙ)/n, Cᵢ i.i.d. standard Cauchy
    o) XₙYₙ + Yₙ where Xₙ ⇒ N(0, 1) and Yₙ → 2 in probability
    p) Xₙ = n with probability 1/n, else 0: the limit, and lim E Xₙ
    q) (Poisson(n) − n)/√n
    r) √n(Ū − ½)·√12, Ū the mean of n i.i.d. U[0, 1]
    s) Sₙ/n for i.i.d. Cauchy Cᵢ
    Answers:
      a) δ₀       b) δ₀       c) none (not tight: mass escapes to ∞)
      d) none (Fₙ(x) → ½ for every x; not a distribution function)
      e) U[0, 1]  f) Poisson(3)           g) Exp(λ)
      h) Exp(1)   i) Gumbel, F(x) = exp(−e^{−x})
      j) Exp(1)   k) N(0, 1)              l) N(0, 1)
      m) U[0, 1] (∫f·(1 + sin 2πnx) → ∫f by Riemann-Lebesgue, although the
         densities do not converge)
      n) Fréchet: P(limit ≤ x) = exp(−1/(πx)), x > 0
      o) N(2, 4)  p) δ₀; E Xₙ = 1 for all n (not UI)
      q) N(0, 1)  r) N(0, 1)
      s) standard Cauchy (it is Cauchy for every n: no LLN)

M9. Characteristic functions: compute φ(t) = E e^{itX}, or identify the

    a) Bernoulli(p)                      b) Bin(n, p)

M10. Moments, inversion, and "is it a characteristic function?"
