M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) E[E[X | 𝒢]] = EX for X ∈ L¹.
     b) If X ⫫ 𝒢 then E[X | 𝒢] = EX.
     c) If E[X | Y] = EX then X and Y are independent.
     d) E[X | 𝒢] = E[X | ℋ] a.s. whenever σ-algebras 𝒢 ⊆ ℋ.
     e) Every L¹-bounded martingale converges in L¹.
     f) Every UI martingale converges a.s. and in L¹.
     g) E M_τ = E M₀ for every martingale and a.s. finite stopping time τ.
     h) The last time before 10 that a random walk visits 0 is a
        stopping time.
     i) Brownian motion is a.s. differentiable at t = 0.
     j) Brownian paths have finite total variation on [0, 1].
     k) B_t² is a martingale.
     l) Convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability.
     m) Xₙ ⇒ X and Yₙ ⇒ Y imply Xₙ + Yₙ ⇒ X + Y.
     n) A pointwise limit of characteristic functions is a ch.f.
     o) If φₙ → φ pointwise and φ is a ch.f., then μₙ ⇒ μ.
     p) If φ_X is real-valued then X is symmetric.
     q) If φ_X is differentiable at 0 then E|X| < ∞.
     r) Xₙ ⇒ X implies E Xₙ → EX.
     s) Every tight sequence of laws on R has a weakly convergent
        subsequence.
     t) Xₙ ⇒ c (a constant) implies Xₙ → c in probability.
     Answers:
       a) T        b) T
       c) F: Z ~ N(0, 1), X = Z, Y = Z²: E[X | Y] = 0 = EX, yet X and Y
          are dependent
       d) F: 𝒢 trivial, ℋ = ℱ gives EX versus X (the tower property
          only says E[E[X | ℋ] | 𝒢] = E[X | 𝒢])
       e) F: ∏ξᵢ with ξ ∈ {0, 2}      f) T
       g) F: simple random walk stopped at the first hit of 1
       h) F: deciding it requires the future path
       i) F: B_t/t = W_{1/t} with W = time inversion, a BM, and
          lim sup_{u→∞} W_u = +∞
       j) F (quadratic variation 1 forces infinite variation)
       k) F: E[B_t² | ℱ_s] = B_s² + t − s; B_t² − t is
       l) F: X ~ N(0, 1), Xₙ = −X for all n: Xₙ ⇒ X but |Xₙ − X| = 2|X|
       m) F: Xₙ = Z, Yₙ = −Z, Y = Z (sum 0, not 2Z)
       n) F: e^{−nt²/2} → 𝟙_{t=0} (N(0, n))
       o) T (Lévy)     p) T (φ_{−X} = conj φ_X = φ_X)
       q) F: symmetric X with P(|X| > x) ~ 1/(x ln x) (only the converse
          direction holds)
       r) F: Xₙ = n w.p. 1/n (M8 p))     s) T (Helly-Prokhorov)
       t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: teach conditional expectation first on FINITE partitions
  ("average over the block you are in"), and insist that E[X | 𝒢] is a
  random variable; then treat the general definition as the same idea
  with blocks replaced by events of 𝒢. For martingales, drill the one-line
  check E[Mₙ₊₁ | ℱₙ] = Mₙ by writing Mₙ₊₁ via Mₙ and the new independent
  step. Before every optional stopping argument, have the student WRITE
  which hypothesis (bounded τ, bounded stopped process, Eτ < ∞ with
  bounded increments) holds, and keep the doubling-strategy walk as the
  warning example. For Brownian motion, reduce everything to Gaussian
  vectors with covariance min(s, t), and draw the reflected path. For
  weak convergence, always compute Fₙ(x) or φₙ(t) explicitly; keep δ_n
  (not tight), N(0, n) (limit not continuous at 0) and "n w.p. 1/n"
  (means do not converge) as the three standard pathologies. Harder:
  construct Brownian motion by the Lévy-Ciesielski (Haar/Schauder)
  series and prove Kolmogorov's continuity criterion; prove the strong
  Markov property and the full reflection principle for the joint law
  of (M_t, B_t); prove nowhere differentiability (Paley-Wiener-Zygmund)
  and the law of the iterated logarithm; prove Lindeberg-Feller and the
  Berry-Esseen bound; prove Prokhorov's theorem and Donsker's invariance
  principle; establish the martingale central limit theorem and
  Azuma-Hoeffding; and study backward martingales to prove the SLLN and
  de Finetti's theorem.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.13 — PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS (GRADUATE): SOBOLEV SPACES,
ELLIPTIC REGULARITY, WEAK SOLUTIONS, PARABOLIC AND HYPERBOLIC EQUATIONS,
VARIATIONAL METHODS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - WEAK DERIVATIVES: for u, v ∈ L¹_loc(Ω), v = ∂ᵅu weakly if ∫u ∂ᵅφ =
    (−1)^|α| ∫vφ for every φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω). Weak derivatives are unique a.e.
    and agree with classical ones for C^|α| functions. Examples: |x|′ =
    sgn x on (−1, 1); the Heaviside function H has NO weak derivative (its
    distributional derivative is δ ∉ L¹_loc). In one variable u ∈ W^{1,1}
    iff u agrees a.e. with an absolutely continuous function (so the
    Cantor function is not weakly differentiable).
  - SOBOLEV SPACES: W^{k,p}(Ω) = {u ∈ Lᵖ : ∂ᵅu ∈ Lᵖ for |α| ≤ k}, norm
    ‖u‖ = (∑_{|α|≤k} ‖∂ᵅu‖ₚᵖ)^{1/p}; a Banach space, reflexive for 1 < p
    < ∞, and Hᵏ = W^{k,2} is a Hilbert space. MEYERS-SERRIN: C^∞ ∩ W^{k,p}
    is dense in W^{k,p}(Ω) (1 ≤ p < ∞). W₀^{k,p}(Ω) = closure of C_c^∞(Ω);
    W₀^{k,p}(Rⁿ) = W^{k,p}(Rⁿ) but H₀¹(Ω) ≠ H¹(Ω) for bounded Ω.
  - POWER-FUNCTION TEST on the unit ball B ⊂ Rⁿ: |x|^(−a) ∈ Lᵖ(B) iff ap <
    n, and ∈ W^{1,p}(B) iff (a + 1)p < n. ln ln(4/|x|) ∈ W^{1,n}(B) is
    UNBOUNDED for n ≥ 2 (W^{1,n} ⊄ L^∞).
  - SOBOLEV EMBEDDINGS: (i) p < n: GAGLIARDO-NIRENBERG-SOBOLEV ‖u‖_{p*} ≤
    C‖∇u‖ₚ on W^{1,p}(Rⁿ), p* = np/(n − p) (forced by scaling u(λx));
    (ii) p = n: W^{1,n} ⊂ L^q for all q < ∞; (iii) p > n: MORREY W^{1,p} ⊂
    C^{0,γ}, γ = 1 − n/p. Iterating: W^{k,p} ⊂ L^q with 1/q = 1/p − k/n
    if kp < n, and Hᵏ(Rⁿ) ⊂ C⁰ if k > n/2. On bounded Lipschitz Ω the same
    holds, and RELLICH-KONDRACHOV makes W^{1,p} ⊂ L^q COMPACT for q < p*
    (not at q = p*, and never on all of Rⁿ: translations).
  - TRACES AND POINCARÉ: for bounded C¹ (or Lipschitz) Ω the TRACE map T :
    W^{1,p}(Ω) → Lᵖ(∂Ω) is bounded, Tu = u|∂Ω for continuous u, and ker T
    = W₀^{1,p}(Ω). POINCARÉ: ‖u‖ₚ ≤ C‖∇u‖ₚ on W₀^{1,p}(Ω), Ω bounded; on
    (0, L) with p = 2 the best constant is L/π. Poincaré-Wirtinger: ‖u −
    ū‖ₚ ≤ C‖∇u‖ₚ on W^{1,p}(Ω), Ω connected Lipschitz.
  - FRACTIONAL SPACES VIA FOURIER: Hˢ(Rⁿ) = {u : (1 + |ξ|²)^{s/2}û ∈ L²},
    ‖u‖²_{Hˢ} = (2π)⁻ⁿ∫(1 + |ξ|²)ˢ|û|² dξ. Hˢ ⊂ C_b for s > n/2; δ ∈ Hˢ iff
    s < −n/2; 𝟙_[−1,1] ∈ Hˢ(R) iff s < 1/2. H⁻¹(Ω) = (H₀¹(Ω))′.
  - WEAK SOLUTIONS OF ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS: for Lu = −∂ᵢ(aᵢⱼ∂ⱼu) + bᵢ∂ᵢu +
    cu, UNIFORMLY ELLIPTIC (aᵢⱼξᵢξⱼ ≥ θ|ξ|², θ > 0) with bounded
    coefficients, u ∈ H₀¹(Ω) is a weak solution of Lu = f, u = 0 on ∂Ω,
    if B[u, v] = ∫(aᵢⱼ∂ⱼu∂ᵢv + bᵢ∂ᵢu v + cuv) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v ∈
    H₀¹. Neumann conditions are NATURAL (built into the form on H¹);
    Dirichlet conditions are ESSENTIAL (built into the space).
  - LAX-MILGRAM: B bounded (|B[u, v]| ≤ M‖u‖‖v‖) and COERCIVE (B[u, u] ≥
    α‖u‖²) on a Hilbert space H ⇒ for every f ∈ H′ a unique u with B[u, v]
    = f(v) ∀v, and ‖u‖ ≤ ‖f‖/α. Symmetry is NOT needed (symmetric case =
    Riesz). GÅRDING: B[u, u] ≥ (θ/2)‖∇u‖² − γ‖u‖², so B + γ is coercive.
  - FREDHOLM ALTERNATIVE AND SPECTRUM: since H₀¹ ⊂ L² is compact, either
    Lu = f has a unique weak solution for every f, or Lu = 0 has non-zero
    solutions, and then Lu = f is solvable iff f ⊥ ker L* (finite-
    dimensional). The Dirichlet Laplacian has eigenvalues 0 < λ₁ < λ₂ ≤
    ... → ∞ with an L²-orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions; λ₁ = min ∫|∇u|²
    /∫u² (RAYLEIGH), simple, eigenfunction of one sign. On (0, L): λₖ =
    (kπ/L)²; on the square (0, π)²: m² + n².
  - ELLIPTIC REGULARITY: interior: aᵢⱼ ∈ C¹, f ∈ L² ⇒ u ∈ H²_loc with
    ‖u‖_{H²(V)} ≤ C(‖f‖_{L²} + ‖u‖_{L²}) (difference quotients); f ∈ Hᵏ,
    aᵢⱼ ∈ C^{k+1} ⇒ u ∈ H^{k+2}_loc; smooth data ⇒ u ∈ C^∞. Up to the
    boundary if ∂Ω ∈ C²: u ∈ H² ∩ H₀¹, ‖u‖_{H²} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²}. Other scales:
    SCHAUDER f ∈ C^{0,α} ⇒ u ∈ C^{2,α}; CALDERÓN-ZYGMUND f ∈ Lᵖ ⇒ u ∈
    W^{2,p} (1 < p < ∞). FAILURES: f ∈ C⁰ does not give u ∈ C²; at a
    corner of angle ω the solution behaves like r^{π/ω} sin(πθ/ω), not in
    H² when ω > π (L-shaped domain: r^{2/3}). WEYL: weakly harmonic ⇒
    smooth.
  - MAXIMUM PRINCIPLES: weak: Lu ≤ 0 (no zero-order term) in Ω ⇒ max_Ω̄ u
    = max_∂Ω u; strong: an interior maximum forces u constant (Ω
    connected); HOPF boundary lemma. Harmonic functions satisfy the MEAN
    VALUE property. Comparison: −Δu = f with 0 ≤ f ≤ M sandwiches u.
    Classification of au_xx + 2bu_xy + cu_yy: b² − ac < 0 ELLIPTIC, = 0
    PARABOLIC, > 0 HYPERBOLIC.
  - VARIATIONAL METHODS: a minimiser of E(u) = ∫F(x, u, ∇u) satisfies the
    EULER-LAGRANGE equation −div(F_p) + F_u = 0 weakly (Dirichlet
    principle: ∫½|∇u|² − fu ↦ −Δu = f; p-Laplacian; minimal surface).
    DIRECT METHOD: coercive (E(u) ≥ α‖u‖^q − β) + weakly lower semi-
    continuous (F convex in ∇u) on a reflexive space ⇒ minimiser exists.
    Failures: non-convex integrands (Bolza ∫((u′)² − 1)² + u²: inf 0 not
    attained) and non-coercive ones (Weierstrass ∫x²(u′)²). Critical
    points that are not minima: MOUNTAIN PASS (Palais-Smale) for −Δu =
    u³ in bounded Ω ⊂ R³ (subcritical: 3 < 2* − 1 = 5).
  - PARABOLIC (HEAT) EQUATION: u_t − Δu = f. On Rⁿ, u = Φ(·, t) * g with
    HEAT KERNEL Φ(x, t) = (4πt)^(−n/2) e^(−|x|²/(4t)), ∫Φ = 1: infinite
    speed of propagation, instant C^∞ SMOOTHING, maximum principle on the
    parabolic boundary. On a bounded domain: u = ∑ gₖ e^(−λₖt) wₖ and
    ENERGY ESTIMATE d/dt ½‖u‖² = −‖∇u‖² ≤ −λ₁‖u‖², so ‖u(t)‖ ≤ e^(−λ₁t)
    ‖g‖. WEAK SOLUTION: u ∈ L²(0, T; H₀¹), u′ ∈ L²(0, T; H⁻¹) (hence u ∈
    C([0, T]; L²)), ⟨u′, v⟩ + B[u, v] = (f, v); built by GALERKIN
    approximation + energy estimates + weak compactness. The BACKWARD heat
    equation is ILL-POSED (Hadamard).
  - HYPERBOLIC (WAVE) EQUATION: u_tt − c²Δu = 0. D'ALEMBERT (n = 1): u =
    ½(g(x + ct) + g(x − ct)) + (1/(2c))∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct} h; KIRCHHOFF (n = 3),
    POISSON (n = 2, by descent). ENERGY E(t) = ½∫(u_t² + c²|∇u|²) is
    CONSERVED; FINITE SPEED: u(x₀, t₀) depends only on data in B(x₀, ct₀);
    HUYGENS' principle (sharp fronts) in odd n ≥ 3, not in n = 2. No
    smoothing: singularities travel along characteristics x ± ct = const.
    Weak solution: u ∈ L²(0, T; H₀¹), u′ ∈ L²(0, T; L²), u″ ∈ L²(0, T;
    H⁻¹), again by Galerkin.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Show that u(x) = |x| has weak derivative sgn x on (−1, 1).
    (b) Show that the Heaviside function H = 𝟙_(0,1) on (−1, 1) has no
    weak derivative. (c) For which p is u(x) = |x|^{1/2} in W^{1,p}(−1, 1)?
    Answer: (a) integrate by parts on each half; (b) the derivative would
    have to be δ; (c) 1 ≤ p < 2.
    Teacher explains: (a) For φ ∈ C_c^∞(−1, 1), split the integral:
       ∫₋₁¹ |x|φ′ dx = ∫₋₁⁰ (−x)φ′ + ∫₀¹ xφ′
                     = [−xφ]₋₁⁰ + ∫₋₁⁰ φ + [xφ]₀¹ − ∫₀¹ φ
                     = −∫₋₁¹ sgn(x) φ dx,
    because the boundary terms vanish (φ(±1) = 0 and x = 0 at the joint).
    That is exactly the definition ∫uφ′ = −∫vφ with v = sgn x ∈ L^∞, so
    |x| ∈ W^{1,p}(−1, 1) for every p ≤ ∞. (b) Suppose v ∈ L¹_loc with
    ∫Hφ′ = −∫vφ. The left side is ∫₀¹ φ′ = −φ(0). So ∫vφ = φ(0) for all
    φ. Taking φ supported in (0, 1) or in (−1, 0) gives v = 0 a.e. there,
    hence ∫vφ = 0 for every φ, contradicting φ(0) ≠ 0. The distributional
    derivative δ is not a function. (c) The same splitting shows the weak
    derivative is the classical one, v = ½ sgn(x)|x|^{−1/2} (the boundary
    term |x|^{1/2}φ vanishes at 0). ∫|v|ᵖ = 2·2⁻ᵖ∫₀¹ x^{−p/2} dx < ∞ iff
    p/2 < 1. So u ∈ W^{1,p} iff p < 2, although u is continuous. Common
    mistakes: thinking "differentiable a.e." suffices (H′ = 0 a.e., but H
    is not weakly differentiable; the Cantor function is the same trap);
    forgetting to check the boundary term at the singular point. Now you
    try: the weak derivative of max(x, 0) on (−1, 1). (H = 𝟙_(0,1))

D2. Let B be the unit ball in Rⁿ and u(x) = |x|^(−a), a > 0. Prove that u
    ∈ W^{1,p}(B) iff (a + 1)p < n. Decide whether |x|^(−1/2) ∈ H¹(B) for
    n = 3, and show that w = ln ln(4/|x|) ∈ H¹(B) for n = 2 although w is
    unbounded.
    Answer: need ∫_B |x|^(−(a+1)p) < ∞; n = 3, a = ½: (3/2)·2 = 3 ⊀ 3, so
    NOT in H¹; ∫|∇w|² = 2π∫₀¹ dr/(r ln²(4/r)) < ∞.
    Teacher explains: Away from 0, u is smooth with ∇u = −a|x|^(−a−2)x, so
    |∇u| = a|x|^(−a−1). In polar coordinates ∫_B |x|^(−β) dx = ωₙ₋₁∫₀¹
    r^(n−1−β) dr is finite iff β < n. Hence |∇u| ∈ Lᵖ iff (a + 1)p < n,
    and u ∈ Lᵖ iff ap < n (weaker). It remains to show the classical
    gradient is the WEAK one. Cut out B_ε: for φ ∈ C_c^∞(B),
       ∫_{B∖B_ε} u ∂ᵢφ = −∫_{B∖B_ε} ∂ᵢu φ − ∫_{∂B_ε} uφνᵢ dS,
    and |∫_{∂B_ε} uφνᵢ| ≤ ‖φ‖_∞ ε^(−a)·ωₙ₋₁εⁿ⁻¹ → 0 since a < n − 1
    (implied by (a + 1)p < n). Let ε → 0 (DCT, both integrands L¹). For n
    = 3, a = ½, p = 2: (a + 1)p = 3 = n, borderline, so |∇u|² ~ r⁻³ and
    ∫r⁻³r² dr = ∞: NOT in H¹. (|x|^(−1/4) is: 2.5 < 3.) For n = 2: ∇w =
    −x/(|x|² ln(4/|x|)), so |∇w| = 1/(r ln(4/r)) and
       ∫_B |∇w|² = 2π∫₀¹ dr/(r ln²(4/r)) = 2π[1/ln(4/r)]₀¹ = 2π/ln 4,
    finite, and ∫w² < ∞ too; yet w(x) → ∞ as x → 0. So H¹ ⊄ L^∞ in R²:
    the Morrey case needs p > n strictly. Common mistakes: forgetting the
    boundary term (for a ≥ n − 1 it does not vanish); confusing the
    conditions for u and ∇u. Now you try: for which a is |x|^(−a) ∈ H¹ of
    the unit ball in R⁵? (a < 3/2)

D3. (a) Use scaling to show that an inequality ‖u‖_{L^q(Rⁿ)} ≤ C‖∇u‖_{Lᵖ}
    for all u ∈ C_c^∞(Rⁿ) can only hold if q = p* = np/(n − p). (b) State
    the Sobolev, Morrey and Rellich-Kondrachov theorems and apply them to
    H¹ and H² in dimension n = 3.
    Answer: (a) scaling gives λ^{−n/q} = λ^{1−n/p}; (b) H¹(Ω) ⊂ L⁶,
    compactly into L^q for q < 6; H² ⊂ C^{0,1/2}.
    Teacher explains: (a) Put u_λ(x) = u(λx). Then ‖u_λ‖_q = λ^(−n/q)‖u‖_q
    and ∇u_λ = λ(∇u)(λx), so ‖∇u_λ‖ₚ = λ^(1−n/p)‖∇u‖ₚ. The inequality for
    u_λ reads λ^(−n/q)‖u‖_q ≤ Cλ^(1−n/p)‖∇u‖ₚ for all λ > 0; letting λ → 0
    or ∞ gives a contradiction unless −n/q = 1 − n/p, i.e. 1/q = 1/p −
    1/n, q = np/(n − p). (b) GNS: for 1 ≤ p < n, ‖u‖_{p*} ≤ C‖∇u‖ₚ on
    W^{1,p}(Rⁿ); on bounded Lipschitz Ω, W^{1,p}(Ω) ⊂ L^q for q ≤ p*.
    MORREY: p > n ⇒ |u(x) − u(y)| ≤ C|x − y|^{1−n/p}‖∇u‖ₚ, so W^{1,p} ⊂
    C^{0,1−n/p}. RELLICH-KONDRACHOV: bounded sequences in W^{1,p}(Ω) have
    subsequences converging in L^q for q < p* (Ω bounded Lipschitz). In n
    = 3, p = 2: 2* = 6/1 = 6, so H¹(Ω) ⊂ L⁶(Ω), compact into L², L⁴,
    L^{5.9} but NOT into L⁶ (concentrating bubbles u(λx) rescaled keep the
    L⁶ norm). For H²: ∇u ∈ H¹ ⊂ L⁶, so u ∈ W^{1,6}, and 6 > 3 gives
    Morrey exponent 1 − 3/6 = ½: H²(Ω) ⊂ C^{0,1/2}(Ω̄). Common mistakes:
    applying GNS when p ≥ n (p* is then negative or infinite); claiming
    compactness at the critical exponent or on unbounded domains. Now you
    try: W^{2,2}(R⁵) ⊂ L^q for which q? (1/q = 1/2 − 2/5, q = 10)

D4. Prove the Poincaré inequality ∫₀ᴸ u² ≤ (L/π)²∫₀ᴸ (u′)² for u ∈
    H₀¹(0, L), show the constant is sharp, and check it on u = x(1 − x)
    with L = 1. Why is there no such inequality on H¹(0, L)?
    Answer: expand in sine series; equality for sin(πx/L); 1/30 ≤ (1/π²)
    (1/3); constants violate it on H¹.
    Teacher explains: The functions sₖ = √(2/L) sin(kπx/L), k ≥ 1, form an
    orthonormal basis of L²(0, L), and so do the cosines √(2/L)cos(kπx/L)
    (with 1/√L) — they are used for u′. For u ∈ H₀¹ write u = ∑aₖsₖ.
    Integration by parts (valid because u(0) = u(L) = 0) gives the cosine
    coefficients of u′ as (kπ/L)aₖ, so by Parseval
       ∫(u′)² = ∑(kπ/L)²aₖ² ≥ (π/L)²∑aₖ² = (π/L)²∫u².
    Equality iff aₖ = 0 for k ≥ 2, i.e. u = c sin(πx/L): sharp. This is
    the statement λ₁ = (π/L)² for −u″ = λu, u(0) = u(L) = 0. Check: u =
    x(1 − x): ∫u² = ∫(x² − 2x³ + x⁴) = 1/3 − 1/2 + 1/5 = 1/30, ∫(u′)² =
    ∫(1 − 2x)² = 1/3, and 1/30 ≈ 0.0333 ≤ (1/π²)(1/3) ≈ 0.0338 ✓ (very
    close, since x(1 − x) is nearly a multiple of sin πx). On H¹(0, L)
    the constant u = 1 has u′ = 0 but ∫u² = L > 0, so no inequality; the
    right replacement is Poincaré-Wirtinger ∫(u − ū)² ≤ (L/π)²∫(u′)²
    (Neumann λ₁ = (π/L)²). Common mistakes: using the inequality without
    zero boundary values; getting the constant as L/(2π) or L². Now you
    try: the best constant C in ‖u‖₂ ≤ C‖u′‖₂ on H₀¹(0, 3). (3/π)

D5. State the Lax-Milgram theorem and use it to prove that −u″ + u = f,
    u(0) = u(1) = 0 has a unique weak solution u ∈ H₀¹(0, 1) for every f ∈
    L²(0, 1) (indeed every f ∈ H⁻¹). Solve it explicitly for f = 1 and
    compute u(½).
    Answer: B[u, v] = ∫(u′v′ + uv) is the H¹ inner product;
    u = 1 − cosh(x − ½)/cosh(½), u(½) = 1 − sech(½) ≈ 0.11318.
    Teacher explains: WEAK FORM: multiply by v ∈ C_c^∞ (or H₀¹) and
    integrate the u″ term by parts; the boundary term u′v vanishes because
    v(0) = v(1) = 0:
       B[u, v] := ∫₀¹ (u′v′ + uv) dx = ∫₀¹ fv dx =: F(v)   ∀v ∈ H₀¹.
    Conversely a smooth weak solution is a classical one (integrate back).
    LAX-MILGRAM: H Hilbert, B bilinear with |B[u, v]| ≤ M‖u‖‖v‖ and
    B[u, u] ≥ α‖u‖², F ∈ H′ ⇒ there is exactly one u with B[u, v] = F(v)
    for all v, and ‖u‖ ≤ ‖F‖/α. Here H = H₀¹ with the H¹ norm, B is the
    inner product itself, so M = α = 1, and |F(v)| ≤ ‖f‖₂‖v‖₂ ≤ ‖f‖₂‖v‖_{H¹}
    by Cauchy-Schwarz. So there is a unique weak solution with ‖u‖_{H¹} ≤
    ‖f‖₂. (Since B is symmetric, this is just the Riesz representation
    theorem; Lax-Milgram is needed when a first-order term makes B
    non-symmetric.) For f = 1: the general solution of u″ = u − 1 is u = 1
    + A cosh(x − ½) + C sinh(x − ½). Symmetry about ½ forces C = 0, and u(0)
    = 0 gives A = −1/cosh(½). So
       u(x) = 1 − cosh(x − ½)/cosh(½),  u(½) = 1 − 1/cosh(½) ≈ 0.11318.
    Common mistakes: putting the boundary condition into F instead of into
    the space; forgetting that coercivity must be in the FULL H¹ norm (here
    automatic; for −u″ alone it needs Poincaré). Now you try: the weak
    solution of −u″ = 1, u(0) = u(1) = 0, and its value at ½.
    (x(1 − x)/2; 1/8)

D6. Let Lu = −u″ + bu′ + cu on (0, 1) with constants b, c and Dirichlet
    conditions. (a) For which c is the bilinear form coercive on H₀¹?
    (b) Prove the Gårding inequality for Lu = −∂ᵢ(aᵢⱼ∂ⱼu) + bᵢ∂ᵢu + cu.
    (c) Use the Fredholm alternative to decide when −u″ − π²u = f,
    u(0) = u(1) = 0, is solvable; solve it for f = sin 2πx.
    Answer: (a) c > −π² (any b); (b) B[u, u] ≥ (θ/2)‖∇u‖² − γ‖u‖²;
    (c) iff ∫₀¹ f sin πx = 0; u = sin(2πx)/(3π²) + C sin πx.
    Teacher explains: (a) B[u, v] = ∫(u′v′ + bu′v + cuv). For v = u the
    middle term is b∫u′u = (b/2)[u²]₀¹ = 0. So B[u, u] = ∫(u′)² + c∫u².
    If c ≥ 0 this is ≥ ∫(u′)². If −π² < c < 0, Poincaré ∫u² ≤ π⁻²∫(u′)²
    gives B[u, u] ≥ (1 + c/π²)∫(u′)², and ∫(u′)² controls the H¹ norm
    (again by Poincaré). If c ≤ −π², take u = sin πx: B[u, u] = (π² + c)/2
    ≤ 0, not coercive. (b) Ellipticity gives ∫aᵢⱼ∂ⱼu∂ᵢu ≥ θ‖∇u‖². The
    lower-order terms: |∫bᵢ∂ᵢu u| ≤ ‖b‖_∞‖∇u‖‖u‖ ≤ (θ/2)‖∇u‖² +
    (‖b‖²_∞/(2θ))‖u‖² (Young), and |∫cu²| ≤ ‖c‖_∞‖u‖². So
       B[u, u] ≥ (θ/2)‖∇u‖² − γ‖u‖²,   γ = ‖b‖²_∞/(2θ) + ‖c‖_∞,
    and B + γ(·, ·) is coercive: L + γ is uniquely solvable (Lax-Milgram).
    (c) Write L = L₀ − γ with L₀ invertible; L₀⁻¹ : L² → H₀¹ ⊂ L² is
    COMPACT (Rellich), so the Fredholm alternative for I − γL₀⁻¹ applies.
    Here ker L = span{sin πx} (π² is the first eigenvalue) and L is
    symmetric, so −u″ − π²u = f is solvable iff ∫₀¹ f(x) sin πx dx = 0.
    For f = sin 2πx the condition holds (orthogonality). Try u = A sin 2πx:
    −u″ − π²u = (4π² − π²)A sin 2πx, so A = 1/(3π²), plus any C sin πx.
    For f = 1: ∫ sin πx = 2/π ≠ 0, NO solution (resonance). Common
    mistakes: thinking uniqueness fails ⇒ existence fails for every f;
    forgetting that the kernel adds a free constant C. Now you try: is
    −u″ − 4π²u = 1, u(0) = u(1) = 0 solvable? (yes: ∫₀¹ sin 2πx = 0)

D7. (a) For u ∈ C_c^∞(Rⁿ) prove ∫|D²u|² = ∫(Δu)², and explain how the
    difference-quotient method turns this into interior H² regularity for
    weak solutions of −Δu = f ∈ L². (b) On the L-shaped (re-entrant
    corner) domain show that u = r^{2/3} sin(2θ/3) is harmonic, vanishes
    on the edges θ = 0 and θ = 3π/2, lies in H¹ near 0 but not in H².
    Answer: (a) integrate by parts twice; (b) |D²u| ~ r^(−4/3) and
    ∫r^(−8/3) r dr = ∞.
    Teacher explains: (a) ∫(Δu)² = ∑ᵢ,ⱼ∫∂ᵢᵢu ∂ⱼⱼu. Move one ∂ᵢ from ∂ᵢᵢu
    onto ∂ⱼⱼu and then one ∂ⱼ back (no boundary terms, compact support):
       ∫∂ᵢᵢu ∂ⱼⱼu = −∫∂ᵢu ∂ᵢⱼⱼu = ∫∂ᵢⱼu ∂ᵢⱼu.
    Summing: ∫(Δu)² = ∑∫(∂ᵢⱼu)² = ∫|D²u|². So ALL second derivatives are
    controlled by the Laplacian alone. For a weak solution we cannot
    differentiate twice, so we use DIFFERENCE QUOTIENTS Dₖʰu(x) = (u(x +
    heₖ) − u(x))/h. Test the weak equation with v = −Dₖ⁻ʰ(ζ²Dₖʰu), ζ a
    cut-off equal to 1 on V ⊂⊂ Ω; after "discrete integration by parts"
    one gets ∫ζ²|∇Dₖʰu|² ≤ C(‖f‖² + ‖u‖²_{H¹}) uniformly in h. A uniform
    bound on ‖Dₖʰ∇u‖_{L²(V)} implies ∂ₖ∇u ∈ L²(V) (weak compactness), so u
    ∈ H²_loc with ‖u‖_{H²(V)} ≤ C(‖f‖₂ + ‖u‖₂). Iterating gives f ∈ Hᵏ ⇒
    u ∈ H^{k+2}_loc, and f ∈ C^∞ ⇒ u ∈ C^∞ (Sobolev embedding). (b) In
    polar coordinates Δ = ∂ᵣ² + r⁻¹∂ᵣ + r⁻²∂_θ², and for rᵅ sin(αθ):
    (α(α − 1) + α − α²)r^{α−2} sin αθ = 0 ✓. With α = 2/3, sin(2θ/3) = 0 at
    θ = 0 and θ = 3π/2 ✓. |∇u| ~ r^(−1/3): ∫r^(−2/3) r dr < ∞, so u ∈ H¹.
    |D²u| ~ r^(−4/3): ∫r^(−8/3) r dr = ∫r^(−5/3) dr = ∞, so u ∉ H². Thus
    −Δ(ζu) = f ∈ L² (ζ a cut-off; f vanishes near 0) with u ∉ H²: global H²
    regularity FAILS without a smooth (or convex) boundary. In general rᵅ,
    α = π/ω, is in H² iff α > 1 iff ω < π (convex corners are fine).
    Common mistakes: claiming the interior argument works up to any
    boundary; thinking f ∈ C⁰ gives u ∈ C² (false even in the interior: u
    = (x² − y²)√(−ln r) has continuous Δu but u_xx → ∞). Now you try: for
    the slit domain ω = 2π, which Hˢ contains r^{1/2} sin(θ/2) near 0?
    (s < 3/2)

D8. (a) Show that a minimiser of the Rayleigh quotient R(u) = ∫|∇u|²/∫u²
    over H₀¹(Ω) ∖ {0} is a weak eigenfunction −Δu = λ₁u, and that it can be
    taken non-negative. (b) Find all Dirichlet eigenvalues of (0, π)² and
    the multiplicity of 50. (c) Bound λ₁ of the unit square with the trial
    function u = xy(1 − x)(1 − y).
    Answer: (a) differentiate R(u + εv) at ε = 0; |u| is also a minimiser;
    (b) m² + n², m, n ≥ 1; 50 has multiplicity 3; (c) λ₁ ≤ 20 (exact
    2π² ≈ 19.739).
    Teacher explains: (a) The infimum λ₁ is attained: normalise ∫u² = 1,
    a minimising sequence is bounded in H₀¹, so a subsequence converges
    weakly in H₀¹ and STRONGLY in L² (Rellich), ∫u² = 1 survives, and ∫|∇u|²
    is weakly lower semicontinuous. At the minimiser, for each v the
    function ε ↦ R(u + εv) has a minimum at ε = 0, so
       0 = d/dε R = (2∫∇u·∇v − 2λ₁∫uv)/∫u²,
    i.e. ∫∇u·∇v = λ₁∫uv ∀v: the weak form of −Δu = λ₁u. Since |∇|u|| =
    |∇u| a.e., R(|u|) = R(u), so |u| is a minimiser too, hence an
    eigenfunction, and by the strong maximum principle (Harnack) |u| > 0
    in Ω: the first eigenfunction does not change sign and λ₁ is simple.
    (b) Separate: sin mx sin ny gives λ = m² + n². 50 = 1 + 49 = 49 + 1 =
    25 + 25: (m, n) = (1, 7), (7, 1), (5, 5): multiplicity 3. The first
    ones: 2, 5 (×2), 8, 10 (×2), 13 (×2). (c) u′ factors: ∫₀¹(1 − 2x)² dx =
    1/3 and ∫₀¹ x²(1 − x)² dx = 1/30. So ∫|∇u|² = 2·(1/3)(1/30) = 1/45,
    ∫u² = (1/30)² = 1/900, and R(u) = 900/45 = 20 ≥ λ₁ = 2π² ≈ 19.739 ✓:
    any trial function gives an UPPER bound. Common mistakes: using trial
    functions that do not vanish on the boundary (they are not in H₀¹ and
    the bound is wrong); forgetting the multiplicity from swapping m, n.
    Now you try: the Rayleigh quotient of 1 − r² on the unit disc, and
    compare with λ₁ = j₀,₁² ≈ 5.7832. (6)

D9. (a) Prove by the DIRECT METHOD that E(u) = ∫_Ω (½|∇u|² − fu) has a
    minimiser on H₀¹(Ω) (Ω bounded, f ∈ L²), and that it is the weak
    solution of −Δu = f. Compute min E for Ω = (0, 1), f = 1. (b) Show
    that the Bolza functional J(u) = ∫₀¹ (((u′)² − 1)² + u²) dx on
    W₀^{1,4}(0, 1) has infimum 0 but no minimiser. Which hypothesis of the
    direct method fails?
    Answer: (a) coercive + weakly l.s.c. + reflexive; min E = −1/24.
    (b) sawtooth functions with slopes ±1; the integrand is not convex in
    u′.
    Teacher explains: (a) THREE STEPS. (1) Coercive: by Cauchy-Schwarz and
    Poincaré (‖u‖₂ ≤ C_P‖∇u‖₂), ∫fu ≤ ‖f‖C_P‖∇u‖ ≤ ¼‖∇u‖² + C_P²‖f‖², so
    E(u) ≥ ¼‖∇u‖² − C_P²‖f‖²: E is bounded below and minimising sequences
    are bounded in H₀¹. (2) Compactness: H₀¹ is a Hilbert space, so a
    bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence uₖ ⇀ u. (3) Lower
    semicontinuity: ‖∇u‖² ≤ lim inf ‖∇uₖ‖² (norms are weakly l.s.c.; more
    generally ∫F(∇u) is weakly l.s.c. when F is CONVEX), and u ↦ ∫fu is a
    continuous linear functional, so E(u) ≤ lim inf E(uₖ) = inf E: u is a
    minimiser. EULER-LAGRANGE: 0 = d/dε E(u + εv)|₀ = ∫∇u·∇v − ∫fv for
    all v, the weak form of −Δu = f (the Dirichlet principle). Strict
    convexity gives uniqueness. For (0, 1), f = 1: u = x(1 − x)/2, ∫(u′)²
    = ∫(½ − x)² = 1/12, ∫u = 1/12, so min E = 1/24 − 1/12 = −1/24. (Using
    the equation, min E = −½∫fu in general.) (b) J ≥ 0. Let uₖ be the
    sawtooth with slopes ±1 and 2k teeth of height 1/(2k): then (u′ₖ)² = 1
    a.e. and |uₖ| ≤ 1/(2k), so J(uₖ) ≤ 1/(4k²) → 0: inf J = 0. If J(u) =
    0 then u = 0 AND |u′| = 1 a.e., impossible. The minimising sequence is
    bounded in W^{1,4} and uₖ ⇀ 0, but J(0) = 1 > 0 = lim J(uₖ): J is
    NOT weakly l.s.c., because p ↦ (p² − 1)² is not convex (its convex
    envelope is ((p² − 1)₊)², whose relaxed problem has minimiser 0).
    Common mistakes: forgetting to check coercivity (Weierstrass: ∫₋₁¹
    x²(u′)² with u(±1) = ±1 has inf 0, not attained); assuming weak limits
    preserve nonlinear quantities. Now you try: minimise ∫₀¹ ((u′)² + u²)
    with u(0) = 0, u(1) = 1. (u = sinh x/sinh 1, min = coth 1 ≈ 1.31304)

D10. Solve u_t = u_xx on (0, π), u(0, t) = u(π, t) = 0, u(x, 0) = x(π − x)
     by separation of variables and compute u(π/2, 1). Prove the energy
     estimate ‖u(t)‖₂ ≤ e^(−t)‖u(0)‖₂ and deduce uniqueness. What is the
     weak formulation, and why is the backward problem ill-posed?
     Answer: u = ∑_{k odd} (8/(πk³)) e^(−k²t) sin kx; u(π/2, 1) ≈ 0.93679.
     Teacher explains: Separation u = X(x)T(t) gives −X″ = λX, X(0) =
     X(π) = 0, so X = sin kx, λ = k², and T = e^(−k²t). Expand the data:
        bₖ = (2/π)∫₀^π x(π − x) sin kx dx = 4(1 − (−1)ᵏ)/(πk³),
     i.e. 8/(πk³) for k odd and 0 for k even. So u(x, t) = ∑_{k odd}
     8/(πk³) e^(−k²t) sin kx. At (π/2, 1): (8/π)(e⁻¹ − e⁻⁹/27 + e⁻²⁵/125 −
     ...) ≈ 0.93680 − 0.00001 ≈ 0.93679. The factors e^(−k²t) kill high
     modes: u(·, t) is C^∞ (even analytic) for every t > 0 — SMOOTHING.
     ENERGY: multiply by u and integrate: d/dt ½∫u² = ∫u u_xx = −∫u_x²
     (boundary terms vanish) ≤ −∫u² by Poincaré on (0, π) (λ₁ = 1). So
     d/dt ‖u‖² ≤ −2‖u‖², ‖u(t)‖ ≤ e^(−t)‖u(0)‖. If u, w solve the same
     problem, u − w has zero data, so ‖u − w‖ ≡ 0: uniqueness. WEAK FORM:
     u ∈ L²(0, T; H₀¹), u′ ∈ L²(0, T; H⁻¹), ⟨u′, v⟩ + ∫u_x v_x = ⟨f, v⟩ for
     all v ∈ H₀¹ and a.e. t, u(0) = g; Galerkin approximations uₘ =
     ∑_{k≤m} dₖ(t) sin kx satisfy the same energy estimates uniformly in m,
     and a weak limit is the solution. BACKWARD: for u_t = −u_xx take
     uₙ = n⁻¹ e^(n²t) sin nx: data ‖uₙ(0)‖_∞ = 1/n → 0 but at t = 1 the
     amplitude eⁿ²/n → ∞: no continuous dependence (Hadamard). Common
     mistakes: using the Neumann eigenfunctions for Dirichlet data;
     dropping the sign in ∫u u_xx = −∫u_x². Now you try: u_t = u_xx on
     (0, π) with Neumann conditions and u(x, 0) = cos²x. (u = ½ +
     ½e^(−4t)cos 2x → ½)

D11. (a) Derive d'Alembert's formula for u_tt = c²u_xx on R and compute
     u(1, 2) for c = 1, u(x, 0) = 1/(1 + x²), u_t(x, 0) = cos x.
     (b) Prove conservation of energy and FINITE SPEED OF PROPAGATION:
     if the data vanish on [x₀ − t₀, x₀ + t₀] then u(x₀, t₀) = 0 (c = 1).
     (c) Contrast with the heat equation.
     Answer: (a) u(1, 2) = 0.3 + cos 1 sin 2 ≈ 0.79129; (b) the energy in
     the backward cone is non-increasing.
     Teacher explains: (a) In characteristic variables ξ = x + ct, η =
     x − ct the equation becomes u_ξη = 0, so u = F(x + ct) + G(x − ct).
     Fitting u(x, 0) = g, u_t(x, 0) = h gives
        u(x, t) = ½(g(x + ct) + g(x − ct)) + (1/(2c))∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct} h(s) ds.
     Here g-part: ½(g(3) + g(−1)) = ½(1/10 + 1/2) = 0.3; h-part: ½(sin 3 −
     sin(−1)) = ½(sin 3 + sin 1) = cos 1 sin 2 ≈ 0.49129. Total ≈ 0.79129.
     (b) E(t) = ½∫(u_t² + u_x²) dx: E′ = ∫(u_t u_tt + u_x u_xt) = ∫(u_t u_xx
     + u_x u_xt) = ∫(u_x u_t)_x dx = 0 for decaying (or Dirichlet/Neumann)
     solutions. For the CONE, let e(t) = ½∫_{x₀−(t₀−t)}^{x₀+(t₀−t)} (u_t² +
     u_x²) dx. Differentiating (Leibniz rule; the interval shrinks at speed
     1 at both ends)
        e′(t) = [u_x u_t]_{ends} − ½(u_t² + u_x²)|_{right} − ½(u_t² +
                u_x²)|_{left} ≤ 0,
     since |u_x u_t| ≤ ½(u_t² + u_x²). As e(0) = 0 and e ≥ 0, e ≡ 0, so u
     is constant in the cone, and it is 0 at t = 0: u(x₀, t₀) = 0. The same
     argument in Rⁿ shows u(x₀, t₀) depends only on data in B(x₀, ct₀).
     (c) The heat kernel is positive everywhere, so heat data supported in
     [−1, 1] give u > 0 at every x for every t > 0: INFINITE speed, but
     smoothing. The wave equation has FINITE speed but NO smoothing: a kink
     in g travels along x ± ct forever. In R³ (Kirchhoff) u(x, t) depends
     only on data on the SPHERE |y − x| = ct (Huygens), in R² on the whole
     disc (waves leave a "tail"). Common mistakes: writing 1/c instead of
     1/(2c) in front of the integral; forgetting the boundary terms in e′.
     Now you try: c = 1, g = 0, h = 𝟙_[−1,1]: u(0, 5) and u(3, 1). (1 and 0)

D12. For u ∈ L²(Rⁿ) with û(ξ) = ∫e^(−ix·ξ)u(x) dx define ‖u‖²_{Hˢ} =
     (2π)⁻ⁿ∫(1 + |ξ|²)ˢ|û|² dξ. (a) Check ‖u‖²_{H¹} = ∫(u² + |∇u|²) and
     compute it for u = e^(−|x|) on R both ways. (b) Prove Hˢ(Rⁿ) ⊂
     C_b(Rⁿ) for s > n/2. (c) For which s are δ, 𝟙_[−1,1] and e^(−|x|) in
     Hˢ(R)?
     Answer: (a) 2; (b) û ∈ L¹ by Cauchy-Schwarz; (c) s < −1/2, s < 1/2,
     s < 3/2.
     Teacher explains: (a) ∂ⱼu has transform iξⱼû, so by Plancherel
     (2π)⁻ⁿ∫(1 + |ξ|²)|û|² = ‖u‖² + ‖∇u‖². For u = e^(−|x|): u′² = u², and
     ∫e^(−2|x|) = 1, so ‖u‖²_{H¹} = 1 + 1 = 2. In Fourier: û = 2/(1 + ξ²),
     so (1/2π)∫(1 + ξ²)·4/(1 + ξ²)² dξ = (2/π)∫dξ/(1 + ξ²) = (2/π)π = 2 ✓.
     (b) By Cauchy-Schwarz,
        ∫|û| = ∫(1 + |ξ|²)^{−s/2}·(1 + |ξ|²)^{s/2}|û|
             ≤ (∫(1 + |ξ|²)^{−s} dξ)^{1/2}·(2π)^{n/2}‖u‖_{Hˢ},
     and ∫(1 + |ξ|²)^{−s} dξ < ∞ iff 2s > n. So û ∈ L¹, and u(x) =
     (2π)⁻ⁿ∫e^{ix·ξ}û(ξ) dξ is continuous (DCT), bounded by C‖u‖_{Hˢ}, and
     → 0 at ∞ (Riemann-Lebesgue). (c) The rule: if |û| ~ |ξ|^(−β) at ∞
     then u ∈ Hˢ(R) iff 2s − 2β < −1, i.e. s < β − ½. δ̂ = 1 (β = 0): s <
     −½. (𝟙_[−1,1])^ = 2 sin ξ/ξ (β = 1): s < ½ — a jump costs half a
     derivative. (e^(−|x|))^ = 2/(1 + ξ²) (β = 2): s < 3/2; the kink costs
     another half. In Rⁿ, δ ∈ Hˢ iff s < −n/2, so δ ∈ H⁻¹(R) (point loads
     on a string are fine) but δ ∉ H⁻¹(R²) (a point load on a membrane
     has infinite energy: the solution is ln r ∉ H¹). Common mistakes:
     forgetting the (2π)⁻ⁿ normalisation; treating s = n/2 as enough (ln
     ln(4/|x|) ∈ H¹(R²) is unbounded). Now you try: for which s is the
     hat function (1 − |x|)₊ in Hˢ(R)? (û = 4 sin²(ξ/2)/ξ², s < 3/2)

    m) backward heat u_t = −u_xx: uₙ = n⁻¹e^{n²t} sin nx at n = 10, t = 1
    n) regularity in time of a weak solution (u ∈ L²H₀¹, u′ ∈ L²H⁻¹)
    o) smoothing: bound ‖u_x(t)‖₂² by ‖g‖₂² for u_t = u_xx, Dirichlet
    p) u_t = u_xx + 1 on (0, π), Dirichlet, u(x, 0) = 0: lim u(π/2, t)
    q) u_t = u_xx on R, u(x, 0) = 𝟙_[−1,1]: is u(10, 0.01) > 0?
    Answers:
      a) e^(−t) sin x                   b) e⁻¹ ≈ 0.36788
      c) (4/π)∑_{k odd} e^(−k²t) sin(kx)/k; ≈ 0.46835
      d) ½ + ½e^(−4t) cos 2x; ½ (the mean)
      e) 1/√(4π) ≈ 0.28209
      f) (1 + 4t)^(−1/2) e^(−x²/(1+4t)); 1/√5 ≈ 0.44721
      g) ½ for all t > 0 (u = ½(1 + erf(x/(2√t))))
      h) x² + 2t        i) e^(−t) cos x     j) e^(−π²t/L²)
      k) −∫|∇u|² ≤ −λ₁∫u²                 l) 0 ≤ u ≤ 1
      m) amplitude e^{100}/10 ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴² from data of size 0.1
      n) u ∈ C([0, T]; L²)
      o) ‖u_x(t)‖² ≤ ‖g‖²/(2t) (‖u_x‖ decreases, ∫₀ᵗ‖u_x‖² ≤ ½‖g‖²)
      p) π²/8 ≈ 1.23370 (steady state x(π − x)/2)
      q) yes (tiny but positive: infinite speed)

M10. Wave equation u_tt = c²u_xx (c = 1 unless stated).
     a) u(x, 0) = 1/(1 + x²), u_t(x, 0) = 0: u(1, 2)
     b) u(x, 0) = 0, u_t(x, 0) = cos x: u and u(0, π/2)
     c) c = 2, u(x, 0) = sin x, u_t = 0: u and u(π/2, π/2)

       p) u ∈ C([0, T]; H₀¹), u′ ∈ C([0, T]; L²)
       q) at x = ±t only (the kink travels, it is never smoothed)

M11. Type, maximum principle and harmonic functions.
     Classify (E = elliptic, P = parabolic, H = hyperbolic):
     a) u_xx + u_yy                     b) u_xx − u_yy
     c) u_xx − u_y                      d) u_xx + 4u_xy + 4u_yy
     e) u_xx + 2u_xy + 5u_yy            f) u_xy = 0
     g) u_xx − 2u_xy − 3u_yy            h) yu_xx + u_yy (Tricomi type)
     i) u_xx + xu_yy
     Compute:
     j) Δu = 0 in the unit disc, u = x² on the circle: u, u(0), max u
     k) Δu = 0 in the unit disc, u = cos 3θ on the circle: u(½, 0)
     l) −Δu = 1 in the unit disc, u = 0: u and max u
     m) −Δu = 1 in the unit ball of R³, u = 0: max u
     n) 0 ≤ −Δu ≤ 2 in the unit disc, u = 0 on ∂: bounds for u(0)
     o) u harmonic in R², u(0) = 5: the mean of u over |x| = 7
     p) u_t = u_xx on (0, 1) × (0, T], u(x, 0) = sin πx, u = 0 at the ends:
        max u and where it is attained
     q) a bounded harmonic function on R²
     Answers:
       a) E      b) H      c) P      d) P (b² − ac = 4 − 4 = 0)
       e) E (1 − 5 < 0)    f) H      g) H (1 + 3 > 0)
       h) E for y > 0, H for y < 0, P on y = 0
       i) E for x > 0, H for x < 0, P on x = 0
       j) ½ + ½(x² − y²); ½; 1 (at (±1, 0), on the boundary)
       k) r³cos 3θ: 1/8                  l) (1 − r²)/4; ¼

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every u ∈ W^{1,1}(0, 1) has a continuous representative.
     b) Every u ∈ H¹ of the unit disc in R² is bounded.
     c) C_c^∞(Ω) is dense in H¹(Ω) for bounded Ω.
     d) H₀¹(Rⁿ) = H¹(Rⁿ).
     e) ‖u‖₂ ≤ C‖∇u‖₂ holds on H¹(Ω) for bounded Ω.
     f) H¹(Ω) ⊂ L²(Ω) is compact for EVERY bounded open Ω.
     g) H₀¹(Ω) ⊂ L²(Ω) is compact for every bounded open Ω.
     h) If −Δu = f with f continuous then u ∈ C².
     i) Lax-Milgram requires B to be symmetric.
     j) For every f ∈ H⁻¹(Ω) (Ω bounded), −Δu = f has a unique weak
        solution u ∈ H₀¹(Ω).
     k) The heat equation has finite speed of propagation.
     l) The wave equation smooths rough initial data.
     m) The backward heat equation is well-posed in L².
     n) A bounded sequence in H₀¹(Ω) has a weakly convergent subsequence.
     o) ∫F(∇u) always attains its infimum over u ∈ W₀^{1,p} if F ≥ 0 is
        continuous.
     p) Huygens' principle holds for the wave equation in R².
     q) The first Dirichlet eigenfunction of a connected domain does not
        change sign.
     r) δ ∈ H⁻¹(R²).
     s) The energy ½∫(u_t² + |∇u|²) of the wave equation with Dirichlet
        boundary conditions is conserved.
     t) For p > n and Ω bounded Lipschitz, every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) is Hölder
        continuous (after modification on a null set).
     Answers:
       a) T (absolutely continuous)        b) F: ln ln(4/|x|)
       c) F: its closure is H₀¹; u = 1 has trace 1 ≠ 0
       d) T                                e) F: u = 1 (constants)
       f) F: needs a regular boundary ("rooms and passages" domains)
       g) T (extend by 0 to a ball)        h) F: (x² − y²)√(−ln r)
       i) F: only bounded + coercive (e.g. −u″ + u′ on H₀¹)
       j) T (Riesz/Lax-Milgram with Poincaré)
       k) F: the heat kernel is positive everywhere
       l) F: kinks travel along x ± ct    m) F: n⁻¹e^{n²t} sin nx
       n) T (Hilbert spaces are reflexive)
       o) F: Bolza (u′² − 1)² type integrands (non-convex)
       p) F: holds only in odd n ≥ 3     q) T
       r) F: δ ∈ Hˢ(R²) iff s < −1 (borderline fails)
       s) T                               t) T (Morrey, γ = 1 − n/p)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a single "exponent card" on the board — |x|^(−a) ∈
  W^{1,p}(B ⊂ Rⁿ) iff (a + 1)p < n; p* = np/(n − p) from scaling; Morrey
  γ = 1 − n/p; Hˢ ⊂ C⁰ iff s > n/2 — and make students derive each from
  a one-line polar-coordinates or scaling computation instead of
  memorising. For every boundary-value problem insist on the same four
  written lines: (1) multiply by v and integrate by parts, (2) name the
  space (Dirichlet in the space, Neumann in the form), (3) check bounded +
  coercive (Poincaré!), (4) quote Lax-Milgram or Fredholm. For evolution
  equations, always compute the energy identity first and solve one
  separation-of-variables example by hand, contrasting e^(−k²t) (heat:
  smoothing, decay) with cos kt (wave: no smoothing, conservation). Harder:
  prove the Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality for p = 1 and bootstrap
  it to all p < n; prove Morrey's estimate via averages over balls; prove
  the trace theorem on a half-space; carry out the full difference-
  quotient proof of boundary H² regularity after flattening the boundary;
  construct weak solutions of the heat and wave equations by Galerkin
  approximation with all energy estimates; prove the mountain pass theorem
  from the deformation lemma and apply it to −Δu = |u|^{p−1}u for 1 < p <
  (n + 2)/(n − 2); and show via Pohozaev's identity that there is no
  non-trivial solution in a star-shaped domain at the critical exponent.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.14 — ALGEBRAIC GEOMETRY: VARIETIES, SCHEMES, SHEAVES, SHEAF
COHOMOLOGY, CURVES AND SURFACES, RIEMANN-ROCH
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - AFFINE VARIETIES (k = k̄): V(J) = {x ∈ Aⁿ : f(x) = 0 ∀f ∈ J} and
    I(Z) = {f : f|_Z = 0}. The V(J) are the closed sets of the ZARISKI
    TOPOLOGY (noetherian, not Hausdorff; on A¹ the closed sets are the
    finite sets and A¹). HILBERT'S NULLSTELLENSATZ: I(V(J)) = √J, so
    radical ideals ↔ closed sets, primes ↔ irreducible closed sets,
    maximal ideals ↔ points (fails over R: V(x² + 1) = ∅). Every closed
    set is a finite union of irreducible components.
  - REGULAR FUNCTIONS AND MORPHISMS: k[V] = k[x₁, ..., xₙ]/I(V); the
    category of affine varieties is anti-equivalent to finitely generated
    reduced k-algebras. DIMENSION = Krull dimension of k[V] = tr.deg of the
    function field k(V); a hypersurface in Aⁿ has dimension n − 1. A
    bijective morphism need not be an isomorphism: t ↦ (t², t³) onto the
    cusp y² = x³ (k[t², t³] ≠ k[t]).
  - PROJECTIVE VARIETIES: Pⁿ = (kⁿ⁺¹ ∖ 0)/k*, closed sets V(homogeneous
    ideal); standard affine charts Uᵢ = {xᵢ ≠ 0} ≅ Aⁿ. Regular functions on
    a connected projective variety are constant. VERONESE v_d : Pⁿ → P^N
    (N = C(n+d, d) − 1, image of degree dⁿ) and SEGRE Pᵐ × Pⁿ → P^(mn+m+n)
    (degree C(m+n, m)). HILBERT POLYNOMIAL P(t) = dim (S/I)ₜ for t ≫ 0:
    leading term (deg/r!)tʳ, r = dim; arithmetic genus pₐ = 1 − P(0) for
    curves. BÉZOUT: plane curves of degrees d, e without common component
    meet in exactly de points counted with multiplicity.
  - SMOOTHNESS: X = V(f₁, ..., fₘ) of dimension r is SMOOTH at p iff the
    JACOBIAN (∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ)(p) has rank n − r, iff dim of the Zariski tangent
    space m/m² equals r, iff O_{X,p} is a regular local ring. Examples:
    node y² = x²(x + 1), cusp y² = x³, cone x² + y² = z²; the singular locus
    is a proper closed subset.
  - SCHEMES: Spec A = prime ideals with closed sets V(a), basic opens D(f),
    structure sheaf with O(D(f)) = A_f and stalks O_p = A_p. A SCHEME is a
    locally ringed space locally isomorphic to some Spec A; morphisms of
    affine schemes ↔ ring maps backwards. Non-closed (GENERIC) points,
    nilpotents (Spec k[ε]/(ε²) = a point with a tangent vector), arithmetic
    schemes (Spec Z, Spec Z[x], Spec Z[i] → Spec Z with fibres over p).
    Proj S for graded rings; fibre products exist (A ⊗_C B); properties:
    reduced, integral, noetherian, separated, proper, finite type.
  - SHEAVES: presheaf F(U) with restrictions; SHEAF = locality + gluing.
    STALK F_p = lim F(U), SHEAFIFICATION F⁺ (same stalks). A map of sheaves
    is surjective iff surjective on stalks, NOT on sections (exp : O → O*
    on C*). Global sections Γ is LEFT exact only. O_X-MODULES:
    QUASI-COHERENT = locally M̃, COHERENT = locally M̃ with M finitely
    generated; on Spec A, M ↦ M̃ is an equivalence (A-mod ≃ QCoh).
  - LINE BUNDLES AND DIVISORS: invertible sheaves form PIC(X) under ⊗.
    Weil divisors ∑nᵢYᵢ (codim-1 prime cycles), principal div(f), Cl(X) =
    Div/Prin; Cartier divisors; Cl = Pic on smooth (locally factorial)
    varieties. Pic Pⁿ = Z·O(1), Pic Aⁿ = 0, Pic(P¹ × P¹) = Z², Cl of the
    cone xy = z² is Z/2 while its Pic is 0; Pic of a Dedekind ring = its
    class group. H⁰(Pⁿ, O(d)) = forms of degree d, dim C(n+d, n).
  - SHEAF COHOMOLOGY: Hⁱ(X, F) = right derived functors of Γ (injective
    resolutions); a short exact sequence of sheaves gives a LONG exact
    sequence; ČECH cohomology of an affine open cover computes it on a
    separated noetherian scheme for quasi-coherent F. GROTHENDIECK
    VANISHING: Hⁱ = 0 for i > dim X. SERRE: X noetherian is affine iff
    Hⁱ(F) = 0 for all quasi-coherent F and i > 0. Euler characteristic
    χ(F) = ∑(−1)ⁱ hⁱ(F) is additive; coherent F on projective X has
    finite-dimensional Hⁱ.
  - COHOMOLOGY OF Pⁿ: Hⁱ(Pⁿ, O(d)) = 0 for 0 < i < n; h⁰ = C(n+d, n) for
    d ≥ 0; hⁿ(O(d)) = h⁰(O(−d−n−1)) (nonzero only for d ≤ −n − 1); K_{Pⁿ}
    = O(−n−1). SERRE VANISHING: F coherent, O(1) ample ⇒ Hⁱ(F(m)) = 0
    (i > 0, m ≫ 0). SERRE DUALITY on smooth projective X of dim n:
    Hⁱ(X, L) ≅ Hⁿ⁻ⁱ(X, K_X ⊗ L⁻¹)*.
  - CURVES (smooth projective over k = k̄): equivalent to function fields
    of transcendence degree 1. deg div(f) = 0. GENUS g = h¹(O_C) = h⁰(K_C).
    Smooth plane curve of degree d: g = (d − 1)(d − 2)/2 (so no smooth
    plane curve has g = 2); with δ nodes/cusps the normalization has genus
    (d − 1)(d − 2)/2 − δ. Complete intersection in P³ of degrees a, b:
    K = O(a + b − 4), 2g − 2 = ab(a + b − 4).
  - RIEMANN-ROCH FOR CURVES: ℓ(D) − ℓ(K − D) = deg D + 1 − g, ℓ(D) =
    h⁰(O(D)). Consequences: deg K = 2g − 2; ℓ(D) = deg D + 1 − g if deg D
    > 2g − 2; D very ample if deg D ≥ 2g + 1; g = 0 ⇔ C ≅ P¹; genus 1 with
    a point is a plane cubic (Weierstrass form from ℓ(nP) = n); CLIFFORD:
    ℓ(D) ≤ deg D/2 + 1 for 0 ≤ deg D ≤ 2g − 2; WEIERSTRASS GAPS: exactly g
    gaps at each point.
  - MAPS OF CURVES: a non-constant f : X → Y is finite and surjective, deg
    f = [k(X) : k(Y)] = ∑_{P ↦ Q} e_P. RIEMANN-HURWITZ (tame): 2g_X − 2 =
    n(2g_Y − 2) + ∑(e_P − 1). Hyperelliptic y² = h(x), h squarefree of
    degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2, has genus g and 2g + 2 Weierstrass points;
    every genus-2 curve is hyperelliptic. No non-constant map P¹ → curve
    of genus ≥ 1. HURWITZ: |Aut C| ≤ 84(g − 1) for g ≥ 2 (Klein quartic:
    168). CANONICAL EMBEDDING of a non-hyperelliptic curve in P^(g−1).
  - SURFACES: intersection pairing C·D on Pic (Bézout on P², (a, b)·(c, d)
    = ad + bc on P¹ × P¹); ADJUNCTION 2pₐ(C) − 2 = C·(C + K); RIEMANN-ROCH
    χ(O(D)) = χ(O_X) + ½D·(D − K); NOETHER 12χ(O_X) = K² + e(X); HODGE
    INDEX: the intersection form on NS(X) has signature (1, ρ − 1).
  - BLOW-UPS AND EXAMPLES: blowing up a point p on a surface gives
    exceptional E ≅ P¹, E² = −1, K = π*K + E, K² drops by 1, Pic gains Z.
    CASTELNUOVO: a (−1)-curve E ≅ P¹ can be contracted smoothly. A smooth
    cubic surface = P² blown up at 6 general points; its 27 lines are Eᵢ
    (6), H − Eᵢ − Eⱼ (15), 2H − ∑_{k≠j}Eₖ (6). Degree-d surface in P³: K =
    O(d − 4), K² = d(d − 4)², χ(O) = 1 + C(d − 1, 3); d = 4 gives K3
    surfaces (K = 0, χ = 2, e = 24).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) State the Nullstellensatz and prove the strong form from the weak
    form. (b) In C[x, y] find √J and V(J) for J = (x²y, xy²) and for J =
    (y − x², y). (c) Find the irreducible components of V(xy, xz, yz) ⊆ A³.
    (d) Show the statement fails over R.
    Answer: (a) Rabinowitsch trick. (b) √(x²y, xy²) = (xy), V = both axes;
    √(y − x², y) = (x, y), V = the origin. (c) the three coordinate axes.
    (d) J = (x² + 1): V(J) = ∅ but √J = J ≠ R[x].
    Teacher explains: WEAK NULLSTELLENSATZ: if k = k̄ and J ≠ (1) then
    V(J) ≠ ∅ (because a maximal m ⊇ J has k[x]/m a finitely generated
    k-algebra that is a field, hence = k by Zariski's lemma, so m =
    (x₁ − a₁, ..., xₙ − aₙ)). STRONG: let f vanish on V(J). In k[x, t] the
    ideal J + (1 − tf) has no zeros (where f = 0 the new generator is 1),
    so 1 = ∑gᵢ(x, t)hᵢ + g(x, t)(1 − tf) with hᵢ ∈ J. Substitute t = 1/f
    and multiply by f^N: f^N ∈ J. So I(V(J)) ⊆ √J; ⊇ is obvious.
    (b) V(x²y, xy²) = {xy = 0}. xy ∉ J (J lives in degrees ≥ 3), but
    (xy)² = x·(xy²) ∈ J, and (xy) is radical, so √J = (xy): the SAME set is
    cut out by a non-radical ideal. For J = (y − x², y) = (y, x²): V is the
    single point 0, √J = (x, y); the extra "x²" records that the parabola
    is TANGENT to the line y = 0 — intersection multiplicity
    dim C[x, y]/(y, x²) = 2, as Bézout predicts (2 · 1 = 2). (c) xy = xz =
    yz = 0 means at least two coordinates vanish: V = {y = z = 0} ∪
    {x = z = 0} ∪ {x = y = 0}, i.e. (x, y, z)-axes, and I = (y, z) ∩ (x, z)
    ∩ (x, y), primes of dimension 1. Common mistakes: confusing V(J) = ∅
    with J = 0; thinking every ideal with V(J) = point is maximal.
    Now you try: √(x³, y²) ? ((x, y))

D2. The twisted cubic C is the image of ν : P¹ → P³, [s : t] ↦ [s³ : s²t :
    st² : t³]. (a) Show C = V(xz − y², xw − yz, yw − z²). (b) Compute the
    Hilbert polynomial, degree and arithmetic genus. (c) Show that the
    first two quadrics alone cut out C plus a line, and check Bézout.
    Answer: (a) rank-1 condition on [[x, y, z], [y, z, w]]. (b) P(t) =
    3t + 1, degree 3, pₐ = 0. (c) V(q₀, q₁) = C ∪ {x = y = 0}; 2·2 = 3 + 1.
    Teacher explains: The three quadrics are the 2 × 2 minors of
          ( x  y  z )
          ( y  z  w ).
    Points of ν(P¹) clearly satisfy them (xz = s⁴t² = y², etc.). Conversely
    if the minors vanish the rows are proportional; if x ≠ 0 scale to x =
    1: then z = y², w = yz = y³, so the point is ν([1 : y]); if x = 0 then
    y² = xz = 0, z² = yw = 0, so the point is [0 : 0 : 0 : 1] = ν([0 :
    1]). (b) The ring map k[x, y, z, w] → k[s, t] has kernel I = (q₀, q₁,
    q₂), and the degree-t part of the image is ALL forms of degree 3t in s,
    t, so dim (S/I)ₜ = 3t + 1. Leading coefficient 3 = degree (a general
    plane a x + b y + c z + d w meets C where a cubic in s, t vanishes: 3
    points). pₐ = 1 − P(0) = 0, consistent with C ≅ P¹. (c) If x = 0, q₀
    forces y = 0 and then q₁ = 0 automatically: V(q₀, q₁) contains the
    line L = {x = y = 0}. Off L it equals C. Two quadric surfaces meet in
    a curve of degree 4 = deg C + deg L = 3 + 1 ✓. So C is NOT the
    complete intersection of two of its quadrics. Common mistakes: using
    the affine Hilbert function; forgetting the point at x = 0. Now you
    try: the Hilbert polynomial of the rational normal curve of degree 4 in
    P⁴. (4t + 1)

D3. (a) State the Jacobian criterion. (b) Find the singular points of the
    projective cubic y²z = x³ + x²z and the tangent lines there. (c) Show
    that ν : A¹ → X = V(y² − x³), t ↦ (t², t³), is a bijective morphism
    but not an isomorphism. (d) Compute the Zariski tangent space of the
    cone x² + y² = z² at 0.
    Answer: (b) only [0 : 0 : 1], a NODE with tangents y = ±x. (c) k[X] =
    k[t², t³] ⊊ k[t]. (d) T₀ = k³, dimension 3 > 2 = dim.
    Teacher explains: (a) X = V(f₁, ..., fₘ) ⊆ Aⁿ, I(X) = (fᵢ), X of pure
    dimension r: p is smooth iff rank (∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ(p)) = n − r; for a
    hypersurface V(F) ⊆ Pⁿ: singular points = common zeros of all ∂F/∂xᵢ
    (Euler: ∑xᵢ∂F/∂xᵢ = (deg F)F). (b) F = y²z − x³ − x²z:
       F_x = −3x² − 2xz,  F_y = 2yz,  F_z = y² − x².
    F_y = 0 gives y = 0 or z = 0. If z = 0 then F_x = −3x² = 0, F_z = y² =
    0: no point. If y = 0 then F_z gives x = 0, and z = 1: the point
    [0 : 0 : 1]. Affinely y² = x² + x³: the lowest-order part y² − x² =
    (y − x)(y + x) is the TANGENT CONE, two distinct lines: a node.
    (c) ν is a morphism (polynomial) and bijective (t = y/x for x ≠ 0, t =
    0 ↦ 0). Its pull-back ν* : k[X] = k[x, y]/(y² − x³) → k[t] has image
    k[t², t³], which misses t; an isomorphism would need ν* onto. Also
    X is singular at 0 (both partials vanish) while A¹ is smooth. ν is the
    NORMALIZATION. (d) f = x² + y² − z² has df(0) = 0, so T₀ = V(linear
    part) = k³. Common mistakes: forgetting the chart at infinity; saying
    "the cusp is not a manifold" without proof (use m/m²: dim 2 > 1). Now
    you try: singular locus of x² = y²z in A³. (the z-axis x = y = 0)

D4. (a) Describe the points of Spec Z[x] and their closures. (b) Describe
    the fibres of Spec Z[i] → Spec Z over (2), (3), (5) and (0). (c) Explain
    why a map Spec k[ε]/(ε²) → X is a tangent vector.
    Answer: (a) (0); (p); (f) with f irreducible in Z[x]; maximal (p, f)
    with f̄ irreducible mod p. (b) 2: one non-reduced point (ramified); 3:
    one point with residue field F₉ (inert); 5: two points (split); (0):
    Spec Q(i). (c) it is a point plus a derivation O_p → k.
    Teacher explains: (a) A prime P ⊆ Z[x] meets Z in (0) or (p). If P ∩
    Z = (p): P corresponds to a prime of F_p[x] — (p) itself or (p, f)
    with f̄ irreducible mod p (closed points, residue field F_{p^deg f}).
    If P ∩ Z = 0: P becomes a prime of Q[x]: (0) or (f), f irreducible.
    Closures: {(0)}‾ = everything (the GENERIC POINT); {(p)}‾ = the
    "vertical line" V(p) ≅ Spec F_p[x]; {(f)}‾ = V(f) ≅ Spec Z[x]/(f), a
    "horizontal curve"; (p, f) is closed. dim Spec Z[x] = 2 (chain 0 ⊂ (p)
    ⊂ (p, x)). (b) The fibre over p is Spec Z[i]/(p) = Spec F_p[x]/(x² +
    1). p = 2: x² + 1 = (x + 1)² in F₂[x], one point with a nilpotent —
    RAMIFIED (2 = −i(1 + i)²). p = 3: x² + 1 irreducible (−1 is not a
    square mod 3): one point, residue field F₉ — INERT. p = 5: x² + 1 =
    (x − 2)(x + 2) mod 5: two points, 5 = (2 + i)(2 − i) — SPLIT. Generic
    fibre Spec Q(i): one point. (c) A morphism Spec k[ε] → X is a local
    homomorphism O_{X,p} → k[ε], a ↦ a(p) + εD(a); multiplicativity says D
    is a derivation, i.e. an element of (m/m²)*. Common mistakes: listing
    only closed points; thinking Spec k[ε] "is" Spec k (same space,
    different sheaf). Now you try: how many points lie over 13 in
    Spec Z[i]? (2, since 13 ≡ 1 mod 4)

D5. (a) Define sheaf, stalk and sheafification. (b) Show that the
    presheaf of constant Z-valued functions is not a sheaf. (c) Prove that
    exp : O → O*, f ↦ e^(2πif), is a surjection of sheaves on X = C* but
    not surjective on global sections. (d) Show that Γ(A² ∖ {0}, O) = k[x,
    y] and deduce that A² ∖ {0} is not affine.
    Answer: (b) on U = U₁ ⊔ U₂ the sections 0, 1 glue to nothing constant.
    (c) z has no global logarithm. (d) Hartogs-type computation.
    Teacher explains: (a) A presheaf F assigns groups F(U) with
    restrictions; it is a SHEAF if (locality) s|_{Uᵢ} = 0 ∀i ⇒ s = 0, and
    (gluing) compatible sᵢ ∈ F(Uᵢ) come from one s ∈ F(⋃Uᵢ). The stalk
    F_p = lim_{U ∋ p} F(U) (germs). The sheafification F⁺ = compatible
    families of germs; F → F⁺ is an iso on stalks and universal.
    (b) Take U = U₁ ⊔ U₂ disjoint opens, s₁ = 0, s₂ = 1: compatible
    (U₁ ∩ U₂ = ∅) but no constant function glues them. Its sheafification
    is the sheaf of LOCALLY constant functions, with value Z² on U.
    (c) On a small disc D around p ≠ 0 every g ∈ O*(D) has a logarithm
    (D is simply connected), so exp is onto on stalks: a surjection of
    sheaves, with kernel the constant sheaf Z. But g(z) = z on C* is not
    e^(2πif) for any holomorphic f (its winding number around 0 is 1 ≠ 0).
    Long exact sequence: 0 → Z → O(C*) → O*(C*) → H¹(C*, Z) = Z →
    H¹(C*, O) = 0: the cokernel on sections is exactly H¹(C*, Z) ≅ Z.
    (d) Cover X = A² ∖ 0 by D(x) and D(y): O(D(x)) = k[x, x⁻¹, y], O(D(y)) =
    k[x, y, y⁻¹], and a global section lies in both; inside k[x^±, y^±]
    their intersection is k[x, y]. If X were affine, X = Spec Γ(X, O) =
    A², but the inclusion X → A² is not onto. Common mistakes: checking
    surjectivity on global sections; forgetting that the ONE point lost has
    codimension 2 (removing a curve adds functions: O(D(x)) ∋ 1/x). Now
    you try: stalk of O_{A¹} at the generic point. (k(x))

D6. (a) Describe O_{P¹}(d) by transition functions and compute
    H⁰(Pⁿ, O(d)). (b) Show Pic Pⁿ ≅ Z. (c) How many independent conditions
    define the cubics through 9 general points of P²?
    Answer: (a) transition t^d; h⁰ = C(n + d, n) for d ≥ 0, 0 for d < 0.
    (b) deg : Cl Pⁿ → Z is an iso. (c) h⁰(O(3)) = 10: a unique cubic.
    Teacher explains: (a) On U₀ = {x₀ ≠ 0} and U₁ = {x₁ ≠ 0} of P¹ with t =
    x₁/x₀, O(d) is trivial on each and glued by the unit t^d on U₀ ∩ U₁
    (equivalently O(d)(U) = degree-d elements of the localized graded
    ring). A global section is a homogeneous polynomial of degree d; the
    monomials x^α, |α| = d, in n + 1 variables number C(n + d, n) ("stars
    and bars"). For d < 0 there are none: O(−1) (the tautological line
    bundle) has no non-zero section. (b) Pⁿ is smooth, so Pic = Cl. A prime
    divisor is V(F) with F irreducible of degree e; define deg V(F) = e.
    Principal divisors div(F/G), deg F = deg G, have degree 0, and any D of
    degree 0 is div(∏Fᵢ^(nᵢ)) — so deg : Cl Pⁿ → Z is an isomorphism, with
    O(1) = O(H) the generator. (c) h⁰(P², O(3)) = C(5, 2) = 10, so cubics
    form P⁹; each point imposes one linear condition, 9 general points
    leave a P⁰: exactly one cubic (Cayley-Bacharach territory: through 8
    general points passes a pencil, whose 9 base points are forced).
    Common mistakes: C(n + d, d) vs C(n + d − 1, d) (the latter counts
    forms in n variables); thinking O(−1) has sections because Pⁿ has
    lines through 0. Now you try: h⁰(P³, O(3)). (20)

D7. Compute H⁰ and H¹ of O(d) on P¹ by Čech cohomology for the cover
    U₀, U₁. Deduce h¹(O(−2)) = 1 and check Serre duality.
    Answer: h⁰(O(d)) = d + 1 (d ≥ 0), h¹(O(d)) = −d − 1 (d ≤ −2), otherwise
    0.
    Teacher explains: With t = x₁/x₀, O(d)(U₀) = k[t] (sections f(t)x₀^d),
    O(d)(U₁) = t^d k[t⁻¹] (sections g(1/t)x₁^d = g(1/t)t^d x₀^d), and
    O(d)(U₀₁) = k[t, t⁻¹]. The Čech complex is
       0 → k[t] ⊕ t^d k[t⁻¹] → k[t, t⁻¹] → 0,  (a, b) ↦ b − a.
    KERNEL: a = b ∈ k[t] ∩ t^d k[t⁻¹] = span{tⁱ : 0 ≤ i ≤ d}: dim d + 1 if
    d ≥ 0, else 0. COKERNEL: k[t^±] modulo span{tⁱ : i ≥ 0} + span{tⁱ :
    i ≤ d}. The survivors are tⁱ with d < i < 0, i.e. i = d + 1, ..., −1:
    there are −d − 1 of them when d ≤ −2. So H¹(O(−2)) = k·[t⁻¹], H¹(O(−3))
    = span[t⁻¹], [t⁻²] (dim 2), and H¹(O(d)) = 0 for d ≥ −1. Čech =
    derived-functor cohomology because the cover is affine and P¹ is
    separated. SERRE DUALITY with K = O(−2): h¹(O(d)) = h⁰(O(−2 − d)) =
    −d − 1 ✓; in particular h¹(O) = 0: g(P¹) = 0. Also χ(O(d)) = d + 1 for
    every d, a polynomial as it must be (Riemann-Roch with g = 0).
    Common mistakes: including t⁰ or t^d in the cokernel; forgetting that
    Grothendieck vanishing kills H² automatically. Now you try: h¹(P¹,
    O(−7)). (6)

D8. (a) State the cohomology of O(d) on Pⁿ. (b) For a smooth plane curve C
    of degree d prove g(C) = h¹(O_C) = (d − 1)(d − 2)/2. (c) For a smooth
    quartic compute h⁰ and h¹ of O_C(1) and check Riemann-Roch.
    Answer: (b) use 0 → O(−d) → O → O_C → 0. (c) h⁰ = 3, h¹ = 1;
    3 − 1 = 4 + 1 − 3 ✓.
    Teacher explains: (a) Hⁱ(Pⁿ, O(d)) = 0 for 0 < i < n and all d;
    H⁰ = S_d (forms of degree d); Hⁿ(O(d)) ≅ H⁰(O(−d − n − 1))* (Serre
    duality, K = O(−n − 1)), spanned by x^α with all exponents negative.
    (b) Multiplication by the equation F gives 0 → O_{P²}(−d) → O_{P²} →
    O_C → 0. Long exact sequence:
       0 → H⁰(O(−d)) → H⁰(O) → H⁰(O_C) → H¹(O(−d)) → H¹(O) → H¹(O_C)
         → H²(O(−d)) → H²(O) → 0.
    Middle terms: H⁰(O(−d)) = 0, H⁰(O) = k, H¹(anything) = 0, H²(O) = 0. So
    h⁰(O_C) = 1 (C connected) and h¹(O_C) = h²(O(−d)) = h⁰(O(d − 3)) =
    C(d − 1, 2) = (d − 1)(d − 2)/2. d = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: g = 0, 0, 1, 3, 6.
    (c) Twist by 1, d = 4: 0 → O(−3) → O(1) → O_C(1) → 0 gives h⁰(O_C(1))
    = h⁰(O(1)) = 3 and h¹(O_C(1)) = h²(O(−3)) = h⁰(O) = 1. Riemann-Roch:
    deg O_C(1) = 4 (Bézout with a line), 3 − 1 = 4 + 1 − 3 ✓. In fact
    K_C = O_C(d − 3) (adjunction), so for d = 4, O_C(1) = K_C: a plane
    quartic is its own canonical embedding. Common mistakes: forgetting
    h⁰(O_C) = 1 needs H¹(O(−d)) = 0; using h²(O(−d)) = h⁰(O(d)) (the
    correct twist is d − 3). Now you try: g of a smooth plane sextic. (10)

D9. (a) State Riemann-Roch for a smooth projective curve C of genus g and
    prove it from Serre duality. Deduce deg K = 2g − 2. (b) Show that g = 0
    implies C ≅ P¹. (c) Let (E, O) have genus 1. Compute ℓ(nO) and derive a
    Weierstrass equation.
    Answer: (a) ℓ(D) − ℓ(K − D) = deg D + 1 − g. (b) ℓ(P) = 2 gives a
    degree-1 map to P¹. (c) ℓ(nO) = n (n ≥ 1); the 7 functions 1, x, y,
    x², xy, y², x³ in L(6O) are dependent: y² + a₁xy + a₃y = x³ + a₂x² +
    a₄x + a₆.
    Teacher explains: (a) Put χ(D) = h⁰(O(D)) − h¹(O(D)). For D = 0: χ = 1
    − g (definition of g = h¹(O)). For a point P the sequence 0 → O(D) →
    O(D + P) → k_P → 0 (k_P the skyscraper) gives χ(D + P) = χ(D) + 1, and
    similarly χ(D − P) = χ(D) − 1. Every D is reached from 0 by adding and
    subtracting points, so χ(D) = deg D + 1 − g. SERRE DUALITY h¹(O(D)) =
    h⁰(K − D) turns this into Riemann-Roch. For D = K: ℓ(K) − ℓ(0) = g − 1
    = deg K + 1 − g, so deg K = 2g − 2. If deg D > 2g − 2 then deg(K − D)
    < 0, ℓ(K − D) = 0 and ℓ(D) = deg D + 1 − g exactly. (b) g = 0: ℓ(P) = 1
    + 1 − 0 = 2, so there is a non-constant f with at most a simple pole
    at P; f : C → P¹ has degree 1, hence is an isomorphism. (c) g = 1,
    2g − 2 = 0: ℓ(nO) = n for n ≥ 1 (and ℓ(O) = 1: only constants).
    ℓ(2O) = 2 adds x with a double pole; ℓ(3O) = 3 adds y with a triple
    pole. Pole orders at O: 1:0, x:2, y:3, x²:4, xy:5, y², x³:6. Seven
    functions in the 6-dimensional L(6O) satisfy a linear relation; y²
    and x³ are the only ones with pole order 6, so both appear, and after
    scaling we get the Weierstrass form. (x, y) : E → P² embeds E as a
    smooth cubic (3O is very ample, deg 3 ≥ 2g + 1). Common mistakes:
    forgetting ℓ(O) = 1, not 2, on an elliptic curve (else E ≅ P¹);
    applying ℓ(D) = deg D + 1 − g when deg D ≤ 2g − 2. Now you try: on a
    curve of genus 3, ℓ(D) for deg D = 7. (5)

D10. (a) State Riemann-Hurwitz. (b) Show that y² = h(x), h squarefree of
     degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2, has genus g. (c) Compute the genus of the
     Fermat curve xⁿ + yⁿ + zⁿ = 0 by projection to P¹. (d) Prove that a
     non-constant f : X → Y forces g_X ≥ g_Y, and that every map from P¹ to
     an elliptic curve is constant.
     Answer: (a) 2g_X − 2 = n(2g_Y − 2) + ∑(e_P − 1). (b) 2g + 2 branch
     points. (c) (n − 1)(n − 2)/2. (d) from (a).
     Teacher explains: (a) For f of degree n, separable (char 0), pull
     back a meromorphic differential ω on Y: near P with e = e_P, f is
     w = z^e, and dw = e z^(e−1) dz, so ord_P f*ω = e_P ord_Q ω + (e_P − 1).
     Summing, K_X ∼ f*K_Y + R with deg R = ∑(e_P − 1); take degrees (deg
     f*D = n deg D). (b) x : C → P¹ has degree 2. Over each root of h
     there is ONE point (y = 0), e = 2. Over ∞: if deg h = 2g + 1 (odd),
     y ~ x^(g + 1/2) is not single-valued, so ∞ is branched; if deg h =
     2g + 2, y ~ ±x^(g+1): two points, unbranched. Either way there are
     exactly 2g + 2 branch points: 2g_C − 2 = 2(−2) + (2g + 2) = 2g − 2 ✓.
     These 2g + 2 points are the WEIERSTRASS POINTS (for g ≥ 2).
     (c) [x : y : z] ↦ [x : y] has degree n (z is the n-th root of −xⁿ −
     yⁿ) and is totally ramified (e = n) exactly over the n points with
     xⁿ + yⁿ = 0. 2g − 2 = n(−2) + n(n − 1), g = (n² − 3n + 2)/2 =
     (n − 1)(n − 2)/2 ✓ (agrees with D8). (d) If g_Y ≥ 1 then 2g_X − 2 ≥
     n(2g_Y − 2) ≥ 2g_Y − 2. For X = P¹, Y = E: −2 = n·0 + (≥ 0) is
     impossible. Common mistakes: counting ramification POINTS instead of
     ∑(e_P − 1); forgetting the point(s) at infinity. Now you try: genus of
     y³ = x⁴ − 1 (∞ is totally ramified since 3 ∤ 4). (3: 2g − 2 = −6 +
     5·2)

D11. Let Q = P¹ × P¹ with Pic Q = Z(1, 0) ⊕ Z(0, 1). (a) Compute K_Q, the
     intersection form and the genus of a smooth curve of bidegree (a, b).
     (b) Verify Riemann-Roch for surfaces for O(a, b), a, b ≥ 0, and
     Noether's formula for Q and P². (c) For a smooth quartic X ⊆ P³ find
     K_X, χ(O_X), e(X) and the genus of a smooth hyperplane section.
     Answer: (a) K = (−2, −2), (a, b)·(c, d) = ad + bc, g = (a − 1)(b − 1).
     (b) χ = (a + 1)(b + 1) = h⁰; 12 = 8 + 4 and 12 = 9 + 3. (c) K = 0,
     χ = 2, e = 24, g = 3.
     Teacher explains: (a) Fibres of the two projections: (1, 0)² = 0
     (two fibres are disjoint), (1, 0)·(0, 1) = 1. So (a, b)·(c, d) = ad +
     bc. K_Q = pr₁*K_{P¹} + pr₂*K_{P¹} = (−2, −2). ADJUNCTION for C = (a, b):
        2g − 2 = C·(C + K) = (a, b)·(a − 2, b − 2) = 2ab − 2a − 2b,
     so g = (a − 1)(b − 1): (2, 2) → 1, (3, 3) → 4, (1, b) → 0 (graphs of
     maps P¹ → P¹ of degree b). (b) RIEMANN-ROCH: χ(D) = χ(O_Q) + ½D·(D −
     K) = 1 + ½(a(b + 2) + b(a + 2)) = 1 + ab + a + b = (a + 1)(b + 1),
     which is h⁰(O(a, b)) = h⁰(O(a))h⁰(O(b)) by Künneth (h¹ = h² = 0). NOETHER
     12χ(O) = K² + e: for Q, K² = (−2, −2)² = 8, e = 4 (topologically S² ×
     S²): 12 = 8 + 4 ✓; for P², K² = 9, e = 3 ✓. (c) Adjunction in P³: K_X =
     (K_{P³} + X)|_X = O_X(−4 + 4) = O_X. From 0 → O(−4) → O → O_X → 0:
     h⁰(O_X) = 1, h¹(O_X) = 0, h²(O_X) = h³(O_{P³}(−4)) = h⁰(O) = 1, so
     χ(O_X) = 2 (a K3 SURFACE). Noether: e = 24 − 0 = 24. A hyperplane
     section H has H² = 4 (Bézout), so 2g − 2 = H·(H + 0) = 4, g = 3 — a
     plane quartic ✓. On a K3 every smooth curve has C² = 2g − 2. Common
     mistakes: (1, 0)² = 1 (that is a line in P²); forgetting χ(O_X) = 1 −
     q + p_g, not h⁰ alone. Now you try: genus of a smooth (3, 4) curve on
     Q. (6)

D12. (a) Blow up P² at a point p. Show E ≅ P¹, E² = −1, compute the strict
     transform of a line through p and K of the blow-up. (b) For X = P²
     blown up at 6 general points show K_X² = 3 and that −K_X embeds X as a
     cubic surface. (c) Find all (−1)-classes and count the 27 lines. How
     many lines meet a given line?
     Answer: (a) L̃ = H − E, L̃² = 0, K = −3H + E, K² = 8. (b) (−K)² = 9 −
     6 = 3, h⁰(−K) = 10 − 6 = 4. (c) Eᵢ, H − Eᵢ − Eⱼ, 2H − ∑_{k≠j}Eₖ: 6 +
     15 + 6 = 27; each meets 10.
     Teacher explains: (a) Locally Bl₀A² = {((x, y), [u : v]) : xv = yu};
     the fibre over 0 is E = P¹ of tangent directions. Let H = π*(line);
     a line L through p pulls back to π*L = L̃ + E. Moving L off p shows
     π*L·E = 0; L̃ meets E once (one direction): L̃·E = 1. Hence E² =
     (π*L − L̃)·E = 0 − 1 = −1 and L̃² = (H − E)² = 1 − 0 − 1 = 0 (the lines
     through p become a pencil of disjoint curves: Bl_p P² → P¹).
     K = π*K_{P²} + E = −3H + E, K² = 9 − 1 = 8. Check adjunction for E:
     E·(E + K) = −1 − 1 = −2, g = 0 ✓. (b) Each blow-up lowers K² by one:
     K² = 9 − 6 = 3. Sections of −K = 3H − ∑Eᵢ = cubics through the 6
     points: 10 − 6 = 4, giving X → P³; the image has degree (−K)² = 3, a
     CUBIC SURFACE. (c) A LINE ℓ on X ⊆ P³ has −K·ℓ = 1 and, being ≅ P¹,
     ℓ² = 2g − 2 − K·ℓ = −2 + 1 = −1. Check: L_{ij} = H − Eᵢ − Eⱼ has L² =
     1 − 2 = −1, K·L = −3 + 1 + 1 = −1; the conic Cⱼ = 2H − ∑_{k≠j}Eₖ has
     C² = 4 − 5 = −1, K·C = −6 + 5 = −1; Eᵢ is clear. Count 6 + C(6, 2) + 6 =
     27. E₁ meets L_{1j} (5) and Cⱼ for j ≠ 1 (5): 10 lines. CASTELNUOVO:
     any (−1)-curve ≅ P¹ can be blown down to a smooth point; a surface
     with none is MINIMAL (P² and P¹ × P¹ are both minimal rational: the
     minimal model is not unique for rational surfaces). Common mistakes:
     E² = +1; forgetting that the 6 points must be general (no 3 collinear,
     not all 6 on a conic). Now you try: K² for P² blown up at 8 points.
     (1)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Varieties and the Nullstellensatz (k = C unless stated). Find the
    radical, the irreducible components, or the dimension as asked.
    a) √(x³) in k[x]                    b) √(x²y³) in k[x, y]
    c) √(x², y²)                         d) √((x − 1)²(x + 2)) in k[x]
    e) components and dim of V(xy, xz) ⊆ A³
    f) components of V(x² − yz, xz − x) ⊆ A³
    g) V(y − x², y − 1)                  h) V(x² + y² − 1, x − 1) and √ of
                                            the ideal
    i) dim C[x, y]/(y − x³, y) as a vector space (intersection
       multiplicity at 0)
    j) Krull dim of k[x, y, z]/(xy − z²)  k) dim of k[x, y]/(x², xy); is
                                            the ideal radical?
    l) is V(y² − x³ + x) irreducible?    m) is V(x² − y²) irreducible?
    n) I(V(J)) for J = (x² + 1) ⊆ R[x]
    o) Zariski closure of Z ⊆ A¹, and of {(n, n) : n ∈ Z} ⊆ A²
    p) Zariski closure of {(t, eᵗ) : t ∈ C} ⊆ A²
    q) is the Zariski topology on A² the product topology of A¹ × A¹?
    Answers:
      a) (x)      b) (xy)      c) (x, y)      d) ((x − 1)(x + 2))
      e) the plane x = 0 and the line y = z = 0; dim 2
      f) the lines {x = y = 0}, {x = z = 0} and the parabola {z = 1, y =
         x²}: three curves
      g) {(1, 1), (−1, 1)}      h) {(1, 0)}; (x − 1, y²) is not radical,
         its radical is (x − 1, y) (the line is tangent)
      i) 3 (the ideal is (y, x³))                      j) 2
      k) 1 (V = the line x = 0); not radical: √ = (x), with an embedded
         point at 0 ((x², xy) = (x) ∩ (x², y))
      l) yes (x³ − x is not a square)   m) no: {y = x} ∪ {y = −x}
      n) R[x] (V = ∅), while √J = J: the Nullstellensatz needs k = k̄
      o) A¹; the line y = x     p) A² (eᵗ is not algebraic over C(t))
      q) no: the diagonal (or xy = 1) is closed in A² but not in the
         product of cofinite topologies

M2. Projective varieties: dimensions of linear systems, degrees, Hilbert
    polynomials, Bézout.
    a) dim of the space of cubic forms in 3 variables
    b) dim of the space of quartic forms in 4 variables
    c) the Veronese v₂ : P² → P^N: N and degree of the image
    d) v₃ : P¹ → P^N                    e) v₂ : P³ → P^N
    f) v₃ : P² → P^N                    g) Segre P¹ × P¹ → P^N: N, degree
    h) Segre P¹ × P² → P^N              i) Segre P² × P² → P^N
    j) Hilbert polynomial of a smooth plane conic
    k) of a plane cubic                 l) of 3 non-collinear points in P²
    m) of the twisted cubic             n) of a smooth quadric surface in P³
    o) of the complete intersection of two quadrics in P³
    p) of the Veronese surface v₂(P²) ⊆ P⁵
    q) number of intersection points of a general conic and a general
       cubic in P²
    r) three general quadrics in P³ meet in how many points?
    s) intersection multiplicity of y²z = x³ and the line z = 0 at [0 : 1
       : 0]
    t) how many general points determine a unique conic, cubic, quartic?
