M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample or reason for F.
     a) ζ(s) ≠ 0 for Re s > 1.
     b) ζ(s) has no zeros with Re s < 0.
     c) ∑_p 1/p converges.
     d) ∑ 1/p over twin primes p converges.
     e) L(s, χ) has a pole at s = 1 for every χ mod q.
     f) L(1, χ) = 0 is possible for a real character χ ≠ χ₀.
     g) For a real primitive χ mod q, τ(χ)² = χ(−1)q.
     h) |τ(χ)| = √q for every character mod q.
     i) π(x) < li(x) for all x ≥ 3.
     j) The PNT is equivalent to M(x) = ∑_{n≤x} μ(n) = o(x).
     k) The Legendre sieve with z = √x gives π(x) ~ x/log x.
     l) Selberg's sieve alone gives π(x) ≫ x/log x.
     m) Every odd n ≥ 7 is a sum of three primes.
     n) Bombieri-Vinogradov implies GRH.
     o) The non-trivial zeros are symmetric about Re s = ½.
     p) A Dirichlet series with non-negative coefficients can be analytic
        at its real abscissa of convergence.
     q) Siegel's theorem is effective.
     r) The Euler product for ζ converges at s = ½.
     s) RH implies ψ(x) = x + O(x^(½+ε)).
     t) The Selberg sieve upper bound for twin primes matches the
        Hardy-Littlewood conjecture.
     Answers:
       a) T (Euler product)       b) F: −2, −4, ...
       c) F (Euler)               d) T (Brun)
       e) F: only for χ₀; L(s, χ) is entire for χ ≠ χ₀
       f) F (Dirichlet; the ζ·L trick with Landau)
       g) T (τ(χ)τ(χ̄) = χ(−1)q)  h) F: τ(χ₀ mod 7) = −1
       i) F: Littlewood, sign changes infinitely often
       j) T                       k) F: x∏_{p≤√x}(1 − 1/p) ~ 2e^(−γ)x/log x
                                     ≈ 1.123x/log x; the error dominates
       l) F: parity problem (Selberg's λ(n) example)
       m) T (Vinogradov for large n; Helfgott for all)
       n) F: it is an average over q only
       o) T (ξ(s) = ξ(1 − s) and ξ(s̄) = ξ(s)‾)
       p) F (Landau's theorem)    q) F: the constant is ineffective
       r) F: ∏(1 − p^(−½))⁻¹ diverges (∑p^(−½) = ∞)
       s) T                       t) F: it is 4 times too large

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep ONE dictionary on the board — "primes ↔ Λ ↔ −ζ′/ζ,
  squarefree ↔ μ² ↔ ζ(s)/ζ(2s), progressions ↔ characters ↔ L(s, χ)" —
  and translate every question into it before computing. Drill partial
  summation until it is automatic, since nearly every asymptotic in M5
  is one line of it. For the functional equation, have students first
  compute ζ(−1) and ζ(−3) mechanically, then see the theta proof. For
  sieves, do Legendre by hand for x = 100 before any theory: the error
  term 2^π(z) and Mertens' 2e^(−γ) then explain why smarter sieves exist.
  For the circle method, start from ∫₀¹ e(mα) dα = 𝟙_{m=0} and compute
  local factors p by p. Harder: prove the zero-free region
  quantitatively and deduce the de la Vallée Poussin error term; prove
  Siegel's theorem and explain its ineffectivity; derive the large sieve
  via Gallagher's lemma and deduce Bombieri-Vinogradov from Vaughan's
  identity; prove Selberg's G(z) ≥ log z carefully and the Brun-
  Titchmarsh inequality; carry out Vinogradov's minor arc estimate; and
  read Maynard's bounded gaps proof as a multidimensional Selberg sieve.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.17 — REPRESENTATION THEORY OF LIE GROUPS, ALGEBRAIC GROUPS AND
QUANTUM GROUPS: COMPACT GROUPS, PETER-WEYL, HIGHEST WEIGHTS, WEYL CHARACTER
FORMULA, REDUCTIVE GROUPS, U_q(sl₂)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - REPRESENTATIONS: a continuous homomorphism π : G → GL(V) (V complex,
    usually finite-dimensional). Subrepresentations, irreducibility,
    intertwiners Hom_G(V, W), direct sums, tensor products V ⊗ W, duals V*
    (g acts by π(g⁻¹)ᵀ), Sym^k V, Λ^k V. SCHUR'S LEMMA: an intertwiner
    between irreducibles is 0 or an isomorphism; End_G(V) = C·id for V
    irreducible (C algebraically closed). Hence irreps of ABELIAN groups are
    1-dimensional; the centre acts by a scalar (central character).
  - COMPACT GROUPS: a compact group has a unique bi-invariant HAAR
    probability measure dg. AVERAGING ⟨v, w⟩_G = ∫⟨gv, gw⟩ dg gives an
    invariant inner product, so every finite-dimensional representation is
    UNITARISABLE and COMPLETELY REDUCIBLE (orthogonal complements of
    subreps are subreps). Fails for non-compact groups: t ↦ (1 t; 0 1) of
    R (or of the algebraic group G_a) is not completely reducible.
  - CHARACTERS: χ_V(g) = tr π(g), a class function; χ_{V⊕W} = χ_V + χ_W,
    χ_{V⊗W} = χ_Vχ_W, χ_{V*} = conj(χ_V). SCHUR ORTHOGONALITY: for
    irreducible unitary π, π′, ∫ π_ij(g) conj(π′_kl(g)) dg = δ_{ππ′}δ_ik
    δ_jl/dim π; so ⟨χ_V, χ_W⟩ = dim Hom_G(V, W), V is irreducible iff
    ‖χ_V‖ = 1, and the multiplicity of an irrep U in V is ⟨χ_V, χ_U⟩.
  - PETER-WEYL THEOREM (G compact): matrix coefficients of irreps are
    uniformly dense in C(G); L²(G) = ⊕̂_{π∈Ĝ} V_π ⊗ V_π* as G × G-modules,
    with ONB {√(dim π) π_ij}; characters form an ONB of the L² class
    functions. Consequences: every compact Lie group has a faithful finite-
    dimensional rep (is a closed subgroup of U(n)); |G| = ∑(dim π)² for G
    finite; for G = U(1) it is Fourier series. For a closed subgroup K,
    the multiplicity of V_π in L²(G/K) is dim V_π^K (FROBENIUS RECIPROCITY):
    L²(S²) = ⊕_l ℋ_l, harmonics of degree l, dim 2l + 1.
  - SU(2) AND SO(3): the irreps of SU(2) are Vₙ = homogeneous polynomials
    of degree n in two variables, dim n + 1, one for each n ≥ 0, with
    χₙ(diag(e^{iθ}, e^{−iθ})) = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ. CLEBSCH-GORDAN:
    V_m ⊗ Vₙ = V_{m+n} ⊕ V_{m+n−2} ⊕ ... ⊕ V_{|m−n|}. The irreps of
    SO(3) = SU(2)/{±1} are the Vₙ with n even (dims 1, 3, 5, ...; "integer
    spin"). WEYL INTEGRATION on SU(2): ∫ f dg = (2/π)∫₀^π f(θ) sin²θ dθ for
    class functions; on SO(3) the density of the rotation angle is
    (1 − cos θ)/π.
  - LIE ALGEBRA REPRESENTATIONS: a rep of G gives dπ of 𝔤 = Lie(G); for G
    simply connected every rep of 𝔤 integrates to G. UNITARY TRICK: f.d.
    reps of SU(n), SL(n, C) (holomorphic) and 𝔰𝔩(n, C) are "the same".
    WEYL'S THEOREM: f.d. reps of a semisimple 𝔤 over C are completely
    reducible.
  - 𝔰𝔩₂ THEORY: basis e, f, h with [h, e] = 2e, [h, f] = −2f, [e, f] = h.
    For each n ≥ 0 there is exactly one irrep V(n) of dim n + 1, basis
    v₀, ..., vₙ with h vₖ = (n − 2k)vₖ, f vₖ = vₖ₊₁, e vₖ = k(n − k + 1)vₖ₋₁.
    Weights are symmetric and unbroken strings; the CASIMIR Ω = h² + 2ef +
    2fe acts on V(n) by n(n + 2).
  - HIGHEST WEIGHT THEORY (𝔤 semisimple, Cartan 𝔥, roots Φ, positive roots
    Φ⁺, simple roots αᵢ, coroots αᵢ∨, fundamental weights ωᵢ with ⟨ωᵢ,
    αⱼ∨⟩ = δᵢⱼ, ρ = ½∑_{α>0} α = ∑ωᵢ, Weyl group W): every f.d. irrep has
    a unique highest weight λ, which is DOMINANT INTEGRAL (λ = ∑aᵢωᵢ,
    aᵢ ∈ Z≥0), and λ ↦ L(λ) is a bijection {dominant integral weights} ↔
    {f.d. irreps}. The weights of L(λ) are W-invariant with multiplicities
    and all lie in λ − Z≥0Φ⁺ inside the convex hull of Wλ.
  - VERMA MODULES: M(λ) = U(𝔤) ⊗_{U(𝔟)} C_λ has a unique irreducible
    quotient L(λ); ch M(λ) = e^λ/∏_{α>0}(1 − e^{−α}). For 𝔰𝔩₂, M(λ) is
    irreducible iff λ ∉ Z≥0; for λ = n ≥ 0, f^{n+1}v is a singular vector
    and L(n) = M(n)/M(−n − 2). DOT ACTION w·λ = w(λ + ρ) − ρ.
  - WEYL CHARACTER FORMULA: ch L(λ) = ∑_{w∈W} ε(w)e^{w(λ+ρ)} / ∑_{w∈W}
    ε(w)e^{wρ}, with DENOMINATOR IDENTITY ∑ε(w)e^{wρ} = e^ρ∏_{α>0}(1 −
    e^{−α}). Equivalent: ch L(λ) = ∑_w ε(w) ch M(w·λ) (BGG resolution).
    WEYL DIMENSION FORMULA: dim L(λ) = ∏_{α>0} ⟨λ + ρ, α∨⟩/⟨ρ, α∨⟩; for
    𝔰𝔩₃, dim L(a, b) = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2. Multiplicities via
    FREUDENTHAL or KOSTANT; for GLₙ they are Kostka numbers.
  - COMPACT CONNECTED LIE GROUPS: maximal torus T, all maximal tori
    conjugate, every element conjugate into T, W = N(T)/T. Irreps ↔
    dominant weights in the character lattice X*(T) (THEOREM OF THE
    HIGHEST WEIGHT); WEYL INTEGRATION FORMULA ∫_G f = (1/|W|)∫_T f(t)
    |Δ(t)|² dt; BOREL-WEIL: L(λ)* = H⁰(G/B, ℒ_λ) (for SL₂: H⁰(P¹, O(n)) =
    Vₙ). Non-compact simple groups such as SL(2, R) have NO non-trivial
    finite-dimensional unitary reps; their unitary irreps are infinite-
    dimensional (principal and discrete series).
  - LINEAR ALGEBRAIC GROUPS over k = k̄: Zariski-closed subgroups of GLₙ.
    Jordan decomposition; unipotent radical R_u(G) = largest connected
    normal unipotent subgroup. G is REDUCTIVE if R_u(G) = 1 (GLₙ, SLₙ, PGLₙ,
    SOₙ, Sp₂ₙ, tori G_mʳ), SEMISIMPLE if its radical is also trivial. NOT
    reductive: G_a, the Borel B of upper triangular matrices, unipotent Uₙ.
    In characteristic 0 reductive ⇔ every rational rep completely
    reducible (linearly reductive).
  - ROOT DATA: (X*(T), Φ, X_*(T), Φ∨) classifies connected reductive groups
    up to isomorphism (Chevalley). GLₙ: X* = Zⁿ, roots eᵢ − eⱼ. SL₂: X* =
    Z, α = 2, α∨ = 1; PGL₂: X* = Z, α = 1, α∨ = 2 — same root system, not
    isomorphic groups. Irreducible rational reps ↔ dominant λ ∈ X*(T);
    for GLₙ: λ₁ ≥ ... ≥ λₙ in Zⁿ; polynomial ones = partitions, dimension by
    the HOOK-CONTENT formula; SCHUR-WEYL: (Cⁿ)^{⊗k} = ⊕_{λ⊢k} S_λ(Cⁿ) ⊗
    Specht_λ as GLₙ × S_k-modules.
  - CHARACTERISTIC p: complete reducibility FAILS; the Weyl module Sym^n(k²)
    of SL₂ can be reducible (Sym^p ⊇ span{x^p, y^p}). STEINBERG TENSOR
    PRODUCT: L(a₀ + a₁p + a₂p² + ...) = L(a₀) ⊗ L(a₁)^{[1]} ⊗ ... (Frobenius
    twists), so for SL₂, dim L(n) = ∏(aᵢ + 1) over the base-p digits of n.
  - QUANTUM GROUP U_q(𝔰𝔩₂) (q ∈ C^×, not a root of unity): generators E,
    F, K^{±1} with KEK⁻¹ = q²E, KFK⁻¹ = q⁻²F, EF − FE = (K − K⁻¹)/(q −
    q⁻¹). HOPF ALGEBRA: Δ(K) = K ⊗ K, Δ(E) = E ⊗ K + 1 ⊗ E, Δ(F) = F ⊗ 1 +
    K⁻¹ ⊗ F, ε(E) = ε(F) = 0, ε(K) = 1, S(E) = −EK⁻¹, S(F) = −KF, S(K) =
    K⁻¹. q-INTEGERS [n] = (qⁿ − q⁻ⁿ)/(q − q⁻¹) = q^{n−1} + ... + q^{1−n}.
  - REPS OF U_q(𝔰𝔩₂): for each n ≥ 0 and σ = ±1 one irrep L(n, σ), basis
    m₀, ..., mₙ, K mᵢ = σq^{n−2i}mᵢ, F mᵢ = mᵢ₊₁, E mᵢ = σ[i][n − i + 1]mᵢ₋₁;
    all f.d. reps are completely reducible and tensor products obey
    Clebsch-Gordan. QUANTUM CASIMIR C = EF + (q⁻¹K + qK⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹)²;
    QUANTUM DIMENSION tr(K) = [n + 1]. Δ is not cocommutative, but V ⊗ W
    ≅ W ⊗ V via the universal R-MATRIX (braiding → knot invariants such as
    the Jones polynomial). At a root of unity ([ℓ] = 0) the theory changes:
    E^ℓ, F^ℓ, K^ℓ become central and non-semisimple reps appear.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Prove Schur's lemma and deduce that every irreducible f.d.
    complex representation of an abelian group is 1-dimensional. (b) Prove
    that every f.d. representation of a compact group G is unitarisable
    and hence completely reducible. (c) Show that π(t) = (1 t; 0 1) of the
    additive group R is not completely reducible.
    Answer: (a) ker and image of an intertwiner are subreps; an eigenspace
    of T ∈ End_G(V) is a subrep. (b) average an inner product with Haar
    measure. (c) the line Ce₁ is invariant but has no invariant complement.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let T : V → W intertwine irreducibles. ker T ⊆ V
    and im T ⊆ W are invariant, so ker T = 0 or V and im T = 0 or W: T = 0
    or T is bijective. If V = W is f.d. over C, T has an eigenvalue c, and
    T − c·id is an intertwiner that is not injective, hence 0: T = c·id.
    For G abelian, each π(g) commutes with all π(h), so π(g) ∈ End_G(V) =
    C·id; then EVERY line is invariant, and irreducibility forces dim V =
    1. (b) Take any inner product ⟨ , ⟩ on V and put
       ⟨v, w⟩_G = ∫_G ⟨π(g)v, π(g)w⟩ dg.
    It is positive definite (integral of a positive continuous function)
    and, by LEFT INVARIANCE of dg, ⟨π(h)v, π(h)w⟩_G = ∫⟨π(gh)v, π(gh)w⟩dg =
    ⟨v, w⟩_G (substitute g ↦ gh⁻¹; Haar measure on compact groups is also
    right invariant). So each π(h) is unitary for ⟨ , ⟩_G. If U ⊆ V is
    invariant, so is U^⊥: for u ∈ U, w ∈ U^⊥, ⟨u, π(h)w⟩ = ⟨π(h⁻¹)u, w⟩ =
    0. Induct on dimension. (c) π(t)e₁ = e₁, so Ce₁ is a subrep. Any other
    invariant line is spanned by an eigenvector common to all π(t); but
    π(t) − 1 = (0 t; 0 0) has kernel Ce₁ only. So Ce₁ has no invariant
    complement; π is indecomposable but reducible. Averaging fails because
    R has no finite invariant measure. Common mistakes: applying Schur over
    R (the rotation rep of SO(2) on R² is irreducible over R with End =
    C); forgetting that Schur needs the vector space f.d. (or at least a
    countable-dimension argument). Now you try: find all irreps of U(1).
    (χₙ(z) = zⁿ, n ∈ Z)

D2. (a) Prove Schur orthogonality ⟨χ_V, χ_W⟩ = ∫χ_V(g) conj(χ_W(g)) dg =
    dim Hom_G(W, V) for a compact group G. (b) For the circle T = U(1)
    and ρ(z) = diag(z², z⁻¹, 1), compute ⟨χ_ρ, χ_ρ⟩ and decompose ρ.
    (c) For the standard 2-dimensional
    representation of S₃ (a compact group!), verify ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 1.
    Answer: (a) the average P = ∫π(g) dg is the projection onto the
    invariants and tr P = dim V^G; apply it to Hom(W, V). (b) ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 3:
    three distinct characters z², z⁻¹, 1. (c) (4 + 3·0 + 2·1)/6 = 1.
    Teacher explains: (a) For any f.d. rep U put P = ∫_G π_U(g) dg. By
    invariance π_U(h)P = P, so im P ⊆ U^G; and P = id on U^G. Hence P² = P
    is a projection onto U^G and dim U^G = tr P = ∫χ_U(g) dg. Apply this
    to U = Hom(W, V) ≅ V ⊗ W*, whose character is χ_V conj(χ_W) (unitary
    eigenvalues satisfy λ⁻¹ = conj λ), and whose invariants are Hom_G(W,
    V). So ∫χ_V conj(χ_W) = dim Hom_G(W, V); by Schur this is δ_{VW} for
    irreducibles. (b) On U(1), Haar measure is dθ/2π, and ∫zᵐ z̄ⁿ = δ_mn.
    So ⟨χ, χ⟩ = ∫|z² + z⁻¹ + 1|² = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 (cross terms vanish): χ is
    the sum of the three distinct irreducible characters χ₂, χ₋₁, χ₀.
    (c) S₃ has classes {e} (size 1, χ = 2), transpositions (size 3, χ =
    0), 3-cycles (size 2, χ = −1). With counting measure divided by 6:
       ⟨χ, χ⟩ = (1·4 + 3·0 + 2·1)/6 = 1,
    so the representation is irreducible. Common mistakes: forgetting the
    complex conjugate (harmless for real characters, fatal on U(1));
    weighting classes without their sizes. Now you try: on U(1) compute
    the multiplicity of χ₀ in (z + z⁻¹)⁴. (∫(2 cos θ)⁴ dθ/2π = 6)

D3. (a) Show that Vₙ = {homogeneous polynomials of degree n in x, y}, with
    (g·p)(x, y) = p((x, y)g), is an irreducible representation of SU(2)
    of dimension n + 1, and compute its character. (b) State the Weyl
    integration formula for SU(2) and check that ⟨χ_m, χₙ⟩ = δ_mn.
    Answer: (a) χₙ(t_θ) = ∑_{k=0}^n e^{i(n−2k)θ} = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ for
    t_θ = diag(e^{iθ}, e^{−iθ}). (b) ∫f = (2/π)∫₀^π f(θ) sin²θ dθ for class
    functions f.
    Teacher explains: (a) The monomials x^{n−k}yᵏ (k = 0, ..., n) are a
    basis: dim n + 1. The torus element t_θ sends x ↦ e^{iθ}x, y ↦ e^{−iθ}y,
    so x^{n−k}yᵏ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue e^{i(n−2k)θ} — these n +
    1 WEIGHTS are distinct (for generic θ). Irreducibility: let W ⊆ Vₙ be a
    non-zero subrep. It is t_θ-stable, hence spanned by the monomials it
    contains; say x^{n−k}yᵏ ∈ W. Apply r_φ = (c, −s; s, c) ∈ SU(2), c =
    cos φ, s = sin φ: r_φ·x^{n−k}yᵏ = (cx + sy)^{n−k}(−sx + cy)ᵏ has
    x^n-coefficient c^{n−k}(−s)ᵏ ≠ 0, so x^n ∈ W (W is spanned by
    monomials); then r_φ·x^n = (cx + sy)^n has ALL coefficients non-zero,
    so every monomial lies in W: W = Vₙ. Character: every element of
    SU(2) is conjugate to some t_θ, θ ∈ [0, π], and
       χₙ(t_θ) = e^{inθ} + e^{i(n−2)θ} + ... + e^{−inθ}
               = (e^{i(n+1)θ} − e^{−i(n+1)θ})/(e^{iθ} − e^{−iθ})
               = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ.
    (b) The conjugacy class of t_θ is the "latitude sphere" tr = 2cos θ in
    SU(2) ≅ S³, of area ∝ sin²θ, which gives the formula (the normalisation
    (2/π)∫₀^π sin²θ dθ = 1 is correct). Then
       ⟨χ_m, χₙ⟩ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin((m + 1)θ) sin((n + 1)θ) dθ = δ_mn,
    by ordinary Fourier orthogonality of sines on [0, π]. The sin²θ weight
    exactly cancels the denominators: this is the Weyl integration formula
    |Δ|² at work. Since the χₙ are orthonormal and (by Peter-Weyl) span the
    class functions, the Vₙ are ALL the irreps. Common mistakes: using
    uniform measure dθ/π (then ⟨χ₀, χ₂⟩ ≠ 0); forgetting that θ and −θ are
    conjugate (Weyl group Z/2). Now you try: χ₂ at θ = π/3. (sin π/sin(π/3)
    = 0: indeed e^{2iπ/3} + 1 + e^{−2iπ/3} = 0)

D4. (a) Prove the Clebsch-Gordan rule V_m ⊗ Vₙ ≅ ⊕_{k=0}^{min(m,n)}
    V_{m+n−2k} for SU(2). (b) Decompose V₁^{⊗3}, Sym²V₂ and Λ²V₃. (c) Which
    Vₙ factor through SO(3), and what are the irreps of SO(3)?
    Answer: (a) compare characters. (b) V₁^{⊗3} = V₃ ⊕ 2V₁; Sym²V₂ = V₄ ⊕
    V₀; Λ²V₃ = V₄ ⊕ V₀. (c) n even: SO(3) has one irrep of each odd
    dimension 2l + 1.
    Teacher explains: A rep of SU(2) is determined by its character, i.e.
    by its multiset of WEIGHTS (exponents of e^{iθ}). (a) The weights of
    V_m ⊗ Vₙ are the sums (m − 2i) + (n − 2j). Write it as a Laurent
    polynomial in z = e^{iθ}: χ_mχₙ = (z^m + ... + z^{−m})(zⁿ + ... + z^{−n}).
    Peel off the top: the highest weight m + n occurs once, so V_{m+n}
    appears; remove its weights m + n, ..., −(m + n). The next highest
    remaining weight is m + n − 2 (it had multiplicity 2), and so on; the
    multiplicity of weight m + n − 2k is k + 1 for k ≤ min(m, n), so each
    step removes exactly one copy. Dimension check: ∑_{k}(m + n − 2k + 1) =
    (m + 1)(n + 1). (b) V₁ ⊗ V₁ = V₂ ⊕ V₀, so V₁^{⊗3} = (V₂ ⊕ V₀) ⊗ V₁ =
    V₃ ⊕ V₁ ⊕ V₁ (8 = 4 + 2 + 2). Sym²V₂: weights of V₂ are 2, 0, −2;
    pairwise sums with repetition: 4, 2, 0, 0, −2, −4, i.e. V₄ ⊕ V₀ (the
    invariant is the quadratic form x² + y² + z² on R³!). Λ²V₃: weights 3,
    1, −1, −3; sums of distinct pairs: 4, 2, 0, 0, −2, −4, so V₄ ⊕ V₀ (the
    invariant is the symplectic form: V₃ is a quaternionic/symplectic rep).
    (c) −1 ∈ SU(2) acts on Vₙ by (−1)ⁿ, since p(−x, −y) = (−1)ⁿp(x, y). So Vₙ
    descends to SO(3) = SU(2)/{±1} iff n is even; writing n = 2l gives the
    irreps D_l of SO(3), dim 2l + 1 (l = 1 is R³ ⊗ C). Common mistakes:
    confusing dimension n + 1 with label n; "spin j" physicists' notation is
    j = n/2 with dim 2j + 1. Now you try: decompose V₂ ⊗ V₂ ⊗ V₂. (V₆ ⊕
    2V₄ ⊕ 3V₂ ⊕ V₀; 27 = 7 + 10 + 9 + 1)

D5. State the Peter-Weyl theorem and give three consequences. Then
    (a) describe the decomposition of L²(SU(2)) and match it with
    harmonic polynomials on S³ ⊂ R⁴; (b) for g = (a, −b̄; b, ā) ∈ SU(2)
    compute ∫|a|² dg and ∫|a|⁴ dg; (c) decompose L²(S²) under SO(3).
    Answer: (a) L²(SU(2)) = ⊕̂ₙ Vₙ ⊗ Vₙ*, dims (n + 1)²; degree-n harmonics
    on R⁴ have dim (n + 1)². (b) 1/2 and 1/3. (c) ⊕_{l≥0} ℋ_l, each SO(3)
    irrep D_l exactly once.
    Teacher explains: PETER-WEYL: for G compact, (i) the span of matrix
    coefficients g ↦ ⟨π(g)v, w⟩ of f.d. irreps is dense in C(G) (sup norm)
    and in L²(G); (ii) L²(G) ≅ ⊕̂_{π∈Ĝ} V_π ⊗ V_π* under (g, h)·f(x) =
    f(g⁻¹xh), and the functions √(d_π) π_ij form an ONB; (iii) characters
    form an ONB of the class functions in L²(G). Proof idea: convolution
    by a continuous approximate identity is a compact self-adjoint operator
    commuting with right translations; its eigenspaces are f.d. and
    invariant. Consequences: a compact Lie group has a FAITHFUL f.d. rep
    (finitely many irreps already separate points near e, so G ⊆ U(N)); a
    finite group has |G| = ∑d_π²; every irrep occurs in L²(G) with
    multiplicity equal to its dimension. (a) The matrix coefficients of Vₙ
    are polynomials of degree n in a, b, ā, b̄ restricted to S³ = SU(2),
    giving the (n + 1)²-dimensional block End(Vₙ). The space ℋₙ(R⁴) of
    harmonic polynomials of degree n has dimension C(n + 3, 3) − C(n + 1,
    3) = (n + 1)², and indeed L²(S³) = ⊕ℋₙ. (b) (a, b) is uniformly
    distributed on S³ ⊂ C², so by symmetry E|a|² = E|b|² = 1/2 (Schur:
    ∫|π_11|² = 1/dim = 1/2 for V₁). |a|² is uniform on [0, 1]
    (Archimedes on S³), so E|a|⁴ = 1/3; equivalently a² = ⟨g·x², x²⟩ is
    a matrix coefficient of V₂ and Schur gives 1/dim V₂ = 1/3. (c) S² = SO(3)/
    SO(2); by Frobenius reciprocity D_l appears in L²(S²) with multiplicity
    dim D_l^{SO(2)} = 1 (the weight-0 space), giving spherical harmonics
    of degree l, dimension 2l + 1. Common mistakes: forgetting the closure
    ⊕̂ (the sum is a Hilbert direct sum, not algebraic); multiplicity is
    dim π, not 1. Now you try: dim ℋ₃(R³) and dim ℋ₃(R⁴). (7 and 16)

D6. Integration over compact groups. (a) Compute ∫_{SU(2)} (tr g)^{2k} dg
    for k = 1, 2, 3 in two ways: by the Weyl integration formula and by
    counting invariants in V₁^{⊗2k}. (b) Derive the density of the
    rotation angle θ of a Haar-random element of SO(3) and compute the mean
    of tr g and of (tr g)². (c) Show ∫_{U(n)} |tr g|² dg = 1 for n ≥ 1.
    Answer: (a) 1, 2, 5 (Catalan numbers C_k = C(2k, k)/(k + 1)).
    (b) (1 − cos θ)/π on [0, π]; means 0 and 1. (c) Cⁿ is irreducible.
    Teacher explains: (a) tr g = χ₁, so ∫χ₁^{2k} = ⟨χ₁^{2k}, χ₀⟩ = number
    of copies of V₀ in V₁^{⊗2k}. Tensoring with V₁ moves Vₙ to V_{n+1} ⊕
    V_{n−1}, so the multiplicities follow a lattice path from 0 back to 0
    that never goes negative: Dyck paths, counted by Catalan numbers 1, 2,
    5, 14, .... By Weyl integration: (2/π)∫₀^π (2cos θ)^{2k} sin²θ dθ; for
    k = 1: (2/π)∫4cos²θ sin²θ = (2/π)∫sin²2θ = (2/π)(π/2) = 1 ✓; k = 2
    gives 2 and k = 3 gives 5 (use cos²θ sin²θ = (1 − cos 4θ)/8 etc.).
    (b) SO(3) = SU(2)/{±1}, and a unit quaternion with angle θ_q (from the
    SU(2) formula) gives a rotation by θ = 2θ_q, folded into [0, π]. Push
    (2/π) sin²θ_q dθ_q forward: sin²(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/2, dθ_q = dθ/2, and
    both θ_q and π − θ_q give the same rotation angle, so the density is
       2 · (2/π) · ((1 − cos θ)/2) · (1/2) = (1 − cos θ)/π.
    (∫₀^π (1 − cos θ)/π dθ = 1 ✓.) The trace of a rotation by θ is 1 +
    2cos θ = χ of D₁ (irreducible, non-trivial), so ∫tr g = 0 and ∫(tr g)² =
    ⟨χ_{D₁}, χ_{D₁}⟩ = 1. Directly: (1/π)∫(1 + 2cos θ)(1 − cos θ) dθ =
    (1/π)(π − π) = 0 ✓. Small angles are RARE: the density vanishes at θ =
    0. (c) |tr g|² = χ conj(χ) for the standard rep Cⁿ, which is
    irreducible (U(n) acts transitively on unit vectors, so any invariant
    subspace is 0 or Cⁿ). So the integral is ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 1. Common mistakes:
    using the uniform measure dθ/π on SO(3) (it is not Haar); ∫|tr g|⁴
    over U(n) is 2 for n ≥ 2 but 1 for n = 1. Now you try: ∫_{SO(3)}(tr
    g)⁴ dg. (3: D₁^{⊗4} contains the trivial rep 3 times)

D7. Classify the finite-dimensional irreducible representations of 𝔰𝔩₂(C):
    show that each has a basis v₀, ..., vₙ with h vₖ = (n − 2k)vₖ, f vₖ =
    vₖ₊₁, e vₖ = k(n − k + 1)vₖ₋₁. Write the matrices for n = 2 and verify
    the Casimir Ω = h² + 2ef + 2fe acts by n(n + 2).
    Answer: one irrep V(n) for each n ≥ 0; for n = 2, Ω = 8·I.
    Teacher explains: STEP 1 (weights move): if hv = μv then h(ev) = ([h,
    e] + eh)v = (μ + 2)ev and h(fv) = (μ − 2)fv. STEP 2 (highest weight):
    V is f.d., so h has an eigenvector, and applying e repeatedly must end:
    there is v₀ ≠ 0 with hv₀ = λv₀, ev₀ = 0. STEP 3: put vₖ = fᵏv₀. By
    induction e vₖ = k(λ − k + 1)vₖ₋₁: indeed e vₖ₊₁ = e f vₖ = (h + fe)vₖ
    = (λ − 2k)vₖ + k(λ − k + 1)vₖ = (k + 1)(λ − k)vₖ. STEP 4 (integrality):
    the non-zero vₖ have distinct h-eigenvalues λ − 2k, so they are
    independent and some v_{n+1} = 0 with vₙ ≠ 0. Then 0 = e v_{n+1} = (n +
    1)(λ − n)vₙ forces λ = n ∈ Z≥0. STEP 5: span{v₀, ..., vₙ} is stable
    under e, f, h, hence equals V by irreducibility; conversely these
    formulas define a rep for every n (ef − fe on vₖ is (k + 1)(n − k) −
    k(n − k + 1) = n − 2k, the h-eigenvalue ✓). For n = 2 (the adjoint
    representation):
       h = diag(2, 0, −2),  f = (0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 1 0),  e = (0 2 0; 0 0 2;
       0 0 0).
    On v₀: h² = 4, 2ef v₀ = 2e v₁ = 2·2v₀ = 4v₀, 2fe v₀ = 0, so Ω v₀ = 8v₀
    = n(n + 2)v₀. Ω is central in U(𝔰𝔩₂), so by Schur it is 8·I on V(2).
    In general Ω = n² + 2n on V(n); it separates the irreps and is the
    "total angular momentum" 4j(j + 1) with j = n/2. Common mistakes:
    normalising vₖ = fᵏv₀/k! and then using the unnormalised e-formula;
    assuming the highest weight is real without first proving integrality.
    Now you try: in V(4), compute e v₂ and the eigenvalue of Ω. (6v₁; 24)

D8. (a) Define the Verma module M(λ) for 𝔰𝔩₂ and show it is irreducible
    iff λ ∉ Z≥0. (b) For λ = n ∈ Z≥0 find the singular vector and show
    L(n) = M(n)/M(−n − 2). (c) Use this to derive the Weyl character
    formula for 𝔰𝔩₂ and explain the general form ch L(λ) = ∑_w ε(w)
    ch M(w·λ).
    Answer: (a) basis fᵏv, e fᵏv = k(λ − k + 1)f^{k−1}v; (b) f^{n+1}v has
    weight −n − 2 and is killed by e; (c) ch L(n) = (e^{n} − e^{−n−2})/(1
    − e^{−2}) = e^n + e^{n−2} + ... + e^{−n}.
    Teacher explains: (a) M(λ) = U(𝔰𝔩₂) ⊗_{U(𝔟)} C_λ, 𝔟 = span(h, e), is
    the "freest" module generated by v with hv = λv, ev = 0. By PBW, fᵏv (k
    ≥ 0) is a basis, and the computation of D7 gives e fᵏv = k(λ − k +
    1)f^{k−1}v, valid for ANY λ ∈ C. Every submodule is a sum of weight
    spaces; if it contains fᵏv (k ≥ 1), applying e k times gives a non-zero
    multiple of v unless some factor j(λ − j + 1), 1 ≤ j ≤ k, vanishes,
    i.e. λ = j − 1 ∈ Z≥0. So for λ ∉ Z≥0 every non-zero submodule contains v
    and is everything: M(λ) is irreducible (and infinite-dimensional). (b) If
    λ = n, then e f^{n+1}v = (n + 1)(n − n)fⁿv = 0: w = f^{n+1}v is a
    SINGULAR (highest weight) vector of weight n − 2(n + 1) = −n − 2, and
    it generates a copy of M(−n − 2) (itself irreducible, since −n − 2 < 0).
    The quotient has basis v, fv, ..., fⁿv: it is L(n) = V(n). Note −n − 2 =
    s·n = s(n + 1) − 1 with ρ = 1 — the DOT ACTION of the reflection s.
    (c) ch M(λ) = e^λ + e^{λ−2} + ... = e^λ/(1 − e^{−α}) with α = 2. So
       ch L(n) = ch M(n) − ch M(s·n) = (e^{n+1} − e^{−(n+1)})/(e^1 − e^{−1}),
    which is ∑ε(w)e^{w(λ+ρ)}/∑ε(w)e^{wρ} for W = {1, s}; at e^1 = e^{iθ} it
    is sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ (D3). In general the BGG resolution 0 → ... →
    ⊕_{ℓ(w)=k} M(w·λ) → ... → M(λ) → L(λ) → 0 gives ch L(λ) = ∑_w ε(w)
    ch M(w·λ), and dividing by the common denominator ∏(1 − e^{−α}) is
    the WEYL CHARACTER FORMULA. Common mistakes: using the ordinary action
    s(n) = −n instead of the dot action −n − 2; claiming M(λ) has a f.d.
    quotient for non-integral λ. Now you try: for λ = −1, is M(λ)
    irreducible? (yes; −1 ∉ Z≥0, and −1 = s·(−1) is the fixed point of the
    dot action)

D9. Highest weights for 𝔰𝔩₃(C). With 𝔥 = traceless diagonal matrices and
    weights εᵢ (∑εᵢ = 0): (a) list roots, simple roots, fundamental
    weights, ρ and W; (b) find the weights (with multiplicities) of the
    adjoint representation and its highest weight; (c) prove dim L(aω₁ +
    bω₂) = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2 and tabulate small cases;
    (d) decompose C³ ⊗ C³ and C³ ⊗ (C³)*.
    Answer: (a) Φ = {εᵢ − εⱼ}, α₁ = ε₁ − ε₂, α₂ = ε₂ − ε₃, ω₁ = ε₁, ω₂ = ε₁ +
    ε₂, ρ = α₁ + α₂, W = S₃. (b) the 6 roots (mult 1) and 0 (mult 2);
    highest weight ε₁ − ε₃ = ω₁ + ω₂. (c) 3, 3, 6, 8, 10, 15, 27. (d) 3 ⊗ 3
    = 6 ⊕ 3̄ and 3 ⊗ 3̄ = 8 ⊕ 1.
    Teacher explains: (a) E_ij (i ≠ j) satisfies [H, E_ij] = (hᵢ − hⱼ)E_ij,
    so the roots are εᵢ − εⱼ; positive ones (i < j) are α₁, α₂, α₁ + α₂.
    Coroots are αᵢ∨ = Eᵢᵢ − Eᵢ₊₁,ᵢ₊₁; ⟨ε₁, α₁∨⟩ = 1, ⟨ε₁, α₂∨⟩ = 0 so ω₁ = ε₁;
    similarly ω₂ = ε₁ + ε₂ = −ε₃. ρ = ½(α₁ + α₂ + α₁ + α₂) = α₁ + α₂ = ω₁ +
    ω₂. W = N(T)/T permutes the εᵢ: W ≅ S₃, order 6. (b) 𝔰𝔩₃ = 𝔥 ⊕
    ⊕CE_ij: weight 0 with multiplicity dim 𝔥 = 2, each root once. The
    highest (α₁ + α₂ + anything is not a root) is θ = ε₁ − ε₃ = ω₁ + ω₂:
    adjoint = L(1, 1), dim 8 = 6 + 2. (c) λ + ρ = (a + 1)ω₁ + (b + 1)ω₂;
    pairing with α₁∨, α₂∨, (α₁ + α₂)∨ = α₁∨ + α₂∨ gives a + 1, b + 1, a + b
    + 2, and for ρ: 1, 1, 2. So dim = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2:
       (1,0), (0,1): 3   (2,0): 6   (1,1): 8   (3,0): 10   (2,1): 15
       (2,2): 27        (3,3): 64
    (d) Weights of C³ ⊗ C³ are εᵢ + εⱼ: the highest 2ε₁ = 2ω₁ gives L(2, 0) =
    Sym²C³ (dim 6), and the rest is Λ²C³ ≅ (C³)* = L(0, 1): 9 = 6 + 3.
    C³ ⊗ (C³)* = End C³ = 𝔰𝔩₃ ⊕ C·I = L(1, 1) ⊕ L(0, 0): 9 = 8 + 1 (the
    physicists' "meson octet and singlet"). Common mistakes: taking ρ =
    α₁ + α₂ as "half the sum" of only the simple roots; forgetting the
    multiplicity 2 of the zero weight (dimension count 6 + 1 = 7 ≠ 8).
    Now you try: dim L(4, 1) and dim L(1, 3). (35 and 24)

D10. (a) State the Weyl character formula and deduce the Weyl dimension
     formula dim L(λ) = ∏_{α>0}⟨λ + ρ, α∨⟩/⟨ρ, α∨⟩. (b) For B₂ = 𝔰𝔬₅, with
     simple roots α₁ = e₁ − e₂ (long) and α₂ = e₂ (short), find the
     dimensions of L(aω₁ + bω₂). (c) Quote the G₂ answer and compute the two
     fundamental dimensions.
     Answer: (a) evaluate the formula at tρ and let t → 0. (b) dim =
     (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)(2a + b + 3)/6: 5, 4, 10, 14, 16. (c) 7, 14.
     Teacher explains: (a) WCF: ch L(λ) = A_{λ+ρ}/A_ρ, A_μ = ∑_{w∈W} ε(w)
     e^{wμ}, where ε(w) = det w = (−1)^{ℓ(w)}, and A_ρ = ∏_{α>0}(e^{α/2} −
     e^{−α/2}) (DENOMINATOR IDENTITY). dim L(λ) = value of the character at
     0, where both A's vanish, so evaluate along tρ: e^μ ↦ e^{t(μ, ρ)}.
     Since (wμ, ρ) = (μ, w⁻¹ρ), A_μ(tρ) = A_ρ(tμ), and the denominator
     identity gives A_μ(tρ) = ∏_{α>0}(e^{t(μ,α)/2} − e^{−t(μ,α)/2}). Hence
        dim L(λ) = lim_{t→0} ∏_{α>0} (2 sinh(t(λ + ρ, α)/2))/(2 sinh(t(ρ,
        α)/2)) = ∏_{α>0} (λ + ρ, α)/(ρ, α),
     and (·, α) may be replaced by ⟨·, α∨⟩ (same factor 2/(α, α) top and
     bottom). (b) Φ⁺ = {e₁ − e₂, e₂, e₁, e₁ + e₂}; ω₁ = e₁ (vector rep),
     ω₂ = (e₁ + e₂)/2 (spin rep); ρ = (3/2, 1/2). With λ + ρ = (a + b/2 +
     3/2, b/2 + 1/2), the coroots e₁ − e₂, 2e₂, 2e₁, e₁ + e₂ give
        a + 1,  b + 1,  2a + b + 3,  a + b + 2;   for ρ: 1, 1, 3, 2.
     So dim = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)(2a + b + 3)/6: (1, 0) → 5 (C⁵),
     (0, 1) → 4 (spinors; Sp₄ = Spin₅), (0, 2) → 10 (adjoint), (2, 0) → 14
     (traceless Sym²C⁵), (1, 1) → 16. (c) For G₂ (ω₁ short) dim L(a, b) =
     (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)(a + 2b + 3)(a + 3b + 4)(2a + 3b + 5)/120:
     (1, 0) → 2·1·3·4·5·7/120 = 7 and (0, 1) → 1·2·3·5·7·8/120 = 14 (the
     adjoint). Common mistakes: using ⟨λ, α∨⟩ without adding ρ (gives 0 for
     λ = 0); mixing up long and short roots in B₂/C₂. Now you try: dim of
     the G₂ representation L(1, 1), and |W(G₂)|. (64; 12)

D11. Reductive algebraic groups (over k = k̄). (a) Show that G_a and the
     Borel subgroup B ⊂ GL₂ of upper triangular matrices are not reductive,
     while GLₙ is. (b) Compute the root data of SL₂, PGL₂ and GL₂, and read
     off the centres and fundamental groups. (c) For GL₃ in characteristic
     0, find dim S_{(2,1)}(k³) and check Schur-Weyl for (k³)^{⊗3}. (d) Show
     Sym²(k²) is reducible for SL₂ when char k = 2, and find dim L(n) for
     p = 3, n = 4, 5, 8.
     Answer: (a) R_u(G_a) = G_a, R_u(B) = {(1 x; 0 1)}; R_u(GLₙ) = 1.
     (b) SL₂: (Z, {±2}, Z, {±1}); PGL₂: (Z, {±1}, Z, {±2}); GL₂: (Z², {±(1,
     −1)}, Z², {±(1, −1)}). Z(SL₂) = μ₂, π₁(PGL₂) = Z/2. (c) 8; 27 = 10 +
     2·8 + 1. (d) span{x², y²}; dims 4, 6, 9.
     Teacher explains: (a) G_a is itself connected unipotent (t ↦ (1 t; 0
     1)), so R_u(G_a) = G_a ≠ 1; in char 0 its rep of D1(c) is not
     completely reducible. In B the unipotent matrices U = {(1 x; 0 1)} form
     a connected normal unipotent subgroup (B/U ≅ G_m²), so R_u(B) ⊇ U ≠ 1.
     For GLₙ, R_u is normal and unipotent, so it fixes a non-zero vector
     of kⁿ; the fixed space is GLₙ-stable, hence all of kⁿ, so R_u = 1.
     (b) SL₂: T = {diag(t, t⁻¹)}, X*(T) = Zχ with χ(diag(t, t⁻¹)) = t;
     conjugation scales e = E₁₂ by t², so α = 2χ; the coroot t ↦ diag(t,
     t⁻¹) generates X_*(T), so α∨ = 1 and ⟨α, α∨⟩ = 2 ✓. PGL₂: T = image of
     diag(t, 1); α(t) = t so α = 1, and α∨ : t ↦ diag(t, t⁻¹) = diag(t², 1)
     is twice the generator: α∨ = 2. Same root system A₁, different root
     data, non-isomorphic groups. The centre is read from X*/ZΦ (Z/2 for
     SL₂, trivial for PGL₂) and π₁ from X_*/ZΦ∨ (trivial for SL₂, Z/2 for
     PGL₂). GL₂: X* = Z² (diag(t₁, t₂) ↦ t₁^{m}t₂^{n}), α = e₁ − e₂ = α∨.
     By CHEVALLEY's classification root data ↔ connected reductive groups;
     irreducible reps ↔ dominant λ ∈ X*(T): for SL₂, λ = n ≥ 0; for GL₂, λ₁
     ≥ λ₂ in Z (e.g. det = (1, 1), det⁻¹ ⊗ Sym² = (1, −1)). (c) HOOK-CONTENT:
     dim S_λ(kⁿ) = ∏_{boxes}(n + c)/h, c = column − row. For λ = (2, 1),
     n = 3: contents 0, 1, −1, hooks 3, 1, 1: (3·4·2)/3 = 8 (≅ 𝔰𝔩₃ ⊗ det:
     highest weight (2, 1, 0) = (1, 0, −1) + (1, 1, 1)). Schur-
     Weyl: (k³)^{⊗3} = S₍₃₎ ⊗ 1 ⊕ S₍₂,₁₎ ⊗ Specht₍₂,₁₎ ⊕ S₍₁,₁,₁₎ ⊗ sgn, dims
     10·1 + 8·2 + 1·1 = 27 ✓. (d) In char 2, g·x² = (ax + by)² = a²x² + b²y²
     (the cross term 2abxy vanishes), so span{x², y²} ≅ the Frobenius twist
     V^{[1]} is a proper subrep of the 3-dimensional Weyl module. STEINBERG:
     dim L(n) = ∏(dᵢ + 1) over base-p digits: 4 = 11₃ → 2·2 = 4; 5 = 12₃ →
     2·3 = 6 (= dim Sym⁵: irreducible); 8 = 22₃ → 3·3 = 9 (Steinberg module,
     p² − 1). Common mistakes: calling O₂ or a torus non-reductive (both
     are reductive; tori have no roots); assuming complete reducibility for
     reductive groups in char p. Now you try: the root datum of G_m. (X* =
     X_* = Z, no roots)

D12. The quantum group U_q(𝔰𝔩₂), q not a root of unity. (a) Verify that
     K mᵢ = q^{n−2i}mᵢ, F mᵢ = mᵢ₊₁ (F mₙ = 0), E mᵢ = [i][n − i + 1]mᵢ₋₁
     defines a representation L(n) of dimension n + 1. (b) Show that the
     quantum Casimir C = EF + (q⁻¹K + qK⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹)² acts on L(n) by
     (q^{n+1} + q^{−n−1})/(q − q⁻¹)², and compute the quantum dimension
     tr_{L(n)}(K). (c) Using Δ(E) = E ⊗ K + 1 ⊗ E, find the highest weight
     vector of L(0) inside L(1) ⊗ L(1). (d) What changes at q = e^{2πi/3}?
     Answer: (a) reduces to [i + 1][n − i] − [i][n − i + 1] = [n − 2i].
     (b) [n + 1] = q^n + q^{n−2} + ... + q^{−n}. (c) m₁ ⊗ m₀ − q m₀ ⊗ m₁.
     (d) [3] = q² + 1 + q⁻² = 0: the module with n = 3 becomes reducible.
     Teacher explains: (a) KEK⁻¹ = q²E: E raises the K-eigenvalue from
     q^{n−2i} to q^{n−2i+2} ✓; similarly for F. The key relation on mᵢ:
        (EF − FE)mᵢ = ([i + 1][n − i] − [i][n − i + 1])mᵢ,
     and (K − K⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹) mᵢ = [n − 2i]mᵢ. The identity [a + 1][b] −
     [a][b + 1] = [b − a] follows by multiplying out: (q − q⁻¹)² times the
     left side is (q^{a+1} − q^{−a−1})(q^b − q^{−b}) − (q^a − q^{−a})(q^{b+1} −
     q^{−b−1}) = −q^{a−b+1} − q^{b−a−1} + q^{a−b−1} + q^{b−a+1} = (q^{b−a} −
     q^{a−b})(q − q⁻¹). Also E m₀ = [0][n + 1]m₋₁ = 0 and F mₙ = 0 cut the
     string off. As q → 1, [k] → k and we recover V(n) of 𝔰𝔩₂ with e vᵢ =
     i(n − i + 1)vᵢ₋₁ (D7). (b) On m₀: EF m₀ = [1][n]m₀ = [n]m₀, and
        [n] + (q^{n−1} + q^{1−n})/(q − q⁻¹)²
        = ((q^n − q^{−n})(q − q⁻¹) + q^{n−1} + q^{1−n})/(q − q⁻¹)²
        = (q^{n+1} + q^{−n−1})/(q − q⁻¹)².
     C is central (check against E, F, K), so it acts by this scalar on
     the irreducible L(n). tr K = ∑ q^{n−2i} = [n + 1] → n + 1 as q → 1.
     (c) Weights (K-eigenvalues) of L(1) ⊗ L(1) are q², 1, 1, q⁻²; so L(1) ⊗
     L(1) = L(2) ⊕ L(0) as for 𝔰𝔩₂. The L(0) vector v = x m₀ ⊗ m₁ + y m₁ ⊗
     m₀ must satisfy Δ(E)v = 0. Since E m₀ = 0, E m₁ = m₀, K m₀ = q m₀:
        Δ(E)v = x(E m₀ ⊗ K m₁ + m₀ ⊗ E m₁) + y(E m₁ ⊗ K m₀ + m₁ ⊗ E m₀)
              = (x + q y) m₀ ⊗ m₀,
     so v = m₁ ⊗ m₀ − q m₀ ⊗ m₁: a q-DEFORMED antisymmetric tensor, which
     shows that the flip V ⊗ W → W ⊗ V is NOT a module map (Δ is not
     cocommutative); the R-matrix repairs it. (d) q = e^{2πi/3} gives q³ = 1
     and [3] = q² + 1 + q⁻² = q² + 1 + q = 0. In the 4-dimensional module
     with n = 3, E m₁ = [1][3]m₀ = 0, so span{m₁, m₂, m₃} is a proper
     submodule: complete reducibility fails. Moreover E³, F³, K³ become
     central (KE³K⁻¹ = q⁶E³ = E³), and irreps have dimension ≤ 3.
     Common mistakes: using E ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ E as coproduct (not an algebra map
     for q ≠ 1); forgetting the second family L(n, −) with K acting by
     −q^{n−2i}. Now you try: at q = e^{πi/5}, compute [2]. (2cos(π/5) =
     (1 + √5)/2, the golden ratio)

M6. Verma modules, the dot action and partition functions.
    a) 𝔰𝔩₂, M(3): the singular vector and its weight
    b) is M(−3) irreducible?         c) is M(1/2) irreducible?
    d) e f³v in M(λ)                 e) λ = 5: the k ≥ 1 with e fᵏv = 0
    f) s·λ = −λ − 2: s·3, s·(−1), s·(−4)
    g) ch M(λ) and ch L(4) as a difference of Verma characters
    h) 𝔰𝔩₃: Kostant partition function p(α₁ + α₂)
    i) p(2α₁ + α₂)          j) p(2α₁ + 2α₂)          k) p(3α₁)
    l) dim of the weight space λ − α₁ − α₂ in M(λ) for 𝔰𝔩₃
    m) 𝔰𝔩₃: the six weights w·0 (in terms of α₁, α₂)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every f.d. representation of a compact group is completely
        reducible.
     b) Every f.d. representation of (R, +) is completely reducible.
     c) Every irreducible real representation of an abelian group is
        1-dimensional.
     d) Every irreducible unitary representation of a compact group is
        finite-dimensional.
     e) SL(2, R) has a non-trivial finite-dimensional unitary rep.
     f) Characters determine f.d. reps of a compact group up to
        isomorphism.
     g) For dim V ≥ 2, V ⊗ V is never irreducible.
     h) The highest weight of the adjoint rep of a simple 𝔤 is the highest
        root.
     i) Every Verma module is reducible.
     j) Every f.d. representation of G_a over C is completely reducible.
     k) SL₂ ≅ PGL₂ as algebraic groups over C.
     l) For SL₂ in characteristic p, Sym^n(k²) is always irreducible.
     m) Distinct dominant weights give non-isomorphic irreps, even when
        their dimensions agree.
     n) Δ on U_q(𝔰𝔩₂) is cocommutative.
     o) Every compact Lie group is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of some
        U(N).
     p) SL(2, R) has finite total Haar measure.
     q) The Weyl group acts simply transitively on the Weyl chambers.
     r) Every representation of U_q(𝔰𝔩₂) is completely reducible at a
        root of unity.
     Answers:
       a) T       b) F: t ↦ (1 t; 0 1)
       c) F: rotations of R² by SO(2) (irreducible over R, dim 2)
       d) T (Peter-Weyl)      e) F: every f.d. unitary rep is trivial
       f) T       g) T (Sym²V and Λ²V are both non-zero subreps)
       h) T       i) F: M(−1) for 𝔰𝔩₂ (M(λ) with λ ∉ Z≥0)
       j) F: the same (1 t; 0 1)
       k) F: centres μ₂ and 1 (same Lie algebra, different root data)
       l) F: n = p, the subrep span{x^p, y^p}
       m) T: e.g. G₂ L(0, 2) and L(3, 0), both of dim 77
       n) F: Δ(E) = E ⊗ K + 1 ⊗ E ≠ K ⊗ E + E ⊗ 1
       o) T       p) F: SL(2, R) has infinite Haar measure (only compact
                     groups have finite Haar measure)
       q) T       r) F: q = e^{2πi/3}, the module with n = 3 (D12)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: reduce everything to WEIGHTS. A representation of SU(2) or
  𝔰𝔩₂ is a symmetric unbroken multiset of integers; decomposing means
  repeatedly peeling off the highest string, and a character is just this
  multiset written as a Laurent polynomial. Draw the weight diagrams of
  𝔰𝔩₃ (triangles for 3, 3̄; the hexagon with a doubled centre for 8) and
  let students find tensor products by adding diagrams before touching
  formulas. Always check a decomposition by dimension, and every Haar
  integral by the normalisation ∫1 = 1. For U_q(𝔰𝔩₂), write everything
  first at q = 1 and only then insert q-integers. Harder: prove Peter-Weyl
  via compact convolution operators; derive the Weyl integration formula
  from the map G/T × T → G and prove the Weyl character formula from it
  (Weyl's original analytic proof); prove the denominator identity and
  Kostant's multiplicity formula; show that Sym²V and Λ²V decide whether
  an irrep is real, quaternionic or complex (Frobenius-Schur indicator);
  prove Borel-Weil for SL₂ via H⁰(P¹, O(n)); verify Steinberg's tensor
  product theorem for SL₂ in characteristic 3 up to n = 8; and construct
  the R-matrix of U_q(𝔰𝔩₂) on L(1) ⊗ L(1) and check the Yang-Baxter
  equation.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.18 — HARMONIC ANALYSIS: FOURIER ANALYSIS ON GROUPS, SINGULAR
INTEGRALS, CALDERÓN-ZYGMUND THEORY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CONVENTIONS used throughout: on R^n, f̂(ξ) = ∫ f(x) e^(−2πix·ξ) dx, so
    (e^(−π|x|²))^ = e^(−π|ξ|²), ∂ⱼ ↔ 2πiξⱼ and Δ ↔ −4π²|ξ|²; on T = R/Z,
    f̂(k) = ∫₀¹ f(x) e^(−2πikx) dx; on Z/N, f̂(k) = ∑ₙ f(n) e^(−2πikn/N).
  - HAAR MEASURE AND CHARACTERS: every locally compact group G carries a
    left-invariant Radon measure, unique up to a constant (dx on Rⁿ,
    counting on Z, dx/|x| on R^×; left da db/a², right da db/a on the
    ax + b group). Compact groups are unimodular. A CHARACTER of an
    abelian G is a continuous homomorphism χ : G → T = {|z| = 1}; they
    form the DUAL GROUP Ĝ. Standard duals: R̂ = R (x ↦ e^(2πixξ)),
    T̂ = Z, Ẑ = T, (Z/N)^ ≅ Z/N, (G × H)^ = Ĝ × Ĥ, Q_p self-dual.
  - PONTRYAGIN DUALITY: the evaluation map G → (Ĝ)^ is an isomorphism;
    G compact ⇔ Ĝ discrete. FOURIER TRANSFORM f̂(χ) = ∫_G f(x) χ̄(x) dx;
    (f ∗ g)^ = f̂ ĝ, Riemann-Lebesgue (f̂ ∈ C₀(Ĝ)), and with Haar measure
    on Ĝ suitably normalised: INVERSION and PLANCHEREL ‖f̂‖₂ = ‖f‖₂.
  - FINITE GROUPS: characters of a finite abelian G are orthonormal for
    ⟨f, g⟩ = (1/|G|)∑ f ḡ, there are exactly |G| of them, and the DFT
    satisfies f(n) = (1/N)∑ₖ f̂(k)e^(2πikn/N), ∑|f|² = (1/N)∑|f̂|²; the FFT
    costs O(N log N). NONABELIAN (Peter-Weyl): f̂(π) = ∑ f(g)π(g)*, the
    irreducible π satisfy ∑ d_π² = |G| (S₃: 1 + 1 + 4 = 6) and
    f(e) = (1/|G|)∑ d_π tr f̂(π).
  - FOURIER SERIES: Sₙf = Dₙ ∗ f with DIRICHLET kernel Dₙ(x) =
    sin((2N + 1)πx)/sin(πx), ‖Dₙ‖₁ = (4/π²)ln N + O(1) → ∞, so (uniform
    boundedness) some continuous f has a divergent Fourier series at 0
    (du Bois-Reymond); Kolmogorov: some f ∈ L¹ diverges a.e.; CARLESON:
    Sₙf → f a.e. for f ∈ L² (Hunt: Lᵖ, p > 1). FEJÉR kernel Fₙ =
    (1/N)(sin(Nπx)/sin(πx))² ≥ 0: σₙf → f uniformly for continuous f and
    in Lᵖ, 1 ≤ p < ∞. Sₙf → f in Lᵖ for 1 < p < ∞ (by boundedness of H).
  - APPROXIMATE IDENTITIES φ_t(x) = t⁻ⁿφ(x/t) with ∫φ = 1: φ_t ∗ f → f in
    Lᵖ (p < ∞); if φ has a radially decreasing integrable majorant then
    sup_t |φ_t ∗ f| ≤ ‖ψ‖₁Mf (ψ the majorant) and φ_t ∗ f → f a.e.
    Examples: Poisson P_t(x) = t/(π(t² + x²)), P̂_t = e^(−2πt|ξ|); heat kernel
    (4πt)^(−n/2)e^(−|x|²/4t), transform e^(−4π²t|ξ|²).
  - Rⁿ: Schwartz space 𝒮 is invariant under ^; PLANCHEREL extends ^ to a
    unitary on L²; POISSON SUMMATION ∑ f(n) = ∑ f̂(k) (theta function
    ∑e^(−πtn²) = t^(−1/2)∑e^(−πk²/t)); HEISENBERG ‖xf‖₂‖ξf̂‖₂ ≥
    ‖f‖₂²/(4π), equality for Gaussians.
  - INTERPOLATION: RIESZ-THORIN (complex method): if ‖T‖ ≤ M₀ on
    L^p₀ → L^q₀ and M₁ on L^p₁ → L^q₁ then ‖T‖ ≤ M₀^(1−θ)M₁^θ on Lᵖ → L^q,
    1/p = (1 − θ)/p₀ + θ/p₁, 1/q = (1 − θ)/q₀ + θ/q₁. Gives
    HAUSDORFF-YOUNG ‖f̂‖_p′ ≤ ‖f‖_p (1 ≤ p ≤ 2) and YOUNG ‖f ∗ g‖_r ≤
    ‖f‖_p‖g‖_q, 1 + 1/r = 1/p + 1/q. MARCINKIEWICZ: sublinear T of weak
    types (p₀, p₀) and (p₁, p₁) is strong type (p, p) in between.
  - WEAK Lᵖ: ‖f‖_{p,∞} = sup_λ λ|{|f| > λ}|^(1/p); |x|^(−n/p) ∈ L^{p,∞}
    ∖ Lᵖ. Chebyshev: Lᵖ ⊆ L^{p,∞}.
  - HARDY-LITTLEWOOD MAXIMAL FUNCTION Mf(x) = sup_r |B(x,r)|⁻¹∫_B |f|.
    VITALI covering lemma (disjoint subfamily with 3× dilates covering)
    ⇒ WEAK (1,1): |{Mf > λ}| ≤ 3ⁿ‖f‖₁/λ; trivially ‖Mf‖_∞ ≤ ‖f‖_∞; so
    ‖Mf‖_p ≤ C_p‖f‖_p for 1 < p ≤ ∞, but Mf ∉ L¹ unless f = 0
    (Mf ≳ |x|⁻ⁿ). Consequence: LEBESGUE DIFFERENTIATION THEOREM, a.e.
    point is a Lebesgue point.
  - HILBERT TRANSFORM Hf(x) = (1/π) p.v.∫ f(y)/(x − y) dy, multiplier
    −i sgn ξ: H² = −I, H* = −H, ‖Hf‖₂ = ‖f‖₂, H cos = sin, f + iHf is the
    boundary value of an analytic function on the upper half-plane
    (conjugate function). H𝟙_[a,b] = (1/π)ln|(x − a)/(x − b)|, so H is
    NOT bounded on L¹ or L^∞. M. RIESZ: ‖Hf‖_p ≤ A_p‖f‖_p, 1 < p < ∞,
    sharp A_p = cot(π/2p*), p* = max(p, p′) (Pichorides).
  - CALDERÓN-ZYGMUND DECOMPOSITION: for f ∈ L¹(Rⁿ), λ > 0 there are
    disjoint dyadic cubes Qⱼ with λ < (1/|Qⱼ|)∫_Qⱼ |f| ≤ 2ⁿλ, |f| ≤ λ a.e.
    off ⋃Qⱼ, ∑|Qⱼ| ≤ ‖f‖₁/λ; f = g + ∑bⱼ with ‖g‖_∞ ≤ 2ⁿλ, ‖g‖₁ ≤ ‖f‖₁,
    supp bⱼ ⊆ Qⱼ, ∫bⱼ = 0, ‖bⱼ‖₁ ≤ 2∫_Qⱼ |f|.
  - CALDERÓN-ZYGMUND THEOREM: let T be bounded on L²(Rⁿ) with Tf = K ∗ f
    off supp f, where |K(x)| ≤ A|x|⁻ⁿ and the HÖRMANDER condition
    ∫_{|x|>2|y|} |K(x − y) − K(x)| dx ≤ B holds (implied by |∇K| ≤
    A|x|^(−n−1)). Then T is weak (1,1), bounded on Lᵖ for 1 < p < ∞ and
    L^∞ → BMO. Model kernels K = Ω(x/|x|)/|x|ⁿ with Ω smooth and MEAN
    ZERO on the sphere; 1/|x|ⁿ itself is not allowed.
  - RIESZ TRANSFORMS Rⱼ: multiplier −iξⱼ/|ξ|, kernel cₙxⱼ/|x|^(n+1),
    cₙ = Γ((n+1)/2)/π^((n+1)/2); ∑Rⱼ² = −I and ∂ⱼ∂ₖΔ⁻¹ = −RⱼRₖ, hence
    ELLIPTIC Lᵖ ESTIMATE ‖∂ⱼ∂ₖu‖_p ≤ C_p‖Δu‖_p (1 < p < ∞, false at
    p = 1, ∞). MIKHLIN-HÖRMANDER: |∂^α m(ξ)| ≤ C|ξ|^(−|α|) for |α| ≤
    ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 ⇒ m is an Lᵖ multiplier, 1 < p < ∞. Counterexample to
    naive hopes: the ball multiplier 𝟙_B (n ≥ 2) is bounded only on L²
    (C. Fefferman).
  - BMO: ‖f‖_* = sup_Q (1/|Q|)∫_Q |f − f_Q| < ∞; L^∞ ⊊ BMO (ln|x|, mean
    oscillation 2/e on every [0, a]); JOHN-NIRENBERG: |{x ∈ Q : |f − f_Q|
    > λ}| ≤ C|Q|e^(−cλ/‖f‖_*); FEFFERMAN: (H¹)* = BMO. A_p WEIGHTS:
    sup_Q (⨍w)(⨍w^(−1/(p−1)))^(p−1) < ∞ ⇔ M (and H) bounded on Lᵖ(w);
    |x|^a ∈ A_p(Rⁿ) ⇔ −n < a < n(p − 1).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Prove that every continuous character of R is x ↦ e^(2πixξ) for
    a unique ξ ∈ R, and deduce T̂ = Z and Ẑ = T. (b) In G = Z/4 × Z/6
    evaluate χ_(1,5)(3, 2), where χ_(a,b)(m, n) = e^(2πi(am/4 + bn/6)),
    and say how many characters G has.
    Answer: (a) χ′ = χ′(0)χ forces χ = e^(cx), |χ| = 1 ⇒ c = 2πiξ.
    (b) e^(2πi·5/12) = e^(5πi/6); 24 characters.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let χ : R → T be a continuous homomorphism. As
    χ(0) = 1 and χ is continuous, choose δ > 0 with c = ∫₀^δ χ(t) dt ≠ 0
    (the integral is ≈ δ for small δ). Then
       χ(x)c = ∫₀^δ χ(x + t) dt = ∫ₓ^{x+δ} χ(s) ds,
    and the right side is differentiable in x (FTC). So χ = (1/c)·(that)
    is C¹, and differentiating χ(x + y) = χ(x)χ(y) in y at y = 0 gives
    χ′(x) = χ′(0)χ(x), so χ(x) = e^(ax), a = χ′(0). |χ| = 1 forces a
    purely imaginary: a = 2πiξ. Uniqueness is clear. For T = R/Z a
    character is a character of R trivial on Z: e^(2πiξ) = 1 ⇔ ξ = k ∈ Z,
    so T̂ = Z. For Z a character is determined by z = χ(1) ∈ T (χ(n) =
    zⁿ), so Ẑ = T. Notice the pattern: compact T ↔ discrete Z. (b) The
    exponent is 1·3/4 + 5·2/6 = 3/4 + 5/3 = 29/12 ≡ 5/12, so the value is
    e^(5πi/6) = −√3/2 + i/2. A finite abelian group has |G| = 24
    characters and Ĝ ≅ G (non-canonically). Common mistakes: forgetting
    continuity (with the axiom of choice there are wild homomorphisms
    R → T); confusing Ĝ ≅ G for finite G (non-canonical) with Pontryagin
    duality G ≅ (Ĝ)^ (canonical). Now you try: list the characters of
    Z/2 × Z/2. (four sign patterns: (m, n) ↦ (−1)^(am+bn), a, b ∈ {0, 1})

D2. On Z/4 compute the DFT of f = (1, 2, 0, 1), verify Plancherel, and
    prove the orthogonality relation ∑ₙ e^(2πi(k−l)n/N) = Nδ_{kl} and the
    inversion formula. Then state the analogue for the nonabelian group
    S₃.
    Answer: f̂ = (4, 1 − i, −2, 1 + i); ∑|f|² = 6 = (16 + 2 + 4 + 2)/4.
    Teacher explains: With ω = e^(−2πi/4) = −i, f̂(k) = ∑ₙ f(n)(−i)^(kn):
       f̂(0) = 1 + 2 + 0 + 1 = 4,  f̂(1) = 1 − 2i + 0 + i = 1 − i,
       f̂(2) = 1 − 2 + 0 − 1 = −2, f̂(3) = 1 + 2i + 0 − i = 1 + i.
    (f is real, so f̂(3) = conj f̂(1): a free check.) Orthogonality: if
    k = l every term is 1; otherwise z = e^(2πi(k−l)/N) ≠ 1 is an N-th
    root of unity and ∑ₙ zⁿ = (z^N − 1)/(z − 1) = 0. Inversion: (1/N)∑ₖ
    f̂(k)e^(2πikn/N) = (1/N)∑ₘ f(m)∑ₖ e^(2πik(n−m)/N) = f(n). Plancherel
    follows the same way: ∑ₖ|f̂(k)|² = N∑|f(n)|². Here (1/4)(16 + 2 + 4 +
    2) = 6 = 1 + 4 + 0 + 1 ✓. For S₃ the "frequencies" are the irreducible
    representations: trivial, sign (dimension 1) and the 2-dimensional
    standard one; ∑d_π² = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 = |S₃|, f̂(π) = ∑_g f(g)π(g)* is a
    d_π × d_π matrix, and Plancherel reads ∑|f(g)|² = (1/6)∑ d_π‖f̂(π)‖²_HS.
    Common mistakes: sign of the exponent (forward −, inverse +);
    forgetting the 1/N in exactly one of the two formulas. Now you try:
    DFT of δ₀ and of (1, 1, 1, 1) on Z/4. ((1, 1, 1, 1) and (4, 0, 0, 0))

D3. (a) Show Dₙ(x) = ∑_{|k|≤N} e^(2πikx) = sin((2N + 1)πx)/sin(πx) and
    that the Fejér kernel Fₙ = (1/N)∑_{n<N} Dₙ equals (1/N)(sin Nπx/sin
    πx)². (b) Prove Fejér's theorem for continuous f. (c) Use Parseval
    for f(x) = x − 1/2 on [0, 1) to find ∑1/k².
    Answer: (a) geometric sums; (b) Fₙ is a positive approximate
    identity; (c) f̂(k) = i/(2πk), ∑1/k² = π²/6.
    Teacher explains: (a) With z = e^(2πix), Dₙ = z^(−N)(z^(2N+1) − 1)/
    (z − 1); multiply top and bottom by z^(−1/2) to get (z^(N+1/2) −
    z^(−N−1/2))/(z^(1/2) − z^(−1/2)) = sin((2N + 1)πx)/sin πx. Summing,
    sin πx·∑_{n<N} sin((2n + 1)πx) = ∑(cos 2nπx − cos 2(n + 1)πx)/2 =
    (1 − cos 2Nπx)/2 = sin²Nπx, which gives the formula for Fₙ.
    (b) Fₙ ≥ 0, ∫₀¹Fₙ = 1 (only k = 0 survives), and for δ ≤ |x| ≤ 1/2,
    Fₙ(x) ≤ 1/(N sin²πδ) → 0. So with ω the modulus of continuity,
       |σₙf(x) − f(x)| ≤ ∫ Fₙ(y)|f(x − y) − f(x)| dy
                       ≤ ω(δ) + 2‖f‖_∞/(N sin²πδ),
    uniformly in x: first pick δ, then N. The same argument FAILS for Dₙ
    because ‖Dₙ‖₁ ~ (4/π²)ln N → ∞ (≈ 2.2234 for N = 10): Dₙ is not a
    bounded approximate identity. (c) ∫₀¹ x e^(−2πikx) dx = −1/(2πik) =
    i/(2πk) for k ≠ 0, and f̂(0) = 0. Parseval: ∑_{k≠0} 1/(4π²k²) =
    ∫₀¹(x − 1/2)² dx = 1/12, so 2ζ(2)/(4π²) = 1/12, ζ(2) = π²/6. Common
    mistakes: thinking Fourier series of continuous functions converge
    (they need not; Fejér means do); forgetting k < 0 in Parseval. Now you
    try: Parseval for 𝟙_[0,1/2) gives ∑_{k odd ≥ 1} 1/k² = ? (π²/8)

D4. (a) Compute the Fourier transform of 𝟙_[−1/2,1/2] and use
    Plancherel to evaluate ∫_R (sin x/x)² dx. (b) Prove the Poisson
    summation formula for f ∈ 𝒮(R) and deduce the theta identity
    ∑ e^(−πtn²) = t^(−1/2)∑ e^(−πk²/t). Check it numerically at t = 2.
    Answer: (a) sin(πξ)/(πξ); ∫(sin x/x)² = π. (b) both sides ≈ 1.003735.
    Teacher explains: (a) ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} e^(−2πixξ) dx = (e^(πiξ) −
    e^(−πiξ))/(2πiξ) = sin(πξ)/(πξ). Plancherel: ∫|sin πξ/(πξ)|² dξ =
    ∫|𝟙|² = 1; substitute x = πξ: (1/π)∫(sin x/x)² dx = 1. (b) Periodise:
    F(x) = ∑ₙ f(x + n) is smooth and 1-periodic (rapid decay makes the
    series converge with all derivatives). Its Fourier coefficients are
       F̂(k) = ∫₀¹ ∑ₙ f(x + n)e^(−2πikx) dx = ∫_R f(y)e^(−2πiky) dy = f̂(k),
    so F(x) = ∑ₖ f̂(k)e^(2πikx) and x = 0 gives ∑f(n) = ∑f̂(k). This is
    Fourier analysis on the pair Z ⊆ R with R/Z = T. For f = e^(−πtx²),
    f̂(ξ) = t^(−1/2)e^(−πξ²/t) (scaling the self-dual Gaussian). At t = 2:
    LHS = 1 + 2e^(−2π) + ... ≈ 1.003735, RHS = (1/√2)(1 + 2e^(−π/2) +
    2e^(−2π) + ...) ≈ 1.003735 ✓. Common mistakes: using 1/(2π) normal-
    isations inconsistently; applying Poisson to f with slow decay (e.g.
    f = 𝟙_[0,1] where the endpoints give half values). Now you try:
    ∑_{n∈Z} 1/(1 + n²) using (1/(1 + x²))^ = πe^(−2π|ξ|). (π coth π ≈
    3.15335)

D5. State the Riesz-Thorin theorem and use it to prove (a) the
    Hausdorff-Young inequality ‖f̂‖_p′ ≤ ‖f‖_p for 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, and (b)
    Young's inequality ‖f ∗ g‖_p ≤ ‖f‖₁‖g‖_p. (c) An operator has norm 2
    on L¹ and norm 8 on L^∞. Bound its norm on L² and on L⁴.
    Answer: (a) interpolate L¹ → L^∞ (norm 1) and L² → L² (norm 1);
    (b) interpolate between p = 1 and p = ∞; (c) 4 and 4√2 ≈ 5.657.
    Teacher explains: RIESZ-THORIN: T linear, ‖T‖_{p₀→q₀} ≤ M₀,
    ‖T‖_{p₁→q₁} ≤ M₁ (1 ≤ pᵢ, qᵢ ≤ ∞, complex scalars) ⇒ for 0 < θ < 1
    ‖T‖_{p_θ→q_θ} ≤ M₀^(1−θ)M₁^θ with 1/p_θ = (1 − θ)/p₀ + θ/p₁ and
    similarly for q. The proof applies Hadamard's three-lines lemma to
    z ↦ ∫(Tf_z)g_z, where f_z, g_z move the exponents analytically.
    (a) |f̂(ξ)| ≤ ∫|f| gives ‖f̂‖_∞ ≤ ‖f‖₁; Plancherel gives ‖f̂‖₂ = ‖f‖₂.
    For 1/p = (1 − θ)/1 + θ/2 = 1 − θ/2 the target exponent is 1/q =
    (1 − θ)/∞ + θ/2 = θ/2 = 1 − 1/p, i.e. q = p′, and the constant is
    1^(1−θ)1^θ = 1. E.g. p = 4/3: θ = 1/2, q = 4. (b) For fixed f ∈ L¹
    the map g ↦ f ∗ g has norm ≤ ‖f‖₁ on L¹ (Fubini) and on L^∞
    (trivial); interpolate. The general Young inequality 1 + 1/r = 1/p +
    1/q follows by interpolating again. (c) L²: 1/2 = (1 − θ)/1 + θ/∞
    gives θ = 1/2, bound 2^(1/2)8^(1/2) = 4. L⁴: 1/4 = 1 − θ gives θ =
    3/4, bound 2^(1/4)8^(3/4) = 2^(1/4 + 9/4) = 2^(5/2) = 4√2. Common
    mistakes: interpolating the exponents p instead of their RECIPROCALS;
    believing Hausdorff-Young for p > 2 (f̂ need not even be a function).
    Now you try: Young with p = q = 4/3 gives r = ? (2)

D6. For f = 𝟙_[0,1] on R compute the centred maximal function Mf, the
    measure of {Mf > λ}, and ‖Mf‖_{1,∞}. Then prove the Vitali covering
    lemma and the weak (1,1) inequality |{Mf > λ}| ≤ 3ⁿ‖f‖₁/λ.
    Answer: Mf = 1 on (0, 1), 1/(2x) for x ≥ 1, 1/(2(1 − x)) for x ≤ 0;
    |{Mf > λ}| = 1/λ − 1 for 0 < λ < 1/2 (= 1 for 1/2 ≤ λ < 1);
    ‖Mf‖_{1,∞} = 1; Mf ∉ L¹.
    Teacher explains: For x ≥ 1 and radius r, the average is |[x − r,
    x + r] ∩ [0, 1]|/(2r). For x − 1 ≤ r ≤ x it is (r − x + 1)/(2r),
    increasing in r (derivative (x − 1)/(2r²) ≥ 0); for r ≥ x it is
    1/(2r), decreasing. The maximum is at r = x: Mf(x) = 1/(2x). By
    symmetry Mf(x) = 1/(2(1 − x)) for x ≤ 0, and Mf = 1 inside. For λ <
    1/2: {Mf > λ} = (1 − 1/(2λ), 1/(2λ)), of length 1/λ − 1.
    Hence λ|{Mf > λ}| = 1 − λ → 1 as λ → 0, and it equals λ < 1 on
    [1/2, 1): the weak norm is 1 = ‖f‖₁, but ∫Mf = ∞ because of the tail
    1/(2|x|). VITALI: from finitely many balls pick greedily the largest,
    discard all balls meeting it, repeat. Any discarded ball B meets a
    chosen B′ of radius ≥ its own, so B ⊆ 3B′. Thus the chosen disjoint
    balls satisfy ∑|B′| ≥ 3⁻ⁿ|⋃B|. WEAK (1,1): if K ⊆ {Mf > λ} is
    compact, each x ∈ K has a ball Bₓ with ∫_Bₓ|f| > λ|Bₓ|; cover K by
    finitely many, extract disjoint B₁, ..., B_m:
       |K| ≤ 3ⁿ∑|Bᵢ| < (3ⁿ/λ)∑∫_Bᵢ|f| ≤ 3ⁿ‖f‖₁/λ.
    Inner regularity gives the claim. With ‖Mf‖_∞ ≤ ‖f‖_∞, Marcinkiewicz
    gives ‖Mf‖_p ≤ C_p‖f‖_p for p > 1, C_p = O(p/(p − 1)). Common
    mistakes: expecting M to be bounded on L¹; forgetting that sup over
    uncountably many balls needs the lower semicontinuity of Mf for
    measurability ({Mf > λ} is open). Now you try: Mf(3) for f =
    𝟙_[−1,1]. (1/4, attained at r = 4)

D7. Deduce the Lebesgue differentiation theorem from the maximal
    inequality. Then for f = 𝟙_[0,1] compute the Poisson integral u(x, t)
    = P_t ∗ f(x) and its limits as t → 0⁺ at x = 1/2, x = 0 and x = 2.
    Explain the value at x = 0.
    Answer: u = (1/π)(arctan(x/t) + arctan((1 − x)/t)); limits 1, 1/2, 0.
    Teacher explains: Let Ω f(x) = lim sup_{r→0} |⨍_{B(x,r)} f − f(x)|.
    For continuous compactly supported g, Ωg = 0, and Ω(f) ≤ Ω(f − g) ≤
    M(f − g) + |f − g|. Given ε > 0 choose g with ‖f − g‖₁ < ε. Then
       |{Ωf > 2λ}| ≤ |{M(f − g) > λ}| + |{|f − g| > λ}| ≤ (3ⁿ + 1)ε/λ.
    As ε is arbitrary, Ωf = 0 a.e. (Same argument with |f(y) − f(x)|
    shows a.e. x is a LEBESGUE POINT.) The pattern "a.e. convergence on a
    dense class + weak-type maximal inequality ⇒ a.e. convergence for
    all" is the central principle; it also proves P_t ∗ f → f a.e.,
    because P_t is radially decreasing with ∫P_t = 1,
    so sup_t |P_t ∗ f| ≤ Mf. Computation: ∫₀¹ t/(π(t² + (x − y)²)) dy =
    (1/π)[arctan((y − x)/t)]₀¹ = (1/π)(arctan((1 − x)/t) + arctan(x/t)).
    As t → 0⁺: at x = 1/2 both arctans → π/2: limit 1; at x = 2,
    arctan(−1/t) + arctan(2/t) → −π/2 + π/2 = 0; at x = 0, arctan(1/t) →
    π/2 and arctan 0 = 0: limit 1/2. The point 0 is not a Lebesgue point
    of f: the symmetric averages are 1/2 there. The limit sees the
    AVERAGE of the one-sided values. Common mistakes: claiming
    convergence at every point; forgetting that u is harmonic in the
    upper half-plane (it is the real part of an analytic function). Now
    you try: which points are Lebesgue points of 𝟙_Q? (exactly the
    irrationals)

D8. Using Hf(x) = (1/π) p.v.∫ f(y)/(x − y) dy compute (a) H𝟙_[a,b],
    (b) H(1/(1 + x²)) via analytic functions, (c) H(cos 2πx) via the
    multiplier −i sgn ξ. (d) Deduce that H is bounded neither on L¹ nor
    on L^∞, and that ‖Hf‖₂ = ‖f‖₂.
    Answer: (a) (1/π)ln|(x − a)/(x − b)|; (b) x/(1 + x²); (c) sin 2πx.
    Teacher explains: (a) For x ∉ [a, b], ∫_a^b dy/(x − y) = [−ln|x −
    y|]_a^b = ln|x − a| − ln|x − b|; for x ∈ (a, b) the principal value
    cuts (x − ε, x + ε), and the two log(ε) terms cancel, giving the same
    formula. It has LOG SINGULARITIES at a and b (so it is unbounded:
    not L^∞) and behaves like (b − a)/(πx) at infinity (so ∫|H𝟙| = ∞:
    not L¹). (b) F(z) = i/(z + i) is analytic and decaying in Im z > 0;
    on the real line F(x) = i(x − i)/(x² + 1) = (1 + ix)/(1 + x²). The
    boundary value of an analytic function is f + iHf, so H(1/(1 + x²)) =
    x/(1 + x²). (c) cos 2πx = (e^(2πix) + e^(−2πix))/2; the frequencies
    ξ = ±1 get multiplied by ∓i: (−ie^(2πix) + ie^(−2πix))/2 = sin 2πx.
    (d) Since |−i sgn ξ| = 1 a.e., Plancherel gives ‖Hf‖₂ = ‖f‖₂, and
    (−i sgn ξ)² = −1 gives H² = −I. Common mistakes: sign of the kernel
    (1/(x − y), not 1/(y − x), with this convention); taking H of a
    constant to be a "constant" (it is 0 as a multiplier, while the
    integral diverges). Now you try: H(x/(1 + x²)). (−1/(1 + x²), as
    H² = −I)

D9. Prove M. Riesz's theorem ‖Hf‖_p ≤ A_p‖f‖_p for 1 < p < ∞ by the
    "squaring" method: show (Hf)² = f² + 2H(f·Hf) for real f ∈ 𝒮, derive
    A_{2p} ≤ A_p + √(A_p² + 1), and compute the bounds obtained for p = 4
    and p = 8. Then extend to all 1 < p < ∞.
    Answer: A₄ ≤ 1 + √2 ≈ 2.41421 = cot(π/8), A₈ ≤ 5.02734 = cot(π/16)
    (both sharp!); duality and Riesz-Thorin do the rest.
    Teacher explains: For real f, F = f + iHf extends analytically to the
    upper half-plane (it is the Poisson extension of the positive-
    frequency part, doubled). Then F² = f² − (Hf)² + 2i f·Hf is also
    analytic with the same decay, so its imaginary part is the Hilbert
    transform of its real part: H(f² − (Hf)²) = 2f·Hf. Apply H and use
    H² = −I: (Hf)² − f² = 2H(f·Hf) — COTLAR'S IDENTITY. Suppose ‖Hg‖_p ≤
    A_p‖g‖_p. Taking L^p norms, with ‖(Hf)²‖_p = ‖Hf‖²_{2p} and Hölder
    ‖f·Hf‖_p ≤ ‖f‖_{2p}‖Hf‖_{2p}:
       ‖Hf‖²_{2p} ≤ ‖f‖²_{2p} + 2A_p‖f‖_{2p}‖Hf‖_{2p}.
    With X = ‖Hf‖_{2p}/‖f‖_{2p}: X² − 2A_pX − 1 ≤ 0, so X ≤ A_p +
    √(A_p² + 1). From A₂ = 1: A₄ ≤ 1 + √2 ≈ 2.41421 and A₈ ≤ 1 + √2 +
    √(4 + 2√2) ≈ 5.02734. Remarkably these equal cot(π/8) and cot(π/16),
    the sharp constants (the half-angle formula cot(θ/2) = cot θ +
    √(cot²θ + 1) is exactly our recursion!). So H is bounded on L^(2^k)
    for all k; by Riesz-Thorin on every 2 ≤ p < ∞; since H* = −H,
    duality gives 1 < p ≤ 2 with A_p = A_p′. At p = 1 and ∞ it fails
    (D8). Common mistakes: applying the identity to complex f (use real
    and imaginary parts separately); forgetting to check that Hf ∈ L^{2p}
    a priori (true for f ∈ 𝒮, then extend by density). Now you try: the
    sharp constant for p = 3. (cot(π/6) = √3)

D10. State and prove the Calderón-Zygmund decomposition. Carry it out in
     one dimension for f = 6·𝟙_[0,1/4) at height λ = 2, starting from
     the dyadic interval [0, 1), and write down g and b.
     Answer: one selected interval Q = [0, 1/2), average 3 ∈ (2, 4];
     g = 3𝟙_[0,1/2), b = 3𝟙_[0,1/4) − 3𝟙_[1/4,1/2).
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: f ∈ L¹(Rⁿ), λ > 0. Partition Rⁿ into
     dyadic cubes so large that ⨍_Q|f| ≤ ‖f‖₁/|Q| ≤ λ. Subdivide each cube
     into its 2ⁿ children; STOP at a child Q if ⨍_Q|f| > λ (select it),
     otherwise keep subdividing. The selected cubes Qⱼ are maximal, hence
     disjoint; the parent Q̃ of Qⱼ was not selected, so
        λ < ⨍_Qⱼ|f| ≤ (|Q̃|/|Qⱼ|)⨍_Q̃|f| ≤ 2ⁿλ.
     Off ⋃Qⱼ, x lies in arbitrarily small cubes with averages ≤ λ, so
     |f(x)| ≤ λ at Lebesgue points (a.e.). Also ∑|Qⱼ| < ∑λ⁻¹∫_Qⱼ|f| ≤
     ‖f‖₁/λ. Put g = f off ⋃Qⱼ, g = ⨍_Qⱼ f on Qⱼ, and bⱼ = (f − ⨍_Qⱼ f)𝟙_Qⱼ.
     Then |g| ≤ 2ⁿλ, ∫bⱼ = 0, ‖bⱼ‖₁ ≤ 2∫_Qⱼ|f|. Example: ⨍_[0,1) f =
     6/4 = 1.5 ≤ 2: not selected. Children: ⨍_[0,1/2) f = (6/4)/(1/2) = 3
     > 2: SELECTED; ⨍_[1/2,1) f = 0: subdivide for ever, never selected.
     Check: 2 < 3 ≤ 2·2 ✓, |Q| = 1/2 ≤ ‖f‖₁/λ = 1.5/2 = 0.75 ✓. So g = 3
     on [0, 1/2), 0 elsewhere (|g| ≤ 4 ✓), b = f − g = 3 on [0, 1/4) and −3
     on [1/4, 1/2), which has integral 0 ✓. Common mistakes: selecting the
     SMALLEST cubes with big average (they must be maximal); forgetting
     the upper bound 2ⁿλ, which is what makes g bounded. Now you try: the
     same f at height λ = 4. (Q = [0, 1/4), average 6 ∈ (4, 8])

D11. State the Calderón-Zygmund theorem and prove the weak (1,1) bound
     from L² boundedness and the Hörmander condition. Verify the
     Hörmander condition for K(x) = 1/(πx), computing the constant
     B = sup_y ∫_{|x|>2|y|} |K(x − y) − K(x)| dx exactly.
     Answer: B = (ln 3)/π ≈ 0.34970.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: T bounded on L²(Rⁿ) with norm A₂, Tf(x) =
     ∫K(x − y)f(y) dy for x ∉ supp f, and ∫_{|x|>2|y|}|K(x − y) − K(x)| dx
     ≤ B. Then |{|Tf| > λ}| ≤ C(A₂ + B)‖f‖₁/λ, hence (Marcinkiewicz)
     L^p-bounds for 1 < p ≤ 2, and by duality (the kernel K(−x) of T*
     satisfies the same conditions) for 2 ≤ p < ∞. PROOF: decompose f =
     g + ∑bⱼ at height λ (D10). Good part: by Chebyshev and L²,
        |{|Tg| > λ/2}| ≤ 4A₂²‖g‖₂²/λ² ≤ 4A₂²(2ⁿλ‖g‖₁)/λ² ≤ 4·2ⁿA₂²‖f‖₁/λ.
     Bad part: let Qⱼ* be the ball with centre cⱼ of Qⱼ and radius
     diam Qⱼ, so |⋃Qⱼ*| ≤ Cₙ∑|Qⱼ| ≤ Cₙ‖f‖₁/λ. For x ∉ Qⱼ* and y ∈ Qⱼ we
     have |x − cⱼ| > 2|y − cⱼ|; using ∫bⱼ = 0,
        Tbⱼ(x) = ∫_Qⱼ (K(x − y) − K(x − cⱼ))bⱼ(y) dy,
        ∫_{(Qⱼ*)ᶜ}|Tbⱼ| ≤ ∫|bⱼ(y)| ∫_{|x′|>2|y′|}|K(x′ − y′) − K(x′)| dx′ dy
                        ≤ B‖bⱼ‖₁   (x′ = x − cⱼ, y′ = y − cⱼ).
     Summing, ∫ off ⋃Qⱼ* of |Tb| ≤ 2B‖f‖₁, so |{|Tb| > λ/2} ∖ ⋃Qⱼ*| ≤
     4B‖f‖₁/λ. Add the three pieces. The CANCELLATION ∫bⱼ = 0 is what turns
     the non-integrable kernel into the integrable difference. For K =
     1/(πx) and y = 1 (the integral is dilation invariant, and y ↦ −y is
     symmetric): ∫_{|x|>2}|1/(x − 1) − 1/x| dx = ∫₂^∞ dx/(x(x − 1)) +
     ∫₂^∞ dx/(x(x + 1)) = ln 2 + ln(3/2) = ln 3; divide by π. Common
     mistakes: forgetting that L² boundedness is a HYPOTHESIS (K = 1/|x|
     in one dimension satisfies Hörmander with the same constant ln 3 but
     gives an unbounded operator); using the size condition alone. Now
     you try: show |∇K(x)| ≤ A|x|^(−n−1) implies Hörmander. (MVT:
     |K(x − y) − K(x)| ≤ A|y|(|x|/2)^(−n−1) for |x| > 2|y|; integrate:
     B ≤ Cₙ A)

D12. (a) Show that the Riesz transforms (multiplier −iξⱼ/|ξ|) satisfy
     ∑Rⱼ² = −I and ∂ⱼ∂ₖu = −RⱼRₖΔu, and deduce ‖D²u‖_p ≤ C_p‖Δu‖_p for
     u ∈ C_c^∞(Rⁿ), 1 < p < ∞. (b) Show it fails at p = ∞ with u =
     x₁x₂ ln|x| near 0 in R². (c) Show ln|x| ∈ BMO(R) ∖ L^∞ by computing
     its mean oscillation on [0, a], and explain why H(sgn) = (2/π)ln|x|
     (modulo constants) fits "H : L^∞ → BMO".
     Answer: (a) symbols; (b) Δu = 4x₁x₂/|x|² bounded, ∂₁∂₂u = ln|x| + 1 −
     2x₁²x₂²/|x|⁴ unbounded; (c) mean oscillation 2/e ≈ 0.73576 on every
     [0, a].
     Teacher explains: (a) ∑(−iξⱼ/|ξ|)² = −∑ξⱼ²/|ξ|² = −1. ∂ⱼ∂ₖ has symbol
     (2πiξⱼ)(2πiξₖ) = −4π²ξⱼξₖ and Δ has −4π²|ξ|², so ∂ⱼ∂ₖΔ⁻¹ has symbol
     ξⱼξₖ/|ξ|² = −(−iξⱼ/|ξ|)(−iξₖ/|ξ|): ∂ⱼ∂ₖ = −RⱼRₖΔ. Each Rⱼ is a CZ
     operator (kernel cₙxⱼ/|x|^(n+1): odd, so mean zero on spheres; L²
     norm 1), hence bounded on L^p, and ‖∂ⱼ∂ₖu‖_p ≤ C_p²‖Δu‖_p. This is
     the L^p theory behind elliptic regularity (Δu ∈ L^p ⇒ u ∈ W^{2,p}).
     (b) With r = |x|: Δ(x₁x₂ ln r) = x₁x₂Δ ln r + 2∇(x₁x₂)·∇ ln r + 0 =
     2(x₂, x₁)·(x₁, x₂)/r² = 4x₁x₂/r², bounded by 2, while a direct
     computation gives ∂₁∂₂u = ln r + 1 − 2x₁²x₂²/r⁴ → −∞ as r → 0
     (multiply by a cutoff to get compact support). (c) On [0, a],
     ⨍ ln x = ln a − 1, and substituting x = at,
        (1/a)∫₀^a |ln x − ln a + 1| dx = ∫₀¹|ln t + 1| dt
          = −[t ln t]₀^{1/e} + [t ln t]_{1/e}^1 = 1/e + 1/e = 2/e.
     By dilation the oscillation on [α, β] depends only on α/β, and it
     stays bounded over all ratios (the supremum, ≈ 0.93, occurs for
     slightly asymmetric intervals around 0), so ln|x| ∈ BMO although it
     is unbounded. For sgn ∈ L^∞, the truncated integral (1/π)∫_{−R}^{R}
     sgn(y)/(x − y) dy = (1/π)(2 ln|x| − ln|R² − x²|): as R → ∞ it
     diverges only by the CONSTANT (2/π)ln R, so Hf is defined modulo
     constants, exactly the way BMO is. Common mistakes: expecting
     L^∞ → L^∞; forgetting BMO is a space modulo constants. Now you try:
     the mean oscillation of 𝟙_[0,∞) on [−a, a]. (1/2)
