       g) yes (∫cos θ sin θ dθ = 0); yes
       h) mean 1/2 ≠ 0: no
       i) yes (cos 2θ); a multiple of the kernel of R₁² − R₂²
       j) yes, yes, yes, no (derivatives do not decay; it is the wave
          propagator, bounded on L^p only for p = 2)
       k) yes (a combination of modulated Hilbert transforms), although
          Mikhlin's theorem does not apply
       l) no (C. Fefferman's ball multiplier theorem)
       m) ln 3 for both (Hörmander alone does not give L² bounds)
       n) π (symbol −iπ sgn ξ)
       o) no: it is a fractional integral (L^p → L^q, q > p), not L^p →
          L^p bounded
       p) −4π²ξⱼξₖ/(1 + 4π²|ξ|²); yes

M11. BMO and Muckenhoupt weights.
     a) is ln|x| in BMO(R)? in L^∞?
     b) the mean oscillation of ln x on [0, a]
     c) the mean oscillation of ln|x| on [−a, a]
     d) the mean oscillation of 𝟙_[0,∞) on [−a, a]
     e) ‖c‖_* for a constant c
     f) is |x|^(−1/2) in BMO(R)?
     g) is sgn(x)ln|x| in BMO(R)?
     h) John-Nirenberg for ln x on Q = [0, 1]: |{x ∈ Q : |ln x + 1| > λ}|
        for λ ≥ 1
     i) the dual of H¹(Rⁿ); the dual of L¹(Rⁿ)
     j) |x|^a ∈ A_p(Rⁿ) iff ... ; for R, p = 2: is |x|^(1/2), |x|, |x|⁻¹
        in A₂?
     k) R², p = 3: is |x|³ ∈ A₃? is |x|⁴?
     l) |x|^a ∈ A₁(Rⁿ) iff ...; is |x|^(−1/2) ∈ A₁(R)?
     m) is eˣ ∈ A₂(R)?
     n) for w = |x|^a on R, (⨍_[0,r]w)(⨍_[0,r]w⁻¹); the value for a = 1/2
     o) is A₂ ⊆ A₃?
     p) for which weights is M bounded on L^p(w), 1 < p < ∞?
     Answers:
       a) yes; no          b) 2/e ≈ 0.73576     c) 2/e (evenness)
       d) 1/2              e) 0
       f) no (the oscillation on [0, a] is ≈ a^(−1/2) → ∞ as a → 0)
       g) no (on [−a, a] the mean oscillation ≈ |ln a| → ∞)
       h) e^(−1−λ) (only ln x < −1 − λ is possible): exponential decay
       i) BMO (C. Fefferman); L^∞ (not BMO: H¹ ⊊ L¹)
       j) −n < a < n(p − 1); yes, no, no
       k) yes (−2 < 3 < 4); no (4 is the endpoint)
       l) −n < a ≤ 0; yes
       m) no (not even doubling: ∫_{x−2r}^{x+2r}/∫_{x−r}^{x+r} ≈ eʳ)
       n) 1/((1 + a)(1 − a)) = 1/(1 − a²); 4/3
       o) yes (A_p increases with p)
       p) exactly w ∈ A_p (Muckenhoupt); the same for H
          (Hunt-Muckenhoupt-Wheeden)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The dual of a compact abelian group is discrete.
     b) The Fourier series of every continuous f on T converges at every
        point.
     c) The Fourier series of every f ∈ L²(T) converges a.e.
     d) The Fourier series of every f ∈ L¹(T) converges a.e.
     e) If f ∈ L¹(R) then f̂ is continuous and f̂(ξ) → 0 as |ξ| → ∞.
     f) If f ∈ L¹(R) then f̂ ∈ L¹(R).
     g) Every sequence (c_k) with c_k → 0 as |k| → ∞ is the sequence of
        Fourier coefficients of some f ∈ L¹(T).
     h) H is bounded on L¹(R).
     i) H maps L^∞(R) into L^∞(R).
     j) M is bounded on L¹(Rⁿ).
     k) Mf ≥ |f| a.e.
     l) The Hausdorff-Young inequality holds for p = 3.
     m) f, g ∈ L²(R) ⇒ f ∗ g ∈ L^∞(R).
     n) The ball multiplier is bounded on L⁴(R²).
     o) An L²-bounded operator with a CZ kernel is bounded on L¹.
     p) L^∞ ⊊ BMO.
     q) Every bounded translation-invariant operator on L²(Rⁿ) is a
        Fourier multiplier with m ∈ L^∞.
     r) Haar measure on a compact group is both left and right invariant.
     s) Haar measure on the ax + b group is bi-invariant.
     t) Weak (1,1) plus L^∞ bounds imply boundedness on L¹.
     Answers:
       a) T
       b) F: du Bois-Reymond (Fejér's explicit example; or ‖D_N‖₁ → ∞ and
          the uniform boundedness principle)
       c) T (Carleson)
       d) F: Kolmogorov's example (even everywhere divergence)
       e) T (Riemann-Lebesgue)
       f) F: 𝟙_[−1/2,1/2], whose transform sin(πξ)/(πξ) is not in L¹
       g) F: the sine series ∑_{k≥2} sin(2πkx)/ln k (for f ∈ L¹, odd
          coefficients bₖ need ∑bₖ/k < ∞, but ∑1/(k ln k) = ∞)
       h) F: H𝟙_[0,1] ~ 1/(πx) at ∞
       i) F: H𝟙_[0,1] = (1/π)ln|x/(x − 1)| (it maps into BMO)
       j) F: M𝟙_[0,1] ~ 1/(2|x|)
       k) T (Lebesgue differentiation)
       l) F: no inequality ‖f̂‖_q ≤ C‖f‖₃ holds for any q (Gaussians
          with complex quadratic phases, or random series)
       m) T (Cauchy-Schwarz; f ∗ g is even in C₀)
       n) F: Fefferman (bounded only for p = 2)
       o) F: the Hilbert transform (only weak (1,1))
       p) T: ln|x|
       q) T
       r) T (compact groups are unimodular)
       s) F: left da db/a², right da db/a
       t) F: M (strong type only for 1 < p ≤ ∞)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: fix ONE Fourier convention (e^(−2πixξ)) and make students
  check every formula on the Gaussian e^(−πx²) and on 𝟙_[−1/2,1/2]
  before trusting it. Teach characters through the chain Z/N → T → R
  (roots of unity, then circles, then lines) and insist on the rule
  "compact ↔ discrete". For singular integrals draw three pictures:
  the kernel 1/(πx) with its cancelling left and right halves, the
  function H𝟙_[0,1] with its two logarithmic spikes and its 1/(πx) tail
  (explaining at once why L¹ and L^∞ fail), and the CZ stopping-time
  tree of dyadic intervals with the selected ones shaded; have them run
  the decomposition by hand on eight-cell vectors (M9) until the bounds
  λ < avg ≤ 2ⁿλ feel inevitable. Repeat the slogan "weak-type maximal
  inequality + dense class ⇒ a.e. convergence" every time it is used.
  Harder: prove the Riesz-Thorin theorem via the three-lines lemma;
  prove Pontryagin duality for finite and compact abelian groups and
  Peter-Weyl for compact groups; prove Cotlar's lemma for almost-
  orthogonal operators; prove the John-Nirenberg inequality with a
  second CZ decomposition and the H¹-BMO duality via atoms; prove the
  Mikhlin multiplier theorem with Littlewood-Paley square functions;
  prove that A_p weights satisfy a reverse Hölder inequality; study the
  T(1) theorem of David-Journé, Carleson's theorem via time-frequency
  analysis, and Fefferman's Kakeya-set proof that the ball multiplier is
  unbounded on L^p(R²), p ≠ 2.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.19 — STOCHASTIC CALCULUS: ITO INTEGRAL, SDEs, APPLICATIONS TO
FINANCE AND PHYSICS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - BROWNIAN MOTION (from 12.12): B₀ = 0, independent stationary Gaussian
    increments B_t − B_s ~ N(0, t − s), continuous paths; E[B_sB_t] =
    min(s, t). QUADRATIC VARIATION: for partitions of [0, t] with mesh → 0,
    ∑(ΔB)² → t in L² (variance 2∑(Δt)²), so [B]_t = t; hence the TOTAL
    VARIATION is infinite and paths are nowhere differentiable. Box rules:
    dB·dB = dt, dB·dt = dt·dt = 0; independent B, W: dB·dW = 0.
  - SETTING: a filtration (𝓕_t) satisfying the usual conditions, B an
    (𝓕_t)-BM. H is ADAPTED if H_t is 𝓕_t-measurable; the class 𝓗²[0, T]
    = progressively measurable H with E∫₀^T H_s² ds < ∞. SIMPLE processes
    H = ∑ ξ_k 𝟙_(t_k, t_{k+1}] with ξ_k bounded and 𝓕_{t_k}-measurable are
    dense in 𝓗².
  - ITO INTEGRAL: ∫H dB = ∑ ξ_k (B_{t_{k+1}} − B_{t_k}) for simple H (LEFT
    endpoint!). ITO ISOMETRY E[(∫₀^T H dB)²] = E∫₀^T H² ds extends the map
    to all of 𝓗² as an L²-limit. Properties: linear, E∫H dB = 0,
    Cov(∫H dB, ∫K dB) = E∫HK ds, t ↦ ∫₀ᵗ H dB is a continuous
    L²-MARTINGALE with [∫H dB]_t = ∫₀ᵗ H² ds; for deterministic H it is
    Gaussian N(0, ∫H²). With only ∫₀^T H² ds < ∞ a.s. the integral is a
    LOCAL martingale (may fail to be a true martingale).
  - THE CHOICE OF EVALUATION POINT MATTERS: left sums give ∫₀ᵗ B dB =
    (B_t² − t)/2 (Ito), midpoint/trapezoid sums give B_t²/2
    (STRATONOVICH ∫H∘dB = ∫H dB + ½[H, B]_t), right sums (B_t² + t)/2.
    Ito integrals are martingales; Stratonovich integrals obey the ordinary
    chain rule (Wong-Zakai: limits of smooth-noise ODEs are Stratonovich).
  - ITO PROCESS dX = b dt + σ dB, [X]_t = ∫σ² ds. ITO'S FORMULA: for f ∈
    C^{1,2}, df(t, X) = f_t dt + f_x dX + ½f_xx d[X] = (f_t + b f_x +
    ½σ²f_xx) dt + σ f_x dB. Multidimensional: df(X) = ∑∂ᵢf dXⁱ +
    ½∑∂ᵢⱼf d[Xⁱ, Xʲ]. PRODUCT RULE d(XY) = X dY + Y dX + d[X, Y].
    TANAKA: d|B| = sgn(B) dB + dL⁰ (local time) since |x| ∉ C².
  - STANDARD EXAMPLES: d(B²) = 2B dB + dt, d(B³) = 3B² dB + 3B dt, moments
    E B_t^{2k} = (2k − 1)!! t^k via Ito; Hermite martingales B² − t,
    B³ − 3tB, B⁴ − 6tB² + 3t²; EXPONENTIAL MARTINGALE exp(θB − θ²t/2);
    stochastic exponential ℰ(X) = exp(X − ½[X]) solves dZ = Z dX.
  - MARTINGALE TOOLS: LÉVY'S CHARACTERISATION (a continuous local
    martingale M with M₀ = 0 and [M]_t = t is a BM); MARTINGALE
    REPRESENTATION (every L²(𝓕_T^B) variable is E F + ∫₀^T H dB); Dambis-
    Dubins-Schwarz (M = W_{[M]}); optional stopping with Ito formulas
    (hitting times, E e^{−λτ_a} = e^{−a√(2λ)}).
  - GIRSANOV: if θ is adapted and Z_t = exp(−∫₀ᵗθ dB − ½∫₀ᵗθ² ds) is a
    martingale (NOVIKOV: E exp(½∫₀^Tθ²) < ∞ suffices), then under dQ =
    Z_T dP the process B̃_t = B_t + ∫₀ᵗ θ ds is a Q-BM on [0, T]. Q ~ P on
    𝓕_T but typically Q ⊥ P on 𝓕_∞. Cameron-Martin for deterministic θ.
  - SDEs dX = b(t, X) dt + σ(t, X) dB, X₀ = ξ. STRONG solution: adapted
    to the given B; WEAK solution: some (Ω, B, X). EXISTENCE AND
    UNIQUENESS: Lipschitz |b(x) − b(y)| + |σ(x) − σ(y)| ≤ K|x − y| and
    linear growth |b| + |σ| ≤ K(1 + |x|), E ξ² < ∞ ⇒ unique strong
    solution, E sup_{t≤T} |X_t|² < ∞ (Picard iteration + Gronwall + Doob).
    Yamada-Watanabe: in 1-d, σ Hölder-½ (e.g. √|x|) still gives pathwise
    uniqueness; weak existence + pathwise uniqueness ⇒ strong solution.
  - COUNTEREXAMPLES: dX = X² dt explodes (X = 1/(1 − t)), no linear
    growth; dX = 3X^{2/3} dt, X₀ = 0 has solutions 0 and t³ (non-
    Lipschitz); TANAKA's dX = sgn(X) dB has weak solutions but no strong
    solution and no pathwise uniqueness.
  - LINEAR SDEs: GBM dS = μS dt + σS dB ⇒ S_t = S₀exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σB_t),
    E S_t = S₀e^{μt}, S_t → 0 a.s. if μ < σ²/2. ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK dX =
    −θX dt + σ dB ⇒ X_t = X₀e^{−θt} + σ∫₀ᵗe^{−θ(t−s)} dB_s, Gaussian,
    stationary law N(0, σ²/(2θ)), covariance (σ²/2θ)e^{−θ|t−s|}.
    Vasicek, Brownian bridge dX = −X/(1 − t) dt + dB; integrating factors.
  - DIFFUSIONS AND PDEs: GENERATOR Lf = b f′ + ½σ²f″; DYNKIN E_x f(X_τ) =
    f(x) + E_x∫₀^τ Lf(X) ds. EXIT PROBLEMS: P_x(hit b before a) solves Lu =
    0, E_xτ solves Lw = −1 (for BM: (x − a)/(b − a) and (x − a)(b − x));
    scale functions. FEYNMAN-KAC: u(t, x) = E[e^{−∫_t^T r ds} g(X_T) |
    X_t = x] solves u_t + Lu − ru = 0, u(T) = g. KOLMOGOROV backward (in
    x, t) and FORWARD/FOKKER-PLANCK p_t = −(bp)_x + ½(σ²p)_xx.
  - FINANCE: Black-Scholes market dS = μS dt + σS dB, bond rate r.
    Self-financing DELTA HEDGE Δ = C_S removes risk ⇒ BLACK-SCHOLES PDE
    C_t + rSC_S + ½σ²S²C_SS − rC = 0 (μ disappears). Risk-neutral
    measure Q via Girsanov with θ = (μ − r)/σ, price = e^{−rτ}E_Q[payoff].
    C = SΦ(d₁) − Ke^{−rτ}Φ(d₂), d₁,₂ = [ln(S/K) + (r ± σ²/2)τ]/(σ√τ).
    Put-call parity C − P = S − Ke^{−rτ}; Greeks Δ = Φ(d₁), Γ =
    φ(d₁)/(Sσ√τ), vega = Sφ(d₁)√τ > 0.
  - PHYSICS: LANGEVIN equation dV = −γV dt + σ dB; FLUCTUATION-
    DISSIPATION σ² = 2γk_BT/m gives equipartition mE V² = k_BT; position
    diffuses with EINSTEIN D = k_BT/(mγ) = k_BT/ζ, MSD ~ 2Dt per dimension
    (ballistic for t ≪ 1/γ). Overdamped dX = −U′(X)/ζ dt + √(2D) dB has
    Boltzmann stationary density ∝ e^{−U/k_BT}; Kramers escape rate
    ∝ e^{−ΔU/k_BT}. Multiplicative noise: Ito vs Stratonovich differ by
    the noise-induced drift ½σσ′.
  - NUMERICS: EULER-MARUYAMA X_{n+1} = X_n + b h + σ ΔB (strong order ½,
    weak order 1); MILSTEIN adds ½σσ′((ΔB)² − h) (strong order 1);
    Monte Carlo error ∝ N^{−1/2}.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let 0 = t₀ < t₁ < ... < t_n = t and Q_n = ∑(B_{t_{k+1}} − B_{t_k})².
    (a) Show E Q_n = t and Var Q_n = 2∑(Δt_k)², so Q_n → t in L² as the
    mesh → 0. (b) Deduce that Brownian paths have infinite total variation
    on [0, t]. (c) For the uniform partition of [0, 1] with n = 100 find
    Var Q_n and E∑|ΔB_k|.
    Answer: (a) Var Q_n ≤ 2t·mesh → 0. (b) ∑|ΔB| ≥ Q_n / max|ΔB| → ∞.
    (c) 0.02 (s.d. 0.1414) and √(200/π) ≈ 7.97885.
    Teacher explains: Write Δ_k = B_{t_{k+1}} − B_{t_k} ~ N(0, Δt_k),
    independent. Then E Δ_k² = Δt_k, so E Q_n = ∑Δt_k = t. For a Gaussian
    Z ~ N(0, v), E Z⁴ = 3v², so Var Z² = 3v² − v² = 2v². By independence
       Var Q_n = ∑ 2(Δt_k)² ≤ 2(max Δt_k)·∑Δt_k = 2t·mesh → 0,
    and E(Q_n − t)² = Var Q_n → 0: this is the statement [B]_t = t.
    (b) Suppose V = sup ∑|Δ_k| < ∞ on some path. Then Q_n ≤ (max_k |Δ_k|)·
    ∑|Δ_k| ≤ V·max|Δ_k| → 0 by uniform continuity of the path. But Q_n → t
    > 0 (along a subsequence a.s.), a contradiction. So a.s. paths are not
    of bounded variation, which is why ∫H dB CANNOT be defined path by
    path as a Riemann-Stieltjes integral. (c) Var Q_n = 2·100·(1/100)² =
    0.02. E|Δ_k| = √(2Δt/π), so E∑|Δ_k| = n√(2/(πn)) = √(2n/π) ≈ 7.979,
    growing like √n. Common mistakes: thinking (ΔB)² ≈ 0 because ΔB is
    small — it is of order Δt, the same as the dt-terms, and that is the
    origin of the extra ½f″ term in Ito's formula. Now you try: uniform
    partition of [0, 2] with n = 50: Var Q_n? (2t²/n = 8/50 = 0.16)

D2. Compute ∫₀ᵗ B_s dB_s directly as a limit of (a) left-endpoint,
    (b) right-endpoint and (c) midpoint-average Riemann sums. Which is the
    Ito integral and why is it the "right" choice for a martingale theory?
    Relate (c) to the Stratonovich integral.
    Answer: (a) (B_t² − t)/2 (Ito); (b) (B_t² + t)/2; (c) B_t²/2
    (Stratonovich).
    Teacher explains: Use the algebraic identity a(b − a) = ½(b² − a²) −
    ½(b − a)². With a = B_{t_k}, b = B_{t_{k+1}}:
       ∑B_{t_k}Δ_k = ½∑(B²_{t_{k+1}} − B²_{t_k}) − ½∑Δ_k² = ½B_t² − ½Q_n,
    which tends in L² to ½B_t² − ½t by D1. Similarly b(b − a) = ½(b² − a²)
    + ½(b − a)², so right sums give ½B_t² + ½Q_n → ½(B_t² + t). The
    average ½(a + b)(b − a) = ½(b² − a²) telescopes EXACTLY to ½B_t².
    For ordinary Stieltjes integrals the three limits would coincide; here
    they differ by multiples of the quadratic variation. The left point is
    chosen because the integrand B_{t_k} is then 𝓕_{t_k}-measurable and
    independent of the increment Δ_k, so each term has mean 0 and the sum
    is a martingale: indeed E[(B_t² − t)/2] = 0. The Stratonovich integral
    ∫H∘dB = ∫H dB + ½[H, B]_t; for H = B, [B, B]_t = t gives (B_t² − t)/2
    + t/2 = B_t²/2, matching the ordinary chain rule. Common mistakes:
    writing ∫B dB = B²/2 "by calculus"; forgetting that the Stratonovich
    integral is NOT a martingale (mean t/2). Now you try: find ∫₀ᵗ B² dB in
    both senses. (Stratonovich B_t³/3; Ito B_t³/3 − ∫₀ᵗ B_s ds)

D3. State and prove the Ito isometry for simple processes. Then, for T = 2,
    compute (a) E[(∫₀^T B dB)²], (b) the law of X = ∫₀^T s dB_s, (c)
    Cov(X, B_T) and Corr(X, B_T), and (d) show X = TB_T − ∫₀^T B_s ds.
    Answer: (a) T²/2 = 2; (b) N(0, T³/3) = N(0, 8/3); (c) T²/2 = 2,
    √3/2 ≈ 0.86603; (d) Ito product rule.
    Teacher explains: For simple H = ∑ξ_k𝟙_(t_k,t_{k+1}], I = ∑ξ_kΔ_k and
       E I² = ∑_k E[ξ_k²Δ_k²] + 2∑_{j<k} E[ξ_jξ_kΔ_jΔ_k].
    Condition on 𝓕_{t_k}: ξ_k² is known and Δ_k is independent of 𝓕_{t_k},
    so E[ξ_k²Δ_k²] = E[ξ_k²]Δt_k; for j < k, ξ_jξ_kΔ_j is 𝓕_{t_k}-
    measurable and E[Δ_k | 𝓕_{t_k}] = 0, so the cross terms vanish. Thus
    E I² = ∑E ξ_k² Δt_k = E∫H² ds. This isometry from simple processes
    (dense in 𝓗²) into L²(Ω) extends uniquely by continuity: that IS the
    definition of the Ito integral. (a) E∫₀^T B_s² ds = ∫₀^T s ds = T²/2 =
    2. Check with D2: E[(B_T² − T)²]/4 = (3T² − 2T² + T²)/4 = T²/2 ✓.
    (b) A deterministic integrand gives a Gaussian (L²-limit of Gaussian
    sums) with variance ∫₀^T s² ds = T³/3 = 8/3. (c) B_T = ∫₀^T 1 dB, so
    by polarization Cov = ∫₀^T s·1 ds = T²/2 = 2; Corr = (T²/2)/√(T³/3·T)
    = √3/2 (independent of T). (d) d(tB_t) = B_t dt + t dB_t (d[t, B] = 0)
    so TB_T = ∫B ds + ∫s dB. Common mistakes: applying the isometry to ds
    integrals: E(∫₀¹B ds)² = 1/3, not ∫₀¹ E B² ds = 1/2. Now you try:
    Var ∫₀¹ e^s dB_s. ((e² − 1)/2 ≈ 3.19453)

D4. State Ito's formula for f(t, X_t) with dX = b dt + σ dB and sketch
    the proof. Use it to (a) write B_t³ as an Ito integral plus a dt
    integral, (b) compute E B_t⁴ and E B_t⁶ recursively, (c) show B_t⁴ −
    6tB_t² + 3t² is a martingale.
    Answer: (a) B_t³ = 3∫B² dB + 3∫B ds; (b) 3t², 15t³; (c) its dt-part
    is zero.
    Teacher explains: FORMULA: df = f_t dt + f_x dX + ½f_xx (dX)², and
    (dX)² = σ² dt by the box rules. PROOF SKETCH (f ∈ C², X = B): Taylor on
    a partition, f(B_t) − f(0) = ∑f′(B_{t_k})Δ_k + ½∑f″(B_{t_k})Δ_k² +
    remainder. The first sum → ∫f′(B) dB (left points!), the second → ½∫
    f″(B) ds because Δ_k² can be replaced by Δt_k (the error ∑f″(Δ_k² −
    Δt_k) has L²-norm² ≈ 2∑(Δt_k)² → 0), and the remainder is bounded by
    sup|ω(Δ)|·Q_n → 0. (a) f = x³: f′ = 3x², f″ = 6x, so d(B³) = 3B² dB +
    3B dt. (b) Taking expectations kills the dB-term (a true martingale
    since E∫B^{2k} < ∞): d(B⁴) = 4B³ dB + 6B² dt gives E B_t⁴ = 6∫₀ᵗ s ds
    = 3t²; d(B⁶) = 6B⁵ dB + 15B⁴ dt gives E B_t⁶ = 15∫₀ᵗ 3s² ds = 15t³. In
    general E B^{2k} = (2k − 1)!! t^k. (c) f = x⁴ − 6tx² + 3t²: f_t = −6x²
    + 6t, ½f_xx = 6x² − 6t, so the drift f_t + ½f_xx = 0 and d f =
    (4B³ − 12tB) dB. Common mistakes: forgetting the f_t term; using
    (dB)² = 0. Now you try: E B_t⁸. (105t⁴)

D5. Show that Z_t = exp(θB_t − θ²t/2) is a martingale and deduce E e^{θB_t}.
    Using optional stopping, find the Laplace transform of the hitting
    time τ_a = inf{t : B_t = a}, a > 0. Evaluate E e^{−2τ₁} and explain why
    E τ_a = ∞.
    Answer: dZ = θZ dB, E e^{θB_t} = e^{θ²t/2}; E e^{−λτ_a} = e^{−a√(2λ)};
    E e^{−2τ₁} = e^{−2} ≈ 0.13534.
    Teacher explains: With f(t, x) = exp(θx − θ²t/2): f_t = −(θ²/2)f,
    f_x = θf, f_xx = θ²f, so dZ = (−θ²/2 + θ²/2)Z dt + θZ dB = θZ dB. Since
    E∫₀ᵗ Z_s² ds = ∫e^{θ²s} ds < ∞, Z is a true martingale and E Z_t = 1,
    i.e. E e^{θB_t} = e^{θ²t/2} (the Gaussian m.g.f. — a good check).
    For θ > 0 the stopped martingale Z_{t∧τ_a} lies in (0, e^{θa}], so it
    is bounded; τ_a < ∞ a.s. (recurrence) and on {τ_a = ∞} Z_t → 0 anyway.
    Bounded convergence in E Z_{t∧τ_a} = 1 gives E exp(θa − θ²τ_a/2) = 1.
    Put λ = θ²/2: E e^{−λτ_a} = e^{−a√(2λ)}. With a = 1, λ = 2: e^{−2}.
    Differentiating at λ = 0⁺: −(d/dλ)e^{−a√(2λ)} = (a/√(2λ))e^{−a√(2λ)}
    → ∞, so E τ_a = ∞ although τ_a < ∞ a.s. Common mistakes: using
    optional stopping for θ < 0 (then Z_{t∧τ} is unbounded); forgetting
    to prove the local martingale is a true martingale. Now you try:
    E e^{−τ₂/8}. (e^{−2·½} = e^{−1} ≈ 0.36788)

D6. Solve the geometric Brownian motion dS = μS dt + σS dB. For S₀ = 100,
    μ = 0.1, σ = 0.2, T = 1 compute E S_T, the median of S_T, Var S_T and
    P(S_T > 100). When does S_t → 0 a.s.?
    Answer: S_t = S₀exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σB_t); 110.517, 108.329, 498.464
    (s.d. 22.326), Φ(0.4) ≈ 0.65542; S_t → 0 iff μ < σ²/2.
    Teacher explains: Apply Ito to Y = ln S: dY = dS/S − ½(dS)²/S² =
    μ dt + σ dB − ½σ² dt. So Y_t = ln S₀ + (μ − σ²/2)t + σB_t and S_t is
    lognormal. Using E e^{σB_t} = e^{σ²t/2}: E S_t = S₀e^{μt} = 110.517;
    E S_t² = S₀²e^{(2μ+σ²)t}, so Var S_t = S₀²e^{2μt}(e^{σ²t} − 1) =
    10⁴e^{0.2}(e^{0.04} − 1) ≈ 498.464. The median is where B_t = 0:
    S₀e^{(μ−σ²/2)t} = 100e^{0.08} ≈ 108.329 < mean (lognormal skew).
    P(S_T > K) = P(σB_T > ln(K/S₀) − (μ − σ²/2)T) = Φ((ln(S₀/K) + (μ −
    σ²/2)T)/(σ√T)) = Φ(0.08/0.2) = Φ(0.4) ≈ 0.65542. Long run: B_t/t → 0
    a.s., so (1/t)ln S_t → μ − σ²/2; if μ < σ²/2 then S_t → 0 a.s. even
    though E S_t = S₀e^{μt} may explode — the mean is carried by rare huge
    paths. Common mistakes: writing S_t = S₀e^{μt + σB_t} (forgetting the
    Ito correction); confusing median and mean. Now you try: μ = 0, σ = 1:
    what happens to S_t and to E S_t? (S_t → 0 a.s., E S_t = S₀: a
    martingale that is not uniformly integrable)

D7. Solve the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE dX = −θX dt + σ dB, X₀ = x, θ > 0.
    Find the mean, variance, the stationary distribution and the
    stationary covariance. Evaluate for θ = 2, σ = 1, x = 3, t = 1.
    Answer: X_t = xe^{−θt} + σ∫₀ᵗe^{−θ(t−s)}dB_s ~ N(xe^{−θt},
    σ²(1 − e^{−2θt})/(2θ)); stationary N(0, σ²/(2θ)); covariance
    (σ²/2θ)e^{−θ|t−s|}; numbers 0.40601 and 0.24542.
    Teacher explains: Integrating factor, exactly as for the linear ODE:
    d(e^{θt}X_t) = θe^{θt}X dt + e^{θt}dX = σe^{θt} dB (no Ito correction
    because e^{θt} has zero quadratic variation). Integrate and multiply by
    e^{−θt}. The stochastic integral has deterministic integrand, so X_t is
    Gaussian with mean xe^{−θt} and, by the isometry, variance σ²∫₀ᵗ
    e^{−2θ(t−s)} ds = σ²(1 − e^{−2θt})/(2θ). As t → ∞ the law tends to
    N(0, σ²/(2θ)); starting from this law, the process is stationary. For
    s < t, X_t = e^{−θ(t−s)}X_s + (independent noise), so Cov(X_s, X_t) =
    e^{−θ(t−s)}Var X_s = (σ²/2θ)e^{−θ(t−s)}. Numbers: 3e^{−2} ≈ 0.40601,
    (1 − e^{−4})/4 ≈ 0.24542 (close to the stationary value 1/4 already).
    Mean reversion half-life: ln 2/θ ≈ 0.347. Common mistakes: variance
    σ²t (that is BM); forgetting the factor 2 in e^{−2θ(t−s)}. Now you
    try: θ = 1, σ = √2, x = 0: Var X₁. (1 − e^{−2} ≈ 0.86466)

D8. State the existence and uniqueness theorem for SDEs and prove the
    uniqueness part. Then show why each hypothesis matters: (a) dX = X² dt,
    X₀ = 1; (b) dX = 3X^{2/3} dt, X₀ = 0; (c) Tanaka's dX = sgn(X) dB.
    Answer: Lipschitz + linear growth ⇒ unique strong solution; (a)
    explodes at t = 1; (b) two solutions 0 and t³; (c) weak solution but no
    pathwise uniqueness, no strong solution.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if |b(t,x) − b(t,y)| + |σ(t,x) − σ(t,y)| ≤
    K|x − y|, |b(t,x)| + |σ(t,x)| ≤ K(1 + |x|) and X₀ ∈ L² is independent
    of B, there is a unique continuous adapted X with E sup_{t≤T}X_t² < ∞.
    UNIQUENESS: if X, Y are solutions, X_t − Y_t = ∫(b(X) − b(Y)) ds +
    ∫(σ(X) − σ(Y)) dB. Using (a + b)² ≤ 2a² + 2b², Cauchy-Schwarz on the
    ds-part and the Ito isometry on the dB-part,
       φ(t) := E|X_t − Y_t|² ≤ 2(T + 1)K² ∫₀ᵗ φ(s) ds,
    so Gronwall gives φ ≡ 0 (localize with stopping times if needed).
    EXISTENCE: Picard iterates X^{n+1} = X₀ + ∫b(Xⁿ) + ∫σ(Xⁿ) dB satisfy
    E sup|X^{n+1} − Xⁿ|² ≤ C(Ct)ⁿ/n! (Doob's inequality), summable, so they
    converge a.s. uniformly (Borel-Cantelli). (a) b = x² is only locally
    Lipschitz, no linear growth: X = 1/(1 − t) blows up at t = 1. (b) b =
    3x^{2/3} is not Lipschitz at 0: both X ≡ 0 and X = t³ (dX/dt = 3t² =
    3(t³)^{2/3}) solve it. (c) Given any BM W, X = W solves the SDE with
    B := ∫sgn(W) dW, a BM by Lévy ([B]_t = t): a weak solution. But −X
    solves it with the same B (sgn is odd, up to the null set {X = 0}),
    so pathwise uniqueness fails, and B = |X| − L generates only the
    filtration of |X|, so X is not adapted to B: no strong solution.
    Common mistakes: thinking local Lipschitz alone prevents explosion.
    Now you try: explosion time of dX = X² dt, X₀ = 2. (1/2)

D9. State Girsanov's theorem. (a) For constant θ, with dQ/dP =
    exp(θB_T − θ²T/2), find the Q-law of B_T and compute E_P[B_T
    exp(θB_T − θ²T/2)] and E_P[B_T² exp(θB_T − θ²T/2)] for θ = 0.5, T = 2.
    (b) Why are P and Q singular on 𝓕_∞?
    Answer: (a) under Q, B_T ~ N(θT, T); 1 and 3. (b) B_t/t → 0 under P
    but → θ under Q.
    Teacher explains: GIRSANOV: let θ be adapted with Z_t = exp(∫₀ᵗθ dB −
    ½∫₀ᵗθ² ds) a martingale (Novikov suffices) and dQ = Z_T dP. Then
    B̃_t = B_t − ∫₀ᵗθ ds is a Q-Brownian motion on [0, T]. (Sign
    convention: density exp(+∫θ dB) ADDS drift θ to B under Q.) Proof idea:
    B̃Z is a P-martingale by the product rule, d(B̃Z) = Z dB̃ + B̃ dZ +
    d[B̃, Z] = Z dB − θZ dt + B̃ dZ + θZ dt, so B̃ is a Q-martingale with
    [B̃]_t = t; apply Lévy. (a) Under Q, B_T = B̃_T + θT ~ N(θT, T), so
    E_P[B_T Z_T] = E_Q B_T = θT = 1, and E_P[B_T² Z_T] = E_Q B_T² = T +
    θ²T² = 2 + 1 = 3. Check directly: E[Be^{θB}] = θTe^{θ²T/2} by Gaussian
    integration by parts ✓. (b) By the strong law B_t/t → 0 P-a.s., while
    B_t/t = B̃_t/t + θ → θ Q-a.s. These events are disjoint, so the
    measures (extended to 𝓕_∞) are mutually singular: Girsanov is a
    FINITE-HORIZON statement. Common mistakes: sign of the drift; using
    Z_T with θ > 0 and claiming B + θt is the new BM. Now you try: θ = 1,
    T = 1: E_P[B₁² e^{B₁ − 1/2}]. (1 + 1 = 2)

D10. Derive the Black-Scholes PDE by delta hedging, state the Black-Scholes
     formula and the risk-neutral interpretation, and price a European
     call and put with S = 100, K = 100, r = 0.05, σ = 0.2, T = 1. Give Δ,
     Γ and vega of the call.
     Answer: C_t + rSC_S + ½σ²S²C_SS − rC = 0, C(T, S) = (S − K)⁺;
     d₁ = 0.35, d₂ = 0.15; C ≈ 10.4506, P ≈ 5.5735; Δ ≈ 0.63683, Γ ≈
     0.018762, vega ≈ 37.524.
     Teacher explains: Model dS = μS dt + σS dB, bond dβ = rβ dt. Let C(t,
     S) be the option price and form Π = C − ΔS, self-financing: dΠ = dC
     − Δ dS. Ito: dC = (C_t + μSC_S + ½σ²S²C_SS) dt + σSC_S dB. With Δ =
     C_S the dB-terms cancel and dΠ = (C_t + ½σ²S²C_SS) dt is riskless, so
     no-arbitrage forces dΠ = rΠ dt = r(C − SC_S) dt, giving the PDE. The
     drift μ has vanished: all investors agree on the price whatever they
     believe about μ. RISK-NEUTRAL VIEW: Girsanov with θ = (μ − r)/σ makes
     B^Q = B + θt a Q-BM and dS = rS dt + σS dB^Q; discounted prices
     e^{−rt}S_t are Q-martingales and C = e^{−rτ}E_Q(S_T − K)⁺. Feynman-Kac
     connects the two views. Computing the expectation of a lognormal:
        C = SΦ(d₁) − Ke^{−rτ}Φ(d₂), d₁ = [ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)τ]/(σ√τ).
     Here d₁ = (0 + 0.07)/0.2 = 0.35, d₂ = 0.15, Φ(d₁) ≈ 0.63683, Φ(d₂) ≈
     0.55962, so C = 63.683 − 95.123·0.55962 ≈ 10.4506. Parity: P = C − S
     + Ke^{−rT} = 10.4506 − 100 + 95.1229 ≈ 5.5735. Δ = Φ(d₁) ≈ 0.63683,
     Γ = φ(d₁)/(Sσ√T) ≈ 0.018762, vega = Sφ(d₁)√T ≈ 37.524 (per unit of
     σ). Common mistakes: using μ instead of r; forgetting to discount K;
     taking d₂ = d₁ + σ√τ. Now you try: S = K = 100, r = 0, σ = 0.2, T =
     1. (C = P ≈ 7.9656, close to the rule of thumb 0.4Sσ√T = 8)

D11. For a diffusion dX = b(X) dt + σ(X) dB with generator L, explain Dynkin's
     formula and use it to solve exit problems. For X = B on (a, b) find
     u(x) = P_x(hit b before a) and w(x) = E_xτ; evaluate at a = 0, b = 3,
     x = 1. For BM with drift μ = 0.5 (σ = 1) find u(1) on (0, 3). State
     Feynman-Kac and check it on u(t, x) = E[B_T² | B_t = x].
     Answer: u = (x − a)/(b − a) = 1/3, w = (x − a)(b − x) = 2; with drift
     u(1) = (1 − e^{−1})/(1 − e^{−3}) ≈ 0.66524; u(t, x) = x² + T − t.
     Teacher explains: For f ∈ C², Ito gives f(X_t) = f(x) + ∫Lf(X) ds +
     martingale, Lf = bf′ + ½σ²f″. At a bounded stopping time (then let t →
     ∞ with E τ < ∞) E_x f(X_τ) = f(x) + E_x∫₀^τ Lf(X_s) ds: DYNKIN. If Lu
     = 0 with u(a) = 0, u(b) = 1, then u(x) = E_x u(X_τ) = P_x(X_τ = b). If
     Lw = −1, w(a) = w(b) = 0, then 0 = w(x) − E_xτ. For BM L = ½d²/dx²:
     u is linear, (x − a)/(b − a) = 1/3; w″ = −2 gives w = (x − a)(b − x) =
     1·2 = 2. With drift μ: μu′ + ½u″ = 0 ⇒ u′ ∝ e^{−2μx} ⇒ u(x) = (1 −
     e^{−2μ(x−a)})/(1 − e^{−2μ(b−a)}) = (1 − e^{−1})/(1 − e^{−3}) ≈ 0.66524
     (up from 1/3: the drift pushes upward). The function s with Ls = 0 is
     the SCALE FUNCTION. FEYNMAN-KAC: u(t, x) = E[e^{−∫_t^T r(X)ds}g(X_T) |
     X_t = x] solves u_t + Lu − ru = 0, u(T, ·) = g. Check: B_T = x +
     (B_T − B_t) gives u = x² + (T − t); u_t + ½u_xx = −1 + 1 = 0 ✓. The
     density p(t, y) of X_t solves the FORWARD equation p_t = −(bp)_y +
     ½(σ²p)_yy (adjoint of L). Common mistakes: using Lu = −1 for the
     probability; forgetting that E τ < ∞ must be checked. Now you try: BM
     on (−1, 2) from 0. (P(hit 2 first) = 1/3, E τ = 2)

D12. A colloidal particle of mass m in a fluid obeys the Langevin equation
     dV = −γV dt + σ dB. (a) Find the stationary E V² and the fluctuation-
     dissipation relation forced by equipartition. (b) Show the position
     X_t = ∫₀ᵗV ds satisfies E X_t² = 2D(t − (1 − e^{−γt})/γ) with D =
     k_BT/(mγ). (c) For a sphere of radius 1 μm in water (ζ = 6πηa, η =
     10⁻³ Pa·s, k_BT = 4.1·10⁻²¹ J) find D and the 1-D MSD after 10 s.
     (d) Find the stationary density of the overdamped dX = −(U′/ζ) dt +
     √(2D) dB.
     Answer: (a) σ²/(2γ) = k_BT/m ⇒ σ² = 2γk_BT/m; (b) integrate the OU
     covariance; (c) D ≈ 0.2175 μm²/s, MSD ≈ 4.35 μm²; (d) ∝ e^{−U/k_BT}.
     Teacher explains: (a) V is OU (D7) with stationary variance σ²/(2γ).
     Equipartition ½mE V² = ½k_BT forces σ² = 2γk_BT/m: the strength of
     the noise is tied to the friction (both come from molecular kicks).
     (b) In stationarity C(u) = E V₀V_u = (σ²/2γ)e^{−γ|u|} and
        E X_t² = ∫₀ᵗ∫₀ᵗ C(s − r) dr ds = 2∫₀ᵗ (t − u)C(u) du
               = (σ²/γ²)(t − (1 − e^{−γt})/γ).
     With D = σ²/(2γ²) = k_BT/(mγ) this is the formula. For γt ≪ 1 it is ≈
     (k_BT/m)t² (ballistic); for γt ≫ 1 it is ≈ 2Dt (diffusive): EINSTEIN'S
     relation D = k_BT/ζ, ζ = mγ. (c) ζ = 6π·10⁻³·10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.885·10⁻⁸ N·s/m,
     D ≈ 2.175·10⁻¹³ m²/s = 0.2175 μm²/s, and 2Dt ≈ 4.35 μm². (d) The
     Fokker-Planck equation is p_t = ∂_x(U′p/ζ + Dp_x). Stationary with
     zero flux: p′ = −U′p/(ζD) = −U′p/k_BT, so p ∝ e^{−U/k_BT}, Boltzmann.
     If instead the noise is multiplicative, g(X)∘dB (physicists' white
     noise limit is Stratonovich, by Wong-Zakai) equals the Ito g dB plus
     the NOISE-INDUCED DRIFT ½gg′ dt. Common mistakes: using MSD 2Dt at
     short times; choosing the Ito interpretation without justification.
     Now you try: convert the Stratonovich dX = X∘dB to Ito and solve.
     (dX = ½X dt + X dB; X_t = X₀e^{B_t})

M4. Martingales, covariations and expectations via Ito.

         2√e ≈ 3.29744          h) 15t

      k) 0 (XY ≡ 1: the drifts ½ + ½ − 1 cancel, and so do the dB-parts)

         (1 − √(1 − 4T))/2 ≤ 1/2)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) ∫₀ᵗ B dB = B_t²/2.
     b) For H ∈ 𝓗²[0, T], t ↦ ∫₀ᵗ H dB is a martingale.
     c) If ∫₀^T H² ds < ∞ a.s., then ∫H dB is a martingale.
     d) Brownian paths have finite total variation on [0, 1].
     e) For deterministic H ∈ L²[0, T], ∫₀^T H dB is Gaussian.
     f) E e^{B_t} = 1.
     g) The Stratonovich integral ∫₀ᵗ H∘dB has mean zero.
     h) Lipschitz b, σ (time-independent) give a unique strong solution.
     i) A non-Lipschitz σ always destroys pathwise uniqueness.
     j) Every weak solution of an SDE is a strong solution.
     k) GBM with μ > 0 tends to ∞ almost surely.
     l) Under Girsanov with constant θ ≠ 0, P ~ Q on 𝓕_∞.
     m) The Black-Scholes call price depends on the drift μ.
     n) A continuous local martingale with [M]_t = t, M₀ = 0, is a BM.
     o) EM has strong order 1 for every SDE with smooth coefficients.
     p) The Black-Scholes call price is increasing in σ.
     q) E(∫₀¹ B_s ds)² = E∫₀¹ B_s² ds.
     r) An OU process with θ > 0 has a Gaussian stationary law.
     s) Every positive local martingale is a supermartingale.
     Answers:
       a) F: (B_t² − t)/2        b) T
       c) F: a strict local martingale, e.g. M = 1/|W| for 3-dim W, W₀ ≠
          0 (= M₀ − ∫(W/|W|³)·dW, but E M_t ↓ 0)
       d) F: infinite (D1)       e) T: N(0, ∫H²)
       f) F: e^{t/2}              g) F: ∫B∘dB = B²/2, mean t/2
       h) T (linear growth follows from Lipschitz)
       i) F: σ = √|x| (Yamada-Watanabe: pathwise uniqueness holds)
       j) F: Tanaka's dX = sgn(X) dB
       k) F: S_t → 0 a.s. when μ < σ²/2 (e.g. μ = 0.1, σ = 0.6)
       l) F: mutually singular (B_t/t → 0 versus → θ)
       m) F: μ cancels in the hedge   n) T (Lévy)
       o) F: ½ for GBM (T for additive noise)
       p) T (vega = Sφ(d₁)√τ > 0)     q) F: 1/3 ≠ 1/2
       r) T: N(0, σ²/(2θ))           s) T (Fatou)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the box calculus (dB·dB = dt, everything else 0) until
  it is automatic, and make every Ito computation a three-column table
  f_t, f_x, ½f_xx before writing df; check each answer by taking
  expectations (the dB-part must vanish, e.g. E B_t⁴ = 3t²) or by
  simulation. Always say which interpretation (Ito or Stratonovich) is
  meant, and derive ∫B dB from left, right and midpoint sums at least once
  by hand. For SDEs, look first for an integrating factor (linear), then a
  log (multiplicative), then f(B) (try Y = f(X) with Ito). For finance,
  derive the Black-Scholes PDE from the hedge before memorising d₁, d₂,
  and check prices with put-call parity. Harder: construct the Ito
  integral for all progressively measurable H with ∫H² < ∞ a.s. via
  localisation; prove Lévy's characterisation and the martingale
  representation theorem; prove Girsanov and Novikov; prove the Picard
  existence theorem and Yamada-Watanabe; show Tanaka's SDE has no strong
  solution; derive Tanaka's formula and the occupation-time formula for
  local time; prove the Feynman-Kac formula with killing and use it for
  the arcsine law; price barrier options by the reflection principle and
  Girsanov; derive Kramers' escape rate by solving the mean exit-time
  ODE asymptotically; and prove that Euler-Maruyama has strong order ½ and
  Milstein order 1.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.20 — ERGODIC THEORY: MEASURE-PRESERVING SYSTEMS, POINCARÉ
RECURRENCE, ERGODICITY AND MIXING, BIRKHOFF AND VON NEUMANN THEOREMS,
EXAMPLES, INVARIANT MEASURES, ENTROPY, ISOMORPHISM, NUMBER THEORY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - MEASURE-PRESERVING SYSTEM (m.p.s.) (X, 𝔅, μ, T): μ a probability
    measure, T : X → X measurable with μ(T⁻¹A) = μ(A) for all A ∈ 𝔅
    (PREIMAGES, not images!). Equivalently ∫f∘T dμ = ∫f dμ for f ∈ L¹.
    It suffices to check μ(T⁻¹A) = μ(A) on a π-system generating 𝔅
    (e.g. intervals, cylinder sets). T need not be invertible.
  - STANDARD EXAMPLES: circle rotation Rα(x) = x + α mod 1 (Lebesgue);
    doubling map x ↦ 2x mod 1 and x ↦ kx mod 1 (Lebesgue); Bernoulli
    shift σ on {1, ..., k}^N or ^Z with product measure (p₁, ..., p_k)^N;
    Markov shift with stochastic P and stationary row vector π (πP = π);
    toral automorphism x ↦ Ax mod Zᵈ, A ∈ GL(d, Z) (Haar measure);
    Gauss map G(x) = {1/x} with Gauss measure dμ = dx/((1 + x) ln 2);
    tent and logistic maps (4x(1 − x) with dx/(π√(x(1 − x)))).
  - POINCARÉ RECURRENCE: if μ(A) > 0 then a.e. x ∈ A returns to A
    infinitely often. Needs μ(X) < ∞ (x ↦ x + 1 on R fails). KAC: if T
    is ergodic and μ(A) > 0 the first return time r_A satisfies
    ∫_A r_A dμ = 1, i.e. the mean return time to A is 1/μ(A).
  - ERGODICITY: T⁻¹A = A (mod μ) ⇒ μ(A) ∈ {0, 1}. Equivalent: every
    invariant f ∈ L² (f∘T = f a.e.) is constant; (1/n)∑_{k<n} μ(T⁻ᵏA ∩ B)
    → μ(A)μ(B) for all A, B. Rα is ergodic iff α ∉ Q (Fourier proof).
  - MIXING HIERARCHY: STRONG MIXING μ(T⁻ⁿA ∩ B) → μ(A)μ(B); WEAK MIXING
    (1/n)∑|μ(T⁻ᵏA ∩ B) − μ(A)μ(B)| → 0 (⇔ T × T ergodic ⇔ no non-constant
    L² eigenfunctions); ERGODIC. Strong ⇒ weak ⇒ ergodic, both strict:
    irrational rotations are ergodic but not weakly mixing (e^{2πix} is
    an eigenfunction); Chacón's map is weakly but not strongly mixing.
    Bernoulli shifts, the doubling map, mixing Markov chains and
    hyperbolic toral automorphisms are (strongly) mixing.
  - VON NEUMANN MEAN ERGODIC THEOREM: U an isometry of a Hilbert space H
    (Koopman Uf = f∘T), P the orthogonal projection onto {f : Uf = f};
    then (1/n)∑_{k<n} Uᵏf → Pf IN NORM. Proof: H = ker(U − I) ⊕
    closure(range(U − I)); averages of coboundaries g − Ug telescope.
  - BIRKHOFF POINTWISE ERGODIC THEOREM: for f ∈ L¹(μ), Aₙf(x) =
    (1/n)∑_{k<n} f(Tᵏx) → f*(x) a.e. and in L¹, where f* = E(f | 𝓘) is
    T-invariant and ∫f* = ∫f (𝓘 = σ-algebra of invariant sets). If T is
    ergodic, f* = ∫f dμ: TIME AVERAGE = SPACE AVERAGE. Key lemma: the
    MAXIMAL ERGODIC THEOREM ∫_{max_{n}Sₙf > 0} f dμ ≥ 0.
  - INVARIANT MEASURES: M(T) = {T-invariant Borel probabilities} is
    convex and weak* compact; KRYLOV-BOGOLYUBOV: M(T) ≠ ∅ for T
    continuous on a compact metric space (limit points of
    (1/n)∑δ_{Tᵏx}). Ergodic measures = EXTREME POINTS of M(T); distinct
    ergodic measures are mutually singular. UNIQUELY ERGODIC: |M(T)| = 1
    ⇔ Aₙf → constant UNIFORMLY for every continuous f (irrational
    rotations; Furstenberg skew product (x, y) ↦ (x + α, y + x)).
  - SHIFTS: cylinders [a₀ ... a_{n−1}] generate; Bernoulli measure of a
    cylinder is the product p_{a₀}...p_{a_{n−1}}; Markov measure is
    π_{a₀}P_{a₀a₁}...P. Markov shift is ergodic ⇔ P irreducible, mixing ⇔
    P irreducible and aperiodic. Periodic points of the topological
    Markov shift with 0-1 matrix M: #Fix(σⁿ) = tr(Mⁿ).
  - TORAL AUTOMORPHISMS: T_A on Tᵈ preserves Haar measure (|det A| = 1);
    T_A is ergodic ⇔ no eigenvalue of A is a root of unity (Fourier: the
    character e^{2πi⟨m,x⟩} is sent to e^{2πi⟨Aᵗm,x⟩}; ergodic ⇔ no finite
    Aᵗ-orbit of m ≠ 0); then it is even mixing. For A ∈ SL(2, Z):
    ergodic ⇔ |tr A| > 2 (hyperbolic). #Fix(T_Aⁿ) = |det(Aⁿ − I)|.
  - ENTROPY: H(ξ) = −∑μ(C) log μ(C) for a finite partition ξ; h(T, ξ) =
    lim (1/n)H(ξ ∨ T⁻¹ξ ∨ ... ∨ T⁻⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾ξ); h(T) = sup_ξ h(T, ξ).
    KOLMOGOROV-SINAI: a (one-sided) generator ξ gives h(T) = h(T, ξ).
    Values: Bernoulli (p) → −∑pᵢ log pᵢ; Markov → −∑πᵢPᵢⱼ log Pᵢⱼ;
    x ↦ kx → log k; toral T_A → ∑_{|λ|>1} log|λ|; rotations, identity
    and any system with discrete spectrum → 0. h(Tⁿ) = |n|h(T),
    h(T × S) = h(T) + h(S).
  - ISOMORPHISM PROBLEM: T ≅ S if there is an invertible m.p. map φ
    (defined mod null sets) with φ∘T = S∘φ. Invariants: ergodicity,
    mixing, SPECTRUM of the Koopman operator, entropy. HALMOS-VON
    NEUMANN: ergodic systems with discrete spectrum are isomorphic iff
    they have the same eigenvalue group (Rα ≅ Rβ ⇔ β = ±α mod 1).
    Spectrum fails for Bernoulli shifts (all have countable Lebesgue
    spectrum); KOLMOGOROV: entropy distinguishes B(½, ½) (log 2) from
    B(⅓, ⅓, ⅓) (log 3); ORNSTEIN: two-sided Bernoulli shifts with equal
    entropy are isomorphic (Meshalkin: B(¼,¼,¼,¼) ≅ B(½,⅛,⅛,⅛,⅛)).
  - NUMBER THEORY: BOREL — a.e. x is NORMAL in every base (Birkhoff for
    x ↦ bx); WEYL — {nα} is equidistributed for α ∉ Q (unique ergodicity
    of Rα), and {p(n)} for a polynomial with an irrational non-constant
    coefficient (skew products); BENFORD — the leading digit of 2ⁿ is d
    with frequency log₁₀(1 + 1/d); CONTINUED FRACTIONS — for a.e. x the
    digit k occurs with frequency log₂(1 + 1/(k(k + 2))), (a₁...aₙ)^(1/n)
    → Khinchin's constant 2.68545..., (1/n) ln qₙ → π²/(12 ln 2);
    FURSTENBERG's multiple recurrence theorem ⇒ SZEMERÉDI's theorem.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Show that the doubling map T(x) = 2x mod 1 preserves Lebesgue
    measure m on [0, 1), and explain why the definition uses preimages.
    (b) Show that the Gauss map G(x) = {1/x} preserves the Gauss measure
    μ(A) = (1/ln 2)∫_A dx/(1 + x). (c) Compute μ([½, 1]) and interpret
    it. (d) Is Lebesgue measure G-invariant?
    Answer: (a) T⁻¹[a, b) has two pieces of length (b − a)/2. (b) the
    preimage of [0, t) telescopes to measure log₂(1 + t). (c) log₂(4/3)
    ≈ 0.41504 = μ{a₁ = 1}. (d) No: m(G⁻¹[0, ½)) = 2(1 − ln 2) ≈ 0.61371.
    Teacher explains: By the π-λ theorem it is enough to test intervals.
    (a) T⁻¹[a, b) = [a/2, b/2) ∪ [(a + 1)/2, (b + 1)/2), total length
    (b − a)/2 + (b − a)/2 = b − a ✓. IMAGES do not work: T[0, ½) = [0, 1)
    has measure 1, not ½. With preimages the identity ∫f∘T = ∫f holds
    (check it on indicators: 𝟙_A∘T = 𝟙_{T⁻¹A}). (b) G(x) < t ⇔ 1/x ∈
    [k, k + t) for some k ≥ 1 ⇔ x ∈ (1/(k + t), 1/k]. So
       ln 2 · μ(G⁻¹[0, t)) = ∑_{k≥1} [ln(1 + 1/k) − ln(1 + 1/(k + t))]
                          = ∑_{k≥1} [ln((k + 1)/(k + 1 + t)) − ln(k/(k + t))].
    This telescopes: the partial sum up to N is ln((N + 1)/(N + 1 + t)) +
    ln(1 + t) → ln(1 + t) = ln 2 · μ[0, t) ✓. (c) μ([½, 1]) = log₂(2/(3/2))
    = log₂(4/3) ≈ 0.41504. Since x ∈ (½, 1] ⇔ the first continued-
    fraction digit a₁(x) = 1, and (by Birkhoff, D12) the digit aₙ = a₁∘Gⁿ⁻¹,
    about 41.5% of all partial quotients of a typical x equal 1.
    (d) m(G⁻¹[0, ½)) = ∑(1/k − 1/(k + ½)) = ∑ 1/(k(2k + 1)) = 2∑(1/(2k) −
    1/(2k + 1)) = 2(1 − ln 2) ≈ 0.61371 ≠ ½. Common mistakes: checking
    μ(TA) = μ(A); forgetting that a non-invertible map has several
    preimage branches. Now you try: show x ↦ 3x mod 1 preserves m.
    (T⁻¹[a, b) is three intervals of length (b − a)/3)

D2. State and prove the Poincaré recurrence theorem. Show that the
    hypothesis μ(X) < ∞ is needed. Verify Kac's lemma for the doubling map
    and A = [0, ½) by computing the distribution of the return time.
    Answer: a.e. point of A returns to A infinitely often; x ↦ x + 1 on R
    fails; P(r_A = k | A) = 2⁻ᵏ, mean 2 = 1/m(A).
    Teacher explains: Let A have μ(A) > 0 and B = {x ∈ A : Tⁿx ∉ A for all
    n ≥ 1}, the points that never come back. CLAIM: B, T⁻¹B, T⁻²B, ... are
    pairwise disjoint. If x ∈ T⁻ᵐB ∩ T⁻ⁿB with m < n, then y = Tᵐx ∈ B and
    T^{n−m}y = Tⁿx ∈ B ⊆ A, so y returns to A: contradiction. All have
    measure μ(B) (invariance), so
       ∑_{n≥0} μ(T⁻ⁿB) = ∑ μ(B) ≤ μ(X) = 1  ⇒  μ(B) = 0.
    INFINITELY OFTEN: a point x ∈ A that visits A only finitely often has
    a last visit time n ≥ 0, and then Tⁿx ∈ B, i.e. x ∈ T⁻ⁿB; but ⋃ₙT⁻ⁿB
    is a countable union of null sets.
    Infinite measure: T(x) = x + 1 preserves Lebesgue measure on R, but
    no point of A = [0, 1) ever returns. KAC for T(x) = 2x mod 1: x ∈ A ⇔
    binary digit d₁ = 0, and Tᵏx ∈ A ⇔ d_{k+1} = 0. So r_A(x) = k ⇔ d₂ =
    ... = d_k = 1, d_{k+1} = 0, with m = ½ · 2⁻⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾ · ½ = 2⁻ᵏ⁻¹. Hence
       ∫_A r_A dm = ∑_{k≥1} k 2⁻ᵏ⁻¹ = ½ · 2 = 1,
    and the conditional mean return time is 1/m(A) = 2 ✓. Common
    mistakes: thinking EVERY point returns (under doubling, ¼ ∈ [¼, ½)
    goes to ½, 0, 0, ... and never returns: a null exception); applying
    the theorem without an invariant measure. Now you try: for the
    doubling map, the mean return time to [0, ¼)? (4)

D3. (a) Prove that Rα(x) = x + α mod 1 is ergodic iff α ∉ Q. (b) Prove that
    T(x) = 2x mod 1 is ergodic. (c) For α = 2/5 exhibit an invariant set of
    measure 1/5.
    Answer: (a) Fourier coefficients of an invariant f satisfy cₙ(e^{2πinα}
    − 1) = 0. (b) c_{2n} = cₙ and Riemann-Lebesgue. (c) ⋃_{j<5}[j/5,
    j/5 + 1/25).
    Teacher explains: USE: T is ergodic ⇔ every invariant f ∈ L²
    (f∘T = f a.e.) is a.e. constant (take f = 𝟙_A for one direction; for
    the other, the sets {f > c} are invariant). (a) Write f(x) = ∑ cₙ
    e^{2πinx} in L². Then f∘Rα = ∑ cₙ e^{2πinα} e^{2πinx}, and by
    uniqueness of Fourier coefficients cₙ = cₙe^{2πinα}. If α ∉ Q then
    e^{2πinα} ≠ 1 for n ≠ 0, so cₙ = 0 for n ≠ 0: f = c₀ is constant. If
    α = p/q then f(x) = e^{2πiqx} is invariant and non-constant.
    (b) f(2x) = f(x) gives ∑ cₙ e^{2πi(2n)x} = ∑ cₘ e^{2πimx}; comparing
    coefficients, c_{2n} = cₙ (and cₘ = 0 for m odd). Hence cₙ = c_{2n} =
    c_{4n} = ... = c_{2ᵏn} → 0 as k → ∞ (∑|cₙ|² < ∞). So cₙ = 0
    for n ≠ 0. (c) For α = 2/5 every point has period 5, and any set of
    the form E ∪ (E + 1/5) ∪ ... ∪ (E + 4/5) is invariant (the rotation
    permutes the translates since 2/5 generates Z/5). With E = [0, 1/25):
    measure 5/25 = 1/5, neither 0 nor 1. Common mistakes: using pointwise
    Fourier series (work in L²); forgetting the trivial invariant sets
    are only defined mod null sets. Now you try: is the map x ↦ −x mod 1
    ergodic? (No: [¼, ¾] is invariant, of measure ½)

D4. (a) Define strong mixing, weak mixing and ergodicity and prove strong
    ⇒ weak ⇒ ergodic. (b) Prove that T(x) = 2x mod 1 is mixing, computing
    m(T⁻ⁿA ∩ A) for A = [0, ¼) and n = 1, 2, 3. (c) For Rα and A = [0, ½)
    show m(Rα⁻ⁿA ∩ A) = ½ − ‖nα‖ (‖·‖ = distance to Z) and conclude that
    Rα (α ∉ Q) is ergodic but not weakly mixing. Evaluate for α = √2 − 1,
    n = 1, 2.
    Answer: (b) 1/8, 1/16, 1/16 (exact independence from n = 2 on).
    (c) ≈ 0.08579, ≈ 0.32843; the Cesàro mean → ¼ but |· − ¼| averages
    to 1/8.
    Teacher explains: Write aₙ = μ(T⁻ⁿA ∩ B) − μ(A)μ(B). Mixing: aₙ → 0;
    weak mixing: (1/n)∑_{k<n}|aₖ| → 0; ergodic ⇔ (1/n)∑aₖ → 0 for all A, B.
    aₙ → 0 ⇒ Cesàro means of |aₙ| → 0 ⇒ Cesàro means of aₙ → 0. And if
    the last holds and T⁻¹A = A, take B = A: μ(A) − μ(A)² = 0, so μ(A) ∈
    {0, 1}. (b) If A is a union of dyadic intervals of level j and B of
    level k, T⁻ⁿA depends only on binary digits n + 1, ..., n + j of x
    while B depends on digits 1, ..., k; for n ≥ k these are independent
    fair coin flips, so m(T⁻ⁿA ∩ B) = m(A)m(B) EXACTLY. Dyadic sets
    approximate every Borel set, giving mixing. For A = B = [0, ¼) =
    {d₁ = d₂ = 0}: n = 1: {d₁ = d₂ = d₃ = 0} has measure 1/8; n = 2:
    {d₁ = ... = d₄ = 0}: 1/16; n = 3: {d₁ = d₂ = d₄ = d₅ = 0}: 1/16 =
    m(A)² ✓. (c) R⁻ⁿA ∩ A is the overlap of [0, ½) with its translate by
    t = −nα; two half-circles at distance ‖t‖ overlap in length ½ − ‖t‖.
    For α = √2 − 1 ≈ 0.41421: ‖α‖ = 0.41421 → 0.08579; 2α ≈ 0.82843,
    ‖2α‖ = 0.17157 → 0.32843. The sequence ‖nα‖ is equidistributed on
    [0, ½] (Weyl), so (1/n)∑(½ − ‖kα‖) → ½ − ¼ = ¼ = m(A)² (ergodic), yet
    (1/n)∑|¼ − ‖kα‖| → mean of |¼ − u|, u uniform on [0, ½], = 1/8 ≠ 0:
    not weakly mixing, and aₙ does not converge: not mixing. Abstractly:
    f = e^{2πix} satisfies f∘Rα = e^{2πiα}f, an eigenfunction, which
    weak mixing forbids. Common mistakes: believing ergodic systems
    "mix"; testing only one pair A, B. Now you try: m(T⁻ⁿA ∩ A) for
    T = doubling, A = [0, ½), n = 1. (¼)

D5. State and prove von Neumann's mean ergodic theorem. For R_{1/2} on
    [0, 1) and f(x) = x, find the L² limit of the averages and check
    ∫Pf = ∫f.
    Answer: (1/n)∑_{k<n}Uᵏf → Pf in H. Here Pf(x) = x + ¼ on [0, ½) and
    x − ¼ on [½, 1); both integrals are ½.
    Teacher explains: Let U be an isometry (‖Uf‖ = ‖f‖), I = {f : Uf = f}
    and C = {g − Ug : g ∈ H}. STEP 1: I = C^⊥. If Uf = f then U*f = f too
    (‖U*f − f‖² = ‖U*f‖² − 2Re⟨U*f, f⟩ + ‖f‖² ≤ 2‖f‖² − 2Re⟨f, Uf⟩ = 0),
    so ⟨f, g − Ug⟩ = ⟨f − U*f, g⟩ = 0. Conversely if f ⊥ C then
    ⟨U*f − f, g⟩ = 0 for all g, so U*f = f, and ‖Uf − f‖² = 2‖f‖² −
    2Re⟨U*f, f⟩ = 0. Hence H = I ⊕ closure(C). STEP 2: on I the averages
    are f. On C they TELESCOPE: (1/n)∑_{k<n}Uᵏ(g − Ug) = (g − Uⁿg)/n, of
    norm ≤ 2‖g‖/n → 0. STEP 3: on closure(C) use ε/2: if ‖h − c‖ < ε with
    c ∈ C, the averages of h are within ε of those of c, since each
    average operator has norm ≤ 1. So Aₙf → Pf. For the Koopman operator
    of an ergodic T, I = constants and Pf = ∫f dμ. EXAMPLE: R_{1/2} is
    not ergodic; the invariant functions are those with period ½, and
    for f(x) = x, A₂f = (f + f∘R)/2 = x + ¼ on [0, ½), x − ¼ on [½, 1);
    A₂ₙf = A₂f and A_{2n+1}f → the same. ∫ = (1/8 + 1/8) + (3/8 − 1/8) = ½
    = ∫x dx ✓. Common mistakes: expecting a.e. convergence from this
    theorem (that is Birkhoff); forgetting that U need not be unitary.
    Now you try: the limit for f(x) = cos(4πx) under R_{1/2}. (f itself:
    it is invariant)

D6. State Birkhoff's ergodic theorem, prove the maximal ergodic theorem
    and deduce the a.e. convergence of Aₙf.
    Answer: see below; key inequality Mₙ ≤ f + Mₙ∘T on {Mₙ > 0}.
    Teacher explains: Let f ∈ L¹, Sₙ = ∑_{k<n} f∘Tᵏ (S₀ = 0) and Mₙ =
    max(S₀, S₁, ..., Sₙ) ≥ 0. MAXIMAL ERGODIC THEOREM: ∫_{Mₙ>0} f dμ ≥ 0.
    Proof (Garsia): for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, Sₖ = f + S_{k−1}∘T ≤ f + Mₙ∘T. On
    {Mₙ > 0} we have Mₙ = max_{1≤k≤n} Sₖ ≤ f + Mₙ∘T. Integrate over
    Eₙ = {Mₙ > 0}:
       ∫_{Eₙ} f ≥ ∫_{Eₙ} Mₙ − ∫_{Eₙ} Mₙ∘T ≥ ∫_X Mₙ − ∫_X Mₙ∘T = 0,
    using Mₙ = 0 off Eₙ, Mₙ∘T ≥ 0 and invariance of μ. Letting n → ∞:
    ∫_E f ≥ 0 on E = {sup Sₙ > 0}; the same holds relative to any
    invariant set. BIRKHOFF: put f̄ = lim sup Aₙf, f̲ = lim inf Aₙf; both
    are T-invariant (Aₙf∘T = ((n + 1)/n)A_{n+1}f − f/n). For rationals a <
    b let E = {f̲ < a < b < f̄}, an invariant set. On E, sup (Sₙ(f − b)) > 0,
    so the maximal theorem for (f − b)𝟙_E gives ∫_E (f − b) ≥ 0; likewise
    ∫_E (a − f) ≥ 0. Adding, (a − b)μ(E) ≥ 0, so μ(E) = 0. A countable
    union over (a, b) shows f̲ = f̄ a.e.: Aₙf → f* a.e. Fatou gives
    f* ∈ L¹; for bounded f DCT gives L¹ convergence, and bounded
    functions are dense (each Aₙ contracts L¹), so Aₙf → f* in L¹ and
    ∫f* = ∫f. f* is invariant, and for an invariant set A, ∫_A f* = ∫_A f,
    so f* = E(f | 𝓘); if T is ergodic, f* = ∫f dμ. Common mistakes:
    claiming convergence for EVERY x (only a.e.; the doubling map at a
    periodic point gives other limits); forgetting f ∈ L¹. Now you try:
    doubling map, f = 𝟙_[0,½), x = 1/3 (binary 0.0101...): limit? (½; the
    orbit 1/3, 2/3 alternates)

D7. Consider the two-state Markov shift on {0, 1}^N with P = (0.9 0.1;
    0.2 0.8). (a) Find the stationary vector π and show the Markov measure
    is shift invariant. (b) Compute μ([0 0 1]) and μ([0] ∩ σ⁻ⁿ[1]) exactly,
    and deduce mixing. (c) Give the mean return time to [1]. (d) Why is
    P = (0 1; 1 0) ergodic but not mixing?
    Answer: (a) π = (2/3, 1/3). (b) 0.06; (2/9)(1 − 0.7ⁿ) → 2/9 = π₀π₁.
    (c) 3. (d) the chain has period 2.
    Teacher explains: The Markov measure of a cylinder is μ[a₀a₁...aₙ] =
    π_{a₀}P_{a₀a₁}...P_{aₙ₋₁aₙ}. (a) πP = π: 0.1π₀ = 0.2π₁ with π₀ + π₁ =
    1 gives π = (2/3, 1/3). Invariance on cylinders: σ⁻¹[a₀...aₙ] =
    ⋃_b [b a₀...aₙ], of measure ∑_b π_bP_{ba₀}·(P's) = (πP)_{a₀}·(P's) =
    μ[a₀...aₙ] ✓; cylinders form a π-system generating the σ-algebra.
    (b) μ[001] = (2/3)(0.9)(0.1) = 0.06. Next μ([0] ∩ σ⁻ⁿ[1]) = π₀(Pⁿ)₀₁.
    P has eigenvalues 1 and tr P − 1 = 0.7, and (Pⁿ)₀₁ = π₁(1 − 0.7ⁿ)
    (check n = 1: (1/3)(0.3) = 0.1 ✓). So μ = (2/9)(1 − 0.7ⁿ) → 2/9 =
    μ[0]μ[1]. The same argument for arbitrary cylinders (Pⁿ → the matrix
    with rows π) gives MIXING; in general a Markov shift is mixing ⇔ P is
    irreducible and aperiodic, ergodic ⇔ P is irreducible. (c) By Kac,
    E(r | start in [1]) = 1/π₁ = 3 (the classical Markov chain formula).
    (d) For P = (0 1; 1 0), π = (½, ½) and the measure lives on the two
    points 0101... and 1010..., swapped by σ: ergodic (one orbit), but
    μ([0] ∩ σ⁻ⁿ[0]) alternates ½, 0, ½, ... and does not tend to ¼.
    Common mistakes: using the uniform vector instead of π; forgetting
    the factor π_{a₀}. Now you try: entropy of the chain in (a),
    −∑πᵢPᵢⱼ ln Pᵢⱼ. (≈ 0.38352 nats)

D8. The cat map T(x) = Ax mod Z², A = (2 1; 1 1). (a) Show T preserves
    Haar (Lebesgue) measure on T². (b) Prove T is ergodic and mixing.
    (c) Find the eigenvalues and the entropy. (d) Count points of period
    n = 1, 2, 3 and find a point of least period 2.
    Answer: (b) Fourier: Aᵗ has no finite orbit on Z² ∖ {0}.
    (c) (3 ± √5)/2 ≈ 2.61803, 0.38197; h = ln((3 + √5)/2) ≈ 0.96242.
    (d) 1, 5, 16; e.g. (3/5, 1/5) ↦ (2/5, 4/5) ↦ (3/5, 1/5).
    Teacher explains: (a) det A = 1 and A⁻¹ = (1 −1; −1 2) is also integer,
    so T is a bijection of T² which is locally the linear map A with
    |det A| = 1: it preserves area. (b) Characters χₘ(x) = e^{2πi⟨m,x⟩},
    m ∈ Z², form an orthonormal basis, and χₘ∘T = χ_{Aᵗm}. If f = ∑cₘχₘ is
    invariant then c_{Aᵗm} = cₘ, so cₘ is constant along the orbit of m;
    ∑|cₘ|² < ∞ forces cₘ = 0 unless the orbit is finite. A finite orbit
    means (Aᵗ)ᵏm = m, so Aᵏ has eigenvalue 1: impossible because the
    eigenvalues λ^{±1} are real ≠ ±1. MIXING: ⟨χₘ∘Tⁿ, χₖ⟩ = 1 iff
    (Aᵗ)ⁿm = k, which for m ≠ 0 happens for at most one n since
    ‖(Aᵗ)ⁿm‖ → ∞; so correlations of trigonometric polynomials are
    eventually exactly 0, and density gives mixing. (c) λ² − 3λ + 1 = 0,
    λ = (3 ± √5)/2 = φ^{±2}. Entropy = ∑_{|λ|>1} ln|λ| = ln φ² ≈ 0.96242.
    (d) x is fixed by Tⁿ iff (Aⁿ − I)x ∈ Z², and the number of solutions
    in T² is |det(Aⁿ − I)| = λⁿ + λ⁻ⁿ − 2: n = 1: 3 − 2 = 1 (only 0);
    n = 2: 7 − 2 = 5; n = 3: 18 − 2 = 16. So there are 4 points of least
    period 2 (two 2-cycles). A² − I = (4 3; 3 1) has inverse
    −(1/5)(1 −3; −3 4), so these points lie in (1/5)Z²; indeed A(3/5,
    1/5)ᵗ = (7/5, 4/5) ≡ (2/5, 4/5) and A(2/5, 4/5)ᵗ = (8/5, 6/5) ≡
    (3/5, 1/5) ✓. Common mistakes: thinking det A = ±1 alone gives
    ergodicity ((1 1; 0 1) is not ergodic: eigenvalue 1); counting
    periodic points in R² instead of T². Now you try: is (0 1; −1 0)
    ergodic? (No: A⁴ = I, every point has period dividing 4)

D9. (a) Prove the Krylov-Bogolyubov theorem. (b) Show that ergodic
    measures are the extreme points of M(T) and that two distinct ergodic
    measures are mutually singular. (c) Find M(T) for T(x) = x² on [0, 1].
    (d) Show that T(x) = x/2 (x > 0), T(0) = 1 on [0, 1] has NO invariant
    probability measure. (e) Why is Rα (α ∉ Q) uniquely ergodic?
    Answer: (a) weak* limits of empirical measures. (c) {aδ₀ + (1 − a)δ₁ :
    0 ≤ a ≤ 1}. (d) T is not continuous. (e) Fourier coefficients of an
    invariant measure vanish.
    Teacher explains: (a) X compact metric, T continuous. Put μₙ =
    (1/n)∑_{k<n} δ_{Tᵏx}. The probability measures on X are weak* compact
    (Riesz + Banach-Alaoglu, C(X) separable), so μ_{n_j} → μ. For f ∈ C(X),
    |∫f∘T dμₙ − ∫f dμₙ| = |f(Tⁿx) − f(x)|/n ≤ 2‖f‖∞/n → 0, and f∘T is
    continuous, so ∫f∘T dμ = ∫f dμ: μ ∈ M(T). (b) If μ is not ergodic,
    take invariant A with 0 < μ(A) < 1; then μ = μ(A)μ_A + μ(Aᶜ)μ_{Aᶜ}
    (conditional measures, both invariant) is a non-trivial convex
    combination. Conversely if μ ergodic and μ = tν₁ + (1 − t)ν₂, then
    ν₁ ≪ μ and dν₁/dμ is invariant, hence constant = 1: ν₁ = μ. If μ ≠ ν
    are ergodic, pick continuous f with ∫f dμ ≠ ∫f dν; the Birkhoff sets
    {Aₙf → ∫f dμ} and {Aₙf → ∫f dν} are disjoint and have full μ-,
    resp. ν-measure: μ ⊥ ν. (c) For 0 < x < 1, x^{2ⁿ} → 0, so the empirical
    measures from any x < 1 converge to δ₀. If μ is invariant and
    [a, b] ⊂ (0, 1), every orbit starting in [a, b] decreases and leaves
    [a, b] for ever, so by Poincaré recurrence μ([a, b]) = 0; hence
    μ((0, 1)) = 0 and M(T) = {aδ₀ + (1 − a)δ₁}, with ergodic measures δ₀
    and δ₁. (d) μ{0} = μ(T⁻¹{0}) = μ(∅) = 0; μ{1} = μ(T⁻¹{1}) = μ{0} = 0;
    and Iₖ = (2⁻ᵏ⁻¹, 2⁻ᵏ] satisfies T⁻¹Iₖ = I_{k−1}, so all Iₖ (k ≥ 0,
    I₀ = (½, 1]) have the same measure, which must be 0 since they are
    disjoint: μ = 0, contradiction. (e) If μ is Rα-invariant, μ̂(n) =
    ∫e^{−2πinx}dμ satisfies μ̂(n) = e^{−2πinα}μ̂(n), so μ̂(n) = 0 for n ≠ 0:
    μ = Lebesgue. Unique ergodicity implies Aₙf(x) → ∫f UNIFORMLY in x for
    f ∈ C(T) — for EVERY x, not just a.e. Common mistakes: forgetting
    compactness (x ↦ x + 1 on R has no invariant probability) or
    continuity (part (d)). Now you try: list the ergodic measures of the
    identity map. (the Dirac measures δₓ)

D10. Define the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy and compute it for (a) the
     Bernoulli shift B(p₁, ..., p_k), in particular B(⅓, ⅔); (b) the
     doubling map; (c) a Markov shift (π, P); (d) an irrational rotation.
     Answer: (a) −∑pᵢ ln pᵢ; B(⅓, ⅔): ln 3 − (2/3) ln 2 ≈ 0.63651 nats
     ≈ 0.91830 bits. (b) ln 2. (c) −∑πᵢPᵢⱼ ln Pᵢⱼ. (d) 0.
     Teacher explains: For a finite partition ξ, H(ξ) = −∑_{C∈ξ} μ(C) ln
     μ(C), and ξⁿ = ξ ∨ T⁻¹ξ ∨ ... ∨ T⁻⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾ξ (common refinement). The
     sequence H(ξⁿ) is subadditive, so h(T, ξ) = lim H(ξⁿ)/n exists;
     h(T) = sup_ξ h(T, ξ). KOLMOGOROV-SINAI: if ξ is a GENERATOR (the
     partitions ξⁿ generate 𝔅 mod μ; for invertible T use T^{±k}), then
     h(T) = h(T, ξ). (a) ξ = {[1], ..., [k]} (first coordinate) is a
     generator and ξⁿ = cylinders of length n with measures p_{a₀}...
     p_{aₙ₋₁}; since coordinates are independent, H(ξⁿ) = nH(p), so
     h = H(p). For (⅓, ⅔): −⅓ ln ⅓ − ⅔ ln ⅔ = ln 3 − ⅔ ln 2 ≈ 0.63651.
     (b) The partition {[0, ½), [½, 1)} is a generator whose ξⁿ is the 2ⁿ
     dyadic intervals of length 2⁻ⁿ: H(ξⁿ) = n ln 2, so h = ln 2 (the
     doubling map IS the one-sided B(½, ½)). (c) H(ξⁿ) = H(π) + (n − 1)
     ∑ᵢπᵢH(Pᵢ₁, ..., P_{ik}) by the chain rule, giving h = −∑πᵢPᵢⱼ ln Pᵢⱼ.
     (d) ξ = {[0, ½), [½, 1)}: ξⁿ is cut by the 2n points R⁻ʲ0, R⁻ʲ(½),
     j < n, so it has at most 2n atoms and H(ξⁿ) ≤ ln(2n); h(Rα, ξ) =
     lim ln(2n)/n = 0. As ξ generates (the endpoints' orbit is dense),
     h(Rα) = 0. Common mistakes: forgetting the sup over ξ (a bad ξ, e.g.
     the trivial partition, gives 0 for every T); mixing logs to base 2
     and e. Now you try: h of x ↦ 10x mod 1 and of T² for the doubling
     map. (ln 10 ≈ 2.30259; ln 4 = 2h(T))

D11. The isomorphism problem. (a) Why are the two-sided shifts B(½, ½) and
     B(⅓, ⅓, ⅓) not isomorphic although they are spectrally isomorphic?
     (b) Check that B(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼) and B(½, ⅛, ⅛, ⅛, ⅛) have equal entropy.
     What does Ornstein's theorem say? (c) Prove, using eigenvalues, that
     for irrational α, β: Rα ≅ Rβ ⇒ β = ±α mod 1. (d) Show the doubling
     map is isomorphic to the one-sided shift B(½, ½).
     Answer: (a) entropies ln 2 ≠ ln 3. (b) both ln 4 ≈ 1.38629; they are
     isomorphic. (c) eigenvalue groups must coincide. (d) binary digits.
     Teacher explains: An ISOMORPHISM is a measure-preserving φ : X → Y,
     invertible mod null sets, with φ∘T = S∘φ. Anything defined from
     (X, μ, T) alone is an invariant: ergodicity, mixing, the Koopman
     spectrum, entropy. (a) Every non-trivial Bernoulli shift has
     COUNTABLE LEBESGUE SPECTRUM on L²₀ (the orthogonal complement of
     constants), so their Koopman operators are unitarily equivalent: the
     spectral invariants, the main tool before 1958, cannot separate
     them. Kolmogorov's entropy can: h = ln 2 ≈ 0.69315 vs ln 3 ≈
     1.09861. (b) H(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼) = ln 4; H(½, ⅛×4) = ½ ln 2 + 4·⅛ ln 8 =
     ½ ln 2 + (3/2) ln 2 = 2 ln 2 = ln 4 ≈ 1.38629. ORNSTEIN (1970): two
     two-sided Bernoulli shifts are isomorphic ⇔ they have the same
     entropy (Meshalkin had built this particular isomorphism by hand).
     Entropy is a COMPLETE invariant within the Bernoulli class, which
     also contains mixing Markov shifts and hyperbolic toral
     automorphisms. (c) If φ∘Rα = Rβ∘φ, then g(x) = e^{2πiφ(x)} satisfies
     g∘Rα = e^{2πiβ}g: an eigenfunction of Rα with eigenvalue e^{2πiβ}. The
     eigenvalues of Rα are exactly {e^{2πinα} : n ∈ Z} (Fourier), so β ≡
     nα, and symmetrically α ≡ mβ ≡ mnα mod 1; α ∉ Q forces mn = 1, i.e.
     n = ±1. (Halmos-von Neumann gives the converse: discrete spectrum
     systems with equal eigenvalue groups are isomorphic; Rα ≅ R₋α via
     x ↦ −x.) (d) φ(x) = (d₁, d₂, ...) (binary digits) is a bijection off
     the null set of dyadic rationals; the cylinder [a₁...aₙ] corresponds
     to a dyadic interval of length 2⁻ⁿ = its Bernoulli measure, and
     φ(2x mod 1) = σφ(x) since doubling deletes the first digit. Common
     mistakes: thinking equal spectra imply isomorphism; applying Ornstein
     to ONE-sided shifts (these are rigid: isomorphic only when the
     probability vectors agree up to order). Now you try: can the cat map
     be isomorphic to B(½, ½)? (No: 0.96242 ≠ 0.69315; it is isomorphic to
     a Bernoulli shift of entropy ln φ²)

D12. Applications to number theory. (a) Prove Borel's theorem: a.e. x ∈
     [0, 1) is normal in base 10. (b) Prove that the leading digit of 2ⁿ
     is d with frequency log₁₀(1 + 1/d); give the frequency of 1 and of 7,
     and check the first 10 powers. (c) For a.e. x find the frequency of
     the continued-fraction digit aₙ = k, for k = 1, 2, 3. (d) State
     Furstenberg's multiple recurrence theorem and its consequence.
     Answer: (a) Birkhoff for x ↦ 10x. (b) {n log₁₀ 2} is equidistributed;
     1: ≈ 0.30103, 7: ≈ 0.05799; first ten: 2,4,8,1,3,6,1,2,5,1 (three 1's).
     (c) log₂(4/3) ≈ 0.41504, log₂(9/8) ≈ 0.16993, log₂(16/15) ≈ 0.09311.
     (d) Szemerédi: dense sets of integers contain long APs.
     Teacher explains: (a) T(x) = 10x mod 1 preserves m and is ergodic (as
     in D3), and the k-th decimal digit of x is d₁(Tᵏ⁻¹x). For a block w =
     w₁...w_ℓ, let f = 𝟙_{I_w}, I_w the interval of numbers beginning
     0.w: then #{k ≤ n : digits k..k+ℓ−1 equal w}/n = Aₙf(x) → m(I_w) =
     10⁻ℓ for a.e. x. There are countably many blocks (and bases), so a.e.
     x is (absolutely) normal. Explicit examples are harder: Champernowne
     0.123456789101112... is normal in base 10. (b) 2ⁿ has leading digit
     d ⇔ d·10ʲ ≤ 2ⁿ < (d + 1)10ʲ ⇔ {n log₁₀ 2} ∈ [log₁₀ d, log₁₀(d + 1)).
     Since log₁₀ 2 ∉ Q (2ⁿ = 10ᵐ is impossible), R_{log₁₀2} is UNIQUELY
     ergodic, so the orbit of the SPECIFIC point 0 is equidistributed
     (Weyl) — an a.e. statement would not suffice. Frequency log₁₀((d +
     1)/d): d = 1: 0.30103; d = 7: log₁₀(8/7) ≈ 0.05799 (first at 2⁴⁶ =
     70368744177664). Powers 2¹..2¹⁰: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512,
     1024: three 1's in ten (and 301 in the first 1000). (c) The Gauss map
     is ergodic for μ (it is even exact/mixing), aₙ(x) = a₁(Gⁿ⁻¹x), and
     a₁ = k ⇔ x ∈ (1/(k + 1), 1/k]. Birkhoff gives frequency μ(1/(k + 1),
     1/k] = log₂((1 + 1/k)/(1 + 1/(k + 1))) = log₂(1 + 1/(k(k + 2))).
     k = 1: log₂(4/3), k = 2: log₂(9/8), k = 3: log₂(16/15). Applying
     Birkhoff to ln a₁ (in L¹(μ)) gives KHINCHIN's constant (a₁...aₙ)^(1/n)
     → 2.68545...; for −ln x one gets LÉVY's (1/n) ln qₙ → π²/(12 ln 2) ≈
     1.18657. (d) FURSTENBERG: if μ(A) > 0 and k ≥ 1, there is n ≥ 1 with
     μ(A ∩ T⁻ⁿA ∩ T⁻²ⁿA ∩ ... ∩ T⁻ᵏⁿA) > 0. Via the CORRESPONDENCE
     PRINCIPLE (a set E ⊆ Z of positive upper density yields a system and
     a set A with μ(A) = d̄(E)), this gives SZEMERÉDI's theorem: E contains
     arithmetic progressions of every length. (k = 1 is Poincaré
     recurrence.) Common mistakes: applying Birkhoff to a specific point
     such as 0 or √2 (Birkhoff says nothing about a given x; unique
     ergodicity does); taking Lebesgue measure for the Gauss map. Now you
     try: frequency with which 2ⁿ begins with the digits 10. (log₁₀(11/10)
     ≈ 0.04139)
