      f) aδ₀ + (1 − a)δ₁          g) δ₀ only
      h) e.g. δ₀, ½(δ_{1/3} + δ_{2/3}), Lebesgue, the image of B(⅓, ⅔)
         under binary expansion (all mutually singular)
      i) two: uniform on {1/7, 2/7, 4/7} and on {3/7, 6/7, 5/7}
      j) none (no invariant probability; Lebesgue is infinite)
      k) none (T is not continuous: D9 d))
      l) 1/((1 + x) ln 2); 1/(π√(x(1 − x)))
      m) ¼(δ_{1/5} + δ_{2/5} + δ_{4/5} + δ_{3/5})       n) Lebesgue
      o) no              p) yes (Furstenberg)
      q) no (each circle y − x = c carries an invariant measure)

M10. Number theory: give the frequency (limit density) asked.
     a) digit 7 in the decimal expansion of a.e. x
     b) block "12" in base 10, a.e. x     c) block "101" in base 2, a.e. x
     d) leading digit 1 of 2ⁿ             e) leading digit 9 of 2ⁿ
     f) leading digit 2 of 3ⁿ             g) leading digit 1 of 10ⁿ
     h) leading digits 99 of 2ⁿ           i) leading base-3 digit 1 of 2ⁿ
     j) n with {n√2} < ¼                  k) n with {n²√2} < ⅓
     l) n with {n/3} < ½                  m) aₖ = 1, a.e. x
     n) aₖ = 4, a.e. x                    o) aₖ ≥ 2, a.e. x
     p) aₖ = 1 for x = √2
     q) lim (a₁...aₙ)^(1/n) and lim qₙ^(1/n), a.e. x
     r) lim (a₁ + ... + aₙ)/n, a.e. x
     Answers:
       a) 1/10     b) 1/100    c) 1/8      d) log₁₀ 2 ≈ 0.30103
       e) log₁₀(10/9) ≈ 0.04576            f) log₁₀(3/2) ≈ 0.17609
       g) 1 (log₁₀ 10 ∈ Q: no equidistribution)
       h) log₁₀(100/99) ≈ 0.00436          i) log₃ 2 ≈ 0.63093
       j) ¼        k) ⅓ (Weyl, via skew products)
       l) ⅔ ({n/3} ∈ {0, ⅓, ⅔})            m) log₂(4/3) ≈ 0.41504
       n) log₂(25/24) ≈ 0.05889            o) log₂(3/2) ≈ 0.58496
       p) 0 (√2 = [1; 2, 2, 2, ...])
       q) 2.68545 (Khinchin); e^{π²/(12 ln 2)} ≈ 3.27582 (Lévy)
       r) ∞ (a₁ ∉ L¹(μ): ∑k log₂(1 + 1/(k(k + 2))) diverges)

M11. Isomorphic? (Y/N and the reason; Bernoulli shifts two-sided unless
     stated.)
     a) B(½, ½) and B(⅓, ⅓, ⅓)            b) B(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼), B(½, ⅛, ⅛, ⅛, ⅛)
     c) B(½, ½) and B(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼)         d) B(½, ½) × B(½, ½), B(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼)
     e) B(⅓, ⅔) and B(⅔, ⅓)               f) Rα and R₋α
     g) Rα and R₂α (α ∉ Q)                h) R_{√2} and R_{√2+1}
     i) cat map and B(p) with H(p) = ln φ²  j) cat map and B(½, ½)
     k) doubling map and tent map          l) doubling map and x ↦ 3x
     m) Rα and the doubling map            n) Rα and Rα × Rα
     o) one-sided B(½, ½) and two-sided B(½, ½)
     p) golden mean Markov shift (Parry measure) and B(p), H(p) = ln φ
     q) doubling map and 4x(1 − x) with the arcsine measure
     r) Markov (0 1; 1 0) and R_{1/2} restricted to the orbit {0, ½}
     Answers:
       a) N (ln 2 ≠ ln 3)      b) Y (Ornstein, both ln 4)
       c) N (ln 2 ≠ ln 4)      d) Y (the product is B(¼, ¼, ¼, ¼))
       e) Y (relabel symbols)  f) Y (x ↦ −x)
       g) N (eigenvalue groups differ)     h) Y (same rotation mod 1)
       i) Y (hyperbolic toral automorphisms are Bernoulli)
       j) N (0.96242 ≠ 0.69315)            k) Y (both one-sided B(½, ½))
       l) N (ln 2 ≠ ln 3)      m) N (entropy 0 vs ln 2; mixing)
       n) N (Rα × Rα is not ergodic)       o) N (invertible vs 2-to-1)
       p) Y (mixing Markov shifts are Bernoulli; Ornstein)
       q) Y (conjugate to the tent map by x = sin²(πy/2))
       r) Y (both are the cyclic permutation of two points)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every m.p. map of a probability space is recurrent (Poincaré).
     b) Poincaré recurrence holds for infinite invariant measures.
     c) Every ergodic system is mixing.
     d) Mixing implies ergodic.
     e) T ergodic ⇒ T² ergodic.
     f) T weakly mixing ⇒ T² and T × T are ergodic.
     g) T ergodic ⇒ T × T ergodic.
     h) Every continuous map of a compact metric space has an invariant
        Borel probability measure.
     i) The Birkhoff averages of f ∈ L¹ converge at every point.
     j) If T is uniquely ergodic, Aₙf → ∫f uniformly for continuous f.
     k) For Rα (α ∉ Q), Aₙ𝟙_A(x) → m(A) for every x and every Borel A.
     l) Spectrally isomorphic systems are isomorphic.
     m) Positive entropy implies ergodic.
     n) An irrational rotation is weakly mixing.
     o) Every A ∈ SL(2, Z) with |tr A| > 2 gives a mixing automorphism.
     p) The Gauss map preserves Lebesgue measure.
     q) Two distinct ergodic invariant measures are mutually singular.
     r) h(T × T) = h(T)².
     s) Entropy is an isomorphism invariant.
     t) An ergodic measure-preserving map on a finite set is a cyclic
        permutation of the support of μ.
     Answers:
       a) T              b) F: x ↦ x + 1 on R
       c) F: Rα, α ∉ Q   d) T
       e) F: the swap of two points (T² = identity)
       f) T              g) F: Rα (e^{2πi(x−y)} is T × T-invariant)
       h) T (Krylov-Bogolyubov)
       i) F: doubling map, f = 𝟙_[0,½), x with binary digits in blocks
          of 0's and 1's of lengths 1!, 2!, 3!, ...: Aₙf(x) oscillates
       j) T              k) F: A = the orbit of x (measure 0, Aₙ𝟙_A = 1)
       l) F: B(½, ½) and B(⅓, ⅓, ⅓)
       m) F: the doubling map on two disjoint copies of [0, 1)
       n) F: e^{2πix} is an eigenfunction      o) T
       p) F: D1 d)       q) T (Birkhoff)
       r) F: h(T × T) = 2h(T) (doubling: 2 ln 2, not (ln 2)²)
       s) T              t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: begin every problem by drawing the map (graph of 2x mod 1,
  the rotation as a clock hand, the cat map stretching a square) and by
  asking three questions in order: "which measure is preserved?" (always
  test PREIMAGES of intervals or cylinders), "what are the invariant
  functions?" (use Fourier series for rotations, doubling and toral maps,
  and look for finite orbits of frequencies) and "do correlations decay?"
  (compute μ(T⁻ⁿA ∩ B) for dyadic sets or cylinders, where the answer is
  exact). Keep the three model examples in mind: rotation (ergodic, zero
  entropy, not mixing), doubling map/Bernoulli shift (mixing, entropy
  ln 2), and x ↦ x² (no interesting invariant measure). Stress that
  Birkhoff is an a.e. statement and that unique ergodicity is what lets
  us talk about SPECIFIC orbits (Weyl, Benford). Harder: prove Kac's
  lemma and the ergodic decomposition; show that weak mixing is
  equivalent to the absence of non-constant eigenfunctions and to
  ergodicity of T × T; prove Weyl's polynomial equidistribution via
  Furstenberg's skew products and van der Corput; prove the
  Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem and Rohlin's formula for the Gauss map;
  compute the entropy of a hyperbolic toral automorphism with Markov
  partitions; study Ornstein's theory and the Halmos-von Neumann
  theorem; and read Furstenberg's proof of Szemerédi's theorem via the
  correspondence principle and multiple recurrence.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.21 — MATHEMATICAL LOGIC: MODEL THEORY, SET THEORY (ZFC, FORCING,
LARGE CARDINALS), RECURSION THEORY, PROOF THEORY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - FIRST-ORDER LOGIC: a language L (constants, function and relation
    symbols), L-structures 𝔐, satisfaction 𝔐 ⊨ φ[ā], theories T, models,
    T ⊨ φ (semantic) versus T ⊢ φ (formal proof). SOUNDNESS (⊢ ⇒ ⊨) and
    GÖDEL'S COMPLETENESS THEOREM (⊨ ⇒ ⊢; equivalently every consistent
    theory has a model, via Henkin constants and a maximal consistent set).
  - COMPACTNESS: T has a model iff every finite subset does. Consequences:
    nonstandard models of Th(N) and of R (infinitesimals); "finite",
    "torsion", "connected graph", "well-ordered" are NOT first-order
    axiomatizable; a theory with arbitrarily large finite models has an
    infinite model; De Bruijn-Erdős (a graph is k-colourable iff every
    finite subgraph is).
  - LÖWENHEIM-SKOLEM: if |L| ≤ κ and T has an infinite model, it has a model
    of every cardinality ≥ |L| + ℵ₀ (upward) and every infinite 𝔐 has an
    ELEMENTARY submodel 𝔑 ≼ 𝔐 of any size between |L| + ℵ₀ and |𝔐|
    (downward; Tarski-Vaught test). Skolem's "paradox": ZFC, if consistent,
    has a countable model although it proves R uncountable.
  - CATEGORICITY: T is κ-categorical if it has exactly one model of size κ
    up to ≅. ŁOŚ-VAUGHT TEST: κ-categorical with no finite models ⇒
    complete. Examples: DLO (ℵ₀-categorical, Cantor back-and-forth); ACF_p
    and Q-vector spaces (categorical in every uncountable κ, not in ℵ₀);
    the random graph (ℵ₀ only). MORLEY: categorical in one uncountable κ
    ⇒ in all. VAUGHT: a complete countable theory never has exactly 2
    countable models.
  - ULTRAFILTERS AND ULTRAPRODUCTS: U ⊆ 𝒫(I) is an ultrafilter if it is a
    filter and for every A exactly one of A, I ∖ A is in U; non-principal
    ones exist by Zorn. ŁOŚ'S THEOREM: ∏𝔐ᵢ/U ⊨ φ[[f]] iff {i : 𝔐ᵢ ⊨
    φ[f(i)]} ∈ U. Gives a second proof of compactness, the hyperreals ∗R,
    and ∏F_p/U, a field of characteristic 0.
  - TYPES AND QUANTIFIER ELIMINATION: a (complete) n-type over A is a
    maximal consistent set of formulas in x₁..xₙ with parameters in A;
    realized versus omitted types; ω-saturated models. T has QE if every
    formula is T-equivalent to a quantifier-free one: DLO, ACF (Chevalley:
    constructible sets), RCF (Tarski-Seidenberg: semialgebraic sets),
    Presburger arithmetic (with congruences ≡ₙ). QE + a decidable
    quantifier-free part ⇒ decidability.
  - ZFC: Extensionality, Foundation, Pairing, Union, Power set, Separation
    (schema), Replacement (schema), Infinity, Choice. ZFC is not finitely
    axiomatizable (Reflection). Useful models of fragments: V_ω ⊨ ZFC −
    Infinity; V_{ω+ω} ⊨ Z but not Replacement; H(ℵ₁) ⊨ ZFC − Power set.
    AC ⇔ Zorn's lemma ⇔ well-ordering theorem.
  - ORDINALS: transitive sets well-ordered by ∈; α + 1 = α ∪ {α}; successor
    and limit ordinals; transfinite induction and recursion. ORDINAL
    ARITHMETIC is not commutative: 1 + ω = ω ≠ ω + 1, 2·ω = ω ≠ ω·2 = ω + ω.
    CANTOR NORMAL FORM α = ω^β₁·c₁ + ... + ω^βₖ·cₖ (β₁ > ... > βₖ). ε₀ =
    sup{ω, ω^ω, ω^ω^ω, ...}, the least α with ω^α = α. The rank hierarchy
    V₀ = ∅, V_{α+1} = 𝒫(V_α), V_λ = ⋃_{α<λ} V_α; V = ⋃V_α (by Foundation).
  - CARDINALS: |A| ≤ |B| via injections; SCHRÖDER-BERNSTEIN; CANTOR |X| <
    |𝒫(X)|; alephs ℵ_α, κ⁺; under AC κ·κ = κ for infinite κ, so κ + λ = κ·λ
    = max. Cofinality cf(κ); regular (cf κ = κ) versus singular (cf ℵ_ω =
    ω). KÖNIG: κ^cf(κ) > κ, hence cf(2^κ) > κ and 2^ℵ₀ ≠ ℵ_ω. Hausdorff:
    ℵ_{n+1}^ℵ₀ = ℵ_{n+1}·ℵ_n^ℵ₀. GCH: 2^κ = κ⁺.
  - INDEPENDENCE OF CH: GÖDEL'S constructible universe L (L₀ = ∅, L_{α+1} =
    definable subsets of L_α) is an inner model of ZFC + V = L + GCH, so
    Con(ZF) ⇒ Con(ZFC + GCH). COHEN FORCING: a countable transitive model
    M, a poset P ∈ M, a generic filter G meeting every dense D ∈ M; M[G] ⊨
    ZFC; forcing theorem (truth in M[G] is forced by some p ∈ G). Adding ℵ₂
    Cohen reals with Fn(ℵ₂ × ω, 2) (ccc, so cardinals are preserved) gives
    2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂; so Con(ZF) ⇒ Con(ZFC + ¬CH). EASTON: 2^ℵ₀ can be any κ
    with cf κ > ω.
  - LARGE CARDINALS: κ is (strongly) INACCESSIBLE if uncountable, regular
    and λ < κ ⇒ 2^λ < κ; then V_κ ⊨ ZFC, so by Gödel II ZFC ⊬ "an
    inaccessible exists". Hierarchy (increasing strength): inaccessible <
    Mahlo < weakly compact < measurable < strong < Woodin < supercompact.
    κ is MEASURABLE if there is a κ-complete non-principal ultrafilter on
    κ ⇔ a nontrivial elementary embedding j : V → M with critical point κ.
    Measurable ⇒ inaccessible; SCOTT: measurable ⇒ V ≠ L. KUNEN: there is
    no nontrivial j : V → V (in ZFC).
  - COMPUTABILITY: Turing machines ≡ partial recursive (μ-recursive)
    functions ≡ λ-calculus (CHURCH-TURING THESIS). Primitive recursive
    functions ⊊ total recursive (the ACKERMANN function). Kleene normal
    form φₑ(x) = U(μs T(e, x, s)); s-m-n theorem; universal machine;
    KLEENE'S RECURSION THEOREM (every total computable f has e with φ_{f(e)}
    = φₑ: quines).
  - UNDECIDABILITY: the HALTING SET K = {e : φₑ(e)↓} is c.e. but not
    computable (diagonalisation). A set is computable iff it and its
    complement are c.e. RICE: every non-trivial index set {e : φₑ ∈ 𝒞} is
    undecidable. Many-one (≤ₘ) and Turing (≤_T) reductions, Turing degrees,
    the jump A′, 0 < 0′ < 0″; POST'S problem (Friedberg-Muchnik: c.e.
    degrees strictly between 0 and 0′). Natural undecidable problems:
    Hilbert's 10th (MRDP), the word problem for groups, Th(N, +, ·).
  - ARITHMETICAL HIERARCHY: Σₙ, Πₙ, Δₙ = Σₙ ∩ Πₙ by quantifier alternation
    over a decidable matrix. Σ₁ = c.e., Δ₁ = computable. POST: A ∈ Σₙ₊₁ ⇔ A
    is c.e. in ∅⁽ⁿ⁾. Complete sets: K (Σ₁), Tot = {e : φₑ total} and Inf
    (Π₂), Fin (Σ₂), Cof and Rec = {e : Wₑ computable} (Σ₃).
  - GÖDEL'S INCOMPLETENESS: for a consistent, computably axiomatized T ⊇ Q
    (Robinson arithmetic): (I) there is a Π₁ sentence G with T ⊬ G (and T ⊬
    ¬G if T is ω-consistent, or always with ROSSER'S sentence); (II) T ⊬
    Con(T). Tools: Gödel numbering, representability of computable
    functions, the DIAGONAL (fixed point) LEMMA, Hilbert-Bernays-Löb
    derivability conditions, LÖB'S THEOREM (T ⊢ Pr(⌜φ⌝) → φ ⇒ T ⊢ φ).
    TARSKI: truth in N is not arithmetically definable. Complete decidable
    contrasts: Presburger arithmetic, Th(R, +, ·, <), ACF_p.
  - PROOF THEORY: sequent calculus LK; GENTZEN'S HAUPTSATZ (cut
    elimination) ⇒ subformula property, consistency of pure logic,
    Herbrand's theorem. GENTZEN (1936): Con(PA) is provable in PRA + TI(ε₀)
    (transfinite induction along ε₀ for primitive recursive predicates),
    while PA proves TI(α) for every α < ε₀ but not TI(ε₀): the
    PROOF-THEORETIC ORDINAL of PA is ε₀ (of PRA and RCA₀: ω^ω; of ATR₀: Γ₀).
  - TRUE BUT UNPROVABLE COMBINATORICS: GOODSTEIN'S THEOREM (every Goodstein
    sequence reaches 0; proof by the ordinals below ε₀ in hereditary base
    notation) is unprovable in PA (Kirby-Paris), as are the hydra game and
    the Paris-Harrington theorem; the fast-growing hierarchy f_{ε₀}
    eventually dominates every PA-provably total function.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) State the compactness theorem and derive it from the completeness
    theorem. (b) Prove that there is no set of first-order sentences in the
    language of groups whose models are exactly the torsion groups.
    (c) Prove that Th(N, 0, 1, +, ·, <) has a model with an element larger
    than every standard numeral n̄ = 1 + ... + 1.
    Answer: (a) proofs are finite; (b) add a constant c and the sentences
    cⁿ ≠ e; (c) add a constant c and the sentences c > n̄.
    Teacher explains: (a) COMPACTNESS: T has a model iff every finite T₀ ⊆
    T has one. If T has no model, then T ⊨ ⊥, so by COMPLETENESS T ⊢ ⊥. A
    formal proof uses finitely many axioms, so some finite T₀ ⊆ T has T₀ ⊢
    ⊥; by SOUNDNESS T₀ has no model. (b) Suppose Σ axiomatizes the torsion
    groups. Add a new constant c and let
       Σ′ = Σ ∪ {cⁿ ≠ e : n = 1, 2, 3, ...}.
    A finite part of Σ′ mentions only cⁿ ≠ e for n ≤ N; it is satisfied in
    the torsion group Z/(N + 1)Z with c = 1. By compactness Σ′ has a model:
    a group satisfying Σ (so torsion) in which c has infinite order.
    Contradiction. (c) Let T = Th(N) ∪ {c > n̄ : n ∈ N}. A finite part
    mentions c > n̄ for n ≤ N only; interpret c as N + 1 in N. By
    compactness T has a model 𝔐 ⊨ Th(N) in which c is "infinite". Every
    such 𝔐 starts with a copy of N; a countable one has order type ω +
    (ω* + ω)·η (η = order type of Q). Common mistakes: trying to add the
    infinitely long sentence "∀x (x = e ∨ x² = e ∨ ...)"; forgetting that
    compactness needs EVERY finite subset, including those containing
    axioms of Σ. Now you try: show "the graph is connected" is not
    first-order. (add constants a, b and "no path of length n from a to b"
    for every n)

D2. (a) Prove by a back-and-forth argument that any two countable dense
    linear orders without endpoints are isomorphic. (b) Deduce with the
    Łoś-Vaught test that DLO is complete. (c) Show DLO is not
    2^ℵ₀-categorical.
    Answer: (a) extend finite partial isomorphisms alternately; (b) DLO is
    ℵ₀-categorical with no finite models; (c) R and R + Q (R followed by
    a copy of Q) are non-isomorphic models of size 2^ℵ₀.
    Teacher explains: (a) Enumerate A = {a₀, a₁, ...}, B = {b₀, b₁, ...}.
    Build finite order-preserving maps f₀ ⊆ f₁ ⊆ ... . At an even step
    take the first aᵢ not in dom fₙ; it lies in some "gap" between points
    of dom fₙ (or beyond all of them); since B is dense without endpoints
    there is b in the corresponding gap of ran fₙ; put fₙ₊₁ = fₙ ∪ {(aᵢ,
    b)}. At odd steps do the same backwards for the first bⱼ not in ran fₙ.
    Then f = ⋃fₙ is total, onto and order-preserving: an isomorphism.
    (b) ŁOŚ-VAUGHT: if T has no finite models and is κ-categorical for some
    κ ≥ |L| + ℵ₀, then T is complete. Proof: if T ⊬ φ and T ⊬ ¬φ, both T ∪
    {φ} and T ∪ {¬φ} have infinite models, hence by Löwenheim-Skolem models
    of size κ; they are isomorphic yet disagree on φ. DLO has no finite
    models (density produces new points), so it is complete, i.e. DLO =
    Th(Q, <). (c) R and R + Q (a copy of R followed by a copy of Q; still
    dense without endpoints, size 2^ℵ₀) are not isomorphic: in R every
    bounded non-empty set has a supremum, while in R + Q the set R has
    upper bounds but no least one. Common mistakes: doing only the
    "forth" direction (gives an embedding, not a bijection); forgetting
    the "no finite models" clause (the empty theory of pure equality is
    ℵ₀-categorical but has finite models, and is not complete: it does
    not decide "there are at least 2 elements").
    Now you try: is the theory of infinite sets (pure equality) complete?
    (yes: κ-categorical for every infinite κ)

D3. Let U be a non-principal ultrafilter on N and ∗R = R^N/U.
    (a) State Łoś's theorem and prove the step for ∃. (b) Show ε =
    [(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...)] is a positive infinitesimal. (c) Show that
    ∏_p F_p/U (p over the primes) is a field of characteristic 0.
    Answer: (b) {n : 0 < 1/n < r} is cofinite, hence in U, for each real
    r > 0; (c) for each n the set {p : n·1 ≠ 0 in F_p} is cofinite.
    Teacher explains: (a) ŁOŚ: for every formula φ and f₁, ..., fₖ ∈ ∏Mᵢ,
       ∏Mᵢ/U ⊨ φ[[f₁], ..., [fₖ]] ⇔ {i : Mᵢ ⊨ φ[f₁(i), ..., fₖ(i)]} ∈ U.
    Induction on φ: atomic by definition; ¬ uses "A ∈ U or I ∖ A ∈ U,
    not both" (this is where ULTRA is needed); ∧ uses closure of U under
    ∩. For ∃x ψ: if the product satisfies ψ[[g], [f]], then {i : Mᵢ ⊨ ψ[g(i),
    f(i)]} ∈ U and it is contained in X = {i : Mᵢ ⊨ ∃x ψ[f(i)]}, so X ∈ U
    (upward closure). Conversely if X ∈ U, choose (AC) g(i) witnessing ψ
    for i ∈ X (arbitrary otherwise); then the set for ψ[[g], [f]] contains
    X, so it is in U. (b) Non-principal ultrafilters contain every
    cofinite set (if a finite F were in U, one of its points would be).
    For r > 0 real, {n : 0 < 1/n < r} ⊇ {n > 1/r} is cofinite, so 0 < ε <
    r in ∗R. (c) Being a field is first-order, each F_p is a field, so by
    Łoś the product is a field. The sentence 1 + ... + 1 (n times) ≠ 0
    holds in F_p for all p > n, a cofinite set, so it holds in the
    ultraproduct: characteristic 0. Common mistakes: using a principal U
    (then ∏Mᵢ/U ≅ M_{i₀}, nothing new); thinking the ultraproduct of the
    F_p is algebraically closed (it is not: x² = a can fail; the
    ultraproduct of the algebraic closures of F_p is ACF₀ of size 2^ℵ₀,
    hence ≅ C). Now you try: is [(n)ₙ] ∈ ∗R larger than every real? (yes)

D4. (a) In RCF = Th(R, +, ·, 0, 1, <) find a quantifier-free equivalent of
    ∃x (ax² + bx + c = 0); in ACF find one for the same formula.
    (b) How many complete 1-types over ∅ and over Q does DLO have? How
    many 2-types over ∅? (c) Explain why QE for ACF₀ plus the
    decidability of the quantifier-free sentences gives decidability.
    Answer: (a) RCF: (a ≠ 0 ∧ b² − 4ac ≥ 0) ∨ (a = 0 ∧ b ≠ 0) ∨ (a = b = c
    = 0); ACF: a ≠ 0 ∨ b ≠ 0 ∨ c = 0. (b) 1; 2^ℵ₀; 3. (c) below.
    Teacher explains: (a) Split by the degree. If a ≠ 0 the quadratic
    formula shows a real root exists iff the discriminant is ≥ 0; if a = 0
    ≠ b there is the root −c/b; if a = b = 0 we need c = 0. In an
    algebraically closed field every non-constant polynomial has a root, so
    only the constant case a = b = 0 needs c = 0. TARSKI-SEIDENBERG says
    this always works in RCF: the projection of a semialgebraic set is
    semialgebraic. (b) By QE for DLO, a 1-type over ∅ is determined by the
    quantifier-free formulas in x, i.e. x = x: exactly 1 type. A 2-type
    over ∅ must decide x < y, x = y or x > y: 3 types. Over the parameter
    set Q a 1-type is determined by the cut x makes in Q: x = q (ℵ₀
    types, realized), "just above q" or "just below q" (q⁺, q⁻), +∞, −∞,
    and the irrational cuts (2^ℵ₀ of them). Total 2^ℵ₀. (In general the
    number of n-types over ∅ is the number of weak orderings of n points:
    1, 3, 13, 75, ...) (c) Given a sentence φ, compute (effectively) a
    quantifier-free ψ with ACF₀ ⊢ φ ↔ ψ. A quantifier-free SENTENCE is a
    Boolean combination of equations m·1 = n·1 between integers, true in
    ACF₀ iff true in Z. So ACF₀ is decidable. Common mistakes: forgetting
    the a = 0 cases; counting only the realized types over Q (types need
    not be realized in the given model). Now you try: quantifier-free form
    in RCF of ∃x (x² = a). (a ≥ 0)

D5. (a) Using the recursive definitions (α + 0 = α, α + (β + 1) = (α + β)
    + 1, α + λ = sup_{β<λ}(α + β), and similarly for ·), compute in Cantor
    normal form: 1 + ω, ω + 1, 2·ω, ω·2, 2·(ω + 1), (ω + 1)², (ω + 3)·(ω +
    2), 2^ω. (b) Show that V_{ω+ω} satisfies Separation and Power set but
    not Replacement. (c) Find the rank of the Kuratowski pair ⟨a, b⟩ =
    {{a}, {a, b}} in terms of rank a and rank b; compute rank ⟨0, 1⟩.
    Answer: (a) ω, ω + 1, ω, ω + ω, ω + 2, ω² + ω + 1, ω² + ω·2 + 3, ω.
    (b) the map n ↦ ω + n has range of rank ω + ω. (c) max(rank a, rank b)
    + 2; rank ⟨0, 1⟩ = 3.
    Teacher explains: (a) 1 + ω = sup(1 + n) = sup(n + 1) = ω, but ω + 1 =
    ω ∪ {ω} > ω: addition is not commutative. 2·ω = sup 2n = ω, whereas
    ω·2 = ω·1 + ω = ω + ω. LEFT distributivity holds: 2·(ω + 1) = 2·ω + 2
    = ω + 2; RIGHT distributivity fails ((1 + 1)·ω = ω ≠ ω + ω). For
    (ω + 1)² = (ω + 1)(ω + 1) = (ω + 1)·ω + (ω + 1): here (ω + 1)·n = ω·n +
    1 (the middle 1's are absorbed: 1 + ω = ω), so (ω + 1)·ω = sup(ω·n +
    1) = ω². Hence (ω + 1)² = ω² + ω + 1. Similarly (ω + 3)(ω + 2) = (ω +
    3)ω + (ω + 3)·2 = ω² + ω + 3 + ω + 3 = ω² + ω·2 + 3 (the first 3 is
    absorbed by the following ω). 2^ω = sup 2ⁿ = ω. RULE: in a sum of CNF
    terms, a term is absorbed by a later term with a larger exponent:
    ω³ + ω⁵ = ω⁵. (b) λ = ω + ω is a limit ordinal, so x ∈ V_λ ⇒ x ∈ V_α
    for some α < λ, so 𝒫(x) ∈ V_{α+2} ⊆ V_λ and every subset of x is in
    V_{α+1} ⊆ V_λ: Separation and Power set hold (V_λ is transitive, so Δ₀
    facts are absolute). But F(n) = ω + n is definable in V_λ, each ω + n ∈
    V_λ, and the range {ω + n : n ∈ ω} has rank ω + ω, so it is not in
    V_λ: Replacement fails. Indeed Z ⊬ "ω + ω exists". (c) rank x = sup{rank
    y + 1 : y ∈ x}. rank{a} = rank a + 1, rank{a, b} = max + 1, so rank
    ⟨a, b⟩ = max(rank a, rank b) + 2. For ⟨0, 1⟩: max(0, 1) + 2 = 3.
    Common mistakes: "simplifying" ω + 1 to ω; computing (ω + 1)² as ω² +
    2ω + 1 by the high-school rule. Now you try: (ω² + 1)·(ω + 1).
    (ω³ + ω² + 1)

D6. (a) Prove Cantor's theorem |X| < |𝒫(X)|. (b) Show that |R| = |𝒫(N)|
    = ℵ₀^ℵ₀ = 2^ℵ₀ and that the set of continuous f : R → R has size 2^ℵ₀
    while R^R has size 2^(2^ℵ₀). (c) Prove KÖNIG'S THEOREM κ^cf(κ) > κ and
    deduce cf(2^ℵ₀) > ℵ₀, so 2^ℵ₀ ≠ ℵ_ω.
    Answer: (a) diagonal set D = {x : x ∉ f(x)}; (b) binary expansions and
    Schröder-Bernstein; continuous f is determined by f|Q; (c) diagonalise
    against a cofinal sequence.
    Teacher explains: (a) x ↦ {x} injects X into 𝒫(X). If f : X → 𝒫(X),
    put D = {x ∈ X : x ∉ f(x)}. If D = f(d) then d ∈ D ⇔ d ∉ f(d) = D,
    absurd; so f is not onto. (b) 𝒫(N) ↔ {0, 1}^N; 2^ℵ₀ ≤ ℵ₀^ℵ₀ ≤
    (2^ℵ₀)^ℵ₀ = 2^(ℵ₀·ℵ₀) = 2^ℵ₀. For R: x ↦ {q ∈ Q : q < x} injects R
    into 𝒫(Q), and A ↦ ∑_{n∈A} 2·3⁻ⁿ injects 𝒫(N) into R (Cantor-set
    points; no double expansions), so Schröder-Bernstein gives |R| = 2^ℵ₀
    = 𝔠. A continuous f is determined by its values on the dense set Q,
    so there are at most 𝔠^ℵ₀ = 𝔠 of them, and at least 𝔠 (constants).
    |R^R| = 𝔠^𝔠 = 2^(ℵ₀·𝔠) = 2^𝔠. (c) Write κ = sup_{i<λ} κᵢ with κᵢ <
    κ, λ = cf κ. Given any F : κ → κ^λ (functions λ → κ), define g : λ →
    κ by choosing g(i) ∉ {F(α)(i) : α < κᵢ}, a set of size ≤ κᵢ < κ. Every
    α < κ is below some κᵢ, and then g(i) ≠ F(α)(i); so g ∉ ran F and κ^λ
    > κ. Now if cf(2^κ) = λ ≤ κ, König gives (2^κ)^λ > 2^κ, but (2^κ)^λ =
    2^(κ·λ) = 2^κ: contradiction. Since cf ℵ_ω = ω, 2^ℵ₀ ≠ ℵ_ω. Common
    mistakes: believing ℵ₀^ℵ₀ = ℵ₀ ("ℵ₀·ℵ₀ = ℵ₀, so powers too"); using
    AC-free arguments where AC is needed (κ·κ = κ needs a well-order).
    Now you try: |{f : N → N bijective}|. (2^ℵ₀)

D7. Let M be a countable transitive model of ZFC + GCH and P = Fn(ω₂ × ω,
    2) (finite partial functions, ordered by reverse inclusion), ω₂ =
    ω₂^M. Let G be P-generic over M. (a) Show F = ⋃G is a total function
    ω₂ × ω → 2 and the reals r_α(n) = F(α, n) are pairwise distinct.
    (b) Explain why ω₁ and ω₂ are not collapsed. (c) Show M[G] ⊨ 2^ℵ₀ =
    ℵ₂. (d) What does Gödel's L contribute?
    Answer: (a) density arguments; (b) P is ccc (Δ-system lemma); (c) ≥ by
    (a), (b); ≤ by counting nice names: (ℵ₂^ℵ₀)^M = ℵ₂. (d) Con(ZF) ⇒
    Con(ZFC + GCH); together: CH is independent of ZFC.
    Teacher explains: GENERIC means G is a filter meeting every dense D ⊆ P
    lying in M; one exists because M is countable (Rasiowa-Sikorski). (a)
    D_{α,n} = {p : (α, n) ∈ dom p} is dense (extend any p there) and in M;
    G meets it, and compatible conditions agree, so F is a total function.
    For α ≠ β, E_{α,β} = {p : ∃n p(α, n) ≠ p(β, n)} is dense (use an n not
    yet mentioned), so r_α ≠ r_β. Each r_α ∉ M (density of {p : p differs
    from x somewhere} for each x ∈ M). (b) Any uncountable family of
    finite domains contains an uncountable Δ-SYSTEM (common root); two
    conditions agreeing on the root are compatible, so every antichain is
    countable: P is CCC. A ccc forcing preserves cofinalities, hence all
    cardinals: if f ∈ M[G] mapped ω onto ω₁^M, each value f(n) would be
    decided by a countable antichain, trapping ran f in a countable set of
    M. (c) So M[G] has ℵ₂ distinct reals and 2^ℵ₀ ≥ ℵ₂. Conversely every
    subset of ω in M[G] has a NICE NAME ⋃_n {ň} × Aₙ with Aₙ countable
    antichains; there are at most (|P|^ℵ₀)^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ of them in M
    (GCH, cf ℵ₂ > ℵ₀). So M[G] ⊨ 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂. (d) L ⊨ ZFC + GCH, so CH is
    not refutable; forcing shows it is not provable. Common mistakes:
    thinking G ∈ M (it never is); forgetting that cardinals of M could
    collapse (Fn(ω, ω₁) makes ω₁^M countable). Now you try: what is 2^ℵ₀
    after adding ℵ_{ω₁} Cohen reals to a GCH model? (ℵ_{ω₁}: cf ω₁ > ω, so
    ℵ_{ω₁}^ℵ₀ = ℵ_{ω₁} under GCH)

D8. (a) Show that if κ is inaccessible then V_κ ⊨ ZFC, and that |V_α| < κ
    for α < κ. (b) Deduce that ZFC (if consistent) does not prove that
    inaccessible cardinals exist. (c) Prove that a measurable cardinal is
    inaccessible. (d) Compute |V_n| for n ≤ 5 and |V_{ω+1}|.
    Answer: (a) regularity gives Replacement, strong limit gives Power
    set; (b) Gödel II; (c) κ-completeness kills a λ-sequence of halvings;
    (d) 0, 1, 2, 4, 16, 65536; 2^ℵ₀.
    Teacher explains: (a) By induction |V_{α+1}| = 2^|V_α| < κ (strong
    limit) and |V_λ| ≤ ∑_{α<λ}|V_α| < κ for λ < κ (regularity). V_κ is
    transitive, closed under pairing, union and 𝒫, contains ω. REPLACEMENT:
    if x ∈ V_κ and F : x → V_κ is definable, |x| < κ and ran F ⊆ V_κ;
    by regularity the ranks of F(y) are bounded below κ, so ran F ∈ V_κ.
    (b) If ZFC ⊢ "there is an inaccessible κ", then ZFC ⊢ "V_κ ⊨ ZFC", so
    ZFC ⊢ Con(ZFC), which contradicts Gödel's second theorem unless ZFC is
    inconsistent. (Large cardinals are measured by CONSISTENCY STRENGTH.)
    (c) Let U be a κ-complete non-principal ultrafilter on κ. U contains no
    set of size < κ (a union of < κ singletons ∉ U). REGULAR: if κ = ⋃_{i<λ}
    Xᵢ with λ < κ and |Xᵢ| < κ, then by κ-completeness some Xᵢ ∈ U, absurd.
    STRONG LIMIT: if 2^λ ≥ κ for some λ < κ, inject κ into {0, 1}^λ, x ↦
    fₓ. For each α < λ exactly one of {x : fₓ(α) = 0}, {x : fₓ(α) = 1}
    is in U; call its value e(α). The intersection of these λ sets is in U
    but contains only x with fₓ = e: at most 1 point. Contradiction.
    (d) |V_{n+1}| = 2^|V_n|: 0, 1, 2, 4, 16, 2¹⁶ = 65536; |V_ω| = ℵ₀,
    |V_{ω+1}| = 2^ℵ₀. Common mistakes: "inaccessible" meaning only
    "regular limit" (that is WEAKLY inaccessible; under GCH they agree);
    thinking large cardinals are provable from ZFC plus more work (they
    are new axioms). Now you try: is the least inaccessible measurable?
    (no: below a measurable κ there are κ inaccessibles)

D9. (a) Prove that K = {e : φₑ(e)↓} is c.e. but not computable. (b) State
    and prove RICE'S THEOREM. (c) Show that Tot = {e : φₑ is total} is Π₂,
    is not c.e. and is not co-c.e.
    Answer: (a) diagonalise; (b) reduce K to the index set; (c) Tot ≡
    ∀x ∃s (φₑ,ₛ(x)↓); K ≤ₘ Tot and K̄ ≤ₘ Tot.
    Teacher explains: (a) K is c.e.: run φₑ(e) and accept if it halts
    (universal machine). If K were computable, so would be
       d(e) = φₑ(e) + 1 if e ∈ K,   d(e) = 0 if e ∉ K.
    d is total computable, so d = φ_c for some c, and c ∈ K; then d(c) =
    φ_c(c) + 1 = d(c) + 1. Contradiction. So K̄ is not c.e. (a set is
    computable iff it and its complement are c.e.). (b) RICE: if 𝒞 is a
    set of partial computable functions with ∅ ≠ I = {e : φₑ ∈ 𝒞} ≠ N,
    then I is not computable. Proof: WLOG the empty function ∉ 𝒞 (else
    use the complement), and fix a with φ_a ∈ 𝒞. By s-m-n there is a
    total computable h with φ_{h(x)}(y) = φ_a(y) if φₓ(x)↓, and undefined
    otherwise (first run φₓ(x), then φ_a(y)). So x ∈ K ⇔ φ_{h(x)} = φ_a ∈ 𝒞
    ⇔ h(x) ∈ I: K ≤ₘ I, and I is not computable. (c) e ∈ Tot ⇔ ∀x ∃s
    [φₑ(x) halts within s steps], a decidable matrix under ∀∃: Π₂.
    K ≤ₘ Tot by h(x) with φ_{h(x)}(y) = φₓ(x) (ignore y): total iff x ∈
    K. So Tot is not co-c.e. K̄ ≤ₘ Tot by g(x) with φ_{g(x)}(y) = 0 if
    φₓ(x) has NOT halted within y steps, undefined otherwise: total iff x
    ∉ K. So Tot is not c.e. (In fact Tot is Π₂-complete.) Common
    mistakes: applying Rice to properties of machines rather than of the
    functions they compute ("halts within 100 steps" is decidable); getting
    the direction of a reduction backwards (to show I hard, reduce K TO I).
    Now you try: is {e : φₑ(3) = 7} computable? c.e.? (not computable by
    Rice; c.e.: Σ₁)

D10. (a) Show the Ackermann function A(0, n) = n + 1, A(m + 1, 0) = A(m,
     1), A(m + 1, n + 1) = A(m, A(m + 1, n)) satisfies A(1, n) = n + 2,
     A(2, n) = 2n + 3, A(3, n) = 2^(n+3) − 3, and compute A(3, 3) and
     A(4, 0). (b) Explain why A is computable but not primitive recursive.
     (c) Use Kleene's recursion theorem to show there is e with φₑ(x) = e
     for all x, and one with Wₑ = {e}. (d) Compute the Cantor pairing
     π(x, y) = (x + y)(x + y + 1)/2 + y at (3, 4) and invert 20 and 100.
     Answer: (a) A(3, 3) = 61, A(4, 0) = 13; (b) A dominates every p.r.
     function; (c) apply the theorem to f(e) = index of "output e";
     (d) 32; π⁻¹(20) = (0, 5), π⁻¹(100) = (4, 9).
     Teacher explains: (a) Induction on n. A(1, 0) = A(0, 1) = 2 and A(1, n
     + 1) = A(1, n) + 1, so A(1, n) = n + 2. A(2, 0) = A(1, 1) = 3 and A(2,
     n + 1) = A(2, n) + 2: A(2, n) = 2n + 3. A(3, 0) = A(2, 1) = 5 and A(3, n
     + 1) = 2A(3, n) + 3; the formula 2^(n+3) − 3 satisfies 2(2^(n+3) − 3)
     + 3 = 2^(n+4) − 3 ✓. So A(3, 3) = 64 − 3 = 61, A(4, 0) = A(3, 1) = 13
     (and A(4, 1) = A(3, 13) = 2¹⁶ − 3 = 65533). (b) The recursion is a
     well-founded (lexicographic) descent on (m, n), so a program computes
     A. For every p.r. f one proves by induction on its construction that
     there is m with f(x₁, ..., xₖ) < A(m, max xᵢ) for all x. If A were p.r.
     so would be g(n) = A(n, n), and g(n) < A(m, n) for all n; at n = m this
     says A(m, m) < A(m, m). (c) RECURSION THEOREM: for total computable
     f there is e with φ_{f(e)} = φₑ. By s-m-n let f(e) be an index of the
     constant function x ↦ e; a fixed point satisfies φₑ(x) = φ_{f(e)}(x)
     = e: a QUINE. For Wₑ = {e}, let f(e) index the function defined only
     at e. (d) π(3, 4) = 7·8/2 + 4 = 32. To invert z find the largest w
     with w(w + 1)/2 ≤ z, then y = z − w(w + 1)/2, x = w − y: for 20, w = 5
     (15), y = 5, x = 0; for 100, w = 13 (91), y = 9, x = 4. Common
     mistakes: thinking "total computable = primitive recursive"; forgetting
     that a p.r. function is always total. Now you try: A(2, 10) and A(3,
     5). (23; 253)

D11. (a) Code finite sequences by (a₁, ..., aₖ) ↦ ∏ pᵢ^(aᵢ+1): code (2, 0,
     1) and decode 360. (b) Prove the DIAGONAL LEMMA: for every ψ(y) there
     is a sentence φ with Q ⊢ φ ↔ ψ(⌜φ⌝). (c) Prove Gödel's first theorem
     for a consistent, computably axiomatized T ⊇ Q using G ↔ ¬Pr_T(⌜G⌝)
     (assume ω-consistency for the second half), and sketch the second.
     (d) State Löb's theorem and apply it to a Henkin sentence H ↔
     Pr_T(⌜H⌝).
     Answer: (a) 2³·3¹·5² = 600; 360 = 2³·3²·5¹ ↦ (2, 1, 0). (b) substitute
     a formula's own code into itself; (c) below; (d) T ⊢ H.
     Teacher explains: (b) Let diag(n) be the code of the result of
     substituting the numeral n̄ for x in the formula with code n; diag is
     computable, so it is represented in Q by δ(x, y). Put θ(x) = ∃y (δ(x,
     y) ∧ ψ(y)), m = ⌜θ⌝ and φ = θ(m̄). Then diag(m) = ⌜φ⌝, so Q ⊢ φ ↔
     ∃y (δ(m̄, y) ∧ ψ(y)) ↔ ψ(⌜φ⌝). (c) Apply (b) to ¬Pr_T(y), where Pr_T(y)
     = ∃p Prf_T(p, y) is Σ₁ (T computably axiomatized). If T ⊢ G, then
     Pr_T(⌜G⌝) is a true Σ₁ sentence, so T ⊢ Pr_T(⌜G⌝) (Σ₁-completeness of
     Q), while T ⊢ G gives T ⊢ ¬Pr_T(⌜G⌝): T is inconsistent. So T ⊬ G;
     hence no n codes a proof of G, and T ⊢ ¬Prf_T(n̄, ⌜G⌝) for every n.
     If also T ⊢ ¬G, i.e. T ⊢ ∃p Prf_T(p, ⌜G⌝), T is ω-INCONSISTENT. (Rosser
     removes ω-consistency by using "for every proof of me there is a
     shorter proof of my negation".) G is TRUE in N (it says it is
     unprovable, and it is). SECOND THEOREM: the argument "if T ⊢ G then T
     is inconsistent" formalizes in T under the derivability conditions:
     T ⊢ Con(T) → G. So T ⊢ Con(T) would give T ⊢ G. (d) LÖB: if T ⊢
     Pr_T(⌜φ⌝) → φ then T ⊢ φ. For H, T ⊢ Pr_T(⌜H⌝) → H, so T ⊢ H: the
     sentence asserting its own provability is provable. Gödel II is the
     case φ = ⊥. Common mistakes: saying "G is true, so T is unsound";
     believing that adding G fixes incompleteness (T + G has its own
     Gödel sentence); forgetting "computably axiomatized" (Th(N) is
     complete). Now you try: does PA ⊢ Con(PA) → Con(PA + ¬Con(PA))? (yes:
     if PA + ¬Con(PA) ⊢ ⊥, then PA ⊢ Con(PA), contradicting Gödel II; this
     argument formalizes in PA)

D12. (a) Compute the Goodstein sequences of 3 and of 4 (first 7 terms):
     write n in hereditary base b, replace b by b + 1, subtract 1.
     (b) Write 266 in hereditary base 2 and compute the next term.
     (c) Assign ordinals below ε₀ (replace the base by ω) to the terms of
     G(4) and prove that every Goodstein sequence terminates. (d) State
     Gentzen's cut-elimination theorem and explain why it proves the
     consistency of first-order logic, and what Gentzen's 1936 result says
     about PA.
     Answer: (a) 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0; 4, 26, 41, 60, 83, 109, 139. (b) 266 =
     2^(2^(2+1)) + 2^(2+1) + 2; next term 3^81 + 83. (c) ω^ω > ω²·2 +
     ω·2 + 2 > ω²·2 + ω·2 + 1 > ...; (d) below.
     Teacher explains: (a) 3 = 2 + 1 → 3 + 1 − 1 = 3; 3 (base 3) = 3 → 4 −
     1 = 3; in base 4, 3 is a digit: 3 − 1 = 2, then 1, then 0. For 4 =
     2²: 3³ − 1 = 26 = 2·3² + 2·3 + 2; → 2·4² + 2·4 + 2 − 1 = 41; → 2·5² +
     2·5 + 1 − 1 = 60; → 2·6² + 2·6 − 1 = 83 = 2·6² + 6 + 5; → 2·7² + 7 + 5
     − 1 = 109; → 2·8² + 8 + 4 − 1 = 139. G(4) reaches 0 only after about
     3·2^402653211 steps. (b) 266 = 256 + 8 + 2 = 2^(2^(2+1)) + 2^(2+1) +
     2¹; bump: 3^(3^(3+1)) + 3^(3+1) + 3 − 1 = 3^81 + 81 + 2 = 3^81 + 83 ≈
     4.4·10³⁸. (c) Replacing the base by ω maps 4 = 2² to ω^ω, 26 to ω²·2 +
     ω·2 + 2, 41 to ω²·2 + ω·2 + 1, 60 to ω²·2 + ω·2, 83 to ω²·2 + ω + 5.
     Changing the base does not change the ordinal; subtracting 1 strictly
     lowers it. A strictly decreasing sequence of ordinals is finite, so
     the sequence hits 0. KIRBY-PARIS: PA ⊬ "every Goodstein sequence
     terminates" (it implies Con(PA)). (d) HAUPTSATZ: every sequent
     provable in LK has a proof without the cut rule. Every other rule has
     the SUBFORMULA PROPERTY: formulas above the line are subformulas of
     those below. The empty sequent ⇒ has no subformulas, and axioms A ⇒ A
     are non-empty, so ⇒ has no cut-free proof, hence no proof at all:
     logic is consistent. GENTZEN: assign ordinals < ε₀ to PA-derivations
     so that each reduction step lowers the ordinal; TI(ε₀) for these
     primitive recursive orderings then proves Con(PA) in PRA. Since PA ⊬
     Con(PA), PA ⊬ TI(ε₀), though it proves TI(α) for each α < ε₀. Common
     mistakes: "Goodstein sequences decrease" (they grow enormously first);
     forgetting to rewrite the EXPONENTS in base b too. Now you try: G(2).
     (2, 2, 1, 0)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Axiomatizability. For each class of structures answer FA (finitely
    axiomatizable), A (axiomatizable, but not finitely) or N (not
    first-order axiomatizable), in the natural language.
    a) groups                          b) abelian groups
    c) infinite groups                 d) finite groups
    e) torsion-free groups             f) torsion groups
    g) fields of characteristic 0      h) fields of characteristic 5
    i) algebraically closed fields     j) well-ordered sets (L = {<})
    k) dense linear orders w/o ends    l) connected graphs
    m) bipartite graphs                n) real closed fields
    o) ordered fields                  p) Archimedean ordered fields
    q) models of PA                    r) sets with exactly 7 elements
    s) infinite sets                   t) groups of exponent dividing 6
    Answers:
      a) FA      b) FA      c) A       d) N (compactness)    e) A
      f) N (D1)  g) A (an ultraproduct of the F_p has char 0)  h) FA
      i) A       j) N (add c₀ > c₁ > c₂ > ...)     k) FA     l) N (D1)
      m) A (no odd cycles; not FA: an ultraproduct of odd cycles C₂ₙ₊₁ is
         bipartite)                    n) A      o) FA
      p) N (add c > 1 + ... + 1 for all n)         q) A (Ryll-Nardzewski)
      r) FA      s) A       t) FA (∀x x⁶ = e)

M2. For each complete theory state: ℵ₀-categorical? (Y/N), categorical in
    uncountable cardinals? (Y/N), number of countable models.
    a) DLO = Th(Q, <)                  b) infinite sets (pure equality)
    c) ACF₀                            d) ACF₇
    e) non-trivial divisible torsion-free abelian groups (Q-vector spaces)
    f) infinite vector spaces over F₂  g) Th(Z, s), s(x) = x + 1
    h) the random graph                i) RCF = Th(R, +, ·)
    j) Th(N, +, ·)                     k) Th(Z, <)
    l) Th((Z/4)^(ω) ⊕ (Z/2)^(ω)) in the language of groups
    m) Ehrenfeucht: DLO + constants c₀ < c₁ < c₂ < ...
    n) Th(Q, <, 0) (DLO with one constant)
    Answers:
      a) Y, N, 1         b) Y, Y, 1          c) N, Y, ℵ₀ (tr. deg 0..ℵ₀)
      d) N, Y, ℵ₀        e) N, Y, ℵ₀ (dim 1..ℵ₀)       f) Y, Y, 1

      h) Y, N, 1         i) N, N, 2^ℵ₀       j) N, N, 2^ℵ₀

      l) Y, N, 1 (uncountable models (Z/4)^(κ) ⊕ (Z/2)^(λ) vary)
      m) N, N, 3 (the cₙ unbounded; bounded with a least upper bound;
         bounded with none) — Vaught: never exactly 2   n) Y, N, 1

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample (or reason) for F.
     a) Every consistent theory in a countable language has a countable
        model.
     b) Every complete theory is κ-categorical for some infinite κ.
     c) A theory with arbitrarily large finite models has an infinite
        model.
     d) The class of finite fields is first-order axiomatizable.
     e) Every uncountable model of DLO is isomorphic to R.
     f) An ultraproduct of finite sets over a non-principal ultrafilter is
        infinite.
     g) ω + 1 = 1 + ω.
     h) Every infinite cardinal is regular.
     i) 2^ℵ₀ can be ℵ_ω.
     j) ZFC proves CH or ZFC proves ¬CH.
     k) Measurable cardinals exist in L if they exist in V.
     l) Every inaccessible cardinal is measurable.
     m) Every c.e. set is computable.
     n) Every total computable function is primitive recursive.
     o) No non-trivial index set is c.e.
     p) If A and its complement are c.e., A is computable.
     q) Every sentence true in N is provable in PA.
     r) PA + ¬Con(PA) is inconsistent.
     s) If T ⊢ Pr_T(⌜φ⌝) → φ then T ⊢ φ (T ⊇ PA computably axiomatized).
     t) Every model of ZFC is well-founded (∈ is well-founded
        externally).
     u) Cut-free LK proofs have the subformula property.
     v) PA proves transfinite induction up to ε₀.
     Answers:
       a) T (downward Löwenheim-Skolem)  b) F: RCF, Th(N, +, ·)
       c) T (compactness)                d) F: the ultraproduct ∏F_p/U is
          an infinite field satisfying the same sentences
       e) F: R + Q (D2)                  f) F: all of size 3 give size 3
          (true if the sizes are unbounded on every set in U)
       g) F: 1 + ω = ω < ω + 1           h) F: ℵ_ω (cf ω)
       i) F: König, cf(2^ℵ₀) > ω         j) F: Gödel (L) and Cohen
       k) F: Scott, V = L ⇒ no measurables
       l) F: the least inaccessible       m) F: K
       n) F: Ackermann                   o) F: {e : Wₑ ≠ ∅} is c.e. (Rice
          only gives "not computable")    p) T (run both enumerations)
       q) F: Gödel's G, Goodstein's theorem
       r) F: consistent by Gödel II (its models are nonstandard)
       s) T (Löb)
       t) F: by compactness add constants cₙ₊₁ ∈ cₙ; also ω-nonstandard
          models exist
       u) T                              v) F: Gentzen; only each α < ε₀

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: organise the whole subject around THREE TOOLS and ask which
  one a problem needs. (1) COMPACTNESS / LÖWENHEIM-SKOLEM: "add new
  constants and finitely satisfiable axioms" answers almost every "is it
  axiomatizable?" or "is there a nonstandard model?" question; always
  check the finite subsets explicitly. (2) DIAGONALISATION: Cantor's D =
  {x : x ∉ f(x)}, the halting set, König's theorem and Gödel's sentence
  are one argument; have students write the four side by side. (3) WELL-
  FOUNDEDNESS: ordinal arithmetic, rank, Goodstein and Gentzen all rest on
  "no infinite descending sequence of ordinals" — drill Cantor normal form
  (absorption rule: a smaller term is swallowed by a later larger one)
  until it is automatic. For computability, insist on "to show I is hard,
  reduce K TO I" and count quantifiers for the arithmetical hierarchy.
  Harder: prove the completeness theorem by Henkin's method; prove
  Morley's theorem for ω-stable theories; prove the Ax-Grothendieck
  theorem (an injective polynomial map Cⁿ → Cⁿ is onto) via ultraproducts
  of the algebraic closures of F_p; prove the Δ-system lemma and the
  forcing theorem; show that adding a Cohen real makes the set of
  ground-model reals meagre; prove the Friedberg-Muchnik theorem with a
  finite-injury priority argument; derive Löb's theorem from the diagonal
  lemma and the derivability conditions; and prove Goodstein's theorem is
  unprovable in PA by showing it implies Con(PA) via the Wainer hierarchy.


================================================================================
TOPIC 12.22 — CATEGORY THEORY: FUNCTORS, NATURAL TRANSFORMATIONS,
ADJUNCTIONS, LIMITS, ABELIAN CATEGORIES, DERIVED FUNCTORS (YONEDA LEMMA,
MONADS, EQUIVALENCES)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CATEGORY 𝒞: objects, sets Hom(A, B), an associative composition and
    identities 1_A. Examples: Set, Grp, Ab, Ring, R-Mod, Vect_k, Top; a
    POSET (one arrow a → b iff a ≤ b); a MONOID or GROUP (one object);
    a GROUPOID (every arrow invertible). The OPPOSITE 𝒞ᵒᵖ reverses arrows
    (DUALITY: every theorem has a dual). MONO: f∘g = f∘h ⇒ g = h; EPI:
    g∘f = h∘f ⇒ g = h; ISO: two-sided inverse. Mono + epi ⇏ iso: Z ↪ Q
    is an epi in Ring; Q ↪ R is an epi in Haus (dense image).
  - FUNCTOR F : 𝒞 → 𝒟 preserves composition and identities (covariant) or
    reverses them (contravariant = 𝒞ᵒᵖ → 𝒟). Examples: forgetful U, free
    F, Hom(A, −), Hom(−, B), abelianization G ↦ Gᵃᵇ = G/[G, G], π₁, Hₙ,
    V ↦ V*, P (power set, both variances), GLₙ, units R ↦ Rˣ. FAITHFUL /
    FULL = injective / surjective on each Hom-set; ESSENTIALLY SURJECTIVE =
    every object is isomorphic to some F(A). Functors preserve isos.
  - NATURAL TRANSFORMATION α : F ⇒ G: arrows α_A : FA → GA with
    G(f)∘α_A = α_B∘F(f) (naturality square). Examples: V → V** (a natural
    iso on finite-dimensional spaces; V ≅ V* is NOT natural), det : GLₙ ⇒
    (−)ˣ, G → Gᵃᵇ, Hurewicz π₁ → H₁. Functor categories [𝒞, 𝒟]; presheaves
    [𝒞ᵒᵖ, Set].
  - EQUIVALENCE: F : 𝒞 → 𝒟 with G and natural isos GF ≅ 1, FG ≅ 1.
    THEOREM: F is an equivalence ⇔ fully faithful + essentially surjective
    (uses choice). Every category is equivalent to a SKELETON (one object
    per iso class). Examples: FinVect_k ≃ Mat_k (objects n ∈ N, arrows
    matrices), FinVect_k ≃ FinVect_kᵒᵖ (duality), FinSetᵒᵖ ≃ finite Boolean
    algebras, R-Mod ≃ Mₙ(R)-Mod (Morita), covering spaces ≃ π₁-sets.
    Equivalence is weaker than isomorphism of categories.
  - YONEDA LEMMA: for F : 𝒞 → Set, Nat(Hom(A, −), F) ≅ F(A), α ↦ α_A(1_A),
    naturally in A and F. Hence the YONEDA EMBEDDING A ↦ Hom(−, A) is fully
    faithful and Hom(−, A) ≅ Hom(−, B) ⇒ A ≅ B. REPRESENTABLE functors:
    U_Grp ≅ Hom(Z, −), U_CRing ≅ Hom(Z[x], −), R ↦ Rˣ ≅ Hom(Z[x, x⁻¹], −),
    P ≅ Hom(−, {0, 1}), open sets ≅ Hom(−, Sierpiński space). Cayley's
    theorem is the Yoneda embedding of a one-object category.
  - UNIVERSAL PROPERTIES: INITIAL and TERMINAL objects are unique up to
    unique iso (Set: ∅, point; Grp: trivial group = ZERO object; Ring: Z
    and 0; Field: neither). Free objects, quotients, tensor products,
    localizations are all defined by universal properties.
  - LIMITS: a limit of D : J → 𝒞 is a terminal cone. PRODUCTS, EQUALIZERS,
    PULLBACKS (fibre products), INVERSE LIMITS (Z_p = lim Z/pⁿ, Ẑ = lim
    Z/n), terminal object (empty limit). COLIMITS (dual): COPRODUCTS (⊔ in
    Set, free product * in Grp, ⊕ in Ab, ⊗ in CRing), COEQUALIZERS,
    PUSHOUTS (amalgams; van Kampen), DIRECT LIMITS (Z[1/p], Z(p^∞), Q/Z).
    In a poset: limit = infimum, colimit = supremum. Products + equalizers
    ⇒ all small limits; lim D ⊆ ∏ D(j) is the set of compatible families.
  - ADJUNCTION F ⊣ G: Hom_𝒟(FA, B) ≅ Hom_𝒞(A, GB) naturally in A, B;
    equivalently unit η : 1 ⇒ GF and counit ε : FG ⇒ 1 with TRIANGLE
    IDENTITIES εF∘Fη = 1_F, Gε∘ηG = 1_G. Examples: free ⊣ forgetful;
    abelianization ⊣ inclusion Ab ⊆ Grp; − ⊗_R M ⊣ Hom_R(M, −); − × A ⊣
    (−)ᴬ (currying); discrete ⊣ U ⊣ indiscrete (Top → Set); Stone-Čech β
    ⊣ inclusion CHaus ⊆ Top; colim ⊣ Δ ⊣ lim; ⌈·⌉ ⊣ (Z ⊆ R) ⊣ ⌊·⌋ (Galois
    connections). Adjoints are unique up to unique natural iso.
  - RAPL: RIGHT ADJOINTS PRESERVE LIMITS, LEFT ADJOINTS PRESERVE COLIMITS
    (hence − ⊗ M is right exact and commutes with ⊕; Hom(A, −) is left
    exact). FREYD'S ADJOINT FUNCTOR THEOREM: G : 𝒟 → 𝒞 with 𝒟 complete and
    locally small has a left adjoint ⇔ G preserves small limits and
    satisfies the SOLUTION SET condition. Used negatively: U : Grp → Set
    has no right adjoint (U(trivial group) = point ≠ ∅).
  - MONADS: T : 𝒞 → 𝒞 with η : 1 ⇒ T, μ : TT ⇒ T, associativity μ∘Tμ =
    μ∘μT and unit laws μ∘Tη = μ∘ηT = 1. Every adjunction F ⊣ G gives T =
    GF, μ = GεF; conversely every monad comes from its KLEISLI and
    EILENBERG-MOORE (T-algebra) adjunctions. Examples: list monad (algebras
    = monoids), maybe X ⊔ {∗} (pointed sets), power set (sup-lattices;
    Kleisli = Rel), ultrafilter β (compact Hausdorff spaces), M × − (M-sets).
    G is MONADIC if 𝒟 ≃ 𝒞ᵀ: Grp, Ab, CHaus → Set are; Top → Set is not.
  - ADDITIVE category: Hom-sets are abelian groups, composition bilinear,
    zero object, finite BIPRODUCTS A ⊕ B. ABELIAN: also every arrow has a
    kernel and cokernel, every mono is a kernel and every epi a cokernel;
    then mono + epi ⇒ iso and im f = ker(coker f) ≅ coim f. Examples: Ab,
    R-Mod, finite abelian groups, sheaves of abelian groups, chain
    complexes Ch(𝒜), G-representations. Non-examples: Grp (not additive),
    free or torsion-free abelian groups, Banach spaces, topological
    groups. FREYD-MITCHELL: a small abelian category embeds exactly and
    fully in some R-Mod, so diagram chases are legitimate.
  - EXACTNESS: A → B → C exact if im = ker. SPLITTING LEMMA; FIVE LEMMA;
    SNAKE LEMMA ker a → ker b → ker c → coker a → coker b → coker c with
    connecting map δ; a short exact sequence of complexes gives a LONG
    EXACT SEQUENCE in homology. Hom(A, −), Hom(−, B) are LEFT exact; − ⊗ M
    is RIGHT exact.
  - PROJECTIVE P: Hom(P, −) exact ⇔ direct summand of a free module
    (over Z or a PID: free). INJECTIVE I: Hom(−, I) exact; BAER: test on
    ideals; over a PID ⇔ divisible (Q, Q/Z). FLAT: − ⊗ M exact (over a
    PID ⇔ torsion-free: Q is flat, not projective). R-Mod has enough
    projectives and enough injectives.
  - DERIVED FUNCTORS: resolve M by projectives P• → M (COMPARISON THEOREM:
    any map lifts to resolutions, unique up to homotopy), then LₙF(M) =
    Hₙ(F(P•)) for F right exact (L₀F = F); RⁿF(M) = Hⁿ(F(I•)) via
    injectives for F left exact. Short exact sequences give long exact
    sequences; the Lₙ, Rⁿ are UNIVERSAL δ-functors (Grothendieck).
    Torₙ^R(A, B) = Lₙ(A ⊗ −)(B), Extⁿ_R(A, B) = Rⁿ Hom(A, −)(B), both
    BALANCED (resolve either variable). Also Hⁿ(G, M) = Extⁿ_ZG(Z, M),
    sheaf cohomology Hⁿ(X, ℱ) = RⁿΓ(ℱ).
  - STANDARD COMPUTATIONS: over Z (d = gcd(m, n)) Z/m ⊗ Z/n ≅ Hom(Z/m,
    Z/n) ≅ Tor₁(Z/m, Z/n) ≅ Ext¹(Z/m, Z/n) ≅ Z/d; Ext¹(Z/n, Z) ≅ Z/n;
    Tor₁(Q/Z, A) = A_tors; Torₙ = Extⁿ = 0 for n ≥ 2 (PID). Over k[x]/(x²):
    Extⁿ(k, k) ≅ k for all n (infinite global dimension). Ext¹(A, B)
    classifies extensions 0 → B → E → A → 0 (Yoneda/Baer). Global
    dimension: field 0, PID 1, k[x₁, ..., xₙ] n (Hilbert syzygy theorem).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Prove that in Grp a homomorphism is a monomorphism iff it is
    injective. (b) Prove that the inclusion Z ↪ Q is an epimorphism in Ring
    (rings with 1), although it is not surjective. (c) In the category of
    divisible abelian groups show that the quotient π : Q → Q/Z is a
    monomorphism. Conclude that "mono + epi ⇒ iso" fails in general.
    Answer: (a) test with homomorphisms out of Z; (b) f(1/n) = f(n)⁻¹ is
    forced; (c) a map into Z from a divisible group is 0.
    Teacher explains: The definitions are ARROW-THEORETIC: f is mono if it
    can be cancelled on the left. (a) If f is injective and f∘g = f∘h then
    f(g(x)) = f(h(x)) gives g(x) = h(x): mono. Conversely suppose f : G →
    H is mono and f(a) = e. The homomorphisms g, h : Z → G with g(1) = a,
    h(1) = e satisfy f∘g = f∘h (both send 1 to e), so g = h, i.e. a = e.
    The trick: Z REPRESENTS elements, Hom(Z, G) = G. (b) Let f, g : Q → R
    be ring maps with f|_Z = g|_Z. For n ≠ 0, n is a unit in Q, so f(n) is
    a unit in R and f(1/n) = f(n)⁻¹ = g(n)⁻¹ = g(1/n); then f(m/n) =
    f(m)f(1/n) = g(m/n). So f = g: the inclusion is epi. It is also mono
    (injective), but not an iso (no ring map Q → Z). (c) Let f, g : D → Q
    with D divisible and π∘f = π∘g. Then h = f − g : D → Z ⊆ Q, and h(D) is
    a divisible subgroup of Z; the only one is 0. So f = g. (π is also epi,
    being surjective, but it is not an iso.) Common mistakes: "mono means
    injective" — true in Set, Grp, R-Mod, false in general; checking epi
    only against surjective test maps. Now you try: show Z → Z[1/2] is an
    epimorphism in Ring. (f(1/2) = f(2)⁻¹ is determined)

D2. (a) Show that the evaluation maps ev_V : V → V**, ev_V(v)(φ) = φ(v),
    form a natural transformation 1 ⇒ (−)** on Vect_k, an isomorphism on
    finite-dimensional spaces. (b) Show that no family of isomorphisms
    φ_V : V → V* on the real vector spaces can be natural with respect to
    all isomorphisms f : V → W (dualizing f by (f⁻¹)*). (c) Show that det
    : GLₙ ⇒ (−)ˣ is natural on commutative rings.
    Answer: (a) f**∘ev_V = ev_W∘f; (b) naturality for f = 2·1_V forces
    φ_V = 4φ_V, so φ_V = 0; (c) ring maps commute with polynomials.
    Teacher explains: (a) For f : V → W, f* : W* → V* is ψ ↦ ψ∘f, and f** :
    V** → W** is Θ ↦ Θ∘f*. For v ∈ V and ψ ∈ W*:
       f**(ev_V(v))(ψ) = ev_V(v)(ψ∘f) = ψ(f(v)) = ev_W(f(v))(ψ).
    So the square commutes. The definition of ev_V uses NO basis — this is
    the informal meaning of "natural". ev_V is injective (for v ≠ 0 extend
    to a basis and pick φ with φ(v) = 1) and dim V** = dim V when finite,
    so it is an iso there; for infinite-dimensional V it is not onto.
    (b) Naturality says (f⁻¹)*∘φ_V = φ_W∘f, i.e. φ_V(v)(u) =
    φ_W(fv)(fu): the bilinear form b(v, u) = φ_V(v)(u) is preserved by
    every isomorphism. Take W = V, f = 2·1: b(v, u) = b(2v, 2u) = 4b(v, u),
    so b = 0, contradicting that φ_V is an isomorphism (V ≠ 0). A choice of
    basis gives V ≅ V*, but never naturally. (c) For φ : R → S, GLₙ(φ)
    applies φ entrywise; det is a polynomial in the entries with integer
    coefficients, so det(φ(A)) = φ(det A): the square commutes. Common
    mistakes: calling a map natural because it is "canonical-looking"
    without checking the square; forgetting that V ↦ V* is contravariant.
    Now you try: show that the quotient maps G → Gᵃᵇ form a natural
    transformation 1_Grp ⇒ (inclusion)∘(ab). (f([G, G]) ⊆ [H, H])

D3. State and prove the Yoneda lemma. Deduce: (a) the Yoneda embedding is
    fully faithful; (b) the natural transformations U ⇒ U for the
    forgetful functor U : Grp → Set are exactly g ↦ gⁿ (n ∈ Z); (c) the
    natural transformations U ⇒ U for U : CRing → Set are r ↦ p(r),
    p ∈ Z[x].
    Answer: Nat(Hom(A, −), F) ≅ F(A) via α ↦ α_A(1_A); (b) U ≅ Hom(Z, −),
    so Nat(U, U) ≅ U(Z) = Z; (c) U ≅ Hom(Z[x], −), Nat ≅ Z[x].
    Teacher explains: Given α : Hom(A, −) ⇒ F put x = α_A(1_A) ∈ F(A). For
    any f : A → B, naturality applied to the element 1_A gives
       α_B(f) = α_B(f∘1_A) = F(f)(α_A(1_A)) = F(f)(x).
    So α is DETERMINED by x. Conversely, for x ∈ F(A) define α^x_B(f) =
    F(f)(x); it is natural because F(g)(F(f)(x)) = F(g∘f)(x). The two
    constructions are inverse: α^x_A(1_A) = F(1_A)(x) = x. (a) Take F =
    Hom(B, −): Nat(Hom(A, −), Hom(B, −)) ≅ Hom(B, A), and every natural
    map is precomposition with a unique arrow — full and faithful
    (contravariantly; the version with Hom(−, A) is covariant). (b) U(G) =
    Hom(Z, G) (g ↔ the map 1 ↦ g), so Nat(U, U) ≅ U(Z) = Z. The element n
    ∈ Z corresponds to α_G(g) = U(g-map)(n) = gⁿ. So every "natural
    operation on elements of groups" is a power map; e.g. g ↦ g⁻¹ is n =
    −1. (c) Hom(Z[x], R) ≅ R via φ ↦ φ(x), and Nat(U, U) ≅ U(Z[x]) = Z[x],
    the polynomial p acting by r ↦ p(r). Common mistakes: applying Yoneda
    to a non-representable functor; confusing Nat(Hom(A, −), Hom(B, −)) ≅
    Hom(B, A) (arrows reversed!). Now you try: find Nat(U × U, U) for U :
    Grp → Set. (U × U ≅ Hom(F₂, −), so Nat ≅ F₂: (g, h) ↦ w(g, h))

D4. (a) Prove that a fully faithful, essentially surjective functor F :
    𝒞 → 𝒟 is an equivalence. (b) Show that FinVect_k is equivalent to the
    category Mat_k whose objects are n = 0, 1, 2, ... and whose arrows
    n → m are m × n matrices, but not isomorphic to it. (c) Show that
    FinSet is equivalent to its skeleton and count |Hom(3, 4)| there.
    Answer: (a) choose G(d) with ε_d : FG(d) ≅ d; (b) n ↦ kⁿ is fully
    faithful and essentially surjective; (c) |Hom(3, 4)| = 4³ = 64.
    Teacher explains: (a) For each d ∈ 𝒟 CHOOSE (axiom of choice) an
    object G(d) and an iso ε_d : F(G(d)) → d. For g : d → d′ the arrow
    ε_{d′}⁻¹∘g∘ε_d : FG(d) → FG(d′) is F of a UNIQUE arrow G(g) (F fully
    faithful); uniqueness makes G a functor and ε : FG ⇒ 1 natural and
    invertible. Finally η_c : c → GF(c) is the unique arrow with F(η_c) =
    ε_{F c}⁻¹; it is an iso because F reflects isos (fully faithful). □
    (b) F(n) = kⁿ, F(M) = the linear map x ↦ Mx. Hom(n, m) = M_{m×n}(k) ≅
    Hom(kⁿ, kᵐ) (fully faithful) and every finite-dimensional V ≅ k^{dim V}
    (essentially surjective). Not an isomorphism: Mat_k has one object per
    dimension, while FinVect_k has many distinct but isomorphic objects
    (k² and the plane x + y + z = 0 in k³). Equivalence is the RIGHT notion
    of sameness: all categorical properties (limits, adjoints, abelian)
    transfer, and it explains why linear algebra "is" matrix algebra.
    (c) The skeleton has objects n = {1, ..., n}; |Hom(3, 4)| = 64, of
    which 4·3·2 = 24 are monos and 0 are epis. Common mistakes: demanding
    GF = 1 on the nose; forgetting that essential surjectivity is "up to
    iso". Now you try: show FinVect_k ≃ FinVect_kᵒᵖ. (V ↦ V*, V ≅ V**)

D5. (a) Define limits and show that a category with all (small) products
    and equalizers has all small limits. (b) Compute in Ab the pullback of
    Z →(×2) Z ←(×3) Z. (c) In the poset (N_{≥1}, |) compute the product of
    12 and 18, and describe all limits in a poset. (d) Describe
    lim(⋯ → Z/8 → Z/4 → Z/2).
    Answer: (a) lim D = equalizer of ∏_j D(j) ⇉ ∏_{u:i→j} D(j);
    (b) {(a, b) : 2a = 3b} = Z·(3, 2) ≅ Z; (c) gcd(12, 18) = 6, limits are
    gcd's (infima); (d) Z₂, the 2-adic integers.
    Teacher explains: A CONE over D : J → 𝒞 is an object L with arrows
    p_j : L → D(j) such that D(u)∘p_i = p_j for all u : i → j; the LIMIT is
    the terminal cone. (a) Put P = ∏_j D(j), Q = ∏_{u : i→j} D(j) (one
    factor per arrow of J). Two maps s, t : P → Q have u-components
    s_u = pr_j and t_u = D(u)∘pr_i. A map x : L → P equalizes s and t iff
    its components form a cone; so the equalizer is the limit. In Set this
    is literally lim D = {(x_j) ∈ ∏D(j) : D(u)(x_i) = x_j}. (b) The pullback
    of f : X → Z, g : Y → Z is {(x, y) : f(x) = g(y)} ⊆ X × Y. Here 2a = 3b
    forces 3 | a: a = 3t, b = 2t, so the pullback is Z generated by (3, 2),
    with projections t ↦ 3t, t ↦ 2t. (c) In a poset an arrow a → b means
    a | b; a product c of 12, 18 must divide both and be divisible by every
    common divisor: c = gcd = 6. In any poset limits are infima and
    colimits are suprema (here lcm). (d) Compatible sequences (xₙ) with
    xₙ ∈ Z/2ⁿ and xₙ₊₁ ≡ xₙ (mod 2ⁿ): exactly the 2-adic integers Z₂;
    e.g. −1 = (1, 3, 7, 15, ...). Common mistakes: computing a pullback as
    X × Y; forgetting the arrows (cone condition) in a limit. Now you try:
    pullback of Z →(×4) Z ←(×6) Z. (Z·(3, 2) again: {4a = 6b})

D6. Compute the following colimits: (a) the coproduct of Z/2 and Z/2 in
    Set, Ab, Grp and CRing; (b) the pushout of Z/4 ← Z/2 → Z/6 (both maps
    injective) in Ab; (c) colim(Z →(×2) Z →(×2) Z → ⋯) in Ab; (d) the
    pushout D² ← S¹ → point in Top.
    Answer: (a) 4 points; Z/2 ⊕ Z/2; the infinite dihedral group D_∞;
    Z/2 ⊗ Z/2 ≅ Z/2. (b) Z/12. (c) Z[1/2]. (d) S².
    Teacher explains: A colimit is an initial cocone; its universal
    property says maps OUT of it are compatible families of maps out of
    the pieces. (a) Set: disjoint union, 2 + 2 = 4 elements. Ab: the direct
    sum (in an additive category coproduct = product = biproduct). Grp:
    the free product ⟨a, b | a², b²⟩; ab has infinite order, and this is
    D_∞ (a, b are reflections of R). CRing: the coproduct of A and B is
    A ⊗_Z B (maps out of it = pairs of maps from A and B), and Z/2 ⊗ Z/2 =
    Z/2. (b) The pushout of B ← A → C in Ab is (B ⊕ C)/{(f(a), −g(a))}.
    Here the generator of Z/2 goes to 2 ∈ Z/4 and 3 ∈ Z/6, so we quotient
    Z/4 ⊕ Z/6 (order 24) by ⟨(2, −3)⟩ (order 2): order 12. Relation matrix
    rows (4, 0), (0, 6), (2, 3): the gcd of entries is 1 and of 2 × 2
    minors is 12, so the Smith form is diag(1, 12): Z/12. (c) A direct limit
    of Z →(×2) Z → ⋯: send the n-th copy to Q by x ↦ x/2ⁿ; the images
    exhaust Z[1/2] and the maps are compatible, so the colimit is Z[1/2].
    (d) Gluing the boundary circle of a disc to a point gives the sphere.
    In Grp, van Kampen says π₁ turns such pushouts (of open covers) into
    pushouts of groups. Common mistakes: using ⊕ as the coproduct in Grp;
    thinking the coproduct in CRing is the product. Now you try: the
    coproduct of Z/2 and Z/3 in CRing. (Z/2 ⊗ Z/3 = 0, the zero ring)

D7. Define an adjunction F ⊣ G by Hom-sets and by unit and counit, and
    show the definitions agree. Then: (a) exhibit abelianization ⊣
    inclusion Ab ⊆ Grp and use it to count |Hom_Grp(S₃, Z/6)|,
    |Hom_Grp(Q₈, Z/4)| and |Hom_Grp(A₄, Z/6)|; (b) verify the currying
    adjunction − × A ⊣ (−)ᴬ in Set for |A| = 2, |B| = 3, |C| = 2.
    Answer: (a) Hom_Grp(G, B) ≅ Hom_Ab(Gᵃᵇ, B): 2, 4, 3; (b) both
    Hom-sets have 2⁶ = 64 elements.
    Teacher explains: F ⊣ G means bijections θ : Hom_𝒟(FA, B) ≅
    Hom_𝒞(A, GB) natural in A and B. Put η_A = θ(1_{FA}) : A → GFA (unit)
    and ε_B = θ⁻¹(1_{GB}) : FGB → B (counit). Naturality gives θ(f) =
    G(f)∘η_A and θ⁻¹(g) = ε_B∘F(g); then θ⁻¹θ = 1 and θθ⁻¹ = 1 become the
    TRIANGLE IDENTITIES ε_{FA}∘F(η_A) = 1_{FA}, G(ε_B)∘η_{GB} = 1_{GB}.
    Conversely, given η, ε with the triangle identities, these formulas
    define inverse natural bijections. Slogan: η_A is the UNIVERSAL arrow
    from A to G. (a) Every homomorphism f : G → B with B abelian kills
    commutators, so it factors UNIQUELY through q : G → Gᵃᵇ: Hom_Grp(G, B)
    ≅ Hom_Ab(Gᵃᵇ, B); the unit is q. S₃ᵃᵇ = S₃/A₃ = Z/2, and |Hom(Z/2,
    Z/6)| = gcd(2, 6) = 2. Q₈ᵃᵇ = Q₈/{±1} = (Z/2)², |Hom((Z/2)², Z/4)| =
    2² = 4. A₄ᵃᵇ = A₄/V₄ = Z/3, |Hom(Z/3, Z/6)| = 3. (b) θ(f)(a)(b) =
    f(a, b) (currying): |Hom(A × B, C)| = 2^(2·3) = 64 and |Hom(A, Cᴮ)| =
    (2³)² = 64. The unit is x ↦ (a ↦ (x, a)), the counit is evaluation
    Cᴬ × A → C. Common mistakes: getting the side wrong — the LEFT adjoint
    is the "free/generated" construction; counting Hom(G, B) directly by
    generators without the abelianization shortcut. Now you try: the free
    group F ⊣ U gives |Hom_Grp(F₂, S₃)| = ? (|S₃|² = 36)

D8. Prove that right adjoints preserve limits. Deduce: (a) the forgetful
    functor U : Grp → Set has no right adjoint; (b) − ⊗_R M is right exact
    and commutes with direct sums; (c) the forgetful functor U : CHaus →
    Set has a left adjoint but no right adjoint. State Freyd's general
    adjoint functor theorem and explain why U : Grp → Set satisfies it.
    Answer: Hom(A, G(lim D)) ≅ lim Hom(A, G D) naturally in A, then
    Yoneda. (a) U does not preserve the initial object; (b) − ⊗ M is a
    left adjoint; (c) U does not preserve coproducts.
    Teacher explains: Let G : 𝒟 → 𝒞 have left adjoint F and let L = lim D.
    For every A ∈ 𝒞, naturally in A,
       Hom(A, GL) ≅ Hom(FA, L) ≅ lim_j Hom(FA, D_j) ≅ lim_j Hom(A, GD_j),
    and the last is the set of cones from A to GD. So GL represents cones
    over GD, i.e. GL is a limit of GD (Yoneda). Dually left adjoints
    preserve colimits. (a) If U had a right adjoint it would be a LEFT
    adjoint and would preserve colimits, in particular initial objects:
    but the initial group is {e}, with U({e}) a point, while the initial
    set is ∅. (U does have a LEFT adjoint, the free group.) (b) − ⊗_R M ⊣
    Hom_R(M, −) (Hom(A ⊗ M, B) ≅ Hom(A, Hom(M, B))). So − ⊗ M preserves
    colimits: direct sums, (⊕Aᵢ) ⊗ M ≅ ⊕(Aᵢ ⊗ M), and cokernels, which is
    exactly right exactness: A → B → C → 0 exact ⇒ A ⊗ M → B ⊗ M → C ⊗ M →
    0 exact. (c) The left adjoint is X ↦ βX (Stone-Čech of the discrete
    space), whose points are ultrafilters. The coproduct in CHaus of
    countably many points is βN (a coproduct must be compact), and U(βN)
    is uncountable, not N: U does not preserve coproducts. FREYD (GAFT): if
    𝒟 is complete and locally small, G : 𝒟 → 𝒞 has a left adjoint iff G
    preserves small limits and, for each A, there is a SET of arrows
    A → G(Dᵢ) through which every A → G(D) factors. For Grp: limits are
    computed on underlying sets; any map X → U(H) factors through the
    subgroup generated by its image, of cardinality ≤ max(|X|, ℵ₀), and
    there is only a set of such groups up to iso. Common mistakes: "U
    preserves products, so it has a right adjoint" (wrong side); assuming
    ⊗ commutes with infinite products (false: (∏Z) ⊗ Q ≠ ∏Q). Now you try:
    does the inclusion Ab → Grp have a right adjoint? (No: Z ⊕ Z ≠ Z * Z,
    it does not preserve coproducts)

D9. (a) Define a monad and show that every adjunction F ⊣ G gives one.
    (b) Work out the monad of the free-monoid adjunction on Set and show
    that its algebras are exactly monoids. (c) Show that the power set
    monad has Kleisli category equal to the category Rel of sets and
    relations. (d) Compute μ([[1, 2], [ ], [3, 1]]) and μ_P({{1, 2}, {2, 3},
    ∅}).
    Answer: (a) T = GF, η = unit, μ = GεF; (b) T X = finite words, μ =
    concatenation; (c) Kleisli arrows X → P(Y) are relations; (d) [1, 2,
    3, 1] and {1, 2, 3}.
    Teacher explains: A MONAD is (T, η, μ) with μ∘Tμ = μ∘μT (flattening a
    triple-nested structure either way agrees) and μ∘Tη = μ∘ηT = 1_T.
    (a) For F ⊣ G: T = GF, η the unit, μ = GεF : GFGF ⇒ GF. Associativity
    is naturality of ε; the unit laws are the triangle identities
    (Gε_F∘η_{GF} = 1 and G(ε_F∘Fη) = 1). (b) F(X) = X* (words, with
    concatenation), so T(X) = UF(X) = X* as a set; η(x) = [x] and μ : X** →
    X* flattens a word of words. A T-ALGEBRA is a : X* → X with a([x]) = x
    and a∘μ = a∘T(a). Put x·y = a([x, y]), e = a([ ]). Associativity of
    · follows from a([a([x, y]), z]) = a([x, y, z]) = a([x, a([y, z])]),
    both being a∘μ of a nested word; unit: a([e, x]) = a([x]) = x. Conversely
    a monoid gives a(word) = product. So the Eilenberg-Moore category is
    Mon: U : Mon → Set is MONADIC. (c) P(X) = subsets, η(x) = {x}, μ =
    union. A Kleisli arrow X → Y is a function X → P(Y), i.e. a relation
    R ⊆ X × Y; Kleisli composition μ∘P(S)∘R is x ↦ ⋃_{y∈R(x)} S(y), which
    is composition of relations. P-algebras are complete sup-lattices.
    (d) μ concatenates: [1, 2, 3, 1]; μ_P takes the union: {1, 2, 3}.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that the monad of discrete ⊣ U : Top → Set
    is the identity (so Top is NOT monadic: its algebras are just sets);
    confusing Kleisli (free algebras) with Eilenberg-Moore (all algebras).
    Now you try: algebras for T(X) = X ⊔ {∗}. (pointed sets)

D10. (a) Define additive and abelian categories and prove that in an
     abelian category a morphism that is mono and epi is an iso. (b) Show
     that the category of torsion-free abelian groups is additive but not
     abelian. (c) State the snake lemma and apply it to multiplication by
     6 on the sequence 0 → Z →(×4) Z → Z/4 → 0.
     Answer: (a) f epi ⇒ f = coker(ker f) = coker(0) is an iso; (b) ×2 :
     Z → Z is mono and epi there but not iso; (c) 0 → Z/2 → Z/6 →(×4)
     Z/6 → Z/2 → 0.
     Teacher explains: ADDITIVE: each Hom(A, B) is an abelian group with
     bilinear composition, there is a zero object and binary biproducts.
     ABELIAN: additive, every arrow has a kernel and a cokernel, every
     mono is the kernel of its cokernel and every epi is the cokernel of
     its kernel. (a) Let f : A → B be mono and epi. Mono ⇒ ker f = 0 (if
     f∘k = 0 = f∘0 then k = 0). Epi ⇒ f is the cokernel of its kernel,
     i.e. of 0 → A, and the cokernel of 0 → A is 1_A: so f ≅ 1_A is an iso.
     (b) Torsion-free groups: Hom-sets, 0 and ⊕ are inherited from Ab.
     ×2 : Z → Z is mono; it is epi because g∘2 = h∘2 gives 2(g − h) = 0,
     and the target is torsion-free, so g = h. It is not an iso: the
     would-be cokernel Z/2 is not torsion-free (in this category the
     cokernel of ×2 is 0). (c) SNAKE: given exact rows A → B → C → 0 and
     0 → A′ → B′ → C′ with vertical maps a, b, c, there is an exact
          ker a → ker b → ker c →(δ) coker a → coker b → coker c,
     with δ(z) = "lift z to B, apply b, pull back to A′". Here a = b = ×6 on
     Z, c = ×6 on Z/4 (which is ×2). ker a = ker b = 0, ker c = {x ∈ Z/4 :
     6x = 0} = {0, 2} ≅ Z/2, coker a = coker b = Z/6, coker c = Z/4/2Z/4 ≅
     Z/2. So 0 → Z/2 →(δ) Z/6 →(×4) Z/6 → Z/2 → 0; check: ×4 on Z/6 has
     kernel {0, 3} and image {0, 2, 4} of index 2 ✓, and the orders
     alternate 2·6 = 6·2. Common mistakes: forgetting the vertical map on
     the quotient is induced (×6 ≡ ×2 on Z/4); believing Grp is abelian (it
     is not even additive: Hom(G, H) is not a group). Now you try: vertical
     ×2 on 0 → Z →(×3) Z → Z/3 → 0. (all kernels 0; coker a ≅ coker b =
     Z/2, coker c = 0; δ = 0 and Z/2 →(×3) Z/2 is an iso)

D11. (a) Prove that Hom(A, −) is left exact but not exact, and that
     − ⊗ M is right exact but not left exact, with explicit examples over
     Z. (b) Show that Q is an injective and flat Z-module but not
     projective, and that Z/n is none of the three over Z but both
     projective and injective over Z/n. (c) Prove that a projective
     Z-module P has Hom(P, −) exact.
     Answer: (a) Hom(Z/2, −) on 0 → Z → Z → Z/2 → 0; − ⊗ Z/2 on the same;
     (b) Q is divisible and torsion-free, Hom(Q, Z) = 0; (c) lift through
     surjections using a basis (or summand of free).
     Teacher explains: (a) If 0 → B′ →(i) B →(p) B″ is exact then 0 →
     Hom(A, B′) → Hom(A, B) → Hom(A, B″) is exact: i∘f = 0 ⇒ f = 0 (i mono);
     if p∘g = 0 then g lands in ker p = im i, so g = i∘f. It is not right
     exact: apply Hom(Z/2, −) to 0 → Z →(×2) Z → Z/2 → 0 to get 0 → 0 → 0 →
     Z/2: the last map is not onto (the identity of Z/2 does not lift).
     − ⊗ M is right exact by D8; applying − ⊗ Z/2 to the same sequence gives
     Z/2 →(×2 = 0) Z/2 → Z/2 → 0: the first map is not injective. The
     failures are MEASURED by Ext¹(Z/2, Z) ≅ Z/2 and Tor₁(Z/2, Z/2) ≅ Z/2.
     (b) Over a PID, injective ⇔ divisible (Baer's criterion: extend
     maps from ideals (n) — possible iff every element is divisible by n),
     and flat ⇔ torsion-free. Q is both. It is not projective: projective
     Z-modules are free, and a free module F ≠ 0 has a nonzero map to Z
     while Hom(Q, Z) = 0 (image divisible in Z). Z/n over Z: torsion (not
     flat), not divisible (not injective), not free. Over Z/n it is free of
     rank 1, hence projective; and Z/n is self-injective (Baer: a map from
     the ideal (d), d | n, sends d to a multiple of d, so it extends).
     (c) Let P be free on a basis (e_s), and p : B → C onto, g : P → C.
     Choose b_s with p(b_s) = g(e_s) and define h(e_s) = b_s; then p∘h = g.
     A direct summand of a free module inherits the lifting. Common
     mistakes: "flat ⇒ projective" (Q); "Z/n is never projective" (it is
     over Z/n); forgetting the choice of preimages. Now you try: is Q/Z
     flat over Z? (no: Tor₁(Q/Z, Z/2) = Z/2 ≠ 0; it is injective)

D12. (a) Define left derived functors via projective resolutions and
     explain why they are well defined. (b) Compute Tor₁^Z(Z/m, Z/n) and
     Ext¹_Z(Z/m, Z/n) for d = gcd(m, n), and Ext¹_Z(Z/n, Z). (c) Compute
     Torₙ^R(k, k) for R = k[x]/(x²). (d) Use Ext¹ to count the extensions
     0 → Z/p → E → Z/p → 0 and identify E.
     Answer: (b) Z/d, Z/d, Z/n; (c) k for every n ≥ 0; (d) |Ext¹(Z/p,
     Z/p)| = p classes: the split one E = (Z/p)² and p − 1 with E ≅ Z/p².
     Teacher explains: (a) Choose a projective resolution ⋯ → P₁ → P₀ → M
     → 0 (exact; R-Mod has enough projectives: free modules). For F right
     exact put LₙF(M) = Hₙ(F(P•)). COMPARISON THEOREM: a map M → N lifts to
     a chain map P• → Q• of resolutions, unique up to chain homotopy, so
     two resolutions of M are homotopy equivalent and Hₙ(F(−)) agrees
     canonically. L₀F = F by right exactness, and 0 → A → B → C → 0 gives
     (horseshoe lemma) a long exact sequence ⋯ → L₁F(C) → F(A) → F(B) →
     F(C) → 0. (b) Resolve: 0 → Z →(×m) Z → Z/m → 0. Tensor with Z/n and
     drop Z/m: 0 → Z/n →(×m) Z/n → 0, so Tor₁ = ker(×m on Z/n) = {x : mx
     ≡ 0 (mod n)} = (n/d)Z/nZ ≅ Z/d, Tor₀ = coker = Z/d = Z/m ⊗ Z/n.
     Apply Hom(−, Z/n): 0 → Z/n →(×m) Z/n → 0, so Hom(Z/m, Z/n) = ker ≅
     Z/d and Ext¹ = coker ≅ Z/d. With Z in place of Z/n: 0 → Z →(×n) Z →
     0 gives Hom(Z/n, Z) = 0, Ext¹(Z/n, Z) = Z/n. (c) Resolution ⋯ →(x) R
     →(x) R →(x) R → k → 0 (ker of x on R is xR = im x). Apply − ⊗_R k:
     every map becomes multiplication by x on k, which is 0; so Torₙ(k, k)
     = k for all n. Hence gl.dim R = ∞, although R is finite-dimensional.
     (d) Ext¹(A, B) is in bijection with equivalence classes of extensions
     (Baer sum = group law, split extension = 0). |Ext¹(Z/p, Z/p)| = p. E
     has order p², so E ≅ (Z/p)² (split class) or Z/p²; the p − 1 nonzero
     classes are the maps Z/p² → Z/p composed with the p − 1 automorphisms
     of the quotient, all with E ≅ Z/p². Common mistakes: not dropping M
     from the resolution before applying F; confusing "iso classes of
     groups E" with "equivalence classes of extensions" (p vs 2). Now you
     try: Ext¹_Z(Z/2, Z/4) and the possible E. (Z/2: Z/4 ⊕ Z/2 or Z/8)

    g) U : Ring → Set preserves coproducts?
    h) U : Top → Set preserves all colimits?
    i) U : CHaus → Set has a right adjoint?
    j) (⊕Mᵢ) ⊗ N ≅ ⊕(Mᵢ ⊗ N)?         k) (∏Mᵢ) ⊗ N ≅ ∏(Mᵢ ⊗ N)?
    l) Hom(⊕Aᵢ, B) ≅ ∏Hom(Aᵢ, B)?    m) Hom(A, ⊕Bᵢ) ≅ ⊕Hom(A, Bᵢ)?
    n) Z³ ⊗ Z/5 and Hom(Z³, Z/5)

    q) representable Hom(A, −) preserves all limits?
    Answers:

         F(1 × 1) = Z ≠ Z × Z)

      g) no (Z[x] ⊗ Z[y] = Z[x, y] ≠ Z[x] ⊔ Z[y])
      h) yes (it has the right adjoint "indiscrete")
      i) no (the coproduct of ℵ₀ points is βN, uncountable)
      j) yes    k) no (M_i = Z, N = Q: (1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) is not in
         (∏Z) ⊗ Q, whose elements have bounded denominators)

      n) (Z/5)³; (Z/5)³     o) yes
      p) no (it would give an initial field; none exists)
